Prescription sales, which accounted for two-thirds of Walgreen's revenue during the quarter, increased by 14% and same-store prescription sales jumped 9%. The company said its gross margins improved by 0.84 percentage point to 28.3%. Drugstore chains are facing a legal settlement that may lower a key pricing benchmark for prescription drugs, a potential hit to profits. Rite Aid reports profits Thursday. --- Dry Cleaner Wins Pants Suit A judge ruled in favor of a dry cleaner who had been sued for $54 million over a missing pair of pants, ruling that the owners of Custom Cleaners didn't violate Washington D.C.'s consumer protection law by failing to live up to Roy L. Pearson's expectations of a "Satisfaction Guaranteed" sign placed in the store's window. Mr. Pearson, an administrative law judge, had originally sought $67 million after he claimed that the cleaners lost the suit pants and then tried to replace them with a pair of pants that weren't his. --- Write to Tim Annett at tim.annett@wsj.com

Title: What's News: Northwest
Text: Gov. Locke May Be Getting Some Bad News in Olympia Gary Locke, Washington's self-styled education governor, may not get the chance to prove it this session. Most bills must be reported out of legislative committees by Friday to make it to the floor of either house, and Senate Education Committee Chairwoman Rosemary McAuliffe, a Bothell Democrat, says she probably won't advance a $1 billion Locke plan to reduce public-school class sizes. Why? She says the Legislature can't afford to pay for that and the $300 million-a-year property-tax-cut measure that Democrats, Mr. Locke included, are backing in the wake of Initiative 695. The initiative reduced fiscal-year 2000 revenue by $750 million, and also set off a tax-cutting craze in Olympia. But Ed Penhale, a Locke spokesman, says the governor isn't crying uncle: "We consider the governor's education proposals very much alive." Katz, 52; Clinton, 89 Portland's mayor, Vera Katz, spoke for 37 fewer minutes than the president did in the annual state-of speech, but tendered nearly as many proposals, including several that observers noted have little to do with City Hall. Ms. Katz allowed as how it would be great if Portland State University added a new engineering school, something to which the Legislature would have to give the nod. She also said that Max, the metro-area light-rail system, should be extended to Vancouver, Wash., perhaps forgetting that Clark County voters said no thanks to that idea in 1995. But the mayor, announcing plans for a run for a third term, also came close to home: She told developers that if they fail to come up with designs that make Portland look prettier, rather than denser, they had better be ready to "build it somewhere else." And she said she supported the establishment of a domestic-partnership registry in which gay couples could officially log their relationships. Crude Salvation Big Oil, in the form of BP Amoco PLC's BP Exploration Alaska Inc. and Atlantic Richfield Co.'s Arco Alaska Inc., promised to spend about $1 billion on projects in the North Slope, Prudhoe Bay and Kuparuk, heartening the oil-revenue-dependent state, which has fretted over the output decline of recent years. And Speaking of Oil Sure, crude oil prices recently hit a nine-year high, but Idaho U.S. Attorney Betty Richardson nonetheless demanded that the U.S. Department of Justice investigate the unfairness of the rising cost of gasoline in the state. "At first blush," she wrote in a letter, "there doesn't seem to be an adequate explanation." The letter was in line with a widespread belief in Idaho, which is that suppliers in Salt Lake City -- not members of OPEC, who make no bones about cutting back on output to push oil values up -- might have somehow colluded to pump up gasoline prices in the state. According to the AAA, Idaho has the eighth-highest pump prices in the nation, while Oregon has the fourth highest. Narrow Decision A Thurston County Superior Court judge dismissed a lawsuit by Gig Harbor-area residents that challenged the state's plan to contract with the private sector to build and operate a toll bridge over the Tacoma Narrows. The plaintiffs plan to appeal. Beaming Bosses The Washington House passed a bill to give employers a $580 million break on unemployment-insurance taxes over the next five years, and to earmark $130 million for the retraining of laid-off workers in the aerospace, fishing and timber industries. Agency's Woes A federal judge slammed the National Marine Fisheries Service, calling its evaluation of the impact of commercial fish trawling on sea lions in the Bering Sea "limited in scope, heavy on general background information and deficient in focused and meaningful discussion and analysis." Not only that, said U.S. District Court Judge Thomas Zilly in Seattle, but NMFS "entirely ignored relevant factors and admittedly failed to analyze and develop projections" based on available information. The agency was ordered back to the drawing board in a lawsuit filed by environmentalists who claim that NMFS has ignored the Endangered Species Act in its management of Bering Sea fisheries, the most lucrative in the nation. The agency said it will get back to work. ---                         The Buzz    The number of stories mentioning the following words in a representative selection of newspapers in the region and the Associated Press:    Jan. 24-Jan. 31  Internet               259 Taxes                  143  Salmon                 86 Initiative 695          68 Rain                    65 Skiing                  30 Ferries                 15 Asian economy           15 Ken Griffey Jr.          6 Snowboarding             4

Title: Congressional campaign to ease curbs on logging business gets under way
Text: The much-anticipated congressional campaign to reduce environmental obstacles to logging has begun.    Aides to Idaho Sen. Larry Craig said he introduced legislation that would exempt so-called salvage logging and certain other timber harvesting techniques from many environmental regulations.    The Idaho Republican said the bill is necessary to allow speedy thinning of densely packed timberlands that are vulnerable to wildfires like last summer's costly infernos, which torched tens of thousands of acres in the Western forests. The bill would also speed logging in burned-out areas, where many trees have been damaged but still retain some commercial value.    Sen. Craig calls the fire danger in federal forests a "crisis," and indeed many environmentalists agree that some forests are perilously overgrown and unhealthy, mainly because of decades of a federal policy, supported by timber companies, to suppress fire to preserve more trees for logging.    The bill is opposed by environmentalists, however, because it takes aim at many procedures they cherish. For example, it would eliminate the right of citizens to challenge some emergency logging with administrative appeals, and would override some provisions of the Endangered Species Act and the National Environmental Policy Act, two of the laws environmentalists have used to win their spotted-owl cases and other legal victories blocking logging. As a result of those court victories, logging on public lands in the Western U.S. has been reduced to less than a quarter of the peak levels of the 1980s.    Moreover, the bill would also promote new logging in untrammeled roadless areas, which environmentalists argue should be essentially left alone because so much other federal forest habitat has been degraded by past logging. "The bill's sole purpose is to increase the cut level on public lands already severely degraded by overlogging" and other practices, said Samantha Mace of the Western Ancient Forest Campaign.    Sen. Craig's proposal is the first of many that are expected in the new Congress to roll back restrictions on logging, and is part of a promised broad review of environmental regulations. For example, Sen. Robert Packwood (R., Ore.) has said he will introduce legislation that would double or triple logging in federal forests in the Northwest.    The effort comes as a new firefight in the West's timber wars has erupted in Sen. Craig's state, triggered by an unusually broad federal-court injunction issued last month that barred logging, road building, mining and grazing in much of six national forests in Idaho. The judge ruled that the activities might damage endangered salmon habitat. The injunction infuriated loggers and others who work the forests, and has been suspended until March -- which has triggered a rush by some companies to push ahead with logging and other projects before the injunction takes effect again.    In recent days, dozens of forest protesters have staged sit-ins in an area known as Cove Mallard, where Shearer Lumber Co. has begun logging in oldgrowth groves. Two protesters were arrested earlier this week for sitting on logging roads and were charged with felonies, the first such charges under a controversial new state law that makes certain logging protests felonies.  Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Water Saga Illuminates Rove's Methods; Bush Strategist Works Agencies in Bid to Make Policy Decisions Jibe With Political Goals
Text: Washington -- In a darkened conference room, White House political strategist Karl Rove was making an unusual address to 50 top managers at the U.S. Interior Department. Flashing color slides, he spoke of poll results, critical constituencies -- and water levels in the Klamath River basin. At the time of the meeting, in January 2002, Mr. Rove had just returned from accompanying President Bush on a trip to Oregon, where they visited with a Republican senator facing re-election. Republican leaders there wanted to support their agricultural base by diverting water from the river basin to nearby farms, and Mr. Rove signaled that the administration did, too. Three months later, Interior Secretary Gale Norton stood with Sen. Gordon Smith in Klamath Falls and opened the irrigation-system head gates that increased the water supply to 220,000 acres of farmland -- a policy shift that continues to stir bitter criticism from environmentalists and Indian tribes. Though Mr. Rove's clout within the administration often is celebrated, this episode offers a rare window into how he works behind the scenes to get things done. One of them is with periodic visits to cabinet departments. Over the past two years Mr. Rove or his top aide, Kenneth Mehlman -- now manager of Mr. Bush's re-election campaign -- have visited nearly every agency to outline White House campaign priorities, review polling data and, on occasion, call attention to tight House, Senate and gubernatorial races that could be affected by regulatory action. Every administration has used cabinet resources to promote its election interests. But some presidential scholars and former federal and White House officials say the systematic presentation of polling data and campaign strategy goes beyond what Mr. Rove's predecessors have done. "We met together and talked a lot about issues of the day, but never in relation to polling results, specific campaigns or the president's popularity," says Lisa Guide, a political appointee at Interior during the Clinton administration. Frank Donatelli, political director in the Reagan White House, says "we were circumspect about discussing specific administration rulings that had yet to be made." Mr. Rove declined to comment. White House spokeswoman Ashley Snee says the agency visits simply were designed to keep political appointees apprised of the president's accomplishments and priorities. Klamath River water levels were an issue at least as far back as the 2000 presidential campaign. During the unusually dry summer of 2001, angry farmers stormed the head gates to forcibly release water, but the Bush administration generally resisted their demands. In 2002, the issue continued to loom large as Mr. Smith faced a potentially difficult re-election challenge. On Jan. 5, Mr. Rove accompanied the president to an appearance in Portland with Mr. Smith. The president signaled his desire to accommodate agricultural interests, saying "We'll do everything we can to make sure water is available for those who farm." The next day, Mr. Rove made sure that commitment didn't fall through the cracks. He visited the 50 Interior managers attending a department retreat at a Fish and Wildlife Service conference center in Shepherdstown, W.Va. In a PowerPoint presentation Mr. Rove also uses when soliciting Republican donors, he brought up the Klamath and made clear that the administration was siding with agricultural interests. His remarks weren't entirely welcome -- especially by officials grappling with the competing arguments made by environmentalists, who wanted river levels high to protect endangered salmon, and Indian tribes, who depend on the salmon for their livelihoods. Neil McCaleb, then an assistant Interior secretary, recalls the "chilling effect" of Mr. Rove's remarks. Wayne Smith, then with the department's Bureau of Indian Affairs, says Mr. Rove reminded the managers of the need to "support our base." Both men since have left the department. An Interior spokesman, Mark Pfeifle, says Mr. Rove spoke in general terms about the Klamath conflict in the course of a broader discussion. Without directing a policy outcome, Mr. Pfeifle says, Mr. Rove simply "indicated the need to help the basin's farmers." In the end, that is what happened when Interior reversed its previous stance and released more water. Mr. Rove's intervention wasn't the only reason. Mr. McCaleb himself says the biggest factor was a report from the independent National Research Council, which questioned the basis on which Interior scientists had made earlier Klamath flow decisions. But Mr. Rove didn't let the matter drop after the Shepherdstown meeting. Weeks later, he returned to Oregon and met with a half-dozen or so farmers and ranchers. Thereafter, the White House formed a cabinet-level task force on Klamath issues. The results became clear on March 29, when the water was released to parched farms. That hasn't ended the controversy. Environmentalists blame the change in water levels for the subsequent death of more than 30,000 salmon, calling it the largest fish kill in the history of the West. A National Marine Fisheries Service biologist, Michael Kelly, has asked for protection under federal "whistle-blower" laws, saying he was subjected to political pressure to go along with the low-water plan and ordered to ignore scientific evidence casting doubt on the plan. This month, a federal judge ruled the administration violated the Endangered Species Act in the way it justified the water diversion. Administration officials note that the judge found fault only with a narrow portion of the biological opinion, and didn't order changes in water flow. Interior is investigating the cause of the fish kill, Mr. Pfeifle says. Oregon farmers point to other factors in the salmon kill, including water temperature and the presence of an infectious disease during salmon-spawning season. And they haven't stopped pressing to keep the irrigation water coming. A few weeks ago, the federal Bureau of Reclamation in Klamath Falls warned farmers that the department would curtail the irrigation flow. Irate, Republican Rep. Greg Walden began making calls to protest. His first one went to Mr. Rove's office. Within hours, the idea was dropped. Interior officials say managers from two cabinet departments agreed on a way to avoid it. ---                 A River Runs Through Him   A look at Karl Rove's involvement in the Klamath River dispute:   -- Jan. 5, 2002: Rove accompanies Bush, who lost Oregon by less than 1% in 2000, to Portland, Ore.; Bush voices support for Klamath Basin farmers.   -- Jan. 6: Rove gives presentation to Interior Department officials connecting regulatory actions in key states, including Oregon's Klamath issue, to Republican prospects in the coming elections.   -- March 2: Rove meets with farmers in Oregon.   -- March 29: Bush administration sides with farmers and diverts Klamath water for agricultural use.   -- Sept. 21: Thousands of salmon die in the shallower Klamath River.   -- June 25, 2003: Regional officials tell Klamath farmers the flow of irrigation water needs to be curtailed; worried congressmen call Rove's office for help. The decision is reversed later in the day.

Title: Court Strikes Down Rules Loosening Habitat Protections
Text: A U.S. appeals court has struck down a federal regulation used by the government to loosen habitat protections for the endangered Gulf sturgeon, in a ruling that could make it easier for environmentalists to block development in many other areas where endangered species are listed.    The opinion Thursday by the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals in New Orleans invalidated a regulation under which the Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service looked only at the survival of an endangered species in determining whether to set aside so-called critical habitat zones.    The agencies used the rule in 1998 to deny environmentalists' requests to designate critical habitat for the Gulf sturgeon, a salmon-like ocean fish whose population has declined precipitously amid pollution and damming on its river spawning grounds along the Gulf Coast. Such a designation could have curbed construction and navigation activities on as many as a dozen rivers from Florida to Louisiana, including the Pascagoula River which runs past the Pascagoula, Miss., hometown of Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott.    Lawyers for the Sierra Club, which filed a suit challenging that decision, argued that the 1973 Endangered Species Act required that critical habitats be designated to assist a species primarily in its recovery -- not just a smaller area tied to its immediate survival. The U.S. District Court in New Orleans sided with the government, but that decision was reversed on appeal to the Fifth Circuit. The court remanded the case to the lower court, with instructions to disregard the survivor-oriented regulation. If left unchallenged before the U.S. Supreme Court, legal observers say the government will have little choice but to apply a far more rigorous standard over lands it protects for endangered species.    "What this means is that the agencies will have to take a much harder look at critical habitat than they have in the past," said Robert Wiygul, staff attorney for the Earthjustice Legal Defense Fund, a San Francisco environmental group that assisted the Sierra Club in its case.    Lawyers for the government weren't available to comment.    Other environmental groups said the case establishes an important legal precedent that can be used in other habitat battles around the country, including some in which they say habitats aren't being protected. In the San Diego area, for example, environmentalists have notified the government that they intend to file suit for permitting a toll road to go through critical habitat either established or proposed for the threatened California gnatcatcher and Quino checkerspot butterfly.    "Loss of habitat is the No. 1 cause of species endangerment in the United States," said David Hogan, a wildlands coordinator for the Center for Biological Diversity group in Berkeley, Calif.  Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Following Timber's Lead, Farmers In Wash. Are Crafting Habitat Plan
Text: Farmers in Washington, taking a page from the timber industry's book, are working with the state and federal governments on a plan that would protect both salmon and profits. The talks with officials from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, the Washington Department of Agriculture and others began in December. The goal: to set land- and water-use guidelines that would abide by the U.S. Endangered Species and Clean Water acts but also keep farming economically viable. "Fish and farms . . . we can do both. We have to do both," says Jim Hazen, executive director of the Washington State Horticultural Association, Wenatchee, which represents 3,700 tree-fruit farmers. Curt Smitch, special assistant to Gov. Gary Locke for natural resources, says he hopes an accord can be ironed out by early next year, but adds that is "optimistic," considering all the players at the table. The negotiators aim to craft a blueprint similar to the so-called forests-and-fish pact approved last year by a number of federal and state agencies and endorsed by the timber industry, though not by many major environmental groups in the state. It allows for the harvesting of trees on eight million acres of privately owned land around the state, in exchange for landowners' pledge to meet certain standards to protect habitat for threatened and endangered species. The agriculture plan would cover more than 30,000 farms around the state, both those that rely on irrigated water and those that don't. The idea would be to reward farmers who voluntarily make habitat-protection improvements -- such as erecting buffer zones around streams -- with a "get out of jail free card" protecting them from some of the stiff civil and criminal penalties the Endangered Species Act, or ESA, requires for the destruction of endangered species or their habitats, according to Jim Jesernig, director of the Washington Agriculture Department. Both the possible agriculture plan and its forests-and-fish model are similar in design to the habitat-conservation plans authorized by Congress in an amendment to the ESA. These are designed to protect fish and wildlife, though often to a lesser degree than the act itself would, while relaxing land-use restrictions. HCPs, as the plans are called, have become a popular method of forestry management, viewed by the Clinton administration and others as successful because they allow economic activity to continue but also satisfy many environmental concerns. In Washington, several timber companies have received or are seeking federal and state approval of HCPs. The fate of the latest such timber plan in Washington, for Simpson Timber Co. of Shelton, could be determined within a few months. Mr. Smitch, Gov. Locke's special assistant, says the governor likes HCPs and comparable plans because they offer long-term certainties for both industry and fish and wildlife. They can also make regulators' jobs easier, he says: Instead of "chasing individual species around," regulators can take an ecosystem-based approach. Still, not everyone favors HCPs and their derivatives. Some tribal governments complain that the plans don't go far enough in protecting fish, and many environmentalists argue that insufficient research goes into dictating guidelines, so that the results are often based in politics, not science. While such plans are "a substantial improvement on current practice," they are "substantially less than what the fish need," says David Bayles, conservation director for the Pacific Rivers Council in Eugene. "The conceptual idea . . . is probably fine, but it's really only as good as the conservation plan that results. And, so far, they're not that good." The Seattle-based Washington Environmental Council pulled out of the fish-and-forest talks last year, objecting to what the council complained was a focus on landowners' needs. David Mann, the council's president, says it hasn't decided yet whether to participate in the agriculture negotiations. In any event, even without environmental opposition, striking a deal with farmers might prove more difficult than it was with timber interests. "The trust level's below zero," says Mr. Jesernig of the Washington Agriculture Department. "We have to find a way to work back up to zero." Tensions between farmers and regulators have been high since the National Marine Fisheries Service last year closed several irrigation ditches in the Methow Valley, claiming their operation could be harmful to fish. Not only that, but the agriculture business is a patchwork of different interests in Washington, where more than 200 crops, from peas to potatoes, are produced. Mr. Jesernig, however, says the Locke administration is committed to forging an agreement, in large part because the alternative is so unattractive. "I think we're on the verge of a litigation Armageddon," he says. "I think the courts are a pathetic place to work out natural-resource issues." Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Timber trade group blames wildfires on less logging, calls for more cutting
Text: The timber industry's main trade group blamed the West's roaring wildfires on insufficient logging and called on Congress to allow more cutting on public lands.    Henson Moore, president of the American Forest & Paper Association, a timber trade group, said the West's fire season, one of the worst in years, results from a "lack of management of these federal forest lands." In the timber industry, "management" means logging. He said that reducing logging levels to protect endangered species has increased the "fuel load and that increases the likelihood for forest fires."    The statements were immediately attacked by the U.S. Forest Service and environmentalists, and further a continuing debate about the role of fire in natural ecosystems and the cause of this year's fires, which have blackened more than 490,000 acres so far. As of yesterday, fires were burning in California, Idaho, Oregon and most other Western states.    While there is little argument that fuel loads are high in public forests, most forestry scientists say that has little to do with the logging limits. Instead, it is the result of decades of a policy of heroically fighting fires in federal forests to preserve more timber for timber companies to cut.    Suppressing fire for so long has eliminated fire's healthy role as a thinner of overcrowded forests and led to the dense packing of trees and brush that fuels many of the current fires. A recent several-year, federally sponsored study by 155 scientists of California's Sierra Nevada area, for example, concluded that "timber harvest, through its effect on forest structure, local microclimates and fuel accumulation, has increased fire severity more than any other human activity."    Moreover, another major reason for this year's fires is simply weather. Much of the West has been hit by record-high temperatures this year, often accompanied by strong winds and dry weather.    Jack Ward Thomas, chief of the Forest Service, called the timber industry position an oversimplification. "This has been a long time in coming," he said. "It didn't come about from a simple situation that we didn't do forest management." Added Sami Yassa, staff scientist with the environmental group Natural Resources Defense Council: "The industry is using fire as a scare tactic. . . . Its position is antiscience, and its motivation is solely to cut more trees, not forest health."    Congress has already opened up formerly restricted areas to so-called salvage logging, a controversial practice that has allowed companies to fell many old-growth trees, in addition to dead and dying trees. President Clinton infuriated environmentalists by signing the bill, and has since said it was a mistake.    Mr. Moore, the trade-group official, said the salvage-logging bill didn't go far enough to prevent fires. He called on Congress to limit citizens' right to challenge planned logging in high-fire danger areas. He also said 120-day limits should be placed on consultations between the Forest Service and federal wildlife agencies required by the Endangered Species Act.    (See related letter: "Letters to the Editor: Loggers' Scare Tactics Focus on Wildfires" -- WSJ Oct. 1, 1996)  Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: U.S. News: Seeing Red Over Green Shrub
Text: SAN FRANCISCO -- In order to protect and restore an endangered species, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service sets aside "critical habitats" in places such as the wilds of Alaska or the pine forests of Louisiana. Now, the agency has targeted a few hundred acres in the heart of this city -- including the backyards of some homeowners. That is drawing fire from some residents who, despite government assurances, fear the proposed protections could constrain land use. Under the proposal, about 270 acres of land mostly in parks would be designated as critical habitat for the Franciscan manzanita, a low-growing shrub thought to have been extinct here since the 1940s until a single example was found in 2009. According to Jennifer Norris, supervisor of the agency's field office in Sacramento, a critical-habitat designation often comes with minimal restrictions on land's use, except perhaps to temporarily fence off a particular area. When it involves private property, she said, cooperation is voluntary -- unless plans by a landowner require federal approval. She said an activity that would raise that concern, such as filling in wetlands, would be rare in a San Francisco backyard. Still, many residents have expressed concern that creating the habitat may curtail recreational activities. "We don't have enough open space for all the recreation needs of city residents as it is," Mary McAllister, a retired-medical school administrator, wrote in a comment regarding the proposal. "We cannot afford to lose huge swaths of this precious resource to become a manzanita garden." The habitat would include about one-third of the 800 acres of undeveloped parklands managed by the city. San Francisco has about 3,470 acres of city-owned parkland in total, according to the Trust for Public Land, a conservation group. Similar debates are playing out across the U.S. The amount of land and water covered by the Fish and Wildlife Service's critical-habitat listings has jumped 46% since 2003 to an area as big as Texas and Tennessee combined. That growth has come in tandem with increased listings under the Endangered Species Act, according to the service. In St. Tammany Parish, La., five landowners in February filed suits against Fish and Wildlife for designating 1,544 acres of a timber farm, which sits on federally supervised wetlands, as critical habitat for the dusky gopher frog. The government estimated the designation could cost them as much as $33.9 million, in part, landowners say, because they wouldn't be able to develop the property. The cases were consolidated into one suit, which is pending in U.S. District Court in New Orleans. "When your land is designated as critical habitat, they do something worse than take your land -- they turn it into a federal preserve," said Reed Hopper, an attorney with the Pacific Legal Foundation, a property-rights group representing plaintiffs in the Louisiana case and others. Fish and Wildlife officials wouldn't comment on the Louisiana case and say most of the opposition stems from a misunderstanding of what the critical habitats mean. Just a designation as a critical habitat can be more significant than any restrictions, said Dave Owen, professor of law at the University of Maine. "There could be economic impacts on properties where someone decides not to develop because of critical habitat," said Mr. Owen, whose analysis found few restrictions occurred on land use, public or private. After the discovery of the single Franciscan manzanita, the Wild Equity Institute -- a group that helps organize environmental causes -- helped get the plant listed as endangered, and in September 2012, Fish and Wildlife proposed the habitat area. In June, the agency added 3.2 acres of private property that would abut as many as 22 homes. The city's Recreation and Park Department supports the habitat. Fish and Wildlife's Ms. Norris said specific plans for its restoration would be made after the habitat is finalized. But affected homeowners remain on edge. "If I wanted to terrace my yard completely, I could potentially run into some resistance," said Owen Randall, a 38-year-old legal-services project manager. The objections have gotten the attention of some city officials. "My hope," said Supervisor Norman Yee, "is that the wildlife folks will work with the local jurisdiction and property owners to come up with an amenable solution." Credit: By Jim Carlton

Title: Salmon Recipes Won't Be Running on This Program
Text: "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire"? Who cares? Now there's something more riveting to watch: Salmon TV.    Seattle, Bellevue and King County governments are sponsoring a monthly half-hour program focusing on the latest government efforts to help save the salmon and spotlighting ways the public can join in.    The first program aired Friday night and featured the executives for King, Snohomish and Pierce counties and Seattle City Council member Margaret Pageler. The program will repeat throughout the month at various times on 20 noncommercial municipal, educational and tribal cable channels to allow as wide a viewership as possible, says Dan Klusman, a spokesman for the King County Endangered Species Act office.    The channels, dubbed the Salmon Information Television Network, can reach 600,000 households from Tacoma to Marysville, Mr. Klusman says, although no one has figures yet on how many households actually chose to tune in for broadcasts so far. Regardless of ratings, the sponsors hope the television programs will drive people to seek out additional information on their Web site, www.salmoninfo.org, or by calling 1-877-SALMON-9.    Future episodes include ways the public can help save salmon as well as a feature on watersheds.    The programs, produced by volunteer efforts with money stitched together from local governments and other sponsors, are meant to be entertaining as well as educational, Mr. Klusman says, and is hosted by aptly named former Northwest comedy "Almost Live" cast member Nancy Guppy.

Title: Judge Bars Land Transfer For Nuclear Waste Dump
Text: SAN FRANCISCO -- A federal court here effectively doomed an attempt by the Interior Department to push through a land transfer for a controversial nuclear-waste dump in the California desert. Judge Marilyn Patel extended a temporary restraining order blocking the transfer of a patch of federal land known as Ward Valley to the state. The state supports an effort to build a low-level nuclear waste dump there, but the proposal has met fierce public resistance. Earlier this month, Interior Secretary Manuel Lujan said he planned to transfer the land to the state, a key requirement for advancing the dump project. Critics of the proposed dump accused Mr. Lujan, who leaves office today, of circumventing normal procedures to ram the transfer through before leaving his post. Dump opponents sued, alleging that the land transfer didn't comply with the Endangered Species Act, among other laws. Judge Patel's decision means the thorny issue of low-level nuclear-waste disposal will fall into the lap of the Clinton administration. That's where dump opponents wanted it, because they believe Mr. Clinton's administration will be more sympathetic to their cause. A federal law passed in 1980 required states to set up low-level nuclear dumps, but not one has yet been built, largely because of public opposition.

Title: The Evening Wrap: Opening the Ad Gates
Text: The nation's highest court ruled that an important package of campaign-finance measures trampled free-speech rights of labor unions and issue advocates, in a decision that likely will have ad-weary voters hitting the mute button often during the coming presidential campaign. The Supreme Court, in a 5-4 decision, loosened restrictions on corporate-and union-funded political advertisements that run close to election day, weakening a key provision of the McCain-Feingold campaign-finance legislation. The law had blocked companies, unions or other interest groups from running broadcast advertisements that reference a candidate for federal office  two months before a general election or a month before a primary. The justices upheld a lower court ruling that Wisconsin Right to Life, an antiabortion group, should have been allowed to broadcast advertisements in the months leading up to the 2004 elections. The ads asked voters to contact Wisconsin's two senators, Democrats Russ Feingold and Herb Kohl, and urge them not to block President Bush's judicial nominees. Sen. Feingold, as circumstance would have it the co-author of the campaign- finance law, was then up for re-election. "Discussion of issues cannot be suppressed simply because the issues may also be pertinent in an election," wrote Chief Justice John Roberts in the majority opinion. "Where the First Amendment is implicated, the tie goes to the speaker, not the censor." The court had previously upheld most of McCain-Feingold from a broad attack brought by Sen. Mitch McConnell in 2003, and while the majority has stopped short of overturning that decision, at least three justices who joined the majority -- Justices Antonin Scalia, Clarence Thomas and Anthony Kennedy -- indicated they would have gone that extra step. Still, the ruling would appear to throw open the ad floodgates in time for the 2008 race. The ACLU, NRA and others that had linked up in an unlikely coalition to get the provision tossed out are almost certain to be blasting at each other's preferred candidates as often as their pocketbooks will allow. Indeed, the effect of today's ruling may be seen as soon as December, as a number of states have moved primaries forward into January. Observers said that the ruling will make an indelible mark in the 2008 race and beyond. "There is no doubt today's decision reflects a constitutional sea change that is likely to have dramatic effects on upcoming elections," said Richard H. Pilbes, a professor at New York University School of Law, on the Supreme Court blog of law firm Akin, Gump. "Some will celebrate that change, others will bemoan it, but that the change is dramatic cannot be doubted." In another speech case before the high court, the justices split 5-4 in upholding the right of an Alaskan school principal to confiscate a 14-foot banner reading "Bong Hits 4 Jesus" from a student who unfurled it away from school grounds at an Olympic torch-relay event in 2002. "We hold that schools may take steps to safeguard those entrusted to their care from speech that can reasonably be regarded as encouraging illegal drug use," Chief Justice Roberts wrote for the majority. Joseph Fredrick, the student who had set up the banner, said that the message was meant to be nonsensical and was intended as an illustration of his right to say anything at all. Also today, the high court threw out, in a 5-4 split, an atheist group's challenge to President Bush's office of faith-based initiatives. And finally the justices ruled -- in yet another decision that broke 5-4 -- that the Endangered Species Act takes a backseat to the Clean Water Act when it comes to the EPA's handing authority to a state to issue water pollution permits. --- Existing-Homes Sales Weaken The National Association of Realtors said existing-home sales skidded by 0.3% during May to a 5.99 million annual pace, the lowest level in almost four years. Given the long downdraft in the housing market, gruesome data from the sector have been piling up like sheets of plywood at a construction site, and the fall in the headline reading was generally within expectations and even tame by recent standards. But economists said that what stood out were worrisome readings on prices and supply. According to the trade group, the national median price was $223,700, 2.1% lower than the same time last year. Steven Wood of consulting service Insight Economics wrote that May marked the 10th consecutive month in which median prices declined in annual terms, "the longest period since data collection began in 1968." And critically, the prolonged prices skid isn't wooing bargain hunters. Prices are poised to come under even greater pressure over the months to come as the inventory of homes on the market continues to surge; in May inventories rose to a level that would take nearly nine months to work off at the current pace of sales. But if prices are heading lower, many homeowners seem to be convinced it isn't going to happen to them. According to the Boston Consulting Group, Americans are confident that their homes are retaining and even climbing in value. And 75% believe they could sell their house within the next six months at a price they think that it's worth. --- Stocks Flatten Out A large inventory increase in the housing market didn't spook markets too much, although by the end of the session the major benchmarks had flattened out. The Dow Jones Industrial Average declined 8.21 points to end at 13352.05, the Nasdaq Composite Index slipped 11.88 points to 2577.08, and the Standard & Poor's 500 Index slid 4.82 points to 1497.74. Slumping crude-oil prices helped stocks early on, but futures resumed their climb late in the day as relief over the end of a general strike in large African oil producer Nigeria was outweighed by reports of more refinery outages, keeping traders' supply concerns alive. The front-month crude-oil futures contract on the New York Mercantile Exchange climbed four cents a barrel to settle at $69.18. Treasury yields dipped, helping ease concern over higher interest rates. The yield on the key 10-year note ended at 5.079%. The dollar was mixed. Markets in Europe and Asia were weaker. --- Hamas Airs Audio of Captured Israeli Soldier Hamas militants posted an audio recording of Israeli Cpl. Gilad Shalit, who was captured a year ago from an army post near the Gaza Strip. It was the first sign that he is still alive since his capture. "I have spent a full year in prison, and my health is still deteriorating, and I need a prolonged hospitalization. I regret the lack of interest on the part of the Israeli government and the Israel Defense Forces in my case," Cpl. Shalit says in the recording. He was captured June 25, 2006, by militants who tunneled into Israel from Gaza. Though it was uncertain when the tape was made, it appeared authentic; Cpl. Shalit's father said that the statement sounded coerced. Human-rights group B'tselem accused the captors of war crimes, noting their refusal to let Red Cross workers to visit Cpl. Shalit. Separately, a video showed the BBC journalist Alan Johnston wearing a suicide bomber's belt packed with explosives, with a message from his captors warning that the charges will be detonated if any effort is made to free him by force. Mr. Johnston was captured in Gaza March 12; a group called Army of Islam claims responsibility. Deposed Palestinian Prime Minister Ismail Haniyeh denounced the kidnapping in a speech yesterday. Al Qaeda's Ayman al-Zawahri called on Muslims to support Hamas and urged the party to unite with al Qaeda. Meanwhile, Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert promised that he'll release 250 Fatah members from Israeli prisons as a gesture of goodwill aimed at bolstering Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas following his party's break with Hamas. Mr. Olmert announced the prisoner release at a summit with Mr. Abbas and the leaders of Egypt and Jordan. "I will bring before the Israeli cabinet a proposal to free 250 Fatah prisoners who do not have blood on their hands, after they sign a commitment not to return to violence," Mr. Olmert said at the gathering. --- Accident Raises Questions on Chinese Tires A lawsuit stemming from a fatal car accident in Pennsylvania is pointing out the potential dangers of tires imported from China. The accident occurred last August, when a steel-belted radial on a cargo van carrying four passengers allegedly experienced a tread separation -- the type of problem that prompted the big Firestone recall of 2000 -- causing the driver to lose control and crash. Two passengers were killed, the two others injured. The tire's U.S. distributor said that it discovered that a safety feature that it had specifically requested the manufacturer to include was omitted from up to 450,000 of the tires imported from China's Hangzhou Zhongce Rubber Co. since 2002. The problem comes amid the discovery of issues with several other types of Chinese imports, such as toys that were discovered to be painted with lead paint and toothpaste that contained hazardous materials, as well as contaminated ingredients that ended up in several brands of pet food. --- Iran Looks to Clear Up Nuclear Questions The International Atomic Energy Agency said that Iran has invited the nuclear watchdog to send a team to Tehran to draw up a plan to resolve questions over the country's contested nuclear program. Iran claims that it wants to use nuclear energy solely for producing electricity, but Washington and its allies worry that Tehran is developing nuclear weapons. The U.N. Security Council has imposed two round of sanctions against the Islamic regime, and is said to be considering a third unless Iran suspends enrichment of uranium. Iran hid past research from the IAEA and has long stonewalled international inspectors. The new invitation followed discussions between Iranian nuclear negotiator Ali Larijani and IAEA director Mohamed ElBaradei. The IAEA said it will send a team to Tehran "as early as practicable." Separately, Iranian lawmakers said the country will begin rationing gasoline next week amid fuel-supply concerns. Though the nation has plentiful crude reserves, its lacks refining capacity and must import about 40% of its gasoline. The threat of rationing has led some Iranians to stockpile fuel. --- Iraqi Cabinet Backs Draft Oil Law Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki's cabinet has approved a U.S.-backed draft oil law, a measure that along with several other pieces of benchmark legislation is seen as a critical step in the Iraqi reconciliation progress. The legislation is still facing a difficult road; Iraq's fractious parliament is expected to take up the bill next week. Violence was meanwhile continuing, after a suicide bomber walked into the lobby of Baghdad's Mansour Hotel and detonated a blast that killed at least seven, including four Sunni Arab tribal leaders gathered at the hotel for a summit. "It was a great breach of security because there are three checkpoints, one outside and two inside," said Saif al-Rubaie, a hotel worker who witnessed the attack. The sheiks were associated with the Anbar Salvation Council, which has been fighting al Qaeda forces in Anbar province. The attack was just one of several that claimed at least 45 lives around Iraq today. Suicide bombers killed at least 13 Iraqi police officers in an attack on a joint U.S.-Iraqi security station in Beiji, north of Baghdad. A U.S. soldier was killed in southern Baghdad. --- Tyson Strikes Fuels Deal Tyson Foods and synthetic-fuel maker Syntroleum confirmed plans to build a $150 million plant that will take fat from the food company's processing plants and turn it into liquid fuel. A newly formed company, Dynamic Fuels, will turn out fuels for the renewable diesel, jet, and military markets. The first facility is expected to produce 78 million gallons a year of renewable synthetic fuels from 569 million pounds of feedstock, starting in 2010. Tyson reached a similar deal with oil giant ConocoPhillips several months ago. Though emblematic of the drive toward alternative fuels, Tyson and Syntroleum's facility would produce only about 5% of the fuel that comes out of a typical U.S. oil refinery annually. --- Prescription Sales Boost Walgreen Drug retailer Walgreen's earnings surged 20% on strong prescription- drug sales and increased market share in most of its major product categories. Prescription sales, which accounted for two-thirds of Walgreen's revenue during the quarter, increased by 14% and same-store prescription sales jumped 9%. The company said its gross margins improved by 0.84 percentage point to 28.3%. Drugstore chains are facing a legal settlement that may lower a key pricing benchmark for prescription drugs, a potential hit to profits. Rite Aid reports profits Thursday. --- Lost-Pants Suit Lost Sure, the Supreme Court is winding down its term by unveiling a collection of important decisions on matters of great constitutional import. But the justices' august perch was only the second most closely watched court in Washington this morning. Enjoying top billing was the District of Columbia Superior Court, where Judge Judith Bartnoff ruled in favor of a dry cleaner who had been sued for $54 million over a missing pair of pants. Roy L. Pearson, an administrative law judge, brought the lawsuit after Custom Cleaners allegedly lost a pair of his suitpants and attempted to replace them with some other pair that didn't belong to him. Mr. Pearson, reduced to tears during trial when speaking of his missing trousers, claimed that the cleaners violated Washington's consumer-protection law by failing to live up to his expectations of "Satisfaction Guaranteed" -- as guaranteed in sign placed in the store's window. Mr. Pearson originally sought $67 million, a number that he says he arrived at by tallying up years of alleged violations and almost $2 million in common law fraud claims. "A reasonable consumer would not interpret 'Satisfaction Guaranteed' to mean that a merchant is required to satisfy a customer's unreasonable demands" or agree to demands that the merchant would have reasonable grounds for disputing," the decision in the case read. Judge Bartnoff ordered the plaintiff to pony up the court costs of defendants Soo Chung, Jin Nam Chung and Ki Y. Chung. --- Write to Tim Annett at tim.annett@wsj.com

Title: U.S. News: U.S. Watch
Text: EDUCATION New Student Loans Set at Higher Rate The cost of borrowing for college is about to get more expensive. New 10-year U.S. Treasurys were sold at auction Wednesday with a 4.483% yield. Interest rates on new federal undergraduate student loans are determined each year by adding the yield on the 10-year Treasury note in the May auction to a fixed premium of 2.05 percentage points. That means that the interest rate on a new student loan should rise to around 6.5% in July, the highest level since 2008, from 5.5% currently. That 10-year Treasury yield has climbed a lot since a year ago. But it could have been worse for borrowers. In secondary-market trading, the 10-year yield reached as high as roughly 5% in October. It was above 4.6% last week, before data showed cooling in the labor market, causing investors to increase bets on interest-rate cuts by the Federal Reserve. -- Sam Goldfarb --- GEORGIA Election Interference Case Likely Delayed A Georgia appeals court on Wednesday agreed to review a lower-court ruling allowing Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis to continue to prosecute the election interference case against Donald Trump. The move seems likely to delay the case and is the second time in as many days that the former president has gotten a favorable ruling that could push any future trials beyond the November election, when he is expected to be the Republican nominee for president. A day earlier, the judge in his Florida classified-documents case indefinitely postponed that trial date. Trump and some other defendants in Georgia had tried to get Willis and her office removed from the case, saying her romantic relationship with special prosecutor Nathan Wade created a conflict of interest. Superior Court Judge Scott McAfee in March found that no conflict of interest existed that should force Willis off the case. -- Associated Press --- CALIFORNIA Two Children Swept Away by Creek Die Two young siblings died after being swept away by a rapidly flowing creek in Southern California's San Bernardino Mountains, authorities said. The tragedy occurred on Tuesday when a mother took her 4-year-old daughter and 2-year-old son to spend the afternoon at Thurman Flat picnic area on Highway 38 near Mill Creek, the San Bernardino County Sheriff's Department said. They were playing along the creek when at one point the mother was attending to her son and her daughter was taken downstream, the department said. "The mother searched for her but could not locate her," the department said. "When she returned, her son was missing and assumed to be down river as well." Rescue crews eventually found both children. The siblings were taken to local hospitals and pronounced dead after extensive efforts to save their lives, the department said. -- Associated Press --- OBITUARY Pete McCloskey, 96, Ran Against Nixon Pete McCloskey, a pro-environment, antiwar California congressman who co-wrote the Endangered Species Act and co-founded Earth Day, has died. He was 96. A Republican "in the mold of Teddy Roosevelt," as he often put it, McCloskey also ran for president against an incumbent Richard Nixon in 1972. He battled party leaders while serving seven terms in Congress and went on to publicly disavow the GOP in his later years. He died at home Wednesday, according to Lee Houskeeper, a family friend. McCloskey cited disillusionment from influence peddling and ethics scandals under the George W. Bush administration as reasons why he switched parties in 2007 at the age of 79. His enduring legacy is the Endangered Species Act, which protects species designated as endangered or threatened and conserves the ecosystems on which they depend. -- Associated Press

Title: U.S. News: White House Considers Ways to Cut Emissions
Text: WASHINGTON -- The Bush administration -- under pressure from Congress, some big businesses and overseas allies -- is weighing proposals to curb U.S. greenhouse-gas emissions. The administration continues to oppose a bill to be debated soon in Congress that would impose mandatory caps on carbon-dioxide emissions, White House press secretary Dana Perino said. "But our views on how to do this [control greenhouse-gas emissions] the right way are things that we are talking about," she said. The White House said President Bush might make a statement in the next few days. Ms. Perino was responding to a report in the Washington Times that Mr. Bush was poised to call on Congress this week to pass legislation to combat global warming. The administration is worried that the current regulatory and legislative framework is poorly designed to deal with climate change and could have harsh unintended effects on many businesses and economic sectors, Ms. Perino said. "You have . . . a regulatory train wreck," Ms. Perino said Monday, citing the Clean Air Act, Endangered Species Act and National Environmental Policy Act, among others, as laws that potentially could be used to rein in greenhouse-gas emissions. Those laws are creating "regulatory paths on climate change that they were never meant to deal with," she added. One option administration officials have discussed, according to individuals close to the administration, is a statement endorsing caps on carbon-dioxide emissions on the condition that such caps wouldn't take effect until technology capable of capturing and storing carbon- dioxide emissions at large power plants is proven commercially viable. Ms. Perino said White House officials internall are engaging in a "very robust discussion" on the issue. The prospect of a Bush shift on climate change stirred unease Monday in the business community, prompting a series of calls from executives and industry lobbyists to the White House, a person familiar with the calls said. Many experts say the technology is at least a decade from being commercially viable on a large scale. The Energy Department withdrew its support for a project to test such technology in January after huge cost overruns. The administration's signal that it might make new proposals on reducing greenhouse gases comes as the president is under increasing pressure on the issue from congressional Democrats and foreign countries, especially in Europe. A statement on the issue also could help the White House firm up a national goal for reductions that it wants to offer to other countries involved in international negotiations over climate change. The leading bill in Congress that attempts to achieve that goal is a measure sponsored by Sens. Joseph Lieberman (I., Conn.) and John Warner (R., Va.) that would cap greenhouse-gas emissions from power plants and other polluters, and allow companies that exceeded the limits to buy credits from other companies that met them with room to spare. The administration has opposed the bill. The Lieberman-Warner bill has been approved by one committee, but faces an uphill fight on the Senate floor, where 60 votes would be needed to move it forward. --- Greg Hitt and Elizabeth Williamson contributed to this article.

Title: Hydro-Plant License Process Is Challenged
Text: A coalition of environmentalists and government agencies is objecting to the time-honored process for licensing hydropower projects in the Northwest, and their legal challenge could have an impact on the fates of dozens of dams and turbines in the region. A three-judge panel of the Ninth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, based in San Francisco, will hear arguments in Portland today over a challenge to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission's decision to issue a new license to a pair of McKenzie River power-generating plants that some say threaten the fish that call the waterway home. The focus of the legal fight is narrow: whether two small turbines on the river in Oregon that generate just 23 megawatts of electricity should be allowed to continue to operate as they have for more than 50 years. But the impact of the appeals court's decision could be far-reaching. Lawyers for the environmentalists and government agencies mounting the challenge say their aim is to force sweeping changes in the way the FERC evaluates applications for the re-licensing of the facilities that generate most of the electricity in the region. The appellants' argument is that the way rivers flowed in the Northwest before the Industrial Revolution -- not the way power-generating dams and canals have since forced them to move -- should serve as the baseline for assessing the merits of hydropower projects, including the more than 300 hydropower dams in the Northwest. Environmentalists favor the longer-range assessment because it takes into account how decades of hydroelectric projects and other developments have affected what they call the "natural" state of the environment. The FERC's approach, on the other hand, looks only at the environmental impact since the previous license was granted. If the appeal is successful, lawyers say, federal energy regulators will be required to put the natural state of the environment on a equal footing with the needs of electricity consumers in the Northwest, the majority of whom buy their power from facilities that rely on water, rather than natural gas or coal or fuel oil, to generate electricity. "No court has ever ruled on how this baseline for decision-making should be set," says Kristen Boyles of Seattle, the lead attorney for the environmental groups. "Now, a court will decide at what point FERC must begin its evaluation." The case "squarely presents the issue of what environmental analysis is required for dam re-licensing," says Myron Marlin, spokesman for the U.S. Justice Department. The effects of hydropower dams on American rivers "can't be assumed away just because the dams were first licensed 50 years ago." In April 1997, the commission approved the Eugene Water and Electric Board's application for a new license for the Leaburg and Walterville power plants, built in 1930 and 1911, respectively. The re-licensing allowed the utility to continue diverting nearly half of the flow of the river into a canal to drive turbines at the two plants. The canal begins at the Leaburg Dam, 25 miles east of Eugene, stretches for six miles along the wall of the McKenzie River Valley and then plunges down the hillside through the Leaburg Powerhouse. About four miles downstream, the water is diverted again and makes a similar trip to the Walterville Powerhouse. After powering the turbines, the water -- 2,575 cubic feet a second at peak flow -- returns to the river near Thurston, 18 miles from Leaburg. Environmentalists and biologists claim the diversion harms several species of fish swimming in the river, including the McKenzie River bull trout -- listed as a threatened species under the U.S. Endangered Species Act in June 1998 -- and the wild spring Chinook salmon, which has been proposed for listing as threatened. So, in January 1998, five environmental groups, led by the Pacific Rivers Council of Eugene and American Rivers of Washington, D.C., appealed the re-licensing to the San Francisco-based court, claiming that the commission violated both the Federal Power and National Environmental Policy acts by considering the present rather than natural condition of the river in making its decision. A group of state and federal agencies also challenged the ruling, and the two appeals were consolidated. In their appeal, the agencies -- the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, the Environmental Protection Agency, the National Marine Fisheries Service and the Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife -- made the same points as the environmentalists. They also argued that the FERC had failed to properly consider the scientific evidence presented by the agencies during the application process. Fisheries managers' own research showed that less water should be diverted into the power canals, especially at times of low water. But the commission disregarded the opinion, "substituting its judgment" and, in so doing, violated the Federal Power Act, says Jas Adams, a deputy Oregon attorney general representing the state's Department of Fish and Wildlife in the appeal. The appellants want the court to order the FERC to start the re-licensing process over again, and to require the commission and the Eugene utility to focus on the way the McKenzie flowed before 1911 in making and considering arguments for renewal. But FERC officials say that the commission fully complied with all federal laws in the Eugene case, and that it would be unreasonable to review a license pretending that a decades-old power plant doesn't exist. Officials of the Eugene Water and Electric Board are "frustrated by accusations regarding harm our projects are doing to the river," says Laurie Power, the utility's environmental manager. The utility will close its Walterville powerhouse -- at a cost of $140,000 annually -- during critical spring weeks when juvenile salmon are flushed to sea. And the utility pledges to spend $12 million on new fish ladders and other protective measures. As for the claim that the plants take too much water, Ms. Power says the utility asked for data justifying the claim, "yet that data was never brought forward." Over the next 10 years, the FERC will be asked to re-license 229 hydroelectric projects around the U.S., including 38 in the Northwest. There are already 12 such power plants in the region in the re-licensing application process. "We want to define the way they should be doing this new business," says Mr. Adams, the deputy Oregon attorney general. "How many fish is FERC willing to kill?" Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Salmon Battle Could Spawn Much Bitterness
Text: Federal officials are expected to propose adding more Northwestern salmon to the list of endangered species, escalating a preservation battle that could exceed the conflict over saving the spotted owl.    The National Marine Fisheries Service, an arm of the Commerce Department, is scheduled to announce Friday whether four species of salmon in the Columbia and Snake Rivers merit protection under the Endangered Species Act.    Wildlife officials, environmentalists and even industry representatives expect the service to propose endangered status for at least one of the species, the fall chinook salmon. The other species may also get protection, although they're considered less likely to be listed as endangered, in part because some may already be extinct. The fish will join another salmon species, the Snake River sockeye, which was recommended for protection in April.    Saving the salmon has momentous implications for the Northwestern economy and will affect other parts of the West Coast as well. Although depleted by habitat destruction and fishing practices, the main culprit in pushing the fish to the brink of extinction is a series of eight huge federal dams built mainly in the 1940s and 1950s in the Columbia and Snake River systems.    The dams produce the cheap hydroelectric power and irrigation water that has fueled the region's development, as well as enabling barges and ships to make their way down the rivers to ports. But they kill salmon in prodigious numbers when baby fish are sucked into the turbine blades, and protecting the fish will almost certainly require allowing more water to flow down the rivers, reducing water available for power generation, irrigation and navigation.    Utility operators, farmers and shippers predict economic calamity, as electricity rates rise, crop production decreases and barge traffic dries up. Fish advocates say that they're exaggerating and that the economic impact will be manageable. The battle seems headed inexorably for the courts and Congress. Many involved predict the salmon fight will eventually become more bitter than the four-year fight over the spotted owl, which has altered U.S. timber policy in the Northwest.    "This is a unique preservation battle, and I fear it will be nasty," said Ed Chaney, president of the Northwest Resource Information Center, an environmental and resource protection group based in Eagle, Idaho.    Many observers believe the salmon battle could be used by opponents of the Endangered Species Act to promote revisions in the law and the way it is applied. In the wake of the owl battle, some Northwestern congressmen, including Sen. Slade Gorton, (R., Wash.), and Sen. Robert Packwood (R., Ore.) have expressed concern about the economic impact of the act. Environmentalists fear the salmon dispute may be used in an effort to gut the law.    No one disputes that Northwestern salmon are in trouble. Salmon runs that totaled some 11 million fish in the early part of the century are down to about two million now. The parties to the salmon dispute convened a series of "salmon summits" this year in hopes of forging some consensus or compromise. But the meetings produced no agreement and subsequent talks haven't either.    Fish supporters now say they're being excluded from negotiations taking place between federal agencies and industry groups. The Sierra Club Legal Defense Fund, which had tremendous court success on the owl issue, has threatened to sue the National Marine Fisheries Service if it doesn't grant the Snake River sockeye special emergency protection.    Under Commerce Department procedures, it usually takes a year between proposing a species for protection and formally granting it protection. The legal defense fund lawyers say the sockeye may be extinct before that period is up.    The big obstacle to solving the salmon problem is the number of water users and interested parties, all of whom seem to have a plan that calls for everybody else to sacrifice a little more than they do. A plan put together by Idaho Gov. Cecil Andrus has the general support of the fish and environmental groups. It would require dam operators to allow more water to flow through the rivers for about two months each spring to aid baby salmon in their drive for the sea.    That plan is opposed by most of the other groups involved in the debate, including shippers and power producers. The Northwest Grain and Feed Association, a trade group of commercial grain producers that use the waterways to ship wheat and other crops to ports, says the plan would force producers to ship grain by rail or truck and cost millions of dollars. The association proposed that flows be augmented for only two weeks in the spring.    "We're saying we won't use our barges during that period," said Jonathan Schleuter, executive vice president of the association. "That's a considerable sacrifice for us. But if we don't see other parties making commensurate contributions, forget it, we're not going to do it."  Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: U.S. Should Help the Muses, Revise Idiotic Ivory Policy
Text: Regarding the letters of Dec. 8 on the import of animal trophies: It is paradoxical that the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service would consider lifting a ban on trophy hunting while at the same time keeping an import ban on antiques made with African elephant ivory, even those which are over 100 years old. Although the Endangered Species Act allows antique ivory items to be traded in interstate commerce in all 50 states, objects of historical, artistic or cultural importance are prohibited from entering the U.S. since President Obama's executive order was signed in 2014. As a member of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species, the U.S. ought to first consider lifting a ban on ivory antiques, which has no nexus with the poaching crisis. Scott Defrin New York

Title: Bush Gets Cautious About Killing Clinton Rules
Text: WASHINGTON -- The Bush administration, in a sign that it has begun to tread carefully on environmental and energy issues, has delayed acting on Clinton regulations on reporting lead emissions and raising efficiency standards for air conditioners.    Decisions on the two rules were widely expected this week, the latest in a series of reviews being made on environmental and energy policy decisions made before Mr. Clinton left office -- decisions that conservatives and business interests hope will be reversed.    "I think it's the fear factor," said Mohammad Akhter, director of the American Public Health Association, of the delays. "After they came up with the ruling on arsenic [levels in water] and got beaten up, they're rethinking things." The group has been pressing for wider reporting of the environmental releases of lead, which is easily ingested by the human body and can cause subnormal intelligence and violent behavior in children.    The White House has been criticized -- and Mr. Bush has been pounded in public-opinion polls -- for blocking several Clinton environmental and energy regulations that administration officials say need further study or are based on insufficient science.    Spokesmen for Environmental Protection Agency and Energy Department said they couldn't comment on the politics surrounding the lead and air-conditioner rules, but noted that reviews of both are still under way, and that no decisions have been made.    The lead rule would require companies that use more than 100 pounds of lead a year to make an annual report of their wastes and emissions. Current reporting regulations apply only to companies that use at least 10,000 pounds of lead.    Some 67 trade groups representing chemical, metal and other manufacturers have sued to block the EPA from expanding the reporting requirements. They charge that the rules wrongly apply standards for dangerous organic chemicals to metals. "If this rule is approved, you will have a methodology in place that is being misused," said Jane Luxton, a lawyer who represents the so-called Ad Hoc Metals Coalition.    Mr. Akhter and others, however, say the rules are needed. Although the level of lead in the environment has been declining, new studies show that it is more dangerous at lower levels than previously believed, Mr. Akhter said.    Meanwhile, the Energy Department announced it was proceeding with some new, higher energy-efficiency standards that the Clinton administration proposed for many household appliances, but didn't include the rules on air conditioners.    The regulations that were approved require washing machines to be 22% more efficient by 2004 and 35% more efficient by 2007. By 2004, hot-water-heater manufacturers must increase efficiency for gas units by 8% and electric units by 4%.    Rumors flew earlier this week that the White House was about to heed industry complaints and lower the proposed air-conditioner standards, which would have required manufacturers to improve energy efficiency by 30%. Then Houston-based Goodman Manufacturing Co., the nation's second-largest air-conditioner maker, announced that it would have no trouble meeting that level, undermining the criticism of other manufacturers.    Steven Nadel, head of the American Council for an Energy Efficient Economy, estimated the standards would save the equivalent energy of about 170 small-to-medium power plants. "We're talking billions of dollars here," he said.    But Edward W. Dooley, spokesman for the Air Conditioning and Refrigeration Institute, said the Energy Department overestimated electricity savings. The rules will make new air conditioners larger, harder to install and more expensive, he said, and "people will live with their existing units until they die."    The Bush administration took another hit on Wednesday when the Sierra Club claimed that a proposal in the Interior Department 2002 budget would gut the Endangered Species Act. The provision would eliminate funds for protecting new species deemed endangered by court actions. The Interior Department said it wants to use some of the money to figure out how to prioritize a backlog of some 200 plants and animals claimed to be endangered.    ---                       Pending Business    In January the Bush administration suspended many Clinton environmental policies and regulations. More than 20 initiatives remain on hold, including:    Interior Department   -- Regulations limiting snowmobiles in Grand Teton and Yellowstone National Parks   -- Regulations simplifying Native American land ownership.   -- Policy on maintaining diversity and environmental health of National Wildlife Refuge System    Energy Department   -- Efficiency standards for residential and central air conditioners    Environmental Protection Agency   -- Regulations requiring more companies to report lead emissions.  Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Roberts Opposition Struggles for Focus; Liberal Groups' Message Gets Muddled as White House Allies Launch TV Ad Campaign
Text: Washington -- THE SUPREME COURT nomination of Judge John Roberts, a likable man with a miniature public record on the bench, risks diluting the strength of a liberal coalition that has been organizing for more than a year for this battle. With momentum building strongly in the judge's favor on Capitol Hill yesterday, the potential opposition was forced to scramble. The National Organization for Women and NARAL Pro-Choice America were seeking to mount letter-writing drives and protests; the Sierra Club told activists it was researching his record. People for the American Way simply urged its 750,000 members to ask senators to reserve judgment until Senate Judiciary Committee hearings in September. "It's a very clever, very smart nomination," said Kate Michelman, president emeritus of NARAL Pro-Choice America. And that has already had an impact, muddling the left's message as it searches for a promising line of attack. White House allies have been able to use their substantial treasuries to introduce the 50-year-old, District of Columbia appeals- court judge to the general public in a positive way. Progress for America, which has pledged to spend nearly $20 million to support Judge Roberts, launched a one-week, $1 million cable television advertising campaign with a biographical theme that was titled: "Brilliant." On Capitol Hill, the Roberts charm offensive has been so effective that the so-called Gang of 14, the bipartisan bloc that ended a showdown over appellate judges, emerged from its first meeting predicting that a filibuster is unlikely. Indeed, momentum appeared to be moving so quickly in Judge Roberts's favor that one veteran Republican urged his colleagues to slow down and take their responsibilities more seriously. "This is a very important confirmation process, not a coronation," cautioned Sen. John Warner of Virginia. Liberal groups could yet find their voices and conduct a formidable opposition campaign. MoveOn.org, an online activists organization, already is building grass-roots opposition. "He is a stealth candidate without a substantial public record," said Wade Henderson, executive director of the Leadership Conference on Civil Rights. "He is strongly embraced by the ultraright, which suggests they know something about his views on important issues that is not apparent to the public at large." A team of attorneys representing civil rights, women, environmentalists and other groups is searching for ammunition. Senate Democratic staffers are also scrubbing his record. Judge Roberts's public file is thin. He didn't write many opinions in his two years on the bench. His most controversial decision was joining a majority opinion allowing Guantanamo prisoners to be prosecuted before military commissions without the constitutional protections that defendants in U.S. courts receive. But two other periods of his government service have emerged as potentially target-rich environments: His service in the Reagan administration from 1981 to 1986, during which the administration sought changes in the Voting Rights Act, and his role in the first Bush administration from 1989 to 1993, when the government joined in abortion cases. In one of those abortion cases, Judge Roberts argued in a brief, "we continue to believe that Roe was wrongly decided and should be overruled," because the court's finding of a fundamental right to an abortion has "no support in the text, structure, or history of the Constitution." Judge Roberts tried to play down the importance of that brief during his confirmation hearings for the appellate court two years ago. He suggested then that he was simply serving as a lawyer representing his client, in that case President George H. W. Bush. In any case, as an appellate-court judge, Judge Roberts said he would be bound by Supreme Court precedents, including the Roe decision. But Democrats and legal veterans of previous administrations are now skeptical of that response, particularly since Judge Roberts at the time was a high-ranking, political appointee. As a Supreme Court justice, he would no longer be bound by the court's previous rulings. "It's the answer you expect a lawyer to give," said Robert Reinstein, dean of Temple University Law School and a former Justice Department attorney in the Carter administration. "He was a political appointee. Presumably, he was working at high levels in the Justice Department for an administration in which he thought there would not be a lot of conflict between his own views of what the law should be and the positions the government was taking." Senate Democrats and their allies have signaled that they intend to request documents from the Justice Department that could shed light on Judge Roberts's role and advice on both the abortion cases and the civil-rights actions. "We want the relevant documents," said Ralph Neas, president of People for the American Way. But the Bush administration has a history of resisting such requests and likely would do so again, which could cause some Democrats to reconsider their early inclination to support Judge Roberts. An Associated Press poll released yesterday found that 52% of Americans -- and a solid majority of women -- think Judge Roberts should explain his views on abortion before he is confirmed. Such findings embolden liberal women's groups to plow ahead, expecting that allies will follow later.
