Title: Taste: Tony & Tacky
Text: Put Out That Fire: When a group of Upper Darby, Pa., volunteer fireman got together to go to a Rolling Stones concert Sunday evening, they decided to commandeer one of the station's fire trucks. Not only that, they brought along a woman who put on a fireman's helmet, stripped off her cutoff shorts and bared her thong while posing "suggestively" for the men who, according to the Philadelphia Daily News, took photos. Upper Darby officials are not amused. "From what we know," the city's chief administrative officer told the paper, "it appears that these firefighters were not at this location on official township firefighter business."    Shoo Fly, Don't Bother Me: The city of Colton, Calif., says it's had it with flies. On Wednesday, according to Associated Press, its mayor said the city would no longer try to provide a healthy habitat for the only fly on the endangered-species list: the Delhi Sands fly, which makes its home in the city's dunes. Officials say that helping the fly has halted development projects and sapped tax revenues. But the Fish and Wildlife Service is not persuaded. Spokesperson Jane Herndon told AP: "The Endangered Species Act does not differentiate between a species that is cute and fuzzy with a species that may not have the charisma but has a value."

Title: Court Hands Setback To Panel on Logging At Spotted Owl Sites
Text: SAN FRANCISCO -- A federal appeals court here ruled that the Bush administration may have illegally interfered with deliberations of the special governmental committee that last year voted to allow logging on timberlands inhabited by the northern spotted owl. The Bush administration convened the special committee in 1991 under a rarely invoked provision of the Endangered Species Act. The law empowers the committee to exempt economic activity, in this case, logging, from requirements of the act, even if the activity will result in the extinction of a species. After the panel voted to permit logging on certain federal lands where owls nest, environmentalists alleged that secret communications between the Bush administration and the panel violated laws requiring that the panel's operations be public. The appeals court didn't rule on whether any such secret communications took place, but held they were illegal if they did. The appeals court threw the whole matter back at the committee, ordering a full investigation of any contacts between the White House and panel members. It isn't clear how the matter will play out now, since the committee is effectively disbanded and the Clinton administration isn't believed to support its decision to permit the logging. Government officials couldn't be reached to comment on the ruling.

Title: U.S. News: Drilling Limited to Aid Sage Grouse
Text: The Obama administration on Thursday laid out plans to conserve the habitat of the greater sage grouse in several Western states, including limits on oil and natural-gas drilling -- a move that could make it less likely the bird will be listed as endangered. The Interior Department, which is to decide by October whether to designate the chicken-like bird as endangered, said the conservation plans could be enough to avoid a listing. Such a designation, which can lead to land-use and other restrictions, could have a broad impact on the West's economy, including energy development. The conservation plan is expected to take effect later this summer. The government initiative to preserve the sage-grouse habitat -- which covers 165 million acres, about the size of Texas -- has been met with concern by the mining, ranching, and oil and natural-gas industries, which have large footprints in several of the 11 affected states. Most of the area targeted for conservation -- about 64% -- is federal land, the department said. Interior Secretary Sally Jewell announced the effort Thursday in Wyoming, the state with the largest affected area. Ms. Jewell has said she wants to work with environmental groups to avoid a listing under the Endangered Species Act. The plans would set limits on energy development in certain parts of the habitat, including establishing buffer zones around areas where male sage grouse gather around breeding season and perform mating rituals -- a rite that attracts bird-watchers from around the world each spring. Ms. Jewell said about 10% of land with sizable oil and natural-gas resources could be placed off limits by the plans. "Some will say the plans lock up development and they will shut down economic activity for a bird," Ms. Jewell said. "The vast majority of the conventional and renewable energy resources that exist in these landscapes that we have in the plans will be available to develop." Kathleen Sgamma, vice president of government and public affairs at Western Energy Alliance, a group representing oil and gas companies with operations in Western states, said the industry supports conservation of the sage grouse but state-led efforts are the best way to accomplish that. "Western Energy Alliance will protest all land use plan amendments that fail to conform with state plans, and will continue to support actions by Congress to delay these land use plans and a final listing decision," Ms. Sgamma said in a statement. Led by Republicans and rural-state Democrats, Congress passed a spending bill in December prohibiting the Interior Department from writing and issuing a proposed endangered-species listing through this fiscal year, which ends Sept. 30. The same day marks a court-mandated deadline for the department to decide whether to place the bird on the endangered species list. It is unclear how or when the Interior Department would write such a listing -- if it decides to do so -- given the congressional prohibition. Many environmental groups cautiously praised the news Thursday and left out any calls to list the bird as endangered. "This planning process definitely has the potential of finally conserving a quintessential American species and landscape, but half measures won't cut it," said Jamie Rappaport Clark, president and CEO of the Defenders of Wildlife. "The future of sage grouse and the sagebrush sea is at stake." Threats to the bird's habitat include wildfires, invasive species and disturbances to habitat caused by oil and gas drilling, the Interior Department said. In April, the department said it would keep a population of sage grouse in California and Nevada off the endangered list, citing voluntary conservation measures by ranchers, tribes and others. That announcement affected only about two million acres, but some observers took it as a signal the department wouldn't move to list the species as endangered in other regions. Credit: By Amy Harder and Jim Carlton

Title: Tribes Present A Threat of Action
Text: Western Washington Indian tribes are threatening to sue the U.S. government and the state Department of Natural Resources if the state doesn't give them more say in managing salmon habitats. A dozen tribes have filed intent-to-sue notices with the federal Commerce and Interior departments, which in January 1997 approved Washington's habitat-conservation plan. The plan was designed to protect local fish and wildlife listed under the U.S. Endangered Species Act while allowing economic activity on 1.6 million acres of state-managed land. The tribes' chief complaint: The state is barring Native Americans -- perhaps illegally, the tribes say -- from playing a role in managing salmon habitats. "I think there's room to arrive at a common understanding," says Jim Anderson, executive director of the Olympia-based Northwest Indian Fisheries Commission, which represents 20 tribes in western Washington. "But the legal clock is running," he says. The tribes plan to file suit by March 1 if they haven't resolved their differences with the state by then. The Endangered Species Act requires filing intent-to-sue notices before taking legal action, but doesn't set a deadline for a lawsuit. The tribes and state officials have been talking for two years, but remain far apart. Kaleen Cottingham, Washington's deputy commissioner of public lands, says that what the tribes want simply isn't permissible under state law. "Frankly, legally we can't give them joint decision making," she says. "The Legislature sets up the rules for decision making on trust lands." But tribal leaders say a 1974 federal court ruling authorizes them to participate in any program aimed at maintaining salmon supplies. The landmark decision by U.S. District Court Judge George Boldt in Seattle was based on the terms of an 1855 treaty that promised tribal access to "usual and accustomed" fishing sites in western Washington. The Boldt decision said that up to half of all fish harvested in Puget Sound and the Columbia River belong to tribes dependent on fish for food or for ceremonial use. Tribal representatives are to meet this week with officials of the Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service to argue their case and ask the federal agencies to broker negotiations with the state agency. The tribes are unhappy with several aspects of the habitat-conservation plan, including what they say are vague definitions of the size of buffer zones between economic activities and bodies of water where endangered salmon live. The Department of Natural Resources says that the plan is written as sharply as possible. "The salmon protections in the HCP are greater than what anyone else is doing in the state," Ms. Cottingham says. Gov. Gary Locke's proposed salmon recovery plan might end up addressing some of the tribes' complaints. A coalition called Five Caucuses -- comprising representatives from federal, state and local governments, tribes and industry -- is working on salmon-protection rules for all nonfederal forest lands, and its plan is expected to be a cornerstone of the governor's plan.

Title: Delayed U.S. Timber Report Prescribes Stricter Logging Curbs to Save Seabird
Text: Federal timber agencies are preparing a report that suggests additional logging restrictions may be needed in the Northwest to protect a rare seabird. They apparently delayed finishing it because they didn't want it released during President Clinton's timber meeting this month. The report covers the implications of permanently protecting the marbled murrelet on about 107 federal timber sales dating back to 1989 covering thousands of acres. Logging has been halted on the land since September, when the government declared the marbled murrelet a threatened species under the Endangered Species Act. Like the spotted owl, the murrelet needs old-growth forest habitat to survive. The report is a much-anticipated milestone in the forest conflict because it will help define how much cutting, if any, will be allowed on the acreage in the future. The report's conclusions also will send a signal about how far-reaching murrelet protections -- and related permanent logging restrictions -- may eventually be on other Northwest timberland. The report was scheduled to be completed March 15. Hugh Black, the top regional fish and wildlife specialist in the U.S. Forest Service's Portland office, declined to comment on the contents of the report, which he said isn't finished. But scientists familiar with recent drafts of the report, done in conjunction with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service scientists, say it implies that potentially severe logging restrictions will have to be imposed to protect the bird. Mr. Black said the agencies held back the report in part because their superiors in Washington "didn't want anything that could hamper the timber summit . . . or divert attention by causing controversy." A spokesman for the Interior Department, the main agency heading the Clinton administration's review of endangered species and forest policy, denied there was any effort to delay work on the report. Forest Service officials in Washington couldn't be reached. A report calling for further logging restrictions would have stirred things up at the Portland forest conference, called by President Clinton to cool emotions on both sides of the fight between logging and wildlife interests. The report's delay has little immediate impact on forests or birds because of the interim logging ban, it heightens the anxiety of Northwest timber interests. "If they didn't want it released before the forest conference, it's probably not full of good news," said Ralph Saperstein, vice president of the Northwest Forestry Association. Mr. Saperstein said some timber interests hope the delay indicates the administration is trying to figure ways to allow at least a bit more cutting than earlier drafts of the report would permit. Still, even some timber interests acknowledge that they probably won't get to log much in the old-growth forests favored by murrelets. A separate study recently released by Forest Service scientists found more than 600 species dependent on oldgrowth habitat. That report implied that logging restrictions in old-growth forest may have to go far beyond anything proposed to date by the government to comply with federal wildlife laws. Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Environmental Lawsuits Face Tough Standard --- Justices Require Plaintiffs To Prove Personal Harm To Challenge U.S. Rules
Text: WASHINGTON -- The Supreme Court made it tougher for environmentalists to get into court to challenge federal regulations. The decision, issued Friday, continued a recent trend in which the high court has tightened access to federal courts for a wide range of suits claiming that government action, or inaction, has caused a generalized injury to citizens. In the court's main opinion, Justice Antonin Scalia said that to avoid having their lawsuits thrown out before trial, environmental advocates must present plausible evidence that they have personally suffered a specific injury or will be harmed "imminently." Six justices concluded that members of Defenders of Wildlife and other groups had failed to meet this requirement in a suit seeking to change the way the government applies part of the Endangered Species Act. The act requires federal agencies to consult with the Secretary of the Interior to insure that their actions aren't likely to threaten species that are considered endangered. The environmentalists were rebuffed in their attempt to challenge a Reagan administration policy that interpreted the act to require consultation only for federal actions in the U.S. or "on the high seas," but not in other countries. The Supreme Court majority, sticking strictly to the court-access issue, didn't address the merits of the policy itself. The high court has for years interpreted the Constitution as requiring that plaintiffs, to proceed with lawsuits, must offer evidence that they have suffered harm that was "concrete and particular," that the harm was caused by the defendant's conduct and that the court has some ability to redress the harm. The high court interpreted these requirements loosely in the early 1970s but has toughened its approach more recently. The environmentalists in Friday's case asserted that they would suffer if endangered species in other countries are jeopardized by U.S.-supported activities abroad. For example, one woman said she would suffer if she weren't able to see the endangered Nile crocodile in Egypt as a result of U.S. assistance in fixing a huge dam on the North African river. Another woman said she feared she wouldn't see the endangered Asian elephant or leopard in Sri Lanka because of U.S. development assistance to that country. "Such `some-day' intentions," Justice Scalia wrote, are "simply not enough" to warrant a federal court's hearing a lawsuit. The alleged harm must be more certain and imminent, he asserted. The environmental advocates also had asserted that they suffered a "procedural injury" from the failure of federal agencies to consult on protecting endangered species abroad. The act does contain a so-called citizen-suit provision that states that "any person" may sue to block anyone, including the government, from violating the statute. But Justice Scalia reasoned that an individual can enforce such procedural rights only "if the procedures in question are designed to protect some threatened concrete interest of his." In a concluding passage that appeared to be unnecessary to the resolution of the case, Justice Scalia implicitly attacked Congress for passing citizen-suit provisions that may "transfer from the president to the courts the chief executive's most important constitutional duty, to 'take care that the law be faithfully executed.' " This appeared to be a warning to lawmakers that they can't try to allow lawsuits such as those filed by the environmentalists simply by passing more expansive citizen-suit provisions that define general environmental concerns as direct injuries. But only three other members of the court -- Chief Justice William Rehnquist and Justices Byron White and Clarence Thomas -- seemed to agree with Justice Scalia's sweeping assertion. Justice Anthony Kennedy, joined by Justice David Souter, concurred with most of the majority's opinion, but acknowledged Congress's authority to pass broad citizen-suit measures. Justice John Stevens concurred with the majority's judgment, but wrote a separate opinion based on different reasoning. Justice Harry Blackmun, in a dissent joined by Justice Sandra O'Connor, accused the splintered majority of "what amounts to a slash-and-burn expedition through the law of environmental standing." (Lujan vs. Defenders of Wildlife). Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Green Group Tries To Drive Ranchers Off Federal Lands --- Activists Aim to Save Species Hurt By Grazing Cattle' If Operators Fail, `So Be It'
Text: WEED, N.M. -- Jimmy Goss has survived wildfires, flash floods and being struck by lightning while herding cows in the Sacramento Mountains. He's not sure he'll survive the Forest Guardians.   Hardline environmentalists, the Guardians are leaders of the zero-grazing movement, which aims to clear every head of cattle off the 265 million acres of wildlands the U.S. government owns in 11 Western states.   The Guardians use an unusual legal approach. First, they track down ranchers who have permits to feed their livestock on federal land for just pennies a head. The next step is to sue under the U.S. Endangered Species Act or other laws, accusing the government of mismanaging the land where the ranchers' cows graze.   If the Guardians win in court, or if the government settles, the number of cows a rancher is allowed to graze with his permit is cut. That hands the Guardians a double victory: Not only does the land get a breather, but the rancher has to pay much more to feed his displaced cows on private land.   Indeed, the Guardians' most controversial tactic is to single out the financially vulnerable -- ranchers who have used their permits as collateral for bank loans, a common form of financing for small ranching operations. "We want to put the squeeze on ranchers to get off the land," says John Horning, the coordinator of the Guardians' antigrazing campaign. "If some ranchers go out of business along the way, so be it."   A Guardians suit forced Mr. Goss and his wife, Frances, to put 200 of their 553 beef cows out to pasture with a neighbor who charges them 10 times as much as the Forest Service did. They have had to dig into retirement savings to make payments on their grazing-permit loan. "It makes you want to cry, what they've done to us," Mrs. Goss says.   About 25,000 ranchers have grazing permits in the West, where upwards of three million cows, or about 10% of America's beef cattle, feed on land owned by the U.S. government. By their own estimate, the Guardians have managed to clear 5,000 cows off two million acres managed by the U.S. Forest Service, winning or settling some 18 lawsuits, and they have dozens more suits pending. In one of the potentially most significant, a federal judge in Tucson ruled last month that the Forest Service failed to properly monitor and restrict grazing on hundreds of allotments across about 15 million acres in New Mexico and Arizona. The judge is considering remedies, including severely restricting the livestock that can graze there.   Mr. Horning says the Guardians sympathize with the ranchers they go after and don't hold them entirely accountable for the damage done by their cattle. According to the Guardians, their main enemy is the U.S. government, and its grazing-permit program, which zero-grazers say subsidizes an industry that threatens hundreds of varieties of plants and dozens of species of animals.   The only way to protect the land, they say, is to put it off-limits to livestock that crush delicate fauna around mountain streams, causing erosion and harm to fish, and destroy meadows that are home to a multitude of wild creatures, including threatened and endangered species.   The Forest Service says the Guardians exaggerate the injury caused by cattle. For one thing, agency officials say, wild animals, including fast-growing herds of elk that roam many Western states, probably do as much harm to pastureland as livestock. The government's main argument is that public land can and should continue to be available for multiple uses, including grazing. "I believe that properly managed grazing has an excellent future in the Forest Service," says David Stewart, director of rangeland management for the Forest Service's Southwestern region.   Formed in 1989, the Forest Guardians have 2,000 members and an annual budget of $400,000, mostly from small contributors, the group says. The group describes itself in its literature as "relentless" and "uncompromising." In fact, it has drawn criticism from mainstream environmental groups uncomfortable with the Guardians' zeal for putting ranchers, especially small-time family operations, into financial binds.   "They're a little too extreme," says George Grossman, a longtime official in the Sierra Club's office in Santa Fe, N.M., where the Guardians are based. "I think zero anything is not the way to go. I mean, we're talking about people losing their livelihoods."   So far, few ranchers targeted by the Guardians have gone out of business, according to lawyers for ranchers, though many say they have been pushed to the brink.   After the Guardians sued last spring, the Forest Service ordered 77-year-old Lena Shellhorn to remove her 80 cows from the Gila National Forest in southwestern New Mexico. Now the cows feed on the 258 acres she and her two sons own in Glenwood, N.M. But it isn't pastureland, so the Shellhorns have to haul feed in, significantly raising operating costs.   "If we can't get these cattle back in the forest, I'll just go broke," says Mrs. Shellhorn, whose ancestors started ranching nearby in 1878.   Like Mrs. Shellhorn and many of the ranchers the Guardians single out, the Gosses aren't well off. They live in a three-bedroom log house that Mr. Goss built in this tiny community of some 20 residents high in the Sacramento Mountains, an Old West refuge for gunslingers and renegade Apaches.   Mrs. Goss's ancestors settled here around 1880. Mr. Goss's grandfather arrived a few years later. The families ran cattle over a roughly 100,000-acre expanse of ponderosa and fir forest now known as the Sacramento Allotment, part of the Lincoln National Forest. Mr. Goss, 65, worked for years as a logger. In his mid-50s, he went back to the ranching he had grown up with. "My grandaddy worked to give us this," Mr. Goss says, "and I'm busting my behind so my grandkids can have it too."   To find ranchers with grazing-permit loans, the Guardians use the federal Freedom of Information Act to get the names of participants in what's known as the escrow-waiver loan program.   Under the program, the U.S. government provides banks with verification of ranchers' grazing permits, so banks can accept the numbers of livestock allowed to feed under the permits as collateral for business loans. In the past 20 years, banks have issued more than $450 million in grazing-permit loans to about 300 ranching operations, according to records obtained by the Guardians.   The Guardians say another New Mexico-based environmental group, called Gila Watch, gave them the inspiration for the grazing-permits tactic. Gila Watch in 1995 successfully sued the Forest Service to remove all cattle from 125,000 acres of the Gila National Forest, home to the endangered Mexican spotted owl. One rancher with a grazing permit there went out of business after he couldn't keep paying his grazing-permit loan, and the Guardians decided to put that kind of financial squeeze on ranchers throughout the West.   The group's lawsuits are filed under the 1973 Endangered Species Act or other federal environmental laws, including the National Forest Management Act and the Clean Water Act. The laws require federal managers of the nation's public land to protect creatures and plants that the government has determined are threatened or endangered. The suits typically argue that the government needs to take action in order to carry out that legally required protection. For example, an endangered spotted owl may be threatened by cattle grazing, in part, because cows trample the land where field mice, a preferred source of food for the spotted owl, live in burrows.   The Guardians don't sue only in cases where ranchers are in debt. The group says it goes to court whenever it thinks it can force the Forest Service or another federal agency to change its grazing policies. But critics say the Guardians go after loan-holders more often than not and acknowledge the tactic can be effective. "It doesn't take a mathematician to figure out how many head of cattle it takes for the rancher to make his bank note," says G. B. Oliver III, an executive at the Western Bank of Alamogordo, in Alamogordo, N.M., which gave the Gosses a $170,000 loan in 1989, with the 553 cows then on their grazing permit as collateral.   The U.S. government doesn't dispute that a lot of the public land in the West has been excessively grazed. When fires were raging across the Southwest last summer, several Forest Service officials said publicly that one reason was a build-up over the past century of dense ponderosa pine forests. The forests grew up in part after cattle mowed down the native grasses that used to catch fire and keep the timber in check. In recent years, the Forest Service has been keeping cows out of burned areas to help forests recover.   The Forest Service and the ranching industry say smarter land management -- not zero-grazing -- is the best answer for all concerned. "There is no question our performance on the public lands has vastly improved," says Ted Hoffman, president-elect of the Idaho Cattle Association.   Many ranchers take protective steps themselves, fencing off streams and declaring some hard-hit meadows off limits until they can recover. In the Lincoln National Forest, Mr. Goss moves his cows regularly so they won't feed too long in one spot. On a sunny afternoon, he showed how he does it. Driving down a dusty road in his pickup truck, Mr. Goss stopped a few yards from where several brown heifers were munching grass in the shade of pine trees. They perked up when they saw him fetch a bucket full of grain cubes from the back of the truck and hurried forward when he started handing them out. "This gives them more incentive to wait for me to come back," said Mr. Goss, surrounded by cows.   The Goss case started in April 2000, when the Guardians sued the Forest Service in U.S. District Court in Albuquerque. The Guardians argued the Gosses' cows had nibbled the threatened Sacramento Mountains thistle and other vegetation, including native grasses and streamside willows, to the nub, putting the threatened Mexican spotted owl at risk and upsetting the ecosystem.   In June 2000, the Forest Service ordered the Gosses to cut their herd from 553 head to 400. In August of that year, the agency ordered them to cut it again, to 335. Forest Service officials say they did so because it was clear they had allowed too many cattle on the land, not because the Guardians had sued. The judge in the case ultimately ruled that 335 was the right number.   Now, the Gosses pay $2,700 more every month to put their cows out to pasture than they did before the Guardians sued. With their grazing-permit loan eating up $30,000 of the $120,000 their operation grosses every year, and other expenses now consuming the rest, the Gosses live on monthly Social Security checks of $900, and what they had saved for retirement.   The strain weighs on the whole Goss family. "It's like we're watching them slowly kill our folks," the couple's 34-year-old daughter, Kendra Mydock, says on her parents' front porch as thunder rumbles. "Hey," her father says, "we're not dead yet."   (See related letters: "Letters to the Editor: Ranchers as Stewards of Public Land" -- WSJ Nov. 19, 2002)

Title: Supreme Court Supports Rights Of Landowners --- Decision on Compensation Could Limit Regulation By States, Washington
Text: WASHINGTON -- The Supreme Court bolstered property owners' rights to seek compensation when government regulation eliminates the entire value of their land. The 6-3 ruling could have the effect of limiting some state and federal regulation of coastal areas, wetlands and regions that are home to endangered animal species. Governments may hesitate to require that private land be left in its natural state if they have to make large payments to the owners. But yesterday's decision applies only in cases where government rules deny owners all of the value of their land. "This case does not rewrite the constitutional law on private property," said Jerold Kayden, a senior fellow at the Lincoln Institute of Land Policy in Cambridge, Mass. "It is my bet that there are few occasions in which property owners can show that government regulations deny all uses of property." The high court concluded its 1991-1992 term without having launched what many in business and conservative circles hoped would be a major revolution increasing constitutional protection for property interests. But the limited nature of yesterday's ruling didn't stop combatants on both sides of the hotly debated property-rights issue from claiming victory. Paul Kamenar of the conservative Washington Legal Foundation called the ruling a "bright jewel that advances property-rights principles." Mona Zeiberg of the U.S. Chamber of Commerce said the decision will benefit small businesses "because their property is usually their most substantial asset, and losing its value would put them out of business." Environmentalists countered that the decision did little to change current law. The ruling "rejects the real estate, oil and mining companies' attempt to harm their neighbors and reaffirms the Constitution's good-neighbor policy," said David Gardiner of the Sierra Club. Generally, the Constitution's Fifth Amendment prohibits government from taking property without paying "just compensation" to the owner. The question decided yesterday was whether South Carolina's regulation of construction on its environmentally fragile Atlantic coastline amounted to taking property rights from a person who intended to build on beachfront real estate. The high court repeated past statements that such a regulation could be considered the equivalent of physically occupying or confiscating land, requiring the government to pay its owner for the value of the property. The property owner who was the subject of yesterday's decision paid $975,000 in 1986 for two beach-front lots on which he planned to build two houses, one for himself and one to sell. A state agency barred the construction under the environmental law, which took effect in 1988. The property owner, David Lucas, sued the state, arguing that the regulation denied him "all economically viable use" of his land. A state court agreed and awarded him $1.2 million for the "regulatory taking" of his property. The South Carolina Supreme Court reversed that decision, ruling that a restriction "enacted to prevent serious public harm" doesn't require a state to compensate landowners for their losses. The U.S. Supreme Court said South Carolina's top court had misunderstood the law on "takings" and reversed its decision. Even if a regulation addresses a serious harm, the government must compensate a property owner denied "all economically viable use of his land," Justice Antonin Scalia wrote in an opinion for the majority. Narrow exceptions to that rule may arise, however, Justice Scalia said. For example, if the legal title to the land forbids the type of uses proscribed by the government regulation, the government may not have to compensate the owner. Under the state's traditional judge-made law, known as common law, another exception could occur if the owner would be forbidden to use the land in the fashion prohibited by a subsequent regulation enacted by a legislature or imposed by an executive-branch agency. The Supreme Court sent the Lucas case back to the South Carolina courts with instructions that he is owed compensation unless one of the exceptions applies. Despite the limited number of cases to which the high court's ruling will apply, some developers viewed it as adding to the momentum of their attack on the Endangered Species Act and other local and federal conservation laws. "The decision should encourage balancing economic arguments with environmental ones, and we're all for that," said Don Steffenson, executive vice president of Lusk Co., an Irvine, Calif.-based developer. The ruling's effect may be felt immediately in Florida, said Ronald Weaver, a Tampa land use lawyer. He said he expects legal challenges to a state growth-management law that prohibits the issuance of new building permits in areas where public services are deemed inadequate. "At stake are hundreds of millions of dollars of Florida property that may now be compensated if traditional nuisance laws in Florida did not prevent development," Mr. Weaver said. But Stanly Spracker, an environmental lawyer here, said the decision will more likely influence future land use negotiations by forcing governments to balance "environmental issues" against economic interests. Justices Harry Blackmun and John Stevens filed dissenting opinions. Justice Blackmun said the majority opinion used unnecessarily "sweeping" language and generally was "misguided." Justice Stevens said people ought to bear the risk when they buy property that may be subject to government regulation. Justice David H. Souter said in a separate statement that the court should have refrained from deciding the case for procedural reasons. (Lucas vs. South Carolina Coastal Commission) Separately, the Supreme Court said it would consider whether the federal racketeering law violates the First Amendment when the government uses it to seize "expressive materials" in an obscenity prosecution. Such materials include sexually explicit magazines and video cassettes. The justices are expected to hear arguments in the case next fall. (Alexander vs. U.S.) Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Cross Country: California Drains Reservoirs in the Middle of a Drought
Text: One of the worst droughts in California's history has devastated more than a half-million acres of the most fertile farmland in America. In communities like Sacramento, "water police" go from door to door to enforce conservation measures. There's even a mobile "app" to report neighbors to city authorities so they can be fined for wasting water. With the Sierra snowpack at 4% of normal as of May 20, Californians will desperately need what little water remains behind its dams this summer. Authorities have warned some towns like Folsom -- home of Folsom Lake -- to expect daily rationing of 50 gallons per person, a 60% cut from average household usage. Yet last month the Bureau of Reclamation drained Folsom and other reservoirs on the American and Stanislaus rivers of more than 70,000 acre feet of water -- enough to meet the annual needs of a city of half a million people -- for the comfort and convenience of fish. Government officials who are entrusted with the careful management of our water squandered it in less than three weeks to nudge baby salmon toward the Pacific Ocean (to which they swim anyway) and to keep the river at just the right temperature for the fish by flushing the colder water stored in the reservoirs. These water releases are so enormous they are called "pulse flows." They generate such swift currents that local officials issue safety advisories to exercise extreme caution when on or near the rivers. While some of the water can be recaptured downstream, most is lost to the ocean. In January pictures of a near-empty Folsom Lake on the American River made national news. Yet on April 21 the Bureau of Reclamation more than tripled water releases from the dams on that river from 500 cubic feet per second to more than 1,500 cubic feet per second for three days -- sending more than 7,000 acre feet of water toward the ocean. Elevated releases have continued for "temperature control." On April 14 a 16-day pulse flow drained nearly 63,000 acre feet of water from dams on the Stanislaus River. Unrealistic laws like the Endangered Species Act administered by ideologically driven officials have now crossed from good intentions to dangerous policy, and the folly cries out for fundamental reforms. The House twice has passed such reforms, most recently in February. HR 3964 would pave the way for hundreds of thousands of acre feet of new water storage across California and promote fish hatcheries and predator control as simple and inexpensive alternatives to protect endangered species. Sadly, it remains bottled up in the Senate. An administration that has never been shy about asserting executive powers has the authority to stop these releases through provisions in the Endangered Species Act that allow a committee of officials to suspend them. It has failed to do so. While homeowners parch their gardens and clog their showerheads with flow restrictors to save a few extra gallons of water, their government thought nothing of wasting 23 billion gallons to lower river water temperatures by a few degrees. The frivolous and extravagant water releases from our dams last month mock the sacrifices that our citizens make every day to stretch supplies in this crisis. In turn, they undermine the government's credibility and moral authority to call for stringent conservation and hardship by the people. California's chronic water shortages won't be solved without additional storage. Despite an abundance of suitable and affordable sites, opposition from environmentalists and the laws they have wrought have delayed these projects indefinitely and made them prohibitively costly. Until unrealistic laws like the Endangered Species Act, the National Environmental Policy Act and the Wild and Scenic Rivers Act are balanced to accommodate a new era of dam construction, our state and federal governments have a responsibility to manage our increasingly scarce water supply as carefully as we ask our citizens to do. Perhaps, at least, the public can draw from this tragic waste a lesson in how unreasonable our environmental regulations have become, and how out of touch are the policy makers responsible for them. --- Mr. McClintock, a Republican, is a U.S. congressman from California. Credit: By Tom McClintock

Title: REVIEW & OUTLOOK (Editorial) -- Asides: Tough Enough
Text: Who needs the Endangered Species Act, with tough customers like opal allotoca out there? The AP reports that researchers have just found the two-inch fish, long feared extinct, in an egg-smelling, scum-covered pond in Mexico. Intrepid icthyologists waded neck-deep in the slime to bring 'em back alive to the New York Aquarium. We guess it'll be hard to know whether these tough fish are happier in the Aquarium's tender care or back home, undisturbed and undiscovered amid the slime and scum of their former habitat.

Title: Now on the Grill, GE May Quit the Kitchen
Text: The Wall Street Journal Online The Morning Brief, a look at the day's biggest news, is emailed to subscribers by 7 a.m. every business day. Sign up for the e-mail here. One of the biggest household names in corporate America may soon be getting out of the house. General Electric and its recently criticized chief executive, Jeffrey Immelt, have hired Goldman Sachs to run an auction for the manufacturing conglomerate's appliances business and the refrigerators, washing machines and air conditioners that front the GE brand across the country, people familiar with the matter tell The Wall Street Journal. The sale could fetch GE from $5 billion to $8 billion at a time when investors have been pushing Mr. Immelt to burnish GE's once seemingly invincible stature, especially in the wake of the unexpectedly poor quarterly earnings GE posted last month. Mr. Immelt has been facing calls to break up GE, whose far-ranging product line -- including jet engines, industrial turbines, credit cards and the NBC entertainment-and-media empire -- was once considered a key part of the company's thrive-in-all-environments strategy. And his "mission has taken on greater urgency with the credit squeeze and the slumping economy, which have affected many of GE's businesses," the New York Times points out. The appliance business is now a relatively small part of GE's operations, the Journal notes, but the iconic nature of the brand is bound to mark the sale as the end of an era -- especially if it's sold to a foreign competitor. While it isn't clear who'll step up to bid, bankers tell the Journal that BSH Bosch & Siemens Hausgerate of Germany and Haier Group of China are possible buyers, and that private-equity firms and Controladora Mabe, GE's partner in Mexico, could   also be interested. Asian manufacturers in particular could be drawn to GE's appliance business and the chance to use the GE brand to become more global, the Times adds. The timing of the sale may prove propitious. As the Journal reports, credit markets have been significantly improving since March, "emboldening more companies to undertake acquisitions and share buybacks that will be financed largely with debt," even as banks and Wall Street have strengthened their balance sheets enough to begin lending to and encouraging corporate borrowers. --- Icahn to Start Proxy Fight for Yahoo Another nameplate of corporate America, one a lot younger than GE, is in play again. Carl Icahn has decided to go ahead with a proxy fight aimed at unseating Yahoo's entire board of directors and pressure the company to restart sale negotiations with Microsoft, a person close to the matter tells the Journal.  On board with Mr. Icahn's effort is Frank Biondi, the former Viacom CEO who has joined forces with the corporate raider in the past, the Journal says. Mr. Icahn bought roughly 50 million Yahoo shares following Microsoft's decision to walk away from its Yahoo offer in the face of price disagreements with Yahoo's leadership. And though Mr. Icahn "failed to get a response from Microsoft about its interest in restarting acquisition talks," he "elected to proceed because he views a deal with Microsoft as beneficial to both companies and one that executives would come to embrace," people close to the matter tell the Journal. --- Obama and the Edwards Timing Better late than never? John Edwards -- whose enduring populist appeal was enough to garner 7% of the votes in West Virginia's primary this week though he quit the presidential race months ago -- yesterday endorsed Barack Obama for the Democratic nomination. He had been courted on a weekly basis by Mr. Obama and Hillary Clinton since he bowed out with no victories to his name. But his endorsement at this stage, with Mr. Obama so far ahead and only five small primaries left, is unlikely to change the game. It comes as another Democratic Party stalwart, the NARAL Pro-Choice America Pac, endorsed Mr. Obama, as The Hill notes. Yet it also comes at a moment when Mrs. Clinton's lopsided victory in West Virginia revived doubts about Mr. Obama's appeal to the kind of blue-collar voters who have favored Mr. Edwards in the past, and as Mr. Obama turns his attention in their direction with an eye on November. It was no coincidence the Edwards endorsement came in Michigan, where Mr. Obama yesterday was touring plants to meet with auto workers, and where, as the Detroit News reports, he announced a manufacturing agenda that includes billions of dollars in potential aid for the Detroit auto makers. While there, the New York Times notes, Mr. Obama was sporting a flag lapel pin, which has seemed to appear more and more on his suits despite his profession several months ago that he didn't feel compelled to wear his patriotism on his sleeve. Assaults questioning the Americanness of a candidate named Barack Obama -- falsely suggesting he's a Muslim and that this would be bad, juxtaposing his name with terrorist groups, and the like -- have been steadily increasing for months. John McCain, the presumptive Republican nominee, despite his war- hero status and long experience on defense matters, has his own foreign-affairs front to worry about. His wife, Cindy McCain, has sold off some $2 million in investments she had in funds with holdings that do business with Sudan, the New York Times reports, an interest that might appear to clash with Mr. McCain's official position on Darfur. That report comes a day after The Wall Street Journal reported a McCain consultant last year hired a PR firm to burnish the image of Vladimir Putin's political allies in Ukraine, and less than a week after two lobbyists quit prominent roles in the McCain campaign after Newsweek reported they had worked for the military junta ruling Myanmar. Mr. McCain's Republican allies in the House are having a much harder week than he is. After losing a longtime Republican seat from Mississippi to the Democrats on Tuesday, House Republicans are scrambling to make changes and wondering how much to blame their leadership, Roll Call reports. The Journal notes the recent loss of three House seats may push congressional Republicans to move farther away from President Bush. --- Also of Note. . . Reuters: The United Nations said up to 2.5 million people might have been affected by the Myanmar cyclone and proposed a high-level donors conference just as the country's ruling junta again limited foreign aid, while the European Union's top aid official said the military government's restrictions on foreign aid workers and equipment were increasing the risk of starvation and disease. Today, Myanmar state radio reported that the army-drafted constitution was overwhelmingly approved in the first phase of a two-stage referendum held in spite of the devastating cyclone, and that 92% of the ballots cast backed the new charter for democracy, which critics say will entrench army rule. Financial Times: The United Nation's Food and Agriculture Organization food price index, considered the best measure of global food inflation, receded in April, marking its first decline in 15 months, as wheat, dairy, sugar and soybean prices fell. New York Times: The polar bear, whose summertime Arctic hunting grounds have been greatly reduced by a warming climate, will be placed under the protection of the Endangered Species Act, Interior Secretary Dirk Kempthorne announced. But he said it would be "wholly inappropriate" to use the long-delayed decision to list the bear as a threatened species as a tool to reduce greenhouse gases, and the Interior Department added stipulations, seldom used under the act, that would allow oil and gas exploration and development to proceed in areas where the bears live. Washington Post: The Lebanese government rescinded two decisions that had targeted Hezbollah and ignited the worst internal fighting since the end of the 15-year civil war, underlining the group's sense of victory in a battle that has recalibrated Lebanese politics. The information minister said that "in view of the higher national interest," the cabinet would step back from last week's probe into a telecommunications network set up by Hezbollah and the reassignment of the head of security at the Beirut airport, who is considered close to the group. Wall Street Journal:  Pakistan freed dozens of militants and started pulling troops from areas of a volatile tribal region as a part of an effort to make peace with Islamist militants. Government officials also said the two sides were close to a deal that could end hostilities in the country's tribal region of South Waziristan and in parts of North West Frontier Province, one of Pakistan's four provinces. Meanwhile, NATO said it is concerned that the Pakistani government's peace efforts have led to a sharp rise in attacks on the coalition's forces in eastern Afghanistan, where they are fighting insurgents. Associated Press: A previously unknown Islamic militant group today claimed responsibility for bombings that killed dozens in the historic Indian city of Jaipur by planting bicycles laden with explosives on crowded streets, police said. The claim, for explosions that killed 61 people and wounded 90, was reportedly made in videos and an e-mail sent to Indian television stations and a Hindu nationalist political party. Nature: A former Environmental Protection Agency scientist is suing the agency's officials and researchers at the University of Georgia in Athens, alleging that they manufactured and published false data to support the use of potentially harmful sewage sludges as fertilizers. The sludges have been linked to health problems in humans and cattle, and even deaths. International Herald Tribune: European antitrust investigators are expanding the scope of a major inquiry into the pharmaceutical market in a bid to determine whether companies are blocking generics makers from getting less-expensive medicines to market quickly. Lawyers and European Union officials said Neelie Kroes, the EU competition commissioner, was also casting her net widely in a bid to determine whether drug companies' efforts to block competitors by extending patents were also distracting them from developing new medicines, which have been slow in coming to market in recent years. Legal Times: Solicitor General Paul Clement, who led the courtroom defense of the Bush administration's antiterror legal policies -- and emerged unscathed -- announced he is leaving his job next month. No successor has been named, though principal deputy solicitor-general Gregory Garre is viewed as likely to close out the Bush administration in an acting position. Los Angeles Times: Federal Regulators accused Broadcom's billionaire founders Henry T. Nicholas III and Henry Samueli of systematically backdating 232 million stock options to make them more valuable, then hiding the fact from other shareholders. --- Quotes of the Day "I feel like I'm already dead," said a man who dangled upside down in a crevice, his left leg pinned under a car-size boulder amid the toppled buildings and giant stones that have covered the Chinese town of Beichuan since Monday's epic earthquake, The Wall Street Journal reports. While the man was alive and rescue workers knew he was there, he continued to dangle, with workers saying there were so many other victims and not enough heavy equipment. While China quickly mobilized one of the largest relief operations in its modern history after the magnitude-7.9 earthquake, the Journal says a trek into one of the worst-hit areas showed that even this effort was falling short for many victims of the vast devastation. The official death toll had risen to 14,867 as of this afternoon in China, according to the official Xinhua news agency, while 14,000 more were missing in the hardest-hit province, Sichuan, with nearly 26,000 buried in debris there, and 64,746 injured, many of them severely. "Correct guidance of public opinion," was how Li Changchun, a member of the Communist Party's supreme Politburo standing committee, described what the goal of domestic reporting on the quake should be, according to the Financial Times, which cites the People's Daily. Mr. Li said that all frontline coverage of the disaster should "uphold unity and encourage stability" while "giving precedence to positive propaganda."
