Title: Saving the Earth While Killing Some Protected Birds
Text: Regarding Robert Bryce's "Fighting Climate Change by Killing Eagles" (op-ed, Oct. 11): While all forms of energy have some type of impact on the environment, wind offers the lowest-impact, most environmentally benign energy technology available to us today. Plus, wind attracted $25 billion in private investment last year and is supported by the major conservation organizations and Americans nationwide (71% per Gallup). American-made wind power enables the U.S. to develop a diverse energy portfolio better equipped to fight climate change -- the number one threat to wildlife, according to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. Installed American wind power displaces enough carbon emissions annually -- 100 million tons -- to take 15 million cars off the road. No one takes wildlife impacts more seriously than the wind industry. The number of bird losses Mr. Bryce claims wind turbines cause is roughly double the estimate of the most reliable studies, and while unfortunately some eagles collide with turbines at some wind farms, this is an uncommon occurrence. In fact, fatalities of golden eagles at modern wind facilities represent only 2% of all documented sources of human-caused eagle fatalities, and only a few bald eagles have collided with turbines in the history of the industry. Groups like the National Wildlife Federation and the Audubon Society, which make it their job to protect birds, including eagles, and other wildlife, support the development of responsibly sited wind turbines. Finally, the Production Tax Credit has given tax relief to wind-power investors looking to support a clean, domestic energy source that relies on American workers to build more than 70% of its parts. That's something that both Main Street and Wall Street can support. John Anderson American Wind Energy Association Washington [confirm] --- Robert Bryce vastly underestimates the scope of the death toll and scandal. Turbine owners operate under double standards that allow them to kill rare, threatened, endangered and protected species without fear of prosecution or penalty, despite violating the Endangered Species Act and other laws. By contrast, oil companies have had permits denied over far-fetched claims that drilling might disturb mating or nesting, and they have been prosecuted for the deaths of a few ducks over an entire state and year. Individuals have been fined thousands of dollars for possessing a bald eagle feather, whereas turbine operators get off scot-free despite killing thousands of eagles. Equally unacceptable is that many wind-energy facilities operate under voluntary regulations and reporting requirements. No other industry is granted such leeway. This allows them to design "studies" that deliberately hide and minimize bird and bat butchery. They make search areas one-twentieth what they should be for the size of today's turbines, which catapult victims far beyond the 60-meter radius, search only random sections of these small areas, and look only once every 30-90 days, ensuring that scavengers make numerous carcasses "disappear." Finally, attempts to justify the subsidies and bird deaths rely on claims that the tiny amount of electricity generated by wind turbines will help reduce global carbon dioxide levels and prevent "dangerous man-made global warming." However, fossil fuels provide 70%-80% of the "nameplate" electricity generation attributed to turbines. The subsidies must end, and Big Wind must follow the same rules that apply to all other industries. Paul Driessen Committee For A Constructive Tomorrow Fairfax, Va. --- The unnamed scandal is the most dangerous, i.e., government selectively enforcing laws, prosecuting groups it doesn't like and failing to enforce laws against groups it favors. This crony government undermines the rule of law, nurtures a cynical electorate and is characteristic of corrupt Third World countries that are republics in name only. Peter F. Reilly West Palm Beach, Fla. (See related letter: "Letters to the Editor: Wind Farms Kill Many Rare Birds" -- WSJ November 6, 2013)

Title: Did You Hear About the Affiliate That Got Away?
Text: Efforts to save the salmon can, at times, look more like a civil war. Consider Washington's building industry, where opposing approaches on fish recovery pit an influential statewide trade group against its largest affiliate. The Building Industry Association of Washington, a 7,900-member trade organization, through Executive Vice President Tom McCabe, has lashed out at a National Marine Fisheries Service decision last week to list seven types of Washington salmon and two types of Oregon salmon as "endangered" or "threatened" under the Endangered Species Act. But while the association was attacking the listing, the trade group's biggest affiliate, the Master Builders of King and Snohomish Counties, appeared shoulder to shoulder with a consortium of local officials to pledge fraternity instead of fighting. Indeed, Sam Anderson, executive officer of the Master Builders, last week stood by while Seattle Mayor Paul Schell declared the city would create "the greenest plan ever developed." Mr. Anderson says he believes working with local officials will reap the best results for the industry. "We're trying not to be reactive," he says. "We're trying to be proactive." But being reactive is Mr. McCabe's modus operandi. "The sweeping regulations being proposed won't save salmon," he says, "but it will effectively squeeze thousands of families out of the housing market" as land and water supplies dwindle and prices rise. That's part of the reason the association's 160-member board decided at its last regular meeting to create a legal-defense fund, with an initial $150,000 in the bank to help members litigate salmon-related issues. "I expect that amount to increase," Mr. McCabe says, adding that the money will be used primarily for builders and developers in litigation because "environmentalists and neighborhood activists" charge that development is hurting salmon. "The majority of members," he adds, "are too small to fight those battles on their own."

Title: Endangered: Sage Grouse, Prarie Chickens, Ranchers
Text: As a fourth-generation cattle rancher in southeast Oregon's high desert outback, I find myself for the first time agreeing with Nevada Sen. Harry Reid, regarding the "major ramifications" listing the greater sage grouse will have on the economies of the rural West ("Sage Grouse Rebellion," Review & Outlook, March 11). It will put rangeland cattle ranching out of business. Any buckaroo and many scientists can tell you that cattle and sage grouse are compatible.Grouse even follow the cattle around. Why? Cattle dung helps produce bugs, which the grouse eat, and grouse prefer grazed areas. The decline of the sage-grouse population coincides with the government's and environmentalists' push to get cattle off the range and to limit predator control. Peak sage-grouse population occurred with peak cattle grazing. I think the sage grouse's worst enemy is the federal government. Mandated removal of livestock from the range often causes desertification of the land. In other instances, it leads to the increase of nonnative grass species and other weeds, resulting in a buildup of fuels. Add federal government mismanagement of firefighting, and you wind up with disastrous rangeland conflagrations. In 2012, a lightning strike sparked a fire on my property. If we ranchers' advice had been followed, the government could have contained the fire with minimal damage. Instead, the Miller Homestead fire consumed 160,801 acres, killed many of my cattle, threatened the hamlet of Frenchglen and destroyed far more sage-grouse breeding and nesting grounds than ever will be preserved by the government's solution, which in my opinion is more about control than preserving sage grouse. My fellow ranchers and I love the land we work, and we work to preserve a vibrant environment, not only for our cattle but for all of God's creatures. Let us do our job. Gary Miller President Frenchglen Rangeland Fire Protection Association Frenchglen, Ore. --- Considering that 91% of all federal lands lie west of the Colorado/Nebraska line, losing ground to sage grouse under the Endangered Species Act is only part of our problem out here in the West. As you note, the federal government owns on average 47% of each Western state. (That compares to an average of less than 5% federal ownership for our Midwestern and Eastern neighbors. Where's Eric Holder with his disparate-impact team when you need him?) These are lands that we can't tax to support education, transportation and other vital programs. Nor can we responsibly manage these lands -- as we have with private and state lands for generations -- to balance human needs with long-term stewardship and conservation goals. Federal payments in lieu of taxes and shared mineral royalties are meant to offset this lack of access to our resources, but those are becoming endangered as well in the current budget environment and only serve to turn us into welfare states anyway -- all for the pleasure of depriving the nation of our enormous natural resource potential. The disconnect between pie-in-the-sky urban desires and the real needs of the rural production economy have never been greater. If we can't prevent the former from imposing their values on the latter, we won't only imperil a way of life, we will geld the nation's economic engine. Carl Graham Director Sutherland Center for Self-Government in the West Salt Lake City --- You talk in sweeping generalities of the potential impacts of conservation efforts on "farming, ranching, mining, road building, water projects and oil and gas drilling" but fail to mention that prairie chickens have declined by more than 90%, or that sage grouse, which once numbered in the millions, have declined to fewer than 200,000. You also fail to mention the harm to humans caused by rampant fossil-fuel extraction resulting in climate change. It's precisely due to the sort of unbridled habitat destruction that has led to the demise of these birds and brought us to a human-caused extinction crisis. Scientists say we're losing life-sustaining biodiversity at thousands of times historic rates, which will be worsened by greenhouse-gas-induced climate change. With your fear mongering about impending economic catastrophe should the law be followed and these imperiled species be saved for generations to come, your editorial actually offers an extremely strong argument for exactly why we need the tools of the Endangered Species Act to help us balance our economic pursuits with our desire to preserve the health of our planet. Randi Spivak Center for Biological Diversity Washington

Title: City News: In Rockaways, Plovers Settle In --- Endangered shorebird gets special protection, but officials struggle to win over local skeptics
Text: Piping plovers once again have taken up residence along a stretch of Queens beach overlooking the Atlantic Ocean, triggering an annual ritual of wildlife conservation that inspires consternation among some beachgoers. Some 40 blocks of prime sunbathing sand has been marked off in the Rockaways for the diminutive shorebird that is protected under the U.S. Endangered Species Act. A city plover team -- four workers with the Department of Parks & Recreation this year -- has begun spending long days walking the beach to follow bird tracks and scout for predators, especially gulls. Piping plovers were given the federal legal protection in 1986. Back then, 550 breeding pairs were counted in the U.S., according to Meagan Racey, a spokeswoman for the Northeast region of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. Now, authorities say there are about 1,900 breeding pairs. "While the Long Island plover population has been dropping in recent years, we believe recovery is achievable" in the region, said Ms. Racey Last season, 16 pairs of birds made nests on the Rockaways beach and produced 22 viable chicks -- those documented to have lived at least 35 days. Statewide, 303 plover pairs were documented. On the stretch of the eastern Rockaway peninsula nearest the Edgemere community, boosting the bird population requires a team of observers, miles of fencing and sometimes a sales pitch for local skeptics. "It's hard to want to protect something you don't see," said Katrina Toal, an Urban Park Ranger plover sergeant. "People think we are closing this [beach] off for no reason and I have to be, like, 'No, there are birds in there, I just saw two. They are the color of sand.'" A plover nest is a slight depression in the sand with a ring of shells or pebbles around the perimeter. It is no bigger than the top half of a bagel. "It's not the most impressive nest," said Richard Simon, deputy director of the city's Urban Park Rangers. This expanse between Beach 19th Street and Beach 57th Street is particularly good for mating because the piping plovers have sufficient space, the beach has brush to provide protection, and there is good access to tiny marine crustaceans, beetles and other plover food, said Sgt. Toal. On top of that, each nest enjoys 50 meters of protective, though purely symbolic, perimeter fencing -- ribbon and signs strung between posts. That fencing, which goes up at the end of March, extends about halfway down the beach from the boardwalk to the water. Once the chicks hatch, the fence will be extended to the water line. Around Memorial Day, the city hires additional staff to sit at both ends of the fencing and prevent people from traversing east to west. The fences can stay up all summer long, or whenever the last bird heads south. That closure is designed to benefit the plovers, but least terns, common terns and American oystercatchers also enjoy the protective measures. New this year, the state Department of Environmental Conservation placed 22 decoy black skimmers within the fenced-off area, in an effort to attract some of that species of bird, which is listed as one of "special concern" by the state. Whatever the reason, the fencing, and the closed beaches, isn't always welcome. City Councilman Donovan Richards Jr., a Democrat who represents the adjacent Edgemere community, noted that residents of the neighborhood already are denied direct access to the beach by some 80 acres of undeveloped, abandoned city land. Based on city plans, the whole area will be developed in the coming years, he said, but shoreline access remains a source of frustration. "You can't really use the beach here because the issue is the piping plovers," said Mr. Richards. "They actually own the beach." For members of the city plover team, such criticism can sting. The team spends a good part of each day encouraging passersby on the beach to take up the conservation cause and understand that the efforts are mandated by the federal government. "Genuinely, a lot of people don't understand what's happening," said Mr. Simon. "A lot of New Yorkers see a fence and just jump over it." Credit: By Melanie Grayce West

Title: U.S. News: U.S. Watch
Text: ENDANGERED SPECIES ACT States Sue to Undo Protection Changes California and more than a dozen other states sued the Trump administration on Wednesday over regulations that they say have weakened the federal law designed to save wildlife from extinction. The Trump administration last month put new restrictions on how future assessments for protecting wildlife under the Endangered Species Act are made, including ending a policy that automatically gave the highest level of protection to species listed as threatened even before they were listed as endangered. The states say federal regulators improperly injected economic considerations into the law's science-driven, species-focused analyses, limiting the circumstances under which species can be listed as threatened and limiting how unoccupied critical habitat would be designated. State officials asked a federal judge to reinstate the prior regulatory regime. The Trump administration said it acted in response to complaints from business interests that the portions of the law had become too onerous. -- Katy Stech Ferek --- FEDERAL RESERVE Evans Doesn't Expect More 2019 Rate Cuts Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago President Charles Evans said Wednesday he didn't expect more interest rate cuts this year but is open to the possibility they might be needed. "I think we're in a good place in terms of the rate setting," Mr. Evans told reporters after a speech in Lake Forest, Ill. But he added, "I'm open-minded to additional action if that's how the discussion goes . . . I'm sympathetic" to more rate cuts. Mr. Evans supported the Fed's two quarter-percentage-point rate cuts in July and last week to cushion the U.S. economy against the risks of the global growth slowdown and trade tensions. He said he entered the Fed's policy meeting last week thinking those two rate reductions likely would be enough, projecting no additional cuts this year. The move last week lowered the central bank's benchmark interest rate to a range between 1.75% and 2%. -- Shayndi Raice --- FLORIDA Official Recommends Reinstating Sheriff The sheriff suspended by Gov. Ron DeSantis over the Parkland high-school shooting should be reinstated, a Florida Senate official said Wednesday, arguing the governor failed to show the sheriff's policies or alleged negligence were to blame for the massacre of 17 people. Florida Senate special master Dudley Goodlette's recommendation sets up a difficult decision for the GOP-led state Senate. Mr. DeSantis, a Republican, suspended Broward County Sheriff Scott Israel as one of his first acts in office and lawmakers will have to choose whether to follow their governor's lead or agree with Mr. Goodlette's conclusion that Mr. Israel should get his job back. Mr. Goodlette, who was appointed by the Senate to review the suspension process, said the governor didn't prove the charges in suspending Mr. Israel in January. "While the governor has offered a plethora of criticism, he has not shown that Sheriff Israel's policies, procedures or trainings on active shooter situations were inconsistent with Florida law enforcement standards," he wrote in a report. -- Associated Press

Title: Cave Bugs Get Bigger Shield, Irking Builders
Text: The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service is proposing new guidelines for protecting endangered cave bugs in Central Texas that could limit development in one of the fastest-growing regions in the state.    The guidelines, still in draft form but already being applied by the service to some projects, recommend that developers set aside at least 69 acres for habitat around the areas where the bugs are found. Previously, they had been setting aside as little as three acres. The guidelines also lay out specific due-diligence protocols for determining whether the bugs live on certain property and what steps to take if they do.    The new rules are coming under heavy fire from developers. "I can't overemphasize what a dramatic negative impact [the guidelines] could have on landowners," says Alan Glen, an Austin lawyer for several developers. Mr. Glen calls the new rules "conservationism to the point of absurdity."    Bill Seawell, assistant field supervisor in the Austin office of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, counters that the new guidelines are "written in a way that we believe is necessary to protect the species."    The guidelines will probably affect development in Williamson, Travis and Bexar counties, part of the rapidly growing Interstate 35 corridor in Central Texas. There are hundreds of caves around Austin and San Antonio where the bugs might be found. Mr. Glen estimates that more than 100,000 acres could be affected by the new rules. Mr. Seawell says he doesn't have an estimate, but doesn't dispute that number.    The cave-bug flap is one of a series of endangered-species disputes between developers and environmentalists in Central Texas; the golden-cheeked warbler and the Barton Springs salamander, among others, have also been involved. Both developers and environmentalists have sued the federal government at various times over its treatment of endangered species.    "If it isn't a bird, it's a salamander," says Mike Schoenfeld, an Austin developer. "If it isn't a salamander, it's a cave bug. What is going to be next?"    The seven endangered bug species are invertebrates and come with colorful names such as the Coffin Cave mold beetle and the Tooth Cave pseudoscorpion. Three are insects, and four are arachnids. They are typically less than an inch long, and most can't be identified except under a microscope. The Fish and Wildlife Service first listed as endangered five species in Williamson and Travis counties in 1988 and added two more species later.    Williamson County commissioners sued the service in 1994, arguing that two of the species should be removed from the list. The suit, which claimed the listing hurt the county's tax base and slowed economic growth, was thrown out by the U.S. Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals.    The service has recommended listing nine more species, all located in Bexar County, but hasn't issued a final decision on those.    Under the guidelines, landowners must survey all areas within 1,500 feet of a development. If possible caves are found, that ground should be excavated by hand and later restored to its original condition. If a cave is found that contains the endangered bugs -- or other species critical to the ecosystem of the endangered bugs -- the landowner should establish a habitat preserve of between 69 and 99 acres.    Previously, Fish and Wildlife had only general guidelines requiring developers to establish buffers around bug habitats. Mr. Seawell says that approach was deemed inadequate, and the service conducted more rigorous research to come up with the more specific rules.    The guidelines aren't binding per se, but developers are subject to the Endangered Species Act, which imposes criminal penalties for damaging the habitat of a listed species. And Fish and Wildlife must issue a permit for any development in the habitat of an endangered species. The service has already sought to apply the guidelines to several landowners in cases that are in negotiations.    Mr. Glen warns the new due-diligence protocols could add months of delays to some projects and cost developers tens of thousands of dollars in fees for biologists and geologists.    Fish and Wildlife hasn't yet sought public input on the proposed guidelines, and is currently distributing them primarily to scientists and consultants. Mr. Seawell says they could change if new information is presented.    But Mr. Schoenfeld, a member of the land-use committee with the Texas Capitol Area Builders Association, foresees another court skirmish. "I'm sure it will just result in more and more litigation," he says.  Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: U.S. News: Fish Boom Makes Splash in Oregon --- Population Surge Comes Despite Forecasts of Decline; Salmon at the Food Bank
Text: NEHALEM, Ore. -- Adam Rice hasn't had a job since October. The 32-year-old carpenter is a victim of the region's housing slump, one of almost 130,000 Oregonians to tumble into the ranks of the unemployed in the past six months. But he is working hard to feed his family: on the river. This month, it's steelhead, the ocean-dwelling member of the rainbow trout family beginning its return migration to Oregon. Steelhead, along with Coho and Chinook salmon, have made a spectacular return to local streams in the past year, leaving sportsmen exultant and putting food on the tables of struggling Oregonians. The Oregon Department of Fish & Wildlife hatchery here has already surpassed last year's count of 1,400 steelhead. Fisheries manager Joe Watkins calculates his crew could take in as many as 3,000 steelhead before the run ends next month -- fish that will spawn tens of thousands of juvenile "smolts" that will be released to swim downstream and mature in the Pacific. Numbers for other species are even more impressive. More than 680,000 Coho salmon returned to Oregon last year, double the number in 2007. The Coho run was so bountiful the ODFW called in volunteers to herd fish into hatchery pens. There were reports of creeks so choked with salmon, "you could literally walk across on the backs of Coho," said Grant McOmie, outdoors correspondent for a television news team in Portland. And ODFW forecasters expect more than half a million spring Chinook salmon to start swimming upstream in March, about two and half times 2009's run, and nearly four times what came home in 2007. That would be the biggest spring Chinook run since 1938, when Oregon began keeping records of returning Pacific fish. It is all part of a fish rebound no one expected. In 2007, one state office warned, "Populations of anadromous [or oceangoing] fish have declined dramatically all over the Pacific Northwest. Many populations of Chinook, Coho, chum and steelhead are at a tiny fraction of their historic levels." The year before that, a naturalist in Seattle wrote: "It is hard to find the silver lining in a situation as dire as the collapse of wild salmon off the Oregon and California coasts." Among the factors blamed for putting fish in peril are pesticide poisoning, overfishing and global warming, as shrinking mountain glaciers lead to reduced spring melt-offs, which means less water in the creeks where fish spawn. Yet today's fish boom doesn't necessarily signal a long-term turnaround in fish fortunes. It might simply indicate that a few generations of fish have been lucky. The main reason for the population surge, scientists here say, is a brief period of cooling in the Northern Pacific ocean in 2008. Cooler currents brought in fatter plankton, which salmon and steelhead smolts thrive on, said ODFW spokesman Rick Swart. Temperatures have since warmed up again. Mr. Swart added that federally mandated outflows of Columbia River water, which increased during the last decade, helped more smolts get past predators and into the ocean, another factor in increased survival rates. Outflow levels are set each year; last year a federal judge maintained the previous year's level. "It was a perfect storm of conditions for the fish," he said. While the ODFW expects a record-breaking run of spring Chinook, it estimates that 80% of the fish will be hatchery-born, not spawned in the wild, said John North, manager of the department's Columbia River Fisheries Program. "The goal is recovery of wild fish listed under the Endangered Species Act," Mr. North said. "We're improving, but we remain below recovery goals." Regardless of the cause, the bounty has come just in time for the Oregon Food Bank, whose demand for emergency food soared this winter as unemployment in the state topped 12%. Working with fisheries staff, the food bank trucked Coho to a cannery in neighboring Washington. There the Coho were filleted and vacuum sealed. Last month 79,000 pounds of frozen Coho returned to Oregon for distribution to needy families. Here on the North Fork of the Nehalem River, fish that are notoriously hard to catch in large rivers practically leap to the banks of this rushing stream. "I got 85 pounds of filleted fish: salmon and steelhead mixed," said Mr. Rice, raising twin 20-pounders. His fishing partner, painter Lloyd Graves, hefted his third steelhead of the month. "No one likes to be unemployed," said Mr. Graves, who took a voluntary one-month furlough from work. "But this couldn't happen at a better time." Credit: By Joel Millman

Title: To Its Detractors, The National Bird Is on a New List --- With Their Numbers Soaring, Bald Eagles Menace Pets; Raising Hackles in Seattle
Text: SEATTLE -- Bald eagles are no longer endangered. Now they're a pest.    Consider the latest squawk at the Woodland Park Zoo here.    Zoo keepers were startled when a gang of wild bald eagles showed up here and started picking fights with the zoo's tame avians. Ernest Rose, Woodland Park's raptor specialist, says he was tending the owls, turkey vultures and the zoo's tame bald eagle, Chinook, when a wild eagle swooped down from a tree and attacked them.    "I waved my arms and yelled," Mr. Rose recalls. But the wild bird attempted a second pass, leaving the zoo birds quivering in fear.    Eagle lovers exulted when Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt announced Wednesday that about two dozen species, including the bald eagle, no longer need Endangered Species Act protection. Mr. Babbitt, speaking in front of a pair of nesting bald eagles, said that the number of nesting pairs has soared to more than 5,000 from just 500 three decades ago.    Indeed, eagles have rebounded so smartly that some communities are beginning to look askance at them. Near Tampa, Fla., last year, developers had to delay plans for a new apartment development after an eagle began cruising the neighborhood. Around Davenport, Iowa, motorists ogling newly arrived wild eagles have caused traffic jams.    "Some people around here call them vultures," says Susan Johnston, the city clerk in Haines, Alaska, where about 3,500 eagles congregate each fall to snatch spawning salmon from the nearby Chilkat River. Eagles have eaten fish from fishermen's nets and even grabbed pets, Ms. Johnston says. Some time ago, one snatched a puppy playing with her neighbor's daughter.    "The little girl wasn't much bigger than the puppy," she says. "You have to think about that."    Here in Washington, eagles have quadrupled in number to about 600 nesting pairs in 15 years. Greater Seattle, which had just three eagle nests a decade ago, now has about 30. Suburbanites have watched in disbelief as roaming eagles dive-bomb duck flocks and fly off with ducklings.    "People see them doing the things that eagles do, and sometimes they're taken aback by the gore of it," says Kelly McAllister, a biologist for the state's Department of Fish and Wildlife.    Indeed bald eagles, a species Benjamin Franklin called "a bird of bad moral character," have been showing their true colors as they proliferate in the Northwest. (Franklin wanted the wild turkey to be our national bird, but the bald eagle won.) Two years ago, eagles terrorized a colony of blue herons in suburban Renton, Wash., dining on the graceful birds in raids that lasted several weeks.    "Were the heron lovers upset? Well, yes," says Martin Muller, a biology teacher and eagle buff. "But what can you do about it? After all, the eagles have been endangered."    At the Woodland Park Zoo, a wild eagle showed up recently and perched ominously atop a tree overlooking a net enclosure where the zoo's two tame eagles reside. "One day, I watched him come off his perch and run back and forth along the enclosure, trying to stick his head under," says Tom Aversa, another zoo raptor keeper. "You could tell he was being aggressive."    Zoo officials say an attendant is now always on hand to protect the tame birds; the zoo has applied for a federal permit to scare away wild eagles with bright lights. The zoo has also enlisted Chinook as an early-warning system. The four-year-old tame eagle caws loudly whenever an interloping eagle approaches his turf. The zoo says that ultimately, it will have to erect a net to protect its birds from marauding wild eagles.    Vincent Muehter, associate director of bird conservation for the National Audubon Society, says one reason wild eagles may be hounding the Seattle zoo this spring is that breeding pairs usually require up to 15 square miles for hunting.    Mr. Muehter says bald eagles also like to feed in groups. "When you get a big bunch of eagles," he says, "they're always looking for sitting ducks."    Under the Endangered Species Act, harassing eagles remains punishable by a fine of up to $10,000 and a year in jail. When developer Steve Cramer discovered an eagle nest near his five-acre plot of new homes in Kirkland, Wash., three years ago, he dutifully notified local officials. They ordered Mr. Cramer to immediately halt construction and put together an "eagle-management plan." It took 18 months and $150,000 in lost time, he says.    Mr. Cramer now uses the nest as a sales tool for the million-dollar homes in his development and watches the eagles with a telescope. Nonetheless, he says, "Sometimes I wonder, `Why me?' "    On Mercer Island, another wealthy Seattle suburb, arborist Brian Gilles says he now spends much of his time protecting eagles. Mr. Gilles recently had to rush to a nesting site after worried residents summoned the arborist, and then police, to stop a contractor whose loud wood-chipper was disturbing a nest of fledgling eagles.    Mr. Gilles persuaded the contractor to shut down the chipper for three weeks. "I said that was a critical time, because the parents might be scared away and the eaglets would fly before they were ready," he recalls.    Mr. Gilles has also been summoned to stop residents from chopping down trees containing eagle perches and has patiently heard out eagle lovers bemoaning the loss of a perching tree blown down in windstorms.    "There is nothing like seeing an eagle on a windy day make a two-point landing on top of a tree," marvels Sharon Werner, a flight attendant who lives on Mercer Island. "Being an urban dweller, it is a constant reminder that there are wild, beautiful things out there."    (See related letter: "Letters to the Editor: Bald Eagle Reflects American Character" -- WSJ June 10, 1998)  Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: A Tale of the Obstacles Facing Resident Aliens
Text: Florida has tried just about everything to boost its dwindling panther population. So, why is the Game and Freshwater Fish Commission looking to give a panther away? Largely, residency problems. In April, a 2 1/2-year-old, 120-pound panther was discovered in the wild near Waldo. (Hence the animal's nickname, "The Waldo Cat.") As they always do when they discover a new panther, Game officials took the cat into captivity to determine if he really is a Florida panther -- and therefore protected by the Endangered Species Act. The answer appears to be no. The National Institutes of Health has determined with DNA tests that The Waldo Cat's mother is a native of the Western U.S. or South America. That's a problem. Florida panthers, because they're an endangered species, can't be held in captivity without special dispensation. Since the cat isn't a native, he gets no protection under the Act. But state officials don't want to release the cat into the wild, where he could infuse new blood into the population, because they're afraid they'll be held liable if he does any damage. So, The Waldo Cat sits in captivity. The commission has taken out ads in zoo publications advertising that the panther is available, but so far there have been no takers. Meanwhile, Alachua County residents have begun rallying for The Waldo Cat's release. As for the cat, he tends to hide in a shelter in his 10-foot-by-20-foot cage. "He's pretty shy," says a keeper.

Title: An Imperfect Truce in Wildlife Battles
Text: FORTUNA, Calif. -- The 10,000 acres of ancient coastal redwoods in the Headwaters Forest are home to the northern spotted owl, the coho salmon and the marbled murrelet, a seabird that nests in old trees. The forest also has been the subject of a three-year court battle between Pacific Lumber Co., which owned most of the forest, and the federal government, which has been restricting logging and other activity here since 1990 to protect endangered wild inhabitants. The legal fight ended this month when the government paid $480 million to buy the forest from Pacific Lumber and another owner. Hikers, not loggers, now trek over its spectacular vistas. The transaction, however, was reached as part of an increasingly common regulatory vehicle known as a habitat-conservation plan, which has left neither environmentalists nor timber companies completely satisfied. HCPs, as they are called, were intended to curb both the severe restrictions on logging and the flood of litigation that resulted from the Endangered Species Act of 1973, which calls for stiff civil and criminal penalties for intentionally destroying endangered animals or their habitats. Authorized by a 1982 amendment to the act, the habitat-conservation plans aim to continue protecting endangered wildlife while also relaxing land-use restrictions. The HCPs have emerged as the timber industry's and the Clinton administration's preferred technique of forestry management. In practice, the use of HCPs has brought far more land and species under federal protection, but the protection is a bit looser than that provided by the Endangered Species Act. The 1973 law sets a standard of zero tolerance for harm to endangered animals and their habitats. HCPs, on the other hand, contemplate that some animals will be lost. Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt calls HCPs a practical compromise in the long-running battle between government and big timber. When he became interior secretary seven years ago, he notes, the Endangered Species Act was being litigated by landowners one species at a time, tying up the courts as well as the timberland. "We were just in gridlock," he says. Environmentalists, though, have doubts about HCPs. The plans often are used as "a license to kill endangered species," contends Mike Paparian, senior regional representative for the Sierra Club's offices in Sacramento, Calif. The Sierra Club and other groups are particularly concerned over the length of HCP contracts, some lasting as long as 100 years, as well as provisions for monitoring and amending the agreements. Industry's use of HCPs is exploding. From 1982 to 1992, the government approved 14 habitat-conservation plans, most of them on small tracts in urban areas. Since then, 300 have gone into effect. At present, some 2.7 million acres in the Northwest are under HCP protection. Another 13.6 million acres in the region would be covered by HCPs that are now awaiting government approval. To apply for an HCP, landowners must go through a costly and time-consuming process of identifying and mapping out the nests and other features in the habitats of rare animals and indicate boundaries for protected zones. They submit the plans to government agencies for approval. Government officials concede HCPs have shortcomings. U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service officials agreed there was room for improvement after an independent panel of 119 scientists from eight universities recently examined 208 HCPs and found the plans often lacked scientific data and adequate monitoring. No HCP has been in effect long enough to fully assess its impact. Partly in response to those findings, the government has taken on a strict supervisory role in the HCP it approved for Pacific Lumber, including a full-time federal monitor. Following the company's takeover in 1985 by Texas financier Charles Hurwitz, Pacific Lumber has come under criticism from environmentalists for aggressive logging practices. The company, a unit of Maxxam Inc. of Houston, has denied improper practices. In addition to providing for the sale of the Headwaters Forest, the Pacific Lumber HCP sets aside about 100,000 acres of adjoining company-owned land in protected zones, where logging is severely restricted. In exchange, Pacific Lumber gets broad leeway to harvest timber in the rest of the roughly 111,000 acres it owns in the region. Over the contract's 50-year life, the northern spotted-owl population in both protected and unprotected Pacific Lumber property will be allowed to decline to about 100 from 150, according to Phil Dietrich, a Fish and Wildlife Service biologist. "This gives us a certainty of operations going into the future," says John Campbell, president and chief executive officer of Pacific Lumber. Environmentalists, however, say the only certainty with HCPs is that some endangered animals and fish will be sacrificed. The HCP "locks in the bad stuff and leaves open to change any good things that may be in there," says Darryl Cherney, a Garberville, Calif., organizer for the environmental group Earth First. In future administrations that may be unsympathetic to environmental causes, he says, strict HCPs could be weakened. On March 9, a coalition of scientists, conservationists and others sent Mr. Babbitt a letter asking the government to halt approval of HCPs and correct shortcomings. Timber companies aren't unanimously in support of HCPs either. Timber giant Boise Cascade Corp., for instance, eschews them, focusing on other initiatives, including continued litigation. The Boise, Idaho, company was recently awarded $1.8 million by an Oregon jury, in a suit it filed against the state seeking compensation for having been prevented from harvesting timber where a pair of spotted owls nested. The state has appealed. In some cases, industry's concerns about HCPs are the mirror image of environmentalists'. "Above all, it seems to us that HCPs are subject to the vagaries of political whim," says Boise Cascade spokesman Doug Bartels. Murray Pacific Corp., a small Tacoma, Wash., company, developed one of the first timber HCPs in 1993, covering 54,000 acres of spotted-owl habitat in the Cascades mountain range near Seattle. The agreement hit an unexpected snag less than a month after it was signed, when an endangered marbled murrelet was seen flying into the same forest. "It was a devastating blow to us," says Toby Murray, vice president of the family-owned firm. Two years later, Murray Pacific amended its plan to cover all protected species, including the murrelet, so that it wouldn't have to redesign its plan with each new species. Now, most forestry companies write HCPs to cover many species. Plum Creek Timber Co. of Seattle, for instance, obtained an HCP in 1996 protecting 285 endangered and threatened species -- including the threatened grizzly bear, gray wolf, spotted owl and marbled murrelet -- on 169,000 acres of wildlands straddling Interestate 90 in the Cascades. "We could see an endless number of species being listed, so it made more sense for us to do a comprehensive plan," says Lorin Hicks, Plum Creek's director of fish and wildlife resources. The company plans more HCPs for its timber holdings in Montana, Arkansas and Louisiana. Another firm, Weyerhaeuser Co., is drawing up an HCP covering spotted owls, endangered fish and other rare species on 400,000 acres of its land near Eugene, Ore. The Tacoma firm already has implemented HCPs covering spotted owls on 209,000 acres near Coos Bay, Ore., as well as a rare burrowing beetle on 30,000 acres in the Ouachita Mountains of Arkansas and Oklahoma. ---                    Out of Harm's Way? Title: In Desert Battle, Dune Buggy Takes On Peirson's Milk-Vetch; Fight About Spiny Plants Blossoms Into a War Over Endangered Species
Text: IMPERIAL SAND DUNES, Calif. -- This stretch of hot, dry, wind-carved sand is one of the least habitable spots in the U.S. But it has become the battleground for advocates of two rugged denizens of these hills. One is the Peirson's milk-vetch, an obscure, shrub-sized member of the pea family. The other is the 21st-century Southern California dune buggy, a snarling, V-8-powered beast in a tubular frame mounted on special tires with rubber flaps. In the milk-vetch's corner is Dan Patterson, a 34-year-old red- bearded ecologist with the Center for Biological Diversity, a Tucson, Ariz., nonprofit. He argues that the vehicle endangers the plant and should be banned from large parts of the dunes, which are 20 miles west of Yuma, Ariz. To prove his point, he likes to drive his battered, dirty, 1992 Toyota SUV down a highway that bisects the dunes. The side where buggies are prohibited is dotted with wildflowers including the purple bloom of the milk-vetch. The side where off-road vehicles are allowed is a mess of tire tracks. For the buggies, there's Dick Holliday, sporting a gray Fu Manchu mustache, who has spent 40 of his 60 years driving on the dunes. He's now a top officer of the American Sand Association, a 19,000-member lobbying group in La Verne, Calif., devoted to improving the image and rights of off-road vehicles. He argues the buggies don't pose a threat to the milk-vetch, and says buggy drivers steer clear of the spiny plants for fear of puncturing one of their $250 tires. The competing claims have sparked multiple lawsuits, fights between rival camps' biologists, and testy public hearings. "I've never been physically pushed, but I've been catcalled," says Eileen Anderson, a botanist for the California Native Plant Society. To try to sift the conflicting assertions of vetch viability, the Department of Interior's Bureau of Land Management will spend $1 million for its annual survey. This month, as the winter off-road-vehicle season ends, a team of 30 government-hired biologists has moved out here, living in tents, tallying the plants in sample five-mile tracts. The milk-vetch squabble is at the center of a broader, escalating, debate over the 31-year-old Endangered Species Act, hailed by backers as a high point of the 1970s environmental movement. Mr. Patterson's center alone -- calling itself "nature's legal eagles" -- claims credit for having used the law's club to get 334 plants and animals formally designated as threatened, more than a quarter of all species on the endangered-species list. Businesses and political conservatives have long attacked the law as imposing additional expenses on property owners, who must often make changes to protect species. They also argue the law is ineffective, noting that of 1,264 plants and animals listed as endangered, only 16 have recovered. They want the Republican-dominated Congress to make it more difficult for the government to limit landowners' options. "Pretending that mankind is not part of the environment doesn't work," California Republican Rep. Richard Pombo, who is spearheading the effort, said recently at a hearing on the subject. The milk-vetch was named after the early 20th-century California botanist F.W. Peirson, who first identified it. There are no known commercial uses for the plant, but biologists marvel at how well it has adapted to severe conditions. It anchors itself in the shifting sand with a sturdy taproot that can snake down 50 feet to find water. It has gray, fuzzy leaves that prevent sunburn, seductive purple flowers that attract a certain type of white-faced bee and lightweight seed pods that float for miles on desert winds which replant the milk- vetch, often where nothing else grows. The buggies came after World War II and have also adapted. They started as converted Volkswagen beetles, so underpowered that most couldn't make it up the steeper dunes. Then hot-rod enthusiasts and manufacturers created bigger, more powerful machines. Today modern buggies costing up to $75,000 and propelled by 600- to 800-horsepower engines can easily claw their way up any dune. Sometimes they climb into the air above the dunes before slamming down on special, air- cushioned shock absorbers copied from airplane landing-gear. Over the past decade, off-road-vehicle traffic here has nearly doubled. Winter holiday weekends can bring 190,000 people, the great majority of them watching the drag races or roaring around on dune buggies, motorbikes and all-terrain vehicles. Moves to separate vetch from vehicles began in 1994, when a Democratic Congress prodded by environmental groups set aside 32,000 acres in the northern part of the dunes as a permanent wilderness area. That didn't bother buggy enthusiasts too much because the steepest dunes are in the south. Then environmentalists sued to have the milk-vetch officially declared an endangered species and to broaden the restrictions. They claimed victory in November 2000, when the Clinton administration as part of a court settlement agreed to fence off an additional 49,300 acres in the popular southern portion of the dunes. Until then, the battle was a legal and political mismatch. Environmental groups like the Center for Biological Diversity have had a long history of coordination, working the Endangered Species Act through regulators and the courts. Off-road enthusiasts mainly just showed up on weekends to ride the dunes and to party. But after the string of court decisions favoring the milk-vetch, buggy riders and manufacturers banded together to form the American Sand Association. In 2001, the group hired a biologist, Arthur M. Phillips III. After counting more than 71,000 of the plants growing in the dune-buggy area, he concluded that the milk-vetch wasn't endangered. Patrolling in dune buggies, and using the satellite-based Global Positioning System, Mr. Phillips said he and five other milk- vetch counters marked out 25 census tracts for a return visit. This year, after heavy rains here, "it looks like the count will be equivalent or greater," he estimates. Mr. Patterson dismisses those findings. "Phillips's work is scientifically invalid," he asserts. "Off-roaders think everything they see out there is a Peirson's milk-vetch." Mr. Phillips replies: "We do our work in the field. They do theirs in court. We have almost nothing in common." Another big part of the ASA's campaign is to try to soften the image of dune-buggy riders as hell-raisers -- a reputation exacerbated over Thanksgiving weekend in 2001, when a drug- and alcohol-using crowd that gathered to watch the competition experienced a fatal shooting, several stabbings and accidents involving more than 150 injuries. Since then, the sand association has started a charm campaign. Members pick up trash and put up billboards emphasizing safety on nearby highways. They are working out rules for uphill drag-races to minimize the danger to crowds. The ASA says in one safety flier to members that "this is important" in part because, after one raucous incident, "the Sierra Club demanded the dunes be closed because a reasonable amount of safety could not be maintained. A nonenvironmental issue, to be sure, but ammunition they could use just the same." The Interior Department, which regulates the dunes, is required by law to keep them open for a variety of recreational uses. Mr. Patterson thinks the department should promote greater use of the dunes by hikers and photographers to offset the domination of off- roaders. As it stands, dune-buggy drivers, seeing the rare person walking in the dunes during busy weekends, sometimes stop to ask whether their vehicles have broken down. Do they need any help? "This is not just about Peirson's milk-vetch," says Mr. Patterson. "This is about a really cool place." His center has notified the Interior Department that it is preparing a new lawsuit that argues 16 other dune species are also endangered, including three exotic beetles, two rare ants and four weevils.

Title: Angry threats targeting federal employees aren't limited to the gun-toting law enforcers
Text: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal  "You could see it coming," he says of the attack, which has been linked to the antigovernment militia movement. "There's too much hate directed at federal workers."  Unlike the federal agents whose 1993 attack on Waco's Branch Davidian compound led to threats of retaliation from the militias, Mr. Hamilton is no gun-toting law enforcer. A bespectacled graduate of Mississippi State University, where he received his bachelor's degree in biology and his master's in fishery management, Mr. Hamilton appears, to the casual observer, embattled mainly by thinning hair (he turns 40 next month).  But when Mr. Hamilton has ventured out lately to meet with community groups, he always has been accompanied by at least one armed plainclothes law-enforcement official. Fish and Wildlife's once-proudly displayed emblem is gone from his fleet of trucks, cars and vans. Nobody in the office (located above a bank in a nondescript glass-sheathed building) wears the service's familiar khaki uniform unless on a wildlife refuge, and most keep their private phone numbers unlisted. "We decided it's in the interest of safety" not to flaunt any government affiliation, Mr. Hamilton explains.  There is a shared sense among other federal workers, too, that displaying a federal government insignia can invite danger. While the offices of the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms are thought to be possible targets of accused Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh, who once visited the Waco site, plenty of other government workers have been the targets of less devastating displays of anger.  For example, the Bureau of Land Management last month sent field offices a memo noting recent threats against federal officials in Nevada and Idaho, and urged officials to travel in pairs and "avoid areas with a known potential for conflict." Also in Idaho recently, there was a bitter clash between local ranchers and federal wildlife officials over a government plan to re-introduce the Canadian Wolf on federal lands. And within the past two years, bombs went off at BLM and U.S. Forest Service offices in Reno and Carson City, respectively, actions many believe were committed by antigovernment extremists.  Mr. Hamilton, who is leaving Texas for a promotion elsewhere in the agency, dates his wariness to the 1980s, when the wave of public anger began to build against federal bureaucrats. But for Mr. Hamilton, that hostility reached its peak last fall as controversy swirled around a proposed federal plan to declare portions of central Texas critical habitat for a songbird called the golden-cheeked warbler, an action that ranchers and developers feared would bring their activities to a halt.  At a public meeting on the plan in tiny Llano, Texas, 1,500 angry citizens turned out to denounce not just the plan, but, to his surprise, Mr. Hamilton himself. When he stepped up to the microphone, he was greeted with boos and curses. "Get a real job," he recalls one participant shouting. "Warblers don't taste good, we don't need 'em," shouted another.  At a separate meeting of the Kerr County Republican party, Marshall Kuykendall, a land broker and president of a property-rights group called Take Back Texas, called Mr. Hamilton "a thief." Today, Mr. Kuykendall says he didn't mean anything personal by it, but "I don't like the Fish and Wildlife Service. They're overbudgeted and overgunned and overbadged."  Even though the policy at issue was being shaped by top Interior Department officials in Washington, Mr. Hamilton, a "GS-15" midlevel career civil servant, became the target of public criticism by local talk-radio hosts and elected officials like Rep. Lamar Smith (R., Texas), a staunch property-rights proponent. Mr. Hamilton's attempts to explain that the critical-habitat plan was less momentous than widely believed only angered opponents further. "To meet with him personally is to meet with someone who knows how to speak in honey-coated words," recalls Rep. Smith. "He tried to dampen the spirits of the opposition."  Mr. Hamilton's notoriety eventually brought death threats. "You come on my land, I'm gonna take you out," said one anonymous caller. Another phoned a member of Mr. Hamilton's staff, spun a gun barrel into the receiver, and said, "This is for you." A friendly congressional aide, after meeting with opponents to the plan, called Mr. Hamilton to warn him that there had been inquiries about where Mr. Hamilton lived and where his children went to school. "I was warned that I should be careful," he said. "It was scary."  For the moment, the critical-habitat plan is on hold. But on a drive last Friday through the rolling Texas hill country, whose green limestone rises are alternately darkened and brightened by the juniper trees and cedars where golden-cheeked warblers nest, Mr. Hamilton said the bitter aftertaste was far from gone. His decision to leave Texas comes partly from wanting to put the ordeal behind him.  Passion stirred in the warbler fight, of course, in no way compares to whatever fevered emotions were behind the Oklahoma City bombing, Mr. Hamilton agrees. He never saw any evidence that the threats against him came from militias or other organized far-right groups. And one of his antagonists, Dan Byfield of the Farm Credit Bank of Texas, who is a vociferous opponent of the warbler proposal, condemns the bombing as "the act of some lunatics." If efforts to "protect and defend the constitutional rights of individuals" lead to "anger and all towards the government," says Mr. Byfield, that is because it's the government that makes the laws. "If you've got to direct it somewhere, I guess that's the direction it can go."  Environmental laws, increasingly, have stoked anger. David Helvarg, author of "The War Against the Greens," which documents recent violent attacks on environmentalists, estimates there have been "dozens" of attacks on federal environmental officials in recent months. Some extremist groups now rank environmental issues next to abortion and gun control.  At a recent congressional hearing on the Endangered Species Act in Boerne, Texas, a group calling itself the Sons of Liberty distributed fliers denouncing Congress for exercising "unlimited, tyrannical powers" over endangered-species and other matters and demanded that it "restore Constitutional Government, or be prepared to stand trial for Treason, Felony, Breach of the Peace, and other High Crimes and Misdemeanors."  For Mr. Hamilton, clad last Friday not in khaki and jackboots but in green Topsiders and a print shirt decorated with bright facsimiles of fishing lures, such attitudes are merely bewildering. "We went to school because we love the outdoors," he says of his fellow bureaucrats. "It seemed at that time that everybody liked Fish and Wildlife. Everybody liked the outdoors."  AUSTIN, Texas -- When Sam Hamilton joined the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service fresh out of grad school in 1978, he never imagined he would become the target of death threats.  Mr. Hamilton, who ended his tour as Texas state administrator for the Fish and Wildlife Service on Friday, is one of many federal employees who experienced the boiling anger of the conservative fringe well before the April 19 bombing of an Oklahoma City federal building.

Title: Dole revises bill to order payment for loss of value
Text: WASHINGTON -- Senate Majority Leader Robert Dole (R., Kan.) has revised his "takings" bill to require federal compensation to landowners whose property loses value because of regulation.    Mr. Dole's decision to push a measure especially popular with conservatives is sure to be seen as another move to win support with his party's right wing in his quest for the 1996 Republican presidential nomination. In recent weeks, Mr. Dole also has declared his opposition to affirmative-action programs and promised to try to reverse a ban on assault weapons passed last year by Congress.    The new takings bill, set to be unveiled at a news conference today, signals that the Senate is moving to the right on the controversial property-rights issue even as it is moderating its stance on a separate regulatory-overhaul measure, the House-passed moratorium on new regulations. That bill's main Senate sponsor, Sen. Don Nickles (R., Okla.), vowed earlier this week to drop the moratorium, which was to last through 1995, and substitute a less sweeping measure that would delay all new regulations for 45 days while Congress considers whether to overrule them.    Sen. Dole's previous takings bill required merely that the federal government evaluate a proposed regulation's effect on property values before the rule is issued. But the new Senate takings bill would require the federal government to compensate any property owner whose land, or a portion thereof, is reduced in value by more than 33% as a result of federal action.    The new measure was crafted following the House's unexpectedly strong vote (277-148) earlier this month for a takings bill that requires compensation to property owners. The Senate plan consolidates elements of Sen. Dole's earlier bill with more aggressive bills proposed by several other Senate Republicans, including Sen. Phil Gramm (R., Texas), Mr. Dole's more conservative rival for the Republican presidential nomination in 1996.    The Senate bill's 33% threshold is less generous to property owners than the House's 20% threshold -- a concession to those who worry that the bill will prove costly to the federal Treasury.    Overall, however, the Senate bill may prove more expensive than its House counterpart.    Unlike the House measure, whose scope is limited to regulations governing wetlands, endangered species, and water use on public lands, the Senate proposal would apply to all regulations. The Senate bill's supporters maintain, however, that because the Senate measure, unlike the House plan, requires federal agencies to tally proposed regulations' likely costs to property owners before the regulations are issued, agencies will learn to avoid issuing regulations that would trigger federal outlays. Environmentalists worry that if regulation is inhibited in this way, environmental protections will be weakened.    Indeed, Congress's mere consideration of this and other regulatory-overhaul measures may already be inhibiting enforcement of environmental laws. Earlier this month, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service sent enforcement officials a memo stating, "Effective immediately, no criminal actions under the [Endangered Species Act] may be taken without prior notification to the Director or Deputy Director." The Humane Society of the U.S., which yesterday released this memo to the press, said the directive will bring endangered-species-related enforcement activities "to a virtual halt."    But a Fish and Wildlife spokeswoman said the new procedure was a "heads-up" rather than a new "approval process," and was generated in response to a recent incident where Fish and Wildlife Service officials got into a heated argument with an Idaho county sheriff while they were investigating a wolf's death on a rancher's property. In that incident, the spokeswoman said, the Fish and Wildlife director, Molly Beattie, had been unaware that the investigation was taking place.    Separately, a third regulatory initiative, also sponsored by Sen. Dole, drew unexpected criticism yesterday from a strong proponent of regulatory overhaul.    In written testimony before the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, John Graham, director of Harvard's Center for Risk Analysis (which is partially funded by industry) said Sen. Dole's bill requiring extensive cost-benefit analysis before many new regulations are issued "may be too inflexible and legalistic in some respects." Elements of Sen. Dole's bill will be incorporated into a cost-benefit measure, sponsored by Sen. William Roth (R., Del.), that the Senate Government Affairs Committee will take up today. The House passed a similar bill earlier this month.    In response to Mr. Graham's criticism, an aide to Sen. Dole said, "It may be legalistic to him, but the whole point is unless you have the means to enforce agencies' performing cost-benefit analysis, it's a paper tiger."  Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: REVIEW & OUTLOOK (Editorial): The Emotional Species Act
Text: Let us introduce you to the Bruneau Hot Springs snail, which earlier this year became the 615th species to be listed by the federal government as worthy of lifetime tenure under the Endangered Species Act. An average Bruneau snail is the size of a pencil point. It can be distinguished from other snails only because of the relative largeness of its sexual organ. Nonetheless, this tiny if well-endowed flyspeck threatens to severely limit agriculture along Idaho's Snake River. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has moved to cut off 59 farms and ranches from their water rights to avoid lowering the water level of the hot springs where the snails are found. The farms involved represent half of the economic activity in the Bruneau area, which logging families in the Northwest learned carries little weight in arguments with higher life forms, such as owls or snails. Local farmers contend that the springs are being replenished now that seven years of drought have ended. They have filed suit asking that the snail be de-listed. "This is an emotional listing, not a scientific one," says Pat Takasugi, an area farmer. He says it is ludicrous to worry about a snail that is so prolific that it can be found in concentrations of more than 6,000 snails per square foot. There's no evidence any other species is directly or indirectly dependent upon it. It sure would be great if our laws against, say, murder and assault were enforced with the same religious zeal as the Endangered Species Act. The act was passed 20 years ago to outlaw the wanton killing off of a species. However, court interpretations have held that it takes priority over other laws and that species must be protected in all cases, regardless of cost. Even partial exemptions from the Act -- as in the case of the Northern Spotted Owl -- can be obtained only after arduous appeals. Enforcement of the Act is being effectively steered by the BANANA movement: Build Absolutely Nothing Anywhere Near Anything. The Bruneau farmers are defending themselves against this mystical law with pluck and humor. They held a snail race to raise money for their lawsuit, admitting that no one would be able to see the contestants. In August, they offered a $500 reward for evidence the snails exist outside Bruneau. So far, none's been found, though 125 other colonies have been located in the area, adding dramatically to the three known to the Fish and Wildlife Service. The Bruneau snail may represent a new extreme in concern for endangered species, but not by much. The protections accorded the kangaroo rat effectively make it the largest landowner in Riverside County, Calif. Elsewhere in California, the costs of saving the Sacramento Delta smelt could run in the billions. Scientists think there may be 100 million species in the world, with only 1% of them yet having a name. World-wide, we may be losing 50,000 a year. Nearly 4,000 species in the U.S. are candidates for future protection. That number would grow if Congress completes approval of the Clinton Administration's proposed National Biological Survey. Massachusetts Democrat Rep. Gerry Studds, its chief congressional sponsor, says the survey would have "a simple, yet awesome mission -- catalog everything that walks, crawls, swims or flies around this country." Dr. Thomas Lovejoy, the Interior Department's scientific adviser, says the survey's findings would "determine development for the whole country and regulate it all, because that is our obligation as set forth in the Endangered Species Act." Congressional opponents fear the survey is a Trojan Horse for the effective taking of private property without compensation. But Democratic Rep. Billy Tauzin of Louisiana hasn't been permitted a vote on his amendment to require that the government compensate landowners if the survey causes a drop in their land's value. He did win approval of an amendment forbidding the use of environmental "volunteers" to conduct the survey. The House nonetheless voted 253 to 174 to approve $163 million for the survey. The Biological Survey bill now goes to the Senate, where opposition is growing and a filibuster is possible. Some of the Endangered Species Act's longtime Senate supporters say the absurd way it is enforced, exemplified by the Bruneau Hot Springs snail, means that Congress has to find a way to protect private property rights. Oregon Senator Mark Hatfield, one of the act's architects, says "it is being applied far beyond the scope of what any of us who helped adopt it intended." Those words of federal bloat could serve as an epitaph for much of what Washington does in our time -- from snails to health care. (See related letter: "Letters to the Editor: If the Snails Suffer, So Do the Farmers" -- WSJ Nov. 23, 1993) 931102-0184 YY93 MM11

Title: Study Says Removal Of Washington Dams Is Best Hope for Fish
Text: WASHINGTON -- Removing four power-producing dams on the lower Snake River in eastern Washington state likely offers the best hope of ensuring the survival of endangered fish species, according to a government study released Friday. Nevertheless, the draft environmental impact statement, or EIS, doesn't rule out acceptable alternatives to dam removal, which would eliminate 3,033 megawatts of peaking power capacity from the Bonneville Power Administration's electricity-generation portfolio. The four dams represent 15% of the federal power agency's total generation, according to a spokesman. For the entire region, breaching the dams would represent eliminating 5% of power production capacity, according to the draft EIS. Replacing the power would cost between $251 million and $291 million annually, the draft environmental assessment found. This would amount to an increase for the average residential customer's electricity bill of between $1.20 to $6.50 per month, depending upon how and what replacement generation facilities are built, the study said. Dam removal is among four options examined by the draft EIS. The other options studied were maintaining the status quo, increasing the transport of migrating fish by barge, and breaching the dams while leaving the dormant power housings in place to increase water flows. Overall, the draft EIS indicates that removing the dams offers the best option for restoring endangered runs of salmon and steelhead trout listed under the Endangered Species Act. While dam passage efforts, such as barging migrating fish around dams, has helped offset extinction, they won't be enough to allow the fish stocks to recover, the study suggests. Credit: Dow Jones Newswires

Title: U.S. News: Court to Hear Navy Sonar Case
Text: WASHINGTON -- The U.S. Supreme Court agreed to hear the Navy's request to overturn restrictions on its ability to train with sonar off the California coast because of concerns about harm to whales and dolphins. The Ninth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, based in San Francisco, in March upheld most of a court ruling that bans high-powered sonar near the California coast and puts other limits on Navy training exercises. Several environmental groups sued the Navy to block its sonar use in the Pacific Ocean near southern California. The area is home to nine threatened or endangered species of whales, dolphins, sea lions and seals. The high court is scheduled to hear the Navy's appeal of the case, Winter v. Natural Resources Defense Council Inc., this fall. Also, the high court also rejected an appeal from environmental groups that have challenged the government's ability to waive environmental review of the impact of a fence along the U.S.-Mexican border. Under a 2005 federal law, the Homeland Security Department received authority to waive the Endangered Species Act and federally required reviews of the potential environmental impact of the border fence's construction. Environmental groups sued after the Army Corps of Engineers began building in the San Pedro Riparian National Conservation Area last September. A U.S. district court initially granted a temporary restraining order that stopped the construction. But the government cited the 2005 law, prompting the federal courts to drop the restraining order. The case is Defenders of Wildlife v. Chertoff.

Title: Bush Taps Roberts for Supreme Court; Conservative Nominee, 50, Is Viewed as Pro-Business; Doubts From Some Democrats
Text: WASHINGTON -- President Bush nominated federal appeals-court judge John G. Roberts Jr. to the Supreme Court, choosing a candidate with a long-enough history in conservative legal circles to delight Republicans and an affable demeanor and short paper trail that could make him hard for liberals to attack. At age 50, Judge Roberts was one of the youngest people on the president's short list of candidates, an important attribute for officials hoping for a justice who will use his lifetime appointment to reshape American law for a generation to come. The White House rushed to make an announcement this week to begin the lengthy Senate confirmation process in time for Judge Roberts to join the high court for its next term in October. Mr. Bush's business backers were cheered by the appointment of Judge Roberts, who worked as a business lawyer for the white-shoe Washington law firm of Hogan & Hartson LLP before becoming a judge two years ago. In that practice, among other things, he defended Toyota Motor Corp. in a workers-disability case. Judge Roberts's name also drew enthusiasm from social conservatives who are hoping that he will side with them more frequently than did Justice Sandra Day O'Connor, a Ronald Reagan appointee who disappointed the right with rulings favoring abortion rights and opposing displays on government property of the religious symbols like the Ten Commandments. Justice O'Connor's retirement, announced July 1, created the opening Judge Roberts hopes to fill. It is social issues such as abortion that are expected to generate the most controversy over the nomination in the Senate, where solid Democratic opposition could delay, or even prevent, a vote on the candidate if the party holds together. On abortion, his views are ambiguous. As a judge, Mr. Roberts has never written a legal opinion on the issue, but as an official in the first Bush administration, he wrote a legal brief stating, "We continue to believe that Roe was wrongly decided and should be overruled." In 2003, however, during his Senate confirmation hearing to his current post, he said Roe v. Wade, the controversial 1973 ruling that legalized abortion across the nation, "is the settled law of the land. . . . There's nothing in my personal views that would prevent me from fully and faithfully applying that precedent," as is required of lower-court judges. That formulation, however, seems to leave open the possibility that he could vote to overturn Roe as a high-court justice. Mr. Bush tapped a white male to replace one of the high court's two women -- and its first female justice -- after a public plea from his wife to name a woman, and after officials publicly reviewed a number of women and at least one Hispanic for the post. President Bush noted in a nationally televised speech last night that Judge Roberts received bipartisan support in his 2003 nomination to the appeals court, and was easily approved by the Senate. Speaking with Judge Roberts at his side, Mr. Bush made clear in his brief remarks that he felt he had found a judge in the mold of Justices Antonin Scalia and Clarence Thomas, the two most conservative members of the high court. The president hailed his nominee as somebody who will "faithfully apply the Constitution and equal justice before the law" and who will "strictly interpret the laws, not legislate from the bench." Some key Democrats quickly signaled they could be ready to give Judge Roberts a hard time by dragging out the confirmation process, if not outright defeating the nomination. Vermont's Sen. Patrick Leahy, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Judiciary Committee, said after the announcement that "it's going to take a fair amount of time" to hold hearings. New York Democratic Sen. Charles Schumer, also on the committee, said he would push Judge Roberts to answer detailed questions about his views on issues, and that, lacking concrete answers, he might try to block the nomination. White House officials said last night that President Bush has been preparing for such an announcement practically from the day he took office in 2001. After the O'Connor retirement, the White House accelerated its review. When Mr. Bush went to Europe the following week for a summit of world leaders, he took with him a notebook with information on 11 candidates, then later met with five. Judge Roberts was teaching a class in London last week when he was summoned to the White House. He attended an hour-long meeting in the White House residence last Friday and was called by the president yesterday at 12:35 p.m., shortly before Mr. Bush had lunch with visiting Australian Prime Minister John Howard. President Bush and Judge Roberts are scheduled to meet again at the White House this morning for breakfast. Born in Buffalo, N.Y., Judge Roberts attended both college and law school at Harvard University, and when not in government service grew wealthy through his private practice. He is intimately familiar with the Supreme Court, having served as a law clerk to Justice William H. Rehnquist prior to his elevation as chief justice, and having appeared before the court more than 30 times as a litigator. In brief remarks on television last night, Judge Roberts said, "I always got a lump in my throat whenever I walked up those marble steps to argue a case before the court, and I don't think it was just from the nerves." Affable, thoughtful and solidly Republican, Judge Roberts worked for the first president Bush under then-solicitor-general Kenneth Starr, who later gained fame as the independent counsel investigating President Clinton. Judge Roberts first was nominated to the U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia by President George H.W. Bush, but the nomination evaporated when the Democratic- controlled Senate stalled on bringing it to a vote as the 1992 presidential election neared. Judge Roberts contributed $1,000 to George W. Bush's recount legal fight in the 2000 presidential election, and Mr. Bush later made good on his father's offer to put Mr. Roberts on the bench. He was confirmed for the D.C. Circuit two years ago. His actions on the bench are sure to get close scrutiny in the Senate. Shortly after joining the D.C. Circuit, for instance, Judge Roberts dissented from a ruling that effectively upheld a regulation under the Endangered Species Act. Judge Roberts urged the full circuit court to rehear the case, reasoning that it had not properly followed two Supreme Court opinions that rolled back federal power over states. He also has rejected broad views of the Fourth Amendment, which bars unreasonable searches and seizures. Last year, he wrote for a unanimous three-judge panel that it was constitutional for police to arrest, handcuff and briefly jail a 12-year-old girl "for eating a single French fry" in a Washington subway station. "No one is very happy about the events," he wrote, but rejected claims that the action was unconstitutional. He likewise joined a unanimous panel that allowed prosecution based on evidence taken from a stopped car's trunk, even though the court found a police officer had no probable cause to search the trunk. Last week, Judge Roberts helped hand the Bush administration a signal victory as part of a unanimous three-judge panel ruling that so-called enemy combatants being held at Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, have no rights under the Geneva Conventions and can be prosecuted before military commissions that lack due-process protections afforded by U.S. courts martial. Business leaders who recently began reviewing the records of the White House finalist list placed Judge Roberts at the top of their candidate lists. After leaving the first Bush administration in 1993, Judge Roberts practiced telecommunications, energy and other business law in private practice. "He has recent experience in business cases. He writes very careful, narrowly crafted opinions. And he's a very smart person who is not committed to his ideology.
