You are in a room with him and he exudes good judgment," said Robert Gasaway, an attorney with Kirkland & Ellis who has helped business groups vet the nominee list. With only two years on the bench, Judge Roberts has a far shorter record than many of the other candidates who came under consideration. That gives the White House a strategic advantage over Democrats bound to be distrustful of a Bush nominee, but who lack enough evidence of his views to build a public case that he is out of the mainstream. Similar strategies were pursued for three of the last four successful Republican appointees to the court, notes John Yoo, a Berkeley law professor and former official in the Bush Justice Department. Antonin Scalia, David H. Souter and Clarence Thomas all had served no more than four years on a federal appeals court, he says. "For all of them, concerns about track records were important," he said. Nan Aron, head of Alliance for Justice, a civil-rights organization, said Judge Roberts's "limited record raises a whole host of concerns." During his two years on the District of Columbia Circuit Court, Ms. Aron said, Judge Roberts joined rulings weakening federal environmental protections that could signal an inclination to undermine "a wide swath of civil rights, public safety and workplace protections." With no paper trail, Ms. Aron said, opponents of Judge Roberts will have to rely on Democratic senators to "conduct thorough hearings that require him to be forthcoming." Wade Henderson, executive director of the Leadership Conference on Civil Rights, also called on Senate allies to aggressively review Judge Roberts's philosophy and ideology. "The public clearly opposes blatantly extreme judicial nominees, perhaps that is why the president has chosen a candidate whose cover story avoids that label," he said. In the past, conservatives have complained about some justices whom they see as having been nominated because they lacked a deep paper trail, particularly Justice Souter. And Judge Roberts's record is unclear on some key issues besides abortion. "I don't know much about John Roberts," said Richard Land, director of the conservative evangelical Southern Baptist Convention. "But I know a lot about President Bush. If President Bush is nominating him, he gets a huge benefit of the doubt from me." Mr. Bush already has been hard at work for weeks cultivating support for his nominee both on Capitol Hill and among voters. Notably, he and his staff sought input from dozens of senators. Sen. Orrin Hatch, a Utah Republican and the influential former chairman of the Judiciary Committee, said yesterday it was "the most consultative process I've ever seen." Less than two hours after the announcement yesterday, two White House aligned conservative groups had posted a pro-Roberts Web commercial and launched a new Web site promoting his confirmation -- while the liberal activist group MoveOn.org swiftly branded him a "Right Wing Corporate Lawyer." Judge Roberts's nomination came after a frenzied final day of speculation about whom Mr. Bush would nominate -- some of which was encouraged by the White House to deflect attention from the real nominee. In the end, Mr. Bush urged senators to conduct "a dignified confirmation process that is conducted with fairness and civility." Judge Roberts will spend the next two weeks making "courtesy calls" on lawmakers. It is not likely that confirmation hearings will begin before late August or early September, after the congressional summer recess. --- John D. McKinnon, Brody Mullins, Christopher Cooper and Zachary Goldfarb contributed to this article. ---                             A Judge's Rise   President Bush s nominee to succeed Justice Sandra Day O'Connor goes tothe 18-member Senate Judiciary Committee, and would face some hot-buttonissues when the court returns in October.   Big cases likely for the 2005-2006 Supreme Court term:   -- Parental notification for abortion  -- Physician-assisted suicide  -- Due-process rights for "enemy combatants"  -- Federal aid to universities banning military recruiters   Prominent members of Senate Judiciary Committee:   -- Chairman Arlen Specter (R., Pa.): Moderate Republican has infuriatedsocial conservatives but strongly backed Clarence Thomas   -- Sam Brownback (R., Kan.): A darling of social conservatives andpotential presidential candidate in 2008   -- Edward Kennedy (D., Mass.): Led the successful attack on Reagan nomineewith "Robert Bork's America" speech   -- Lindsey Graham (R., S.C.): Member of the "Gang of 14" centrists whohold balance of power in a heated battle   -- Patrick Leahy (D., Vt.): Senior panel Democrat who works closely withMr. Specter but vigorously defends the minority's right to block candidates

Title: City News: Greater New York Watch
Text: NEW JERSEY Gov. Christie Should Resign, Voters Say A survey of New Jersey voters found that the majority think Gov. Chris Christie should step down now that he has declared he is running for president. The Monmouth University Polling Institute survey released Thursday also found that Mr. Christie's popularity had sunk to a five-year low among registered voters, with 34% approving of the Republican's work as governor and 60% disapproving. In New Jersey, Mr. Christie's popularity surged after his handling of superstorm Sandy in 2012 earned him high marks, with Monmouth University polling showing a high of 70% approval in February 2013. Mr. Christie's numbers starting falling in the wake of the George Washington Bridge scandal early last year and have yet to plateau. His frequent out-of-state travels on behalf of the Republican Party in 2014 and earlier this year as he contemplated a run for president appear to have also hurt his favorability. Monmouth University's survey of 453 registered voters found that 75% believed Mr. Christie is more concerned about his political future than governing the New Jersey. Sixty-eight percent of the voters surveyed thought Mr. Christie wouldn't make a good president, and 54% of registered voters thought he should resign as governor now. A spokesman for Mr. Christie declined to comment Thursday. The Monmouth poll had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.6 percentage points. -- Heather Haddon --- NEW JERSEY Former First Gentleman John Whitman Dies John Whitman, the husband of former Republican Gov. Christine Todd Whitman and New Jersey's first-ever first gentleman, died Thursday. He was 71. He died at Morristown Medical Center after suffering a catastrophic brain injury in mid-June, said Heather Grizzle, a spokeswoman for Ms. Todd Whitman. John Whitman was an investment banker who served as a managing partner at Princeton-based Sycamore Ventures. He served as New Jersey's first gentleman from 1994 to 2001. "He was a wonderful husband, father, and grandfather, and we are heartbroken to lose his presence in our lives," Ms. Todd Whitman said in a statement. -- Associated Press --- NEW YORK Fast-Food Minimum Wage Under Review A state board studying whether to increase the minimum wage for fast-food workers is set to issue its recommendation this month. A spokesman for the state Department of Labor said Thursday the Wage Board plans to meet on July 13 to continue its deliberations. Gov. Andrew Cuomo convened the board to study whether to raise the wage, now $8.75 an hour, for workers in the fast-food industry. Members of the board said last week that they think the wage should be raised but would continue their talks before writing a formal recommendation. It will be up to Mr. Cuomo's labor commissioner to accept, reject or modify the recommendation. Some business groups have said they think an increase is a foregone conclusion. -- Associated Press --- NEW YORK City to Review Trump Contracts City officials are reviewing the city's contracts with Donald Trump after statements the GOP presidential hopeful made about Mexican immigrants. A spokeswoman for Mayor Bill de Blasio said Wednesday that the review is ongoing. It follows controversial statements Mr. Trump made at his presidential kickoff event last week. Mr. de Blasio's spokeswoman didn't provide any further details about the review. The Trump Organization operates several city concessions, including a golf course, two ice skating rinks and a carousel. The Trump Golf Links at Ferry Point Park opened in April in the Bronx and the Trump Organization has a 20-year concession agreement to operate the facility. On Thursday, City Councilman Mark Levine, chairman of the council's parks committee, said the city should exercise "terminate-at-will clauses" that are written into the contracts for Trump's concessions. "All of Mr. Trump's parks concessions include terminate-at-will clauses," he said in a statement. "The Parks Department should exercise this option to sever all ties with Mr. Trump immediately." Ron Lieberman, Trump's executive vice president, said Thursday that he was surprised by Mr. de Blasio's call for a review and believes the city has no legal ground to terminate them. He said Mr. Trump has had a "great public-private partnership" with the city after revitalizing the concessions. "There's no right to terminate these contracts because of something that was said," Mr. Lieberman said. "These contracts are binding." -- Associated Press --- NEW JERSEY Prosecutors Seek Imported Tiger Pelt Federal prosecutors are seeking to seize a taxidermic tiger that was shipped to New Jersey as part of a household move from France. Prosecutors say the fully mounted animal skin was imported into the U.S. in violation of the Endangered Species Act. It was seized by wildlife inspectors at Port Newark in December. Authorities say the shipment included a certificate that permitted its transport only within the European Union. The owner challenged the seizure, which prompted prosecutors to seek its forfeiture. Authorities say the tiger is a captive-bred female that was born in 2000. -- Associated Press --- CONNECTICUT State Police Seize Fireworks in Danbury Connecticut state police say illegal fireworks worth about $250,000 have been seized from a home and storage barn in Danbury. State police said Thursday that drugs were also found during the search and they expect several people will be arrested on felony charges. The investigation began after a complaint was made about the illegal use and sale of fireworks. -- Associated Press

Title: Some waste cleanups exempted by Senate from its reform bill
Text: WASHINGTON -- The Senate agreed to exempt from the regulatory-reform bill hazardous-waste cleanups conducted under the Superfund law.    Environmentalists had voiced strong concerns about disruptions to Superfund cleanups that might occur as a result of the bill, which requires elaborate cost-benefit analysis before a federal agency issues a regulation.    In the end, proponents of the bill were willing to drop earlier language applying the bill's provision to Superfund cleanups, leaving the matter to be decided by House and Senate members currently drafting a rewrite of the Superfund law. The language was struck from the bill without a recorded Senate vote.    But the Senate narrowly rejected a separate attempt by Sen. Frank Lautenberg (D., N.J.) to strip from the bill language likely to reduce the number of chemicals on the Environmental Protection Agency's toxic release inventory. The program requires large manufacturers to release data about the quantity of potentially hazardous chemicals they release into the air and water.    Separately, Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt said that he would be willing to consider granting estate-tax credits in exchange for conservation agreements by private property holders under the Endangered Species Act.    Mr. Babbitt was apparently responding to pressure from property-rights advocates who favor another regulatory reform bill, now awaiting action in the Senate Judiciary Committee. That measure would require federal compensation to individuals and businesses whose property loses value due to regulations. Currently the Endangered Species Act doesn't grant tax breaks of any kind in exchange for species protection, although an Internal Revenue Service rule does allow income-tax deductions for certain land easements.

Title: EPA Proposals Worry Industry And Agencies
Text: Northwest timber officials fear that clean-water rules recently proposed by the Environmental Protection Agency could prove too tough to meet. They may not have anything to worry about, though -- state environmental officials are complaining that the laws may be too tough to enforce. The rules, proposed by the EPA in August, would have states establish cleanup plans, and prioritize them, for those bodies of water within their borders that they've identified as too polluted for fishing and swimming. And states would be beholden to reduce contaminants from a broader range of sources than ever before. These would include logging activities -- the felling of trees, the building of roads -- that discharge sediments into nearby streams, rivers or lakes and might imperil the habitats of fish and other animals. The rules, timber-industry leaders say, place so many restrictions on where and how trees could be harvested that it's all but certain that jobs would be lost. "It would have a drastic, negative effect," says Dale Riddle, president of Seneca Sawmills in Eugene, Ore. "It's basically Big Brother appropriating our land and telling us when it's OK to harvest it." At the same time, the state agencies that would be in charge of implementing the rules say they don't have the manpower or money to enforce them. "At a time when we're struggling to find resources to carry out the existing rules, it's going to be hard to be able to say we're going to be able to do this," says Dave Peeler, watershed management supervisor for Washington's Department of Ecology. For more than 20 years, the focus of the Clean Water Act has been on stemming contaminants coming from specific, easily identifiable sources such as factory discharge pipes or sewage plants. Now the Clinton administration has decided it's time to expand the focus of the act. "Having largely succeeded with one part of the problem, we now realize we need to deal with the rest of it," says Tim Hamlin, the EPA's regional water quality unit manager in Seattle. If the rules are adopted, "the long-term effect could be to place many, many acres off-limits to forestry," says Jim Geisinger, president of the Northwest Forestry Association, a Portland-based trade group with 65 members. State water-quality rules governing the timber business are already strict enough, Mr. Geisinger adds. "To have the feds step in now and say they're going to get their hunk of flesh is pretty frightening," he says. In addition, timber officials say, the industry is reeling from federally imposed limits on harvests. In Washington and Oregon, the number of board feet cut has decreased 52% over the past 10 years, to 7,501,807 from 15,660,427, according to Timber Data Co. in Eugene, and the number of timber jobs in the two states has dropped by some 16% to around 119,000 since 1988. State officials in Washington and Oregon say they support the proposed rules in concept, but worry that without additional resources, enforcing them might be close to impossible. Mr. Peeler, with Washington's DOE, says the department is having "a hard enough time" contending with existing clean-water decrees. Finding the money to do the job in Oregon "would be a stretch in that all the resources we have are allocated to current programs," says Dick Pedersen, manager of the standards and assessments section with the Oregon Department of Environmental Quality. For example, spending cuts enacted by the Legislature in 1994 slashed about 35 positions in Washington's DOE. Of those, four have since been filled. Oregon's DEQ can hire only 52 full-time staffers to look into water permits, down from 60 five years ago, and four fewer than the department had budgeted for. There simply wasn't enough revenue to pay for all the positions. And the EPA seems to be in a rush, state officials say. The federal agency set Oct. 22 as the end of the public-comment period, and expects the new rules to be in place by the end of the year. "There's just no way that can happen," Mr. Peeler says. "It's a very complicated set of rules. The states are very concerned the EPA put us in a situation where we're bound to fail." Mr. Hamlin of the EPA says the timber industry's dire predictions about the rules are unfounded. "That environmental regulations increase costs is a legitimate concern," he says. "But to say this is going to destroy the industry is unconvincing. Industries that fall under environmental regulations have called wolf a few too many times for this claim to be convincing on its face." As for state agencies' concerns, Mr. Hamlin says that finding funds to enforce the rules is Congress and state legislators' problem. But there are more concerns among some state officials. In Washington, officials fear that the EPA proposal is at odds with the forest-and-fish plan the state and the timber industry signed off on earlier this year. The plan, which is designed to help Washington comply with the Endangered Species Act, allows continued logging on private land in return for a promise from the timber industry that it will take certain steps to protect aquatic species on 60,000 miles of forested stream habitat. As part of the agreement, the industry and state gave themselves 10 years to establish something called total maximum daily loads -- plans to limit the amount of contaminants a given body of water can take -- and to determine what needs to be done to bring the quality of polluted bodies of water up to standards. The EPA's proposed regulations strongly recommend that states come up with maximum loads for high-priority bodies of water within five years. High-priority waters include those that are home to species listed as endangered or threatened -- about half the bodies of water currently considered impaired under the Clean Water Act in Washington and Oregon. "It's counter to the agreement," says Chris West, a spokesman for the Northwest Forestry Association. Department of Ecology officials agree. "It's important for the industry to get stability," says Dick Wallace, a policy analyst with DOE. "That assurance came from the fact that we wouldn't change the rules on them through TMDL. The assurance was they knew how and when changes would occur. But now it's changing." State officials and timber-industry leaders have asked the EPA to extend the deadline for comments. Agency officials say they're sympathetic to the requests, but haven't decided whether to give them more time. Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Cattle Prod: Catron County, N.M., Leads a Nasty Revolt Over Eco-Protection --- U.S. Agency's Plan to Trim Grazing Rights Sparks Laws -- and Lawlessness --- An End to Cowboy Welfare?
Text: CATRON COUNTY, N.M. -- Last spring, federal wildlife biologist Tim Tibbitts sat in his car after a meeting with local ranchers to outline how protections for endangered species could curtail cattle grazing on federal land here. One rancher popped open the passenger door. Mr. Tibbitts vividly recalls him saying: "If you ever come down to Catron County again, we'll blow your f--- head off." Federal law-enforcement agents are still looking for the rancher, whom, in the darkness, Mr. Tibbitts didn't recognize. But the rhetoric of rebellion just grows louder here in the mesa and mountain country along the Gila River near the Continental Divide. And it is echoing throughout rural America. At issue here are attempts by federal land managers to curb decades of what they say are environmentally damaging cattle grazing and other practices on the public lands that make up 80% of the county's 7,000 square miles. In revolt, the citizens of Catron County have paraded out a number of novel -- and detractors say ludicrous -- weapons: a slew of ordinances aimed at superseding federal law, and the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo of 1848. But death threats and guns have also played a role. The guiding principle of this revolt: The federal government stole the lands it owns in New Mexico more than a century ago; thus, people here need not heed modern-day federal laws regulating their use. So it is that in Catron County, local ordinances have been passed that make it illegal for the Forest Service to regulate grazing, even on Forest Service lands in the heart of the federally owned Gila and Aldo Leopold wilderness areas that straddle the county. The county sheriff has threatened to arrest the head of the local Forest Service office, prompting the U.S. attorney to threaten to arrest the sheriff. Other Catron County ordinances seek to prohibit the federal government from enforcing a host of laws aimed at sparing the Gila River area from what Sally Stefferud, a biologist for the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, describes as "imminent environmental collapse." For emphasis, Catron County passed a measure requiring heads of households to own firearms to "protect citizens' rights." By way of warning, the county passed a resolution predicting "much physical violence" if the government persists with its "arrogant" grazing reform plans. Many mainstream legal scholars say Catron County is on shaky legal ground with much of this. Nonetheless, the movement born here -- now known officially as the "county movement" -- has tapped into a deep well of discontent in the West and other rural regions, where mainstays of rural culture like ranching, mining and logging are colliding with demographic shifts and increased environmental protection. In the past two years, more than 100 counties in Western states have passed ordinances, mimicking Catron County's, that repudiate federal control of public lands. In Nevada, 16 of the state's 17 counties have passed county-movement ordinances. The movement has spread eastward in recent months, picking up counties in Michigan and North Carolina. Federal agencies early on dismissed Catron County's campaign, but they don't anymore. "Do not underestimate these people," Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt warned a crowd of environmentalists at the Sierra Club's annual awards dinner in San Francisco several months ago. "They are out to divest the public of its lands." The West has seen many antigovernment movements in the past -- and Catron County has often been in the vanguard. In the 1890s, people here torched tens of thousands of acres to protest the government's original plan to set aside national forests. But historians think the county movement runs deeper than similar revolts of the past. It overlaps with the so-called Wise Use movement, a well-funded campaign backed by big timber, mining, oil and ranching concerns to roll back environmental restrictions. Yet it may have broader appeal, because it casts its cause as the defense of individual liberty and property rights against an overweening federal government -- an increasingly popular theme, as recent elections have shown. "For many traditional Westerners, there is a feeling that this is the last stand for their way of life, and that generates a new level of desperation," says Patricia Nelson Limerick, a historian at the University of Colorado. That feeling is strong in Catron County. Bigger than Connecticut, the county has been cattle country since the arrival of the Spaniards in the 16th century. Cows still outnumber people about eight to one. But like the entire West, Catron County and environs have been changing. In Silver City, bistros and art galleries have moved into offices vacated by mining suppliers. Newly arrived "green" groups have filed numerous lawsuits and endangered-species actions, leading to federal protection for the Mexican spotted owl and the willow flycatcher, among other creatures. The change that has really got Catron County stirred up is in the Forest Service's approach to its grazing operations. The service has always allowed grazing on public lands, even in wilderness areas, at dirt-cheap fees. A few years ago, under pressure from environmentalists, federal range managers began to acknowledge that a century of heavy grazing had worn much public rangeland in the West to the nub, causing severe environmental damage, especially along streams and rivers. In late 1993, the Forest Service proposed cutting the herds on public land in Catron County by about 30%. To ranchers, these are all changes to fear and to fight. At a "Protect Your Rights Rally" in Silver City, between the barbecue and the cold beer, anger pours forth. "Our way of life is under attack by eco-Nazis," rails Zeno Kiehne, a fourth-generation Catron County rancher. Nearby, rancher Betty Hyatt nods approvingly as a state game commissioner gives a speech suggesting "ignoring" the Endangered Species Act. "All we want is for our children to be able to live and work out here the way we always have," Ms. Hyatt says. It is to that end that local leaders launched Catron County's crusade. James Catron, county attorney and a descendant of the pioneer ranching family that gave the county its name, says the movement in part reflects a nostalgia for a time "when someone causing pain to the community was simply shot." Some of the legal concepts underpinning Catron County's crusade similarly look back in time. One is the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, which ended the Mexican War in 1848 and granted territory from California to the Texas border to the U.S. Mr. Catron argues that the treaty gave the residents of what would become New Mexico the right to graze cattle, free from interference by any federal agency. Another of the county's arguments holds that ranchers have been grazing cattle so long on the federally owned lands here that they in effect own the grazing rights themselves. Another holds that the federal government simply doesn't have a right to own any land. "Nowhere in the Constitution does it say that the federal government can own real estate," Mr. Catron observes. Then there are the ordinances. The latest proposed one, which county commissioners have yet to vote on, would require environmentalists to register with the county. Under the measure, practicing environmentalism without a license could theoretically result in arrest. The county also has drawn up its own land-use plan, which it says can't be contravened by federal land managers. It calls for few restrictions on grazing and other such activities. The only time to date that a county-movement ordinance was actually tested directly, in a case in Idaho state court early last year, it was thrown out as unconstitutional. Nonetheless, the movement has rung up successes. Last month, a federal judge in Albuquerque revoked the Fish and Wildlife Service's designation of critical habitat for two tiny fish in the Gila River as a result of a Catron County lawsuit. The judge accepted the county's argument that the designation procedure dragged on past allowable federal deadlines; the agency, arguing that the designation process was slowed by county protests and legal challenges, is appealing. Even when the movement isn't on firm legal ground, it serves as a potent force for converting the free-floating anger in the region into action. Amid opposition, Interior Secretary Babbitt last month decided to abandon some of his more ambitious proposals for grazing reform. And last summer, the Fish and Wildlife Service shelved an effort to bring back native Gila trout to Mineral Creek. The job required the service to first poison non-native species like brown trout -- a sportsman's favorite but a predator that has contributed to the sharp decline in Gila trout. Before the biologists could get to Mineral Creek, protests and threats of armed intervention forced them to reconsider. The nastiest battles, though, have to do with cattle. The Diamond Bar is one of the biggest grazing allotments in the Forest Service system, 227 square miles, most of it in the rugged Gila and Aldo Leopold wilderness. The current permit holder is Kit Laney, a fourth-generation Catron County rancher who bought his 40-acre ranch and the giant Diamond Bar grazing permit associated with it in 1984 for more than $800,000. (Typically, a rancher buys a piece of private property surrounded by Forest Service land; the private property has a grazing allotment of publicly owned land associated with it, which the property owner has the first option to lease.) When he bought it, the permit allowed Mr. Laney to graze up to 1,188 head of cattle. However, much of the Diamond Bar, the Forest Service now says, has been badly overgrazed for decades and can no longer support more than 600 head; environmentalists say even that's too many. Indeed, throughout the Diamond Bar, as on much Western rangeland, the damaging legacy of cattle is apparent. The banks of Main Diamond Creek, one of several Gila River tributaries weaving through the Diamond Bar, are bare and crumbling, mainly because creekside willows and cottonwoods that once checked erosion were long ago devoured or trampled by cows. Though the Main Diamond once brimmed with fish and bird life, the creek is now a muddy, cow-patty-littered trickle much of the year. Its current condition, say biologists, helps explain why every native fish species existing in the Gila River 50 years ago is now either extinct, endangered or under consideration for federal protection. Mr. Laney, an amiable, broad-chested cowboy, vows not to trim his herd -- and to defend it with bullets if need be. "I'd go broke," he says of the proposed cutbacks. The Forest Service -- badly outnumbered here and its ranks still sprinkled with old-guarders sympathetic to ranchers' concerns -- hasn't said what it intends to do about Mr. Laney's defiance. Recently, the service proposed penalizing Mr. Laney 10 cows because his stock repeatedly had been lolling in a badly damaged, off-limits streamside. A tense public hearing on the matter ended with a local county-movement leader, Brub Stone, following ranger Sue Kozacek out to her car. He called her "a communist" and screamed at her to "think hard about what you're going to do, because we'll hard-ass you to death, and you won't get away with it." Later, Danny Fryar, a rancher and the Catron County manager, says if Mr. Laney's herd is cut, "there'll be all sorts of trouble. Kit won't have to face them alone." The leaders of Catron County's movement portray it as a revolt of hard-working stewards of the land against elitist greens and unfeeling bureaucrats. "It's just honest country folk who have cared for this land and have made something of it standing up against government and outsiders that want to take it all away from us," drawls Richard Manning, a tall, weather-beaten rancher who owns thousands of acres of rangeland and is considered the county's richest man. But critics say that Mr. Manning and other ranchers have grown prosperous precisely because the government's cheap grazing fees have amounted to fat, perpetual subsidies -- derided as "cowboy welfare." "It's the height of hypocrisy," says Peter Galvin, a conservation biologist with the Greater Gila Biodiversity Project, an area environmental group. "They rail about the federal government taking over their lives, but they're first in line when the feds are handing out subsidies." Environmentalists and some federal regulators also wonder about some of the ranchers' stewardship. In addition to the battered condition of the local range, there is Mr. Manning's ongoing feud with the Forest Service over his plan to open up a mill he owns at the Challenger Mine, which is on Forest Service land in the Mogollon Mountains. (Mr. Manning, citing various legal concepts, regards the mill site as his property, not the Forest Service's.) The Forest Service and state regulators suspect that toxic mine tailings at the mill may be leaching into watercourses. Mr. Manning refuses to agree to let them check, and according to several Forest Service and state officials, has threatened to greet any regulator who comes out to the mine with "100 men with rifles." Mr. Manning denies having made any such threat. In any case, the rhetoric in Catron County is baleful, even by the inflamed standards of Western land battles. People here threaten mayhem with a casualness and frequency that alarms regulators and environmentalists. And, in a development that troubles even some movement leaders, the cause has attracted elements with some peculiar ideas. At the recent rights rally, Frank Nagol hands out a schematic of how to make a pipe bomb. He has a .25-caliber pistol tucked in his waistband. "You have to be prepared to defend yourself from the oppressors at all times," Mr. Nagol says. Others in the crowd talk of an FBI plot to recruit the Bloods and the Crips off the streets of Los Angeles to form a secret army. "It will be the instrument of a complete government takeover of private property," observes Ed Cramer, a barrel-chested Arizona man. Mr. Cramer is sure this is true because of his contacts in law enforcement; he was a police officer for 31 years, and now serves as a magistrate in Arizona's Hidalgo County. Still others at the rally warn of imminent invasions by United Nations shock troops, Mexican drug dealers and space aliens. Howard Hutchinson, another leader of Catron County's campaign, acknowledges that the movement has attracted "fringe elements -- all movements do." He has an interesting history himself: He helped found Earth First!, the radical environmental group that got its start here in the Gila area. Now Mr. Hutchinson lives in a trailer, raises organic artichokes and, as a stalwart in the county movement, battles what he calls "environmental extremists." So far, despite the tension and threats, nobody has been shot over land use in Catron County. But authorities are investigating the vandalism of several Forest Service signs and outback buildings, and the service's deputy chief for the region, Carl Pence, worries that a showdown may be inevitable. "We take these threats very seriously," Mr. Pence says. ". . . The tinder is there. It wouldn't take much to set it off." (See related letters: "Letters to the Editor: Why Cattle Eat Federal Grass" -- WSJ Feb. 7, 1995) 950103-0078 YY95 MM02 Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: World-Wide
Text: ROBERTS TOOK the oath as chief justice after a 78-22 vote to confirm. Sworn in by Stevens, the oldest justice, Roberts vowed fealty to the Constitution as "strong and vibrant" as Rehnquist's, and Bush praised his "astute mind and kind heart." At age 50, assessing the aptness of that description may stretch decades. Attention shifted to the choice of an O'Connor successor, expected early next week, and signs if it will touch off the political war Roberts didn't. The Supreme Court, which convenes Monday, will weigh at an Oct. 14 conference whether to overturn a lower court and reinstate a potential $280 billion penalty for tobacco companies. --- GENERALS GAVE a sobering Iraq forecast just as insurgents hit hard. Three suicide car bombs killed at least 60 in the mostly Shiite town of Balad, and an IED in Ramadi killed five U.S. soldiers, deadliest one-day toll in weeks. In Washington, Rumsfeld and senior commanders conceded shortcomings of Iraqi forces, said divisions over a new constitution could impede efforts to withdraw any time soon and estimated it might take nine years to defeat insurgents. Generals promised to investigate media concern about rising numbers of reporters detained or killed. A federal judge ordered the release of government-withheld Abu Ghraib photos. --- Judith Miller left jail after agreeing to testify to a grand jury investigating the Plame leak. The New York Times reporter decided to cooperate after her source, reportedly Cheney aide Libby, released her from a confidentiality vow, a half-a-loaf outcome for both sides in the media-prosecutor standoff over reporters' right to keep their sources secret. --- FEMA spending came under more scrutiny as senators zeroed in on lucrative contracts for cruise ships and trailers that remain unfilled. Disaster-zone schools were given a one-year pass on penalties for failing to meet No Child Left Behind standards. Wild rumors of New Orleans lawlessness made rescue workers hesitant to enter the city after Katrina. House-Senate negotiators approved a $31.9 billion Homeland Security budget giving the White House more latitude to target disaster aid. --- DeLay stays a "powerful adviser" despite indictment, an aide to Hastert said. Events have conspired to scale back Republicans' agenda. Key senators requested an inspector-general inquiry into Crawford's resignation as head of the FDA and whether ethics issues played a role. --- The House voted 229-193 to ease Endangered Species Act curbs on property rights, to environmentalist dismay. Senate chances are uncertain. --- A Pentagon aide will plead guilty to charges of passing along classified data to an Israeli official and lobbyists, a federal court in Virginia said. --- Palestinian police banned public displays of weapons as they tried to impose order on Gaza. Hamas tested its clout in local Palestinian elections. --- China has sided with North Korea's demand to mention promises of a civilian reactor in its nuclear accord, complicating the talks, diplomats say. --- The U.N. said Sudan Arab militiamen brazenly raided a Darfur refugee camp this week, killing 29. Until now, such camps were relatively safe. African migrants staged a mass invasion of Morocco Spanish enclaves, scaling razor-wire fences to gain entry to a scrap of the EU. Five died. --- Indonesian militants are fighting in the Muslim insurgency in southern Thailand despite Bangkok's denials, an adviser to Premier Thaksin said. --- Ukraine's new premier vowed no more privatization reviews, inquiries that had put the ousted government into conflict with powerful interests. --- Recruiting began for the biggest federal study of U.S. children ever, in which 100,000 in 105 localities are to be monitored from birth to age 21.

Title: U.S. News: Senate GOP Targets Biden Regulations
Text: WASHINGTON -- Republicans don't control the Senate. But on some days, they have controlled the Senate's agenda. While Democrats run the Senate floor on account of their 51-49 majority, Republicans are using various tools to force votes on issues dear to the GOP, over the opposition of Senate Democratic leaders and President Biden. They have employed the Congressional Review Act and other provisions of federal law to target rules written by administration agencies and hold votes on hot-button issues, sometimes peeling off centrist Democrats positioning themselves ahead of the 2024 elections. More GOP-led votes are expected in the coming weeks, testing Democratic unity and potentially forcing vetoes from Mr. Biden. Republicans are billing these votes as critical tools of legislative oversight and accountability over the executive branch. "As a legislative branch, we must protect our authority. The Biden administration is trying to subvert our laws, and it must be stopped," Sen. Pete Ricketts (R., Neb.) said on the Senate floor last month. A primary tool has been the Congressional Review Act, which allows Congress to overturn rules and regulations written by federal agencies within 60 days of their enactment by passing resolutions of disapproval. Disapproval resolutions are exempt from the filibuster rule and can't be blocked by the Senate's majority leader, meaning they need just a simple majority in both chambers to reach the president's desk. They are still subject to a presidential veto, which would then require a two-thirds majority in each chamber to override. Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R., W.Va.) introduced a disapproval resolution targeting the administration's Waters of the United States rule, which expanded the definitions of waterways subject to federal pollution regulations. After clearing the House, it passed 53-43 in the Senate, with Democratic Sens. Jacky Rosen and Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada, Joe Manchin of West Virginia and Jon Tester of Montana joining all Republicans to pass the measure. Sen. Kyrsten Sinema, an Arizona independent who caucuses with Democrats, also voted with Republicans. The Senate also voted 50-46 to pass a disapproval resolution introduced by Sen. Mike Braun (R., Ind.) targeting Labor Department rules that allowed retirement-plan managers to consider environmental, social and corporate-governance issues, or ESG, in their investment decisions. Messrs. Manchin and Tester joined Republicans to pass the measure. With Congress coming back into session, Republicans plan additional efforts to keep their agenda in the spotlight. A series of disapproval resolutions on environmental regulations is expected to receive votes in the coming weeks, among them a resolution introduced by Sen. Deb Fischer (R., Neb.) to overturn rules governing trucking emissions and one introduced by Sen. Cynthia Lummis (R., Wyo.) that would overturn new definitions of habitats for purposes of enforcing the Endangered Species Act. Democrats defend such regulations as critical to protecting the environment, while Republicans cast them as costly government overreach. Mr. Biden has used his veto power against these disapproval resolutions. He vetoed Mr. Braun's disapproval bill on ESG, the first veto of his presidency, and an effort to override the veto in the House failed. Mr. Biden also vetoed Ms. Capito's water-regulations bill. In a message to Congress, the White House said that "the increased uncertainty caused by [the bill] would threaten economic growth, including for agriculture, local economies, and downstream communities." Disapproval resolutions rarely succeed. Of the 249 disapproval resolutions that were introduced by members of Congress since the law's inception in 1996 to October 2022, only 20 have successfully managed to overturn federal regulations, according to a new study by researchers at George Washington University. All the successes occurred immediately after a change in presidential administrations and when the president's party held majorities in both houses of Congress, and all but three have occurred during a Republican presidency. But the resolutions can serve political purposes, even if their odds of overturning regulations are poor. For moderate lawmakers like Messrs. Manchin and Tester, breaking with their party and voting in favor of disapproval resolutions can bolster an image of legislative and political independence with voters. For Republicans, getting Democratic support makes the efforts bipartisan. A spokesperson for Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer (D., N.Y.) didn't respond to a request for comment. Credit: By Eric Bazail-Eimil

Title: Board of Contributors: In Defense of Government
Text: Recent months have witnessed an attack of unprecedented passion and ferocity against the national government. The Republican Party has apparently embarked on a crusade to destroy national standards, national projects and national regulations and to transfer domestic governing authority from the national government to the states. A near majority of the Supreme Court even seems to want to replace the Constitution by the Articles of Confederation. There has not been so basic an assault on the national government since the Civil War. Unbridled rhetoric is having consequences far beyond anything that anti-government politicians intend. The flow of angry words seems to have activated and in a sense legitimized what the historian Richard Hofstadter called the "paranoid strain" in American politics. For historians there is a certain charm in watching the Rev. Pat Robertson resurrect the old hysteria about the sinister influence of Adam Weishaupt and the Illuminati of 18th century Bavaria. On the wilder shores of unreason, the national government is seen as a diabolical conspiracy to take away the people's guns in order that the United Nations, flushed no doubt by its victories in Bosnia, might send in its black helicopters to destroy American freedom and enslave Americans in a despotic New World Order. Even this excellent newspaper recently ran a book review under the headline "Fix Washington Before It Enslaves Us All" -- rough language for Bill Clinton in the century of Stalin and Hitler. Private militias prepare to defend American liberties by assault weapons and bombs. Federal officials, even those from benevolent nature-loving agencies like the Forest Service and the Fish and Wildlife Service, become targets of crazed gunmen and must maintain constant radio contact with their offices. A fanatic, Mr. Dooley reminds us, "does what he think th' Lord wud do if He only knew th' facts in th' case." Fanaticism reached its unspeakable climax in Oklahoma City. This, as noted, is certainly not what House Speaker Newt Gingrich had in mind in his denunciations of the national government. But the speaker blamed the murder by a South Carolina woman of her two children on the poisoning of the culture by liberal Democrats, and his own logic must indict the antigovernment demagogues as unwitting accomplices in the Oklahoma City outrage. Is it too much to hope that this will encourage the speaker in rhetorical restraint? (Answer: Yes, it is probably too much to hope.) Oklahoma City, according to the polls, has led the general public to reconsider the cliches and to decide that the national government is not such a monster after all. But it has not deterred the antigovernment wrecking crew on Capitol Hill in their mania for devolution and deregulation -- that is, for dismantling the national government, shifting its functions to the states and repealing or eviscerating national laws that protect the consumer, the investor, the worker, the minorities, the poor and the dispossessed or that benefit scientific research and development, education, the environment and the arts. Moreover, in a lobbyists' saturnalia, industry representatives present willing Republican legislators with statutes designed to increase corporate profits at the expense of the general welfare. Thus Sen. Slade Gorton's proposed castration of the Endangered Species Act was drafted, the New York Times informs us, by a group of Washington, D.C., lawyers representing the timber, mining, ranching and utility interests that have a heavy financial stake in the outcome. The assault on the national government is represented as a disinterested movement to "return" power to the people. But the withdrawal of the national government does not transfer power to the people. It transfers power to the historical rival of the national government and the prime cause of its enlargement -- the great corporate interests. Theodore Roosevelt, a Republican, was the father of "big government." As he observed of the greedy trusts of his day, "If this irresponsible outside power is to be controlled in the interest of the general public, it can be controlled in only one way -- by giving adequate power of control to the National Government." The fight against government regulation of corporate privilege, TR added, "is chiefly done under cover; and especially under the cover of an appeal to State's rights." Getting the government off the back of business really means putting business on the back of government. It is a delusion to say that because state government is closer to the people it is therefore more responsive to their needs and concerns. Local government is the government of the locally powerful. Historically it has been the national government that has served as the protector of the powerless -- workers, farmers, minorities, children, disabled, old folks -- against local exploitation or neglect. Had the state rights creed triumphed, we would still have slavery in the U.S. And historically the national government has been more honest and efficient than state government. State governments are doubtless better now than they used to be. But how well in fact are they doing today with problems that lie primarily within their own jurisdiction, like deteriorating schools and escalating crime? Are state governments doing such a swell job in meeting local responsibilities that we should now dump on the statehouses a carload of national responsibilities? As for bureaucracy, duplication, waste and fraud, will there be more or less if a single federal agency is replaced by 50 separate state agencies? Just wait till local pols get their little hands on those federal block grants. Social Security and Medicare, nationally administered, are much better run than state-administered welfare and Medicaid. Washington is in a position to recruit abler people than most state capitals. As the Economist said the other day in an article on the resurgence of tuberculosis in America: "National surveillance worked well until the 1970s. When, against expert advice, responsibility for this work was given to the states, the programme fell apart." A lot of programs will fall apart if the speaker has his way. Almost unnoticed have been the proposed cuts on funds for scientific R&D. "If approved," Dr. David Baltimore, a Nobel laureate, writes, "they will threaten the very foundations of science in this country." And what will happen when states engage in a debasing competition to attract business and keep out the poor by cutting costs through low wages, minimal working conditions, minimal environmental protection, no unions and no benefits? A contest in meanness will not enhance the quality of American civilization. Before the devolutionists go too far in destroying national authority, the speaker might read his followers the sixth and seventh Federalist papers where Hamilton points out the dangers arising from "rivalships and competitions of commerce" among the states. He might even remind them that the Constitutional Convention was called to stop economic warfare within the Articles of Confederation. National problems require national remedies. Alexis de Tocqueville was no admirer of centralized authority, but he was a sharp observer. It remains as generally true today as it was when Tocqueville visited America in 1832 that, as he put it, "the business of the Union is incomparably better conducted than that of any individual state. . . . It has more prudence and discretion, its projects are more durable and more skillfully combined, its measures are executed with more vigor and consistency." The know-nothing crusade against government springs from a conviction that, if we get government off our backs, our problems will solve themselves. But, far from solving problems, the old unregulated laissez-faire economy of the 19th century generated the problems that produced class war and the Communist Manifesto. What rescued capitalism from Marxist prophecy in the 20th century was the work of reformers like the two Roosevelts who used the national government to humanize the industrial order, to cushion the operations of the economic system, to strengthen the bargaining position of workers and farmers and consumers, to reduce the economic gap between the classes, to ensure against recurrent depression by built-in economic stabilizers; above all, to combine individual opportunity with social responsibility. Things have been slipping back in this era of supply-side, trickle-down economics. "Top Heavy," Prof. Edward N. Wolff's study for the Twentieth Century Fund, shows the U.S. to be first among industrial nations in the inequality of wealth. Britain is notorious as a class-ridden society, but the top 1% of families in Britain own only about 18% of the nation's wealth. In America the top 1% own more than 40%. The Gingrich drive to cripple the national government and to cut taxes for the rich and social programs for the poor will only embitter these inequalities. Unless something is done, Felix Rohatyn sees the America of 2000 as divided and demoralized, "a nation of outcasts within a nation of wealth." Ralph Waldo Emerson, the transcendent American individualist, was also, like Tocqueville, a sharp observer, and he became at times exasperated by the grousing about government he kept hearing around him. "It is folly," he wrote in his journal, "to treat the state as if it were some individual arbitrarily willing this and so. . . . I confess I lose all respect for this tedious denouncing of the state by idlers who rot in indolence, selfishness, & envy in the chimney corner." --- Mr. Schlesinger is Schweitzer professor emeritus at the City University of New York and a winner of Pulitzer Prizes in history and biography. Title: Both parties paint themselves green, but trend of looser environmental rules is seen continuing
Text: WASHINGTON -- As Election Day approaches, Democrats and Republicans alike are talking greener than they are likely to govern.    For Democrats, environmental protection is what race was for Republicans in previous election years -- a "wedge" issue that can separate middle-class voters from the opposing party. President Clinton, in his acceptance speech at last month's Democratic convention, uttered the word "environment" no fewer than seven times and proclaimed, "We should make it a crime even to attempt to pollute."    Republicans, meanwhile, are muting their 1995 argument, made while trying to slash the Environmental Protection Agency's budget, that excessive environmental regulation is strangling the economy. Though Republican presidential nominee Robert Dole more often talks about tax cuts, he included a regulatory-reform proposal in his main economic plan and talked it up last weekend in Pennsylvania. His campaign literature asserts he's "the only presidential candidate ever to have voted for and help [sic] pass every major piece of environmental protection legislation in the past 25 years."    But while Democrats emphasize environmental protection and Republicans try to neutralize the issue, both parties are likely to continue a trend, begun in the late 1980s, toward more flexible environmental regulation that is less intrusive for businesses and individuals.    The fact that both parties tend to favor looser environmental regulation in the 1990s is largely obscured by their sharp disagreement over how much looser it should be. The Clinton administration, for example, has sought to exempt small landowners from penalties under the Endangered Species Act, while Republicans want to reimburse large and small businesses for losses in property value attributable to the law.    Poll after poll shows that voters see Democrats as more vigilant about the environment than Republicans. In a June Wall Street Journal-NBC News survey, 54% of respondents said Mr. Clinton would "do a better job" protecting the environment; only 16% thought Mr. Dole would do the better job. The poll gave Mr. Clinton higher ratings on the environment than on such issues as abortion, Medicare, education or jobs and unemployment. That may help explain why the administration is considering strict new protections for as many as 1.8 million acres in Utah that the GOP Congress had sought to open for development.    But Mr. Clinton's strong standing on environmental issues is somewhat ironic given the slight interest he has shown in past years. In the 1992 campaign, then-Gov. Clinton received some of his sharpest criticism over the dumping of chicken feces into Arkansas rivers and streams. During the first half of his presidential term, his "legislative tactics and inconsistency doomed many of his legislative proposals" on the environment, a recent League of Conservation Voters pamphlet asserted, including proposals for an energy tax and grazing and mining reform that he quickly scuttled after complaints from a then-Democratic Congress. The only major environmental legislation passed by that Congress created parkland in the California desert but had only minimal White House involvement.    "They didn't do anything wrong," says Rep. Sherwood Boehlert of New York, a rare House Republican who is strongly sympathetic to environmental causes. "They just didn't do anything right, either."    After the Republican takeover of Congress, the administration focused more attention on the environment in order to block various Republican proposals, including a measure that would have significantly weakened wetlands protection. But many of these proposals -- for example, then-Sen. Dole's sweeping plan to subject new regulations to cost-benefit analysis -- weren't inconsistent with Clinton policies; they were merely more extreme.    Republicans are well aware that voters don't trust them on the environment, and have attempted to soften their image. In a May 17 memo to House Republican candidates, Rep. Bill Paxon (R., N.Y.), chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee, advised candidates to engage in such activities as holding news conferences and issuing news releases "on the importance of a cleaner, safer environment," hosting river or park cleanups "and invite the press to attend," and designating "a local environmental hero, perhaps a student in a local high school who has instituted a recycling program."    Mr. Dole, for his part, sent Rep. Boehlert as his personal representative to a natural resources summit in Birmingham, Ala., attended by environmentalists and sportsmen. At the conference, Mr. Boehlert said "this Congress got off to what might charitably be called a rocky start on the environment," but "under Bob Dole's leadership, cooler heads prevailed."    But both Mr. Dole and fellow Republicans remain committed to ideas such as regulatory reform and a "takings" bill that Mr. Dole sponsored in the Senate that would require the federal government to compensate businesses and other private property owners for any loss of property values attributable to regulation. The Clinton administration opposes the "takings" bill on cost grounds; Mr. Dole maintains costs would be minimal because federal agencies would learn to avoid actions that reduce private property values. Both regulatory reform and takings have been pushed hard by business interests, which will expect Republicans in Congress and the White House, if Mr. Dole is elected, to press for them next year.    Despite the environmental gulf between Democrats and Republicans, lately they have found some areas of agreement. This summer President Clinton signed a revision of the Safe Drinking Water Act easing some requirements for small-town drinking water systems; he also signed a pesticide bill scuttling the Delaney Clause, an absolutist 1958 prohibition on carcinogens in processed foods that scientists have long believed out of date.    According to Environmental Protection Agency Chief Carol Browner, the two laws were "in large measure what we proposed" years earlier. "The Republicans, recognizing that they needed to improve their image, had nowhere to go but where the president had been on these issues," she said.    New compromises seem unlikely before Election Day. But after Nov. 5, talks will resume on two controversial measures: Superfund and the Endangered Species Act.    On Superfund, Democrats say they oppose GOP proposals to free big polluters from cleanup costs, while Republicans staunchly oppose rewriting the hazardous-waste law to finance cleanups by higher taxes. But a 1994 Clinton administration plan that stalled in Congress proposed reducing (though not eliminating) polluters' cleanup liability. That plan was opposed by congressional Republicans, but won support from many industries -- though it would impose a new tax on insurers to help meet cleanup costs at hazardous-waste dumps. Should Republicans and their business allies fail to accept new Superfund taxes after Election Day, the Democrats might accept a compromise to tap an existing Superfund trust fund that is currently running a surplus.    The Endangered Species Act has sparked especially heated debate between Democrats, who accuse opponents of trying to gut the law, and Republicans, who say it places greater value on spotted owls and gnatcatchers than on jobs for people. But Rep. Jim Saxton (R., N.J.), with the support of House Speaker Newt Gingrich, spent the spring and summer negotiating with the Environmental Defense Fund and other green groups on a possible compromise bill. The talks are suspended for now, but Michael Bean, chairman of the Environmental Defense Fund's wildlife program, said "we got substantial agreement on a number of significant issues," including putting more emphasis on preserving habitats rather than trying to save individual species. According to Rep. Saxton, the negotiations will resume Nov. 19.    For now, however, Democrats likely will remain on the offensive. "Their rhetoric is improving," says Ms. Browner of the Republicans. But "the reality has lagged behind."    ---             Issues Check-Off: The Environment    Here is a look at proposals of President Clinton and Robert Dole on the environment.    Bill Clinton    -- Favors scaling back, but not eliminating, the amount polluters must pay for Superfund hazardous-waste cleanups.    -- Opposes a bill requiring that new regulations pass a a rigorous cost-benefit analysis.    -- Opposes a bill to compensate businesses and other property owners for property-value loss due to regulation.    -- Favors increased spending to restore the Florida Everglades, financed in part with a penny-a-pound tax on Florida sugar growers.    -- Favors maintaining, though downsizing, the Energy Department.    Robert Dole    -- Favors sharply reducing or eliminating the amount polluters must pay for Superfund hazardous-waste cleanups.    -- Favors a bill requiring that new regulations pass a rigorous cost-benefit analysis.    -- Favors a bill to compensate businesses and other property owners for property-value loss due to regulation.    -- Favors increased spending to restore the Florida Everglades, but opposes a penny-a-pound tax on Florida sugar growers.    -- Favors eliminating the Energy Department, but keeping its national labs by transferring them to the Pentagon.  Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Suits Against Maxxam Take Unusual Tack
Text: EUREKA, Calif. -- In a downtown Victorian in this North Coast port, the oldest of professional traditions and the cutting edge of legal activism can be found together in the offices of Pacific Law. There, attorney Steven Schectman, a transplant from San Francisco, is training six apprentices to master the law the old-fashioned way. Just as in the days before California had its first law school, the aspiring lawyers prepare for the bar by working as a practitioner's clerks. But the subject of their work is as modern as the environmental movement: The entire focus of Pacific Law is suing Pacific Lumber Co., and its much-larger parent company, Maxxam Inc. of Houston. The Scotia, Calif., unit owns 200,000 acres of prime Humboldt County timberlands. Maxxam and its chairman, Charles E. Hurwitz, gained control of the venerable Pacific Lumber in 1985 in a highly leveraged hostile takeover. Since then, waves of protests and environmental lawsuits have tried to make Maxxam, which increased its logging to pay off junk bonds, slow its timber harvesting and spare America's last stands of ancient, old-growth redwood trees. "We don't want to crush Pacific Lumber," Mr. Schectman says, "but we want to bring it into legal compliance." Over the past nine months, Mr. Schectman and Bill Bertain, a local attorney who has long fought Pacific Lumber, have filed a trio of lawsuits against Maxxam in state and federal courts. Two actions in Humboldt County Superior Court accuse Maxxam of violating state unfair business practices and federal racketeering statutes and claim such violations inflicted hardship on local residents. A third suit in U.S. District Court in San Francisco alleges that the company fraudulently siphoned $60 million in excess funds from Pacific Lumber's employee pension fund. (All three allegations are untrue, say officials from Maxxam and Pacific Lumber.) Pacific Lumber President and Chief Executive John Campbell says of the complaints: "I don't know what the purpose is, I don't think what [Mr. Schectman's] doing has a lot of merit. We have to ask the question why he's parachuting in to set up a law office in Eureka to litigate one company." As significant as the cases themselves is the unusual operation that is pursuing them. Mr. Schectman, 46 years old, boasts that he works "on the outside edge" of his profession by specializing in "human dignity and corporate responsibility" cases. Last summer -- bankrolled by a lucrative 1997 settlement of an age-discrimination complaint against the San Francisco law firm, Pillsbury, Madison & Sutro LLP -- Mr. Schectman moved lock, stock and law books up to this logging town to stalk big legal game. Establishing the apprenticeship program was part of his self-professed dream of leveraging the law to right social and economic wrongs. Twenty years ago, the future litigator apprenticed under Berkeley civil-rights attorney Len Holt. Now, Mr. Schectman declares, "we're going to produce the most dangerous lawyers in America. They're going to learn by doing it." Six local activists signed up, as did environmental lawyers eager to help train. But as Mr. Schectman can personally attest, becoming a lawyer through apprenticeship -- which requires at least four years of preparation -- is no easy feat. In 1980, he was one of only 11 apprentices out of a total of 7,000 students who qualified to take the bar examination. Nine passed. Since then, apprentices have had an even poorer showing. According to the State Bar of California, only two of 25 apprentices who took the exam since 1997 have passed. The long odds, however, don't seem to daunt Mr. Schectman's students, including Josh Kaufman, a 47-year-old former paleontologist at the Los Angeles County Natural History Museum. "We don't entirely know what we're getting into, and getting by the first-year exam is kind of sobering," says Mr. Kaufman, who moved to Humboldt County 12 years ago to join the environmental movement. The arrival of Mr. Schectman and his "law school" has provided welcome reinforcement for Mr. Bertain, the Eureka attorney who has been battling Pacific Lumber since the takeover. Mr. Bertain, a solo practitioner who graduated from the University of San Francisco Law School, grew up around Scotia where his family ran a Pacific Lumber contract laundry from 1905 until 1992. The affiliation with Mr. Schectman, he says, "could very well turn out to be a good match" even though the two men come from totally different backgrounds. "He has a sense of the need for social and economic justice," says Mr. Bertain. Not all are mesmerized by Mr. Schectman's endeavor, however. The San Francisco lawyer's decision to head into redwood country and wage an all-out legal assault on Pacific Lumber is probably more "about money" than environmental zeal, says Jared Carter, whose Ukiah-based firm is defending the company in the two state-court complaints, which have been consolidated by a Humboldt County Superior Court judge. "He seems to be a competent lawyer, but I'm not swept off my feet by his legal theories," adds Mr. Carter. But both Mr. Carter and Mr. Schectman agree that Pacific Law's state-court cases have injected some "novel arguments" in the continuing legal wrangling between activists and Pacific Lumber. The two complaints allege that Pacific Lumber's logging practices have caused severe economic damages to two communities downslope from timber harvesting. A case filed on May 4 of last year for residents of the hamlet of Stafford claims that logging crews from Pacific Lumber and a second company caused massive mudslides in late December 1996 and early January 1997 that destroyed seven houses and severely damaged seven others. The lawsuit charges the two companies with violating state laws on unfair business practices and the federal Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organization Act by conspiring to go against their state-approved timber-harvesting plans and improperly logging on a hillside. The second suit, filed last Aug. 31 on behalf of another group of residents along the Elk River, accuses Maxxam and Pacific Lumber of knowingly employing similarly unsound hillside-logging practices that caused soil erosion. The shifting soil made river water undrinkable and unusable for household and agricultural purposes, the suit says. Both complaints seek compensatory, general and punitive damages and compensation for emotional distress; dollar amounts weren't specified. And because of the federal racketeering allegations, Mr. Schectman's clients could collect triple damages if successful in court. The cases, Mr. Schectman notes, depart from previous legal efforts against Pacific Lumber that alleged violations of the federal Endangered Species Act, such as logging that damaged the habitat of the marbled murrelet bird and other fauna. "I'm not interested in doing litigation that's already been done. I don't have an expertise in environmental law," Mr. Schectman says. The new cases, he says, are about "poor people going against powerful entities" and are designed to hurt Maxxam's bottom line by making it pay large damage awards. "He's doing something for people who had little or no voice up here," says Michael R. O'Neal, a Stafford resident whose home suffered severe damage in the 1996-97 slide. "We personally don't have the money to fight ourselves." Mr. Carter, Pacific Lumber's attorney, concedes that, at least in the Stafford slide case, residents did suffer severe damages. But blame, he says, can't necessarily be tied to his client's logging practices. "The question zeroes in on whether or not the slides were caused by extraordinary rainfall and would have occurred whether or not there had been any logging," he says. At Elk River, he adds, the legal question is "whether the logging which occurred and admittedly occurred over a period of years was done in an inappropriate manner and resulted in degrading the stream more so than if it had been done correctly." The damages in both cases, Mr. Carter says, aren't the fault of Pacific Lumber. Moreover, he notes that a 1982 state law specifically protects timber companies from being targeted by neighbors' nuisance suits if the logging is being conducted according to state regulations. Meanwhile, Pacific Lumber's already high profile is expected to get higher as a Feb. 28 deadline nears for accepting a joint federal- and state-government offer to pay the company $480 million for the 3,000-acre Headwaters Forest grove of ancient redwoods it owns, along with 7,000 more acres of scenic timberlands. The company, however, must agree to comply with tighter federal and possibly state regulations over how it logs all its Humboldt County holdings. The impending deal has heightened tensions among all participants in the redwoods negotiations. And those tensions will probably increase next week, when Mr. Schectman says he will file a wrongful-death lawsuit in U.S. District Court in San Francisco -- accusing Pacific Lumber of causing the Sept. 17 death of anti-logging protester David Chain of Austin, who was crushed by a tree. Such a move, while not unexpected, would be lamentable, says Mr. Carter, the Pacific Lumber attorney. "I would be very sorry if that matter was not allowed to just go away as a tragic accident that happened to an apparently nice young man," he says. (Humboldt County District Attorney Terry Farmer has found that the death was accidental and said the logger who cut the tree wasn't aware of protesters in the area.) Mr. Schectman, who says he will file the suit on behalf of the victim's mother, Cindy Allsbrooks, of Coldsprings, says the death of Mr. Chain galvanized him into putting together his single-focus law office and in-house law school to take on Maxxam and Pacific Lumber. "This is a case," he says, "crying out for punitive damages." Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: U.S. News: U.S. Watch
Text: MASSACHUSETTS Teixeira Enters Not-Guilty Plea Massachusetts Air National Guardsman Jack Teixeira pleaded not guilty to federal charges that he retained and shared highly classified intelligence documents that prosecutors say endangered national security. Authorities arrested the 21-year-old in April at his home in Dighton, Mass., and he has been in custody since then. His not-guilty plea at a federal courthouse in Worcester, Mass., follows a grand-jury indictment announced last week. The government accuses Teixeira of being the hub for a leak that sent the U.S. government rushing to protect its secrets. The leak also exposed details of American surveillance of adversaries and allies, causing diplomatic tensions with some U.S. partners and raising concerns about undermining Ukraine's fight against Russia. -- Jon Kamp --- WASHINGTON, D.C. New Protection For Wildlife The Biden administration proposed new rules Wednesday for protecting imperiled plants and animals as officials moved to reverse changes under former President Donald Trump that weakened the Endangered Species Act. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service said it would reinstate a decades-old regulation that mandates blanket protections for species newly classified as threatened. That provision was dropped three years ago. Under Wednesday's proposal, officials also would no longer consider economic impacts when deciding if animals and plants need protection. The proposed rules will face pushback from Republican lawmakers, who say President Biden's administration has hampered oil, gas and coal development, and favors conservation over development. -- Associated Press --- ARIZONA Ballot Initiatives Law Affirmed The Arizona Supreme Court ruled that a law criminalizing per-signature payment is constitutional, possibly complicating efforts for groups trying to get initiatives on the ballot. The seven-member panel unanimously agreed the 2017 law doesn't violate the First Amendment rights of petition circulators, reversing an Arizona Court of Appeals opinion. "The statute forbids only per-signature compensation, leaving other productivity-based compensation intact," Justice Clint Bolick wrote. The ban on per-signature payments is one of several restrictions on petition collectors enacted by the Republican-controlled Legislature after liberal groups used the citizen initiative process to make changes lawmakers opposed, including an increase in the minimum wage. -- Associated Press --- WASHINGTON, D.C. Train Accident Rule Proposed Federal regulators want first responders to a train derailment to know exactly what they are dealing with even before they reach the scene, because the dangerous chemicals trains carry might require a specialized response. The Pipelines and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration proposed a new rule Wednesday that would require all railroads to immediately send the details of everything aboard their trains to every emergency responder within 10 miles as soon as the railroad becomes aware of an accident. The new rule comes one day ahead of a National Transportation Safety Board hearing to scrutinize emergency responses to the fiery Feb. 3 derailment of a Norfolk Southern train outside East Palestine, Ohio. The NTSB is still working to determine exactly what caused that wreck. -- Associated Press

Title: Atlanta Is Flexing Muscles in Its War On a Little Bivalve; Both Rely on Reservoirs Drying Up in a Drought; Army Corps on the Spot
Text: They are unassuming little creatures that spend their lives burrowing into sandy beds of Florida's Apalachicola River, filtering water and ingesting detritus. They are too tough for people to eat, but they make tasty snacks for blue herons. They are members of an endangered species, Amblema neislerii, more commonly known as the fat threeridge mussel. Until this summer, few people in Georgia had heard of the humble bivalves. But a prolonged drought has changed all that. The protected mussels depend for sustenance on the same river system that provides drinking water for millions of people in metro Atlanta. That's causing an intensifying struggle for the same resource that Georgia state officials consider an epic battle of Man versus Mussel. At stake is a looming water shortage in Georgia, as well as the survival of a species considered a bellwether for the health of the coastal ecosystem along Florida's Panhandle. Metro Atlanta's main source of drinking water is 39,000-acre Lake Lanier, a 50-year-old reservoir built and controlled by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. Under a 2006 deal with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, which co-administers the Endangered Species Act, the Corps sends a minimum flow of water from Lanier and other reservoirs into the Chattahoochee River and connecting rivers downstream, including Florida's Apalachicola River, where the endangered mussels live. The flow also cools two power plants -- one in Alabama and one in Florida -- located between Atlanta and the mouth of the Apalachicola in the Florida Panhandle 350 miles away. The river's delivery of fresh water also feeds the Gulf Coast spawning grounds of the threatened Gulf sturgeon. As months with little rain steadily lowered the level of Lake Lanier, which provides drinking water for roughly three million people, marooning boat docks and exposing vast flats of red mud, the Corps has continued to open the Lake Lanier dam enough to maintain a steady stream of the millions of gallons of water believed necessary to keep the mussels in Florida alive. State officials in Georgia estimate that if severe drought conditions persist, the reservoir could be nearly dry by the end of January. "If this water isn't conserved now, it's going to be lost for everyone," says Atlanta attorney Bruce Brown, who heads the state's legal efforts in the water crisis. Last weekend, with a shriveled Lake Lanier as a backdrop, Georgia Gov. Sonny Perdue lashed out, blaming "silly federal bureaucratic rules" for the state's dilemma. An onlooker displayed a placard asking, "Where in the U.S. Constitution does it say, 'protect the mussels?'" And U.S. Rep. John Linder, a Republican, said the Corps is behaving "as though mussels are more important than our children and grandchildren." Georgia filed suit against the Corps last week, demanding it hold back more Lake Lanier water. A court hearing is scheduled for Nov. 19. Gov. Perdue also fired a separate volley Saturday, beseeching President Bush to declare a major disaster in Georgia -- a step the state's lawyers say would exempt the Corps from compliance with the Endangered Species Act. Governors both Florida and Alabama countered by asking President Bush not to. The Federal Emergency Management Agency, which is weighing the disaster request, says it's not necessarily that simple. The last drought-related federal disaster decree was three decades ago, a FEMA spokesman says. The White House Council on Environmental Quality, which coordinates environmental policy, says it's studying the situation. "I can't emphasize how complicated this is," says the FEMA spokesman, Aaron Walker. Alabama's governor opposes a reduction in water flow partly because it could force the shutdown of a nuclear plant near his state's border with Georgia. South of the state line in Florida, state officials and wildlife advocates say Georgia's behavior is unneighborly, and putting at risk not only mussels and sturgeon but the oyster and seafood industry in Apalachicola Bay. The bay produces 90% of Florida's oysters, which depend on a balance of freshwater and saltwater to thrive.
