The Forest Service originally planned to allow the harvest of 109 million board feet of timber in the fire-salvage operation, but protests from environmental groups delayed the harvest and reduced it to 50 million board feet. Mr. Batty says Grant County receives 25% of the receipts from timber sales on federal land. That amounted to between $10 million and $12 million a year from 1986 to 1996, according to the intent-to-sue document. But in the past year, the county has received only $1.4 million. That's why last year the John Day and Monument School Districts -- two of the five districts in the county -- were forced to cut back to four-day school weeks, says Mr. Batty. "This has had a devastating effect on our schools." Such community-wide effects are what prompted Don Lundbom, owner of John Day Auto Parts Inc. in John Day, to join the suit along with a number of other local business owners. "Logging is a way of life here," he says. "This is a small town. If something starts tearing at part of our community, everybody feels it." John Day has about 2,100 residents; Grant County has 8,000. Environmentalists, however, scoff at the group's claim that more logging would be good for the environment. "Those people are in denial about the environment and the endangered species," says Asante Riverwind, co-director of the Blue Mountain Biodiversity Project, a conservation group based in Fossil. "They don't care about the fish. They just want to find any way to log that they can." Last year, Mr. Riverwind's group and five other environmental organizations sued the Forest Service, arguing its plans to offer 50 million board feet of burned and damaged trees was too much. The suit claimed that the road building and loss of trees would cause runoff into the streams that feed the John Day River, home to five types of threatened or endangered fish. But while that suit was awaiting action in U.S. District Court in Portland, the Forest Service awarded contracts to cut the timber and that harvest is now nearly complete, says Mr. Holloway. The environmentalists lost a motion for a stay on any harvest while the case was under way. The environmentalists haven't withdrawn their suit, though Mr. Riverwind says it's moot now. But he says he and others will watch closely any legal action taken by the Grant County group. "There is no science that backs the notion that more logging is the answer to restoration of this forest and its streams," he says. "At this point, they are in a bind in Grant County, but that is because they have logged so much in the past, not because of the fire, or the beetles." Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Audubon Society In Tentative Pact With Ranchers
Text: A tentative settlement between the National Audubon Society and some ranchers in Okeechobee County bodes well for a colony of endangered Florida grasshopper sparrows. It's also a big relief for the environmental group. Because the society owns the sanctuary where the sparrows are, "we could be held liable for harming the sparrow" under the Endangered Species Act, says Paul Gray, manager of the Ordway-Whittell Kissimmee Prairie Sanctuary. The dispute was triggered by a series of wet winters that have flooded parts of the sanctuary. Audubon officials initially welcomed the extra water, figuring it would help restore some wetland areas. But then the society got a warning from the federal government: The sanctuary was also home to 30 pairs of endangered grasshopper sparrows, which nest on the ground and need dry prairie land to breed. Audubon tried to drain some of the water through culverts onto neighboring land owned by ranchers. But one of the neighbors accused Audubon of releasing too much water onto ranchers' grazing land, and the landowners began plugging up the culverts. Audubon then sued the landowners in federal court in Miami, and was joined in the suit by the federal government. Last week, lawyers for Audubon and the ranchers reached a tentative settlement, agreeing to split the costs of installing a series of canals and culverts to drain the sanctuary without flooding the pasture land. A final agreement is expected to be signed next week. Mr. Gray says his group is pleased. "It's been doubly frustrating," he says. "Not only were the birds getting their habitat destroyed, but . . . we could be held liable." Ted Brown, a lawyer who represented one of the landowners, 101 Ranch Inc., says his client is happy with the proposed settlement, but is tickled nonetheless by watching Audubon itself face trouble with the Endangered Species Act. Says Mr. Brown: "The irony to me is that they had their own linens soiled on this one."

Title: Environmentalists, White House strike accord on logging
Text: The Clinton administration and 12 environmental groups struck a deal meant to allow logging in some spotted-owl territory in the Pacific Northwest.    The pact seeks to permit some 83 million board feet of timber to be logged in federal forests where cutting is currently banned, under injunctions issued by Judge William Dwyer of U.S. District Court in Seattle. The ban is meant to protect the spotted owl, a threatened species under the Endangered Species Act.    The 12 environmental groups, which include national heavyweights like the Wilderness Society and the National Audubon Society as well as numerous local organizations, are plaintiffs in cases that resulted in the injunctions. Under the deal, they have agreed not to oppose a motion in Judge Dwyer's court by the Forest Service to permit the logging.    In return, the Clinton administration has agreed not to seek legislation that would insulate its new forest policy from court challenge. That policy, which emerged from the much-ballyhooed Timber Summit in Portland, Ore., earlier this year, is controversial among environmentalists; they have feared that the adminstration might win such protective legislation.    The deal furthers one of the main objectives of the administration's new forest plan, which is to free up some timber to help preserve Northwestern logging jobs. But it is no panacea: It was immediately attacked by some environmentalists, who complain that the land targeted for logging contains some of the pristine old-growth forest that has been at the heart of the timber wars. Some loggers, meanwhile, don't think the deal frees up enough timber. And there is no guarantee that Judge Dwyer will approve the agreement.    "The logging wouldn't be environmentally benign, and the agreement should not be seen in any way as an endorsement" of the Clinton forest plan, said Vic Sher, a Sierra Club Legal Defense Fund lawyer who has been one of the leaders of the legal assault that resulted in the logging bans. "But it preserves citizens' rights to improve the forest plan, including by going to court if necessary."  Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Bush Gains Two More Cabinet Members As Senate Confirms Thompson, Mineta
Text: WASHINGTON -- The Senate voted unanimously to confirm Tommy Thompson as secretary of health and human services and Norman Mineta as transportation secretary, bringing President Bush two steps closer to a full cabinet.    Elaine Chao, Mr. Bush's choice for labor secretary, is expected to sail through a Senate vote scheduled for Tuesday after yesterday's friendly hearing before the Senate health and education panel. At the hearing, Ms. Chao left open the possibility -- if she is confirmed -- of seeking changes in new ergonomics rules aimed at reducing repetitive-motion injuries on the job and in other controversial policies introduced by the Clinton administration.    Asked whether she would commit to implementing the rules, she said, "I understand the concerns people have on this. My commitment to you is that I will have an open and full dialogue with all of you. I will take every point of view into consideration."    Ms. Chao, who is married to Sen. Mitch McConnell, a Kentucky Republican, also said she would support Mr. Bush's position on giving communities flexibility on the minimum wage.    Under such a plan, local governments would have to maintain the current minimum wage of $5.15 but could effectively decide whether to implement any new increase mandated by Congress.    The Senate is also expected to vote Tuesday on Gale Norton for interior secretary.    The Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee approved her nomination yesterday in an 18-2 vote, with Democratic Sens. Charles Schumer of New York and Ron Wyden of Oregon voting no. "I strongly hope her record in office proves me wrong," said Mr. Wyden.    Environmental groups have lobbied against Ms. Norton's nomination. The former Colorado attorney general used her confirmation hearing last week to soften, and even reverse, some of her most contentious positions on issues such as global warming and the Endangered Species Act. Democrats now say her confirmation is all but assured.    The Senate's confirmation of Mr. Thompson to head the Department of Health and Human Services will place him in the middle of any clashes over abortion rights and Medicare reform. Democrats have criticized Mr. Bush's plans to initially offer a short-term prescription-drug plan just for poor retirees instead of all beneficiaries. At his confirmation hearing last week, Mr. Thompson assured lawmakers he would weigh their views on Medicare policy.    Abortion-rights groups have expressed worry over Mr. Thompson's statement during his hearing last week that he would review "safety concerns" about abortion pill RU-486, which won Food and Drug Administration approval in September.    As head of the department that oversees the FDA, Mr. Thompson could attempt to restrict or withdraw the abortion pill, known by the brand name Mifeprex.    But Democrats said they could tolerate some differences. The Wisconsin governor won praise for welfare-to-work programs in his home state and was confirmed on a 100-0 vote.    A spokesman for Mr. Thompson said he will sell most of his stocks, including those of cigarette maker Philip Morris Co., to avoid any conflict of interest as he takes over the agency responsible for health programs. According to his financial disclosure form, his Philip Morris holdings are valued at $15,000 to $50,000. The stocks are in a blind trust, and he "didn't know they were in there," said Kevin Keane, the spokesman. "He understands the need to sell them."    The Senate also unanimously voted to confirm Mr. Mineta, the only Democrat in Mr. Bush's cabinet and a former executive of Lockheed Martin Corp.    Mr. Mineta won praise from Senate Democrats and Republicans after pledging to modernize the nation's air-traffic system.    But the former Clinton commerce secretary and California congressman gave few clues on how aggressive he would be as a watchdog over the airline industry.    Meanwhile, Postmaster General William Henderson, 53, said he would retire at the end of May.    A successor will be picked by the Postal Service's board of governors, although no candidates have been named.    ---    Stephen Power contributed to this article.

Title: Pacific Northwest Facing Higher Prices in Wake Of U.S. Move to Add Salmon to Endangered List
Text: The booming Pacific Northwest may be inching closer to water restrictions and higher home and utility prices, following federal action to add nine species of wild salmon to the Endangered Species Act. One of those salmon, the Puget Sound chinook, is found throughout the lakes, streams and tributaries of the greater Seattle area which is home to about three million people. The others are found through much of the rest of Washington state, and parts of Oregon, including Portland. They include the Lower Columbia River chinook, Upper Columbia River chinook, Upper Willamette River chinook, Hood Canal chum, Columbia River chum, Upper Willamette River steelhead, Middle Columbia River steelhead and Ozette Lake sockeye. The listings represent the first federal species protection affecting such a populated area, and signal the Clinton administration's determination to appease environmental interests despite the burden it will put on local communities. "Writing off salmon is not an option," said Rollie Schmitten, director of the National Marine Fisheries Service that issued the listings. "Humans and salmon can peacefully coexist and even enhance each other's quality of life." But that won't be easy, or cheap. In anticipation of the action, officials of the three counties that comprise the Seattle area, King, Snohomish and Pierce, have drawn up a salmon recovery plan that calls for such steps as making golf courses use recycled water instead of local waterways. The plan also recommends that the counties upgrade old sewer systems, replant vegetation along stream banks and steer new development out of rural areas. "People have to be greener, quite frankly," said King County Executive Ron Sims, who estimates his county will have to spend $200 million over the next decade to carry out the plan. Others, though, say the salmon listings will exact too severe an economic toll. Besides the probability of higher sewer and water bills, for example, builders say Seattle's already high housing prices likely will climb even higher. The median price for a three-bedroom home in King County, where corporate giants such as Microsoft Corp. and Boeing Co. are located, has already nearly doubled to $255,000 over the past 10 years. "What will happen is there will be an artificial restriction of land supply," said Tom McCabe, executive vice president of Washington state's Building Industry Association, which is contemplating a suit to overturn the listings. "In our opinion, the Endangered Species Act is being used as an excuse here to stop growth." That sentiment is shared by many others in the Northwest, particularly in rural areas where farmers and ranchers could be required to significantly curtail their use of pesticides and water intake. Indeed, few counties outside the most populated ones in Washington state have prepared any recovery plans. "We have 38 counties and they are all over the map on how they view this problem," said Curt Smitch, an aide to Washington Gov. Gary Locke. Environmentalists hold little sympathy for the detractors, saying it was such practices as excessive building that pushed salmon to the brink of extinction in the first place. "It's time for all these people to join the 21st century," said Bill Arthur, Northwest regional director of the Sierra Club. Federal officials vow to see to it that the salmon are protected, through force if necessary. The unauthorized "taking" of an endangered species is punishable by fines or jail time. "Because the law requires that we recover a listed species, we will do that even if we must do that on our own," said Mr. Schmitten, who said the National Marine Fisheries Service would prefer to let communities come up with their own recovery plans. No enforcement is planned until after the marine fisheries service hammers out its recovery rules with state and local agencies over the next two months. Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Georgia-Pacific Agrees to Provide Woodpecker Shield
Text: WASHINGTON -- A major timber industry concern opted out of future legal logjams by volunteering to protect the red-cockaded woodpecker living on its land. Georgia-Pacific Corp., based in Atlanta, became the first business to commit to managing habitat for endangered species in what Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt hopes will become a trend. "This is an unprecedented agreement in terms of cooperation, in terms of the four million acres it protects, and in terms of the jobs it saves," Mr. Babbitt said at a news conference to unveil the plan. Georgia-Pacific President A.D. Correll agreed. "The plan embraces not just the letter of the law," he said, "but the spirit of the Endangered Species Act, while enabling us to continue managing our lands for commercial value." The agreement will protect 113 redcockaded woodpecker colonies -- one or more birds live in each colony -- which need relatively few old trees to maintain a suitable habitat. The colonies are scattered throughout four million acres of forest in the southeastern United States that is owned by Georgia-Pacific. As part of the nonbinding agreement, the company promised to uphold the Endangered Species Act and to maintain a 200-foot buffer zone around each woodpecker colony. Species that are listed as threatened or endangered under the federal law are protected from development. In addition, Georgia-Pacific will provide roughly 100 acres of foraging habitat for each colony, bringing the total protected land for all the birds to 56,000 acres. And selective tree-cutting in those areas will minimize Georgia-Pacific's losses. The accord follows a similar situation surrounding the California gnatcatcher in which real-estate developers cooperated with the government to develop private land that was also home to an endangered species. But in the case of the gnatcatcher, the government, in effect, exempted the owners of the bird's habitat from complying with the law's absolute prohibitions on killing any members of a protected species, as long as the landowners agree to preserve substantial parts of their gnatcatcher habitat. At the news conference, Mr. Babbitt hinted that arrangements to protect the red-cockaded woodpecker are in the works with other companies, but he declined to elaborate. He said he hopes the Georgia-Pacific agreement will prevent a crisis situation like the one that developed in the Pacific Northwest with the northern spotted owl. "The essence of this agreement is sitting down and negotiating to keep this thing out of the legal process," Mr. Babbitt said. Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Mutual Effort to Sustain Forests and Communities
Text: The issues involved in the Endangered Species Act are more complex than Kimberley A. Strassel acknowledged in her Oct. 19 editorial-page commentary "Owls of Protest." Anyone flying into the Northwest can see that the region's forests have been logged to excess. Clear-cuts and logging roads abound. The destruction of important habitat for endangered species such as spotted owls and marbled murrelets is not the only troubling result. This past forest "management" dumped sediments into spawning beds for wild salmon species, which are now endangered. Many jobs in this region are dependent on salmon and have been lost. Fortunately, there is a growing consensus among conservationists, forest workers and community activists that we can actively employ forest workers to restore our public watersheds -- and at the same time get some dollars from logs and other commodities that our forests can provide. But it takes thoughtfulness, creativeness and commitment to the long-term sustainability of our forests and communities. Robert Freimark The Wilderness Society Seattle --- The spotted owl debacle is just the tip of the iceberg for federal forest policy. The Forest Service, originally established to manage all the leftover land that couldn't be farmed or was unwanted by the railroads, is so completely hamstrung by Clinton-era regulations that a reformed ESA would release little timber. Right now, a home could be built for every single Katrina victim on the volume of trees that simply die each year on Forest Service lands in the West. An even greater amount of  housing could be built just using the growth, without reducing the standing inventory. And we're not talking about federal parks or wilderness areas, just national forests in the West. Arne Hultgren Professional Forester Mount Shasta, Calif.

Title: U.S. to Tighten Farmers' Water Supply in California in Effort to Save Salmon
Text: California's water wars are about to boil over again.    The federal Bureau of Reclamation is expected to announce today limitations on how much irrigation water will go to California farmers from federal dam systems this year, according to people familiar with the bureau's plans. The cuts are largely a result of California's drought, well into its sixth year. Even with the heavy storms lashing the state this week, rainfall remains about 40% below normal in most areas.    However, this year's water limits will be far tougher than they've ever been, partly because federal wildlife officials are forcing the bureau to conserve water that would otherwise go to farmers to try to save the fast-disappearing winter run of Chinook salmon up the Sacramento River, the key artery of the big federal water system known as the Central Valley Project. The salmon, which are listed as a threatened species under the federal Endangered Species Act, have seen their numbers reduced to 191 from 118,000 over the past 20 years, largely because the water system's dams and pumps kill many fish outright or make it impossible for them to spawn.    The restrictions are certain to trigger predictions of economic doom from farmers, many of whom will receive no federal water for the first time since the drought began. More significantly, the situation also will move toward center stage in the increasingly bitter national debate over the Endangered Species Act's impact on economic growth. The act is up for congressional reauthorization this year, and many business interests are calling for a major overhaul to reduce the economic cost of protecting wildlife.    In California, farmers contend that they are being sacrificed for a fish that even some biologists believe is too far gone to save. Environmentalists counter that farmers' voracious and inefficient water use -- farmers sop up 80% of the state's water resources but produce only about 3% of its economic output -- threatens not only salmon, but numerous other fish species and ultimately humans, since two-thirds of the states' 30 million people draw their drinking water from the same river systems used by the fish and the farmers.    "The federal bureaucracy has looked at a fish in trouble and farmers in trouble and chosen the fish," lamented Steve Hall, executive director of the Farm Water Coalition, a lobbying group for agricultural interests.    "That's ridiculous," says David Behar, executive director of the Bay Institute, an environmental group. "Farmers want to blame the species because it's been nearly exterminated by the farmers' (and the Bureau of Reclamation's) own practices."    The Central Valley Project normally provides about a third of the water used by farms in California, the nation's biggest agriculture state. Under the Bureau of Reclamation plan, farmers who received only 25% of their usual federal allotments last year will get no federal water this year.    Moreover, the bureau is contemplating reducing deliveries to so-called "water rights holders" -- farmers who owned water rights on the system's rivers before the Central Valley Project was constructed in the 1920s -- by about half. That is a potentially explosive move, because water rights holders, many of whom are among the biggest and most politically well-connected agricultural barons in the state, have always maintained that water rights laws and guarantees made by the bureau assure that they can't receive less than 75% of their allotments in a given year, no matter how severe a drought is. The matter likely would end up in court.    Barring months of heavy rain, farmers also face steep cuts in water deliveries from the state's other major water system, the state-owned State Water Project. State water officials have predicted that the state project may ship only about 20% of the water it sends to farmers in a normal year. That's actually an improvement: Last year, farmers got no state water. The overall impact on agriculture is likely to exceed $500 million, by some estimates. That's real money, but California's farm economy typically generates about $17 billion a year.    Both the state and federal water agencies' hands have been forced by National Marine Fisheries Service, which is charged with evaluating their impact on troubled species like the salmon. Federal biologists say fisheries service has ruled that Central Valley Project's normal operations seriously jeopardize salmon and thus must be modified under provisions of the Endangered Species Act.    Also figuring in California's water picture are two bills pending in Congress that would mandate changes in the way the Bureau of Reclamation operates and reduce agriculture's disproportionate hold on the state's water. The bills also would require more environmentally sound practices. Last week, Republican Gov. Pete Wilson appealed to Congress to hold off on the bills, but his request has been received icily. Although congressional critics have tried for years to pass legislation reforming bureau practices, many observers believe the bills will be enacted this year.  Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: REVIEW & OUTLOOK (Editorial): The Unspotted Sturgeon
Text: It's hard to believe, but the endangered species gears are grinding toward shutting down a good chunk of southern Alabama. The reason? A fish that either hasn't been seen in a decade or is plentiful from Montana to the Mississippi delta, depending on your taxonomic sympathies. This wrecking ball got swinging two years ago because of an article in the Bulletin of the Alabama Museum of Natural History. After examining a stuffed museum specimen, the authors tossed out 100 years of scientific opinion and declared the Alabama sturgeon a separate species from the Mississippi shovelnose. That was all the local U.S. Fish and Wildlife office needed to nominate the rarely spotted sturgeon for the endangered list. The "phantom fish" has become a running joke in the Alabama papers. State officials have launched a frantic hunt using gill nets, hoop nets, electroshock as well as the fish poison Rotenone, but can't seem to scare one up for view. Nobody will be laughing if the fish wins federal protection. Under a federal rule already drafted, the sturgeon would be awarded some of the nation's busiest commercial waterways as "critical habitat," including the lower reaches of the Alabama, Cahaba and Tombigbee Rivers. Owing to vague hopes that somewhere a lonely sturgeon may still be snuffling along these bottoms in search of snails and whatnot, dredging would be sharply curtailed, causing the navigation channels to silt up. If the state's barge traffic stops moving, 20,000 jobs could vanish. No wonder Alabama's entire Congressional delegation has come out against a listing. At a public meeting last month in Mobile, hundreds had to stand outside and peep through the open windows. These folks cheered the 59 speakers who bad-mouthed the sturgeon and booed the fish's only supporter. Jim Stewart, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife biologist who has taken on the mission of shepherding the sturgeon through the bureaucracy, is puzzled that "seemingly intelligent people" would rise up against Scaphirhynchus platorynchus. It's not the fish that scares folks, but the crowbar it would give litigious activists. Citizens in Alabama have heard tell of the spotted owl, exploited by environmentalists to kill off much of the Northwest timber industry. U.S. Senator Richard Shelby warned the Mobile meeting that an endangered listing can "open a pandora's box that would wreck thousands of lives." We don't question Mr. Stewart's devotion to saving rare species, but the law's myopic absolutism makes him a dangerous fellow. He takes credit for putting "15 or 20" on the list, so Mr. Stewart clearly knows how to work the process. It was Mr. Stewart who orchestrated the study that dubbed the sturgeon a unique species in the first place. He drafted the proposal for an endangered listing and plotted out its critical habitat. Inopportunely, he submitted his first package to Interior's Division of Endangered Species during the presidential campaign, and it quickly came back to him. But after Bill Clinton's election, he got a call from Washington inviting him to resubmit. His friends in the bureaucracy came to his rescue again when Alabama's Congressmen began throwing rocks at Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt. Mr. Babbitt promised to appoint an independent scientific panel, but somehow the job of picking the members landed back on Mr. Stewart's desk. Now a court has blocked the report. Mr. Stewart considers himself a simple scientist, but he clearly understands the importance of remedial flackery. He's frequently quoted in the Alabama press pooh-poohing the potential job losses, and he almost has a war going with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, which predicts that without steady dredging the rivers would be impassable in 12 months or less. The taxonomic questions, though, may be the real zinger for future preservationist battles. In Mr. Stewart's view, any population that undergoes a period of geographic isolation can be deemed a separate species, regardless of its potential for interbreeding with outsiders. If it looks different, it is different. And compared to the Mississippi shovelnose, the Alabama sturgeon has a bigger eye, and a slightly different arrangement of scales. "If that definition is adopted, we're all in trouble," says Mike Howell, an ichthyologist at Birmingham's Samford University. Mr. Howell led the recovery effort for Alabama's first endangered fish, the watercress darter. This time he's joined the sturgeon's opponents, and even briefed Mr. Babbitt on their behalf. Mr. Howell's point is well taken. It's inevitable that contiguous animal populations will get sectioned off by the spread of human societies. If geographic isolation becomes the legal rule, two guppies living on either side of a dam could be deemed different species. No wonder many ecologists are talking less about species these days and more about preserving habitats, where the animals and plants presumably can be left to figure out their own identities. But then that's been the problem with the Endangered Species Act from the beginning. Its scattershot attempt to preserve everything defies any sensible attempt to make rational choices. Scientists have only cataloged about three million of the estimated 100 million species on Earth. Unless the law is changed, it's only a matter of time before zoologists identify enough rare critters to make the planet legally off limits to humans.

Title: U.S. News: Owl Protections Questioned as Blazes Rage
Text: TALENT, Ore. -- The wildfires that ravaged the West Coast in recent weeks have renewed a debate in Oregon and Northern California over protections for the northern spotted owl, which some say prevented logging that would have thinned out forests and made the blazes less destructive. The northern spotted owl was listed as a federally threatened species in 1990, which added restrictions to tree-cutting on millions of acres of the region's national forests. Projects ranging from major logging efforts to small efforts to reduce the overgrowth of trees have been delayed or blocked by lawsuits under the federal Endangered Species Act. "We have crippled the whole process to do effective federal land management there," said John Bailey, professor of forestry and fire management at Oregon State University. The West Coast's latest wildfires are burning in California's wine country. But they have been fueled by dry brush, rather than trees deep in the forest where owls live. Cutting down trees in old-growth forests can threaten local wildlife like the northern spotted owl, but such activities are critical to reducing combustible fuel and lowering the risk of wildfires growing and spreading quickly, according to forest-management experts. Timber officials say reduced logging likely contributed to the ferocity of some of the latest wildfires. A 204,340-acre fire that leveled the small town of Detroit in northwestern Oregon spread in a section of national forest where only about one-third of the needed tree thinning was being done, said Mike Cloughesy, director of forestry for the Oregon Forest Resources Institute, a government agency funded by timber taxes. In 2016, the U.S. Forest Service began planning a 13,271-acre thinning project on Oregon's Mount Hood to help reduce what it called the high fire threat in the fir and pine forests there, including in a spotted-owl habitat. But the Ninth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals put a hold on the Crystal Clear Restoration Project in May after a lawsuit filed by environmental groups, in part because the area includes spotted-owl habitat. On Aug. 17, a lightning strike ignited a fire that forest-service officials say ripped through about 1,400 acres of the project area. The blaze grew to more than 17,383 acres. Activists at Bark, an environmental group that led the suit, said it is too early to draw conclusions about the fire's impact on the project area, pending post-burn assessments. They said the thinning project aimed to chop down too many of the large, old-growth trees that spotted owls depend on. "I have supported small-diameter tree removals, [but] what they want to take are the big trees that make the forest more resilient," said Brenna Bell, staff attorney and policy coordinator with Bark. A spokeswoman for the Forest Service declined to comment because of the pending litigation. The three-decade saga of the spotted owl has been one of the most contentious environmental issues in the Pacific Northwest, pitting conservationists against residents of small rural towns whose economies have shrunk along with a decline in logging, due in part to endangered-species protections. The amount of timber harvested from federal lands in Oregon plummeted from four billion board feet in 1990 to 486 million in 2019, according to the Oregon Forest Resources Institute, a state agency. Now, large wildfires that are primarily affecting rural communities are adding to anger over the issue. "Something needs to change. These cities are being leveled -- it is really devastating," said Nicole Ruyle, a real-estate agent whose family lost their vacation home to the wildfire in Detroit. Ms. Ruyle, who is married to a firefighter, said her in-laws lost their permanent home in the blaze. Lawmakers from the two major parties have blamed each other for either not easing endangered-species protection rules or underfunding thinning projects. Shane Jimerfield, program director for a nonprofit called the Lomakatsi Restoration Project that thins trees in thousands of acres of forests every year, said it is possible to do so while respecting the spotted owl's needs. "We don't clear cut, we do restoration," he said. "Yeah, if you want to go in and clear cut and liquidate the forest, you're going to come up against lots of barriers."   Credit: By Jim Carlton and Zusha Elinson

Title: Local Effort to Save Salmon Is Held Up by Infighting
Text: It was supposed to be a Northwest solution to a Northwest problem. Instead of letting the federal government -- or worse, a federal court -- dictate how to save the threatened Puget Sound chinook salmon, three counties around the Sound would rely on the region's vaunted cooperative culture to find the answer. The resulting partnership of local governments, environmentalists, business interests and Indian tribes -- dubbed the Tri-County ESA Response Effort -- was held up as a model for community action on endangered-species efforts. But things aren't going as planned. The group is months behind schedule, and its 18-member negotiating committee is beset by infighting. Some representatives say delegates from Seattle, Tacoma and Everett are holding up the process and are thwarting salmon recovery by stifling proposals on limiting development near water. The urban delegates retort that the proposed solutions are untested: While they may work for rural areas, the delegates argue, nobody knows if they'll work in cities. Recently, the cities' delegates have begun meeting on their own to come up with a strategy they think is workable. The result is frustration -- and yet another missed deadline. "We're frustrated because it's taking a hell of a lot longer than we thought," says Pierce County Executive Doug Sutherland. "In all probability, we'll find ourselves continuing to work until October." Unless the Tri-County team can buy itself more time -- which officials are trying to do -- a delay will have major consequences. That's because in June, the National Marine Fisheries Service plans to lay down its own rules for protecting salmon. If the tri-county group doesn't settle the matter by then, its plan won't be incorporated into the government's guidelines, called the "4(d) rule" for chinook. Not only is it easier for the plan to be adopted before a 4(d) rule is in place, but the rule's issuance throws the door wide open for lawsuits under the Endangered Species Act. The 4(d) rule is a set of regulations that prohibits the harming of at-risk salmon or degrading their habitat. Individuals can sue if they think the rule is being violated. A decade ago, there was so much legal action over alleged violations of the spotted owls' 4(d) that a federal judge called a halt to virtually all logging in millions of square miles in the Northwest. Indeed, the whole point of forming the tri-county effort -- named for King, Pierce and Snohomish counties -- was to avoid an explosion of lawsuits. To prevent a repeat of the spotted owl furor, the fisheries service is giving states an escape hatch to the 4(d): a so-called local-option alternative. Under the local option, any entity that comes up with an agency-approved conservation plan is exempt from Endangered Species Act prosecution. While it's possible to win an exemption after a 4(d) rule is handed down, environmental-policy experts say it is much easier to secure one beforehand. At the beginning, the tri-county panel seemed confident it could meet its schedule. The group started meeting in 1998 -- in anticipation of the chinook's listing as threatened, which came in March 1999 -- and last December elected officials boasted that the committee would have a plan by January, with a period for public comment in February. "I think we all said we can get this over with very quickly," says King County Executive Ron Sims. "That just didn't prove to be the case." Even a draft plan from the committee shouldn't be expected anytime soon, says panel member Sam Anderson, executive officer of the Master Builders Association of King and Snohomish Counties in Bellevue. "We can't get over all the hurdles that we have to get over" by June. The committee isn't without anything to show for its work. Members say they are close to agreeing on a package of basic guidelines for maintaining roads in an environmentally sensitive way, including repaving roads and repairing culverts. But there is bitter disagreement on other important matters. The biggest fight: whether all future development should be banned in a 100-foot-wide buffer zone along Puget Sound, Lake Union, Lake Washington and other salmon-supporting waterways in the three counties. The representatives from Seattle, Tacoma and Everett think that's far too strict -- particularly because, they argue, no one really knows whether creating buffer zones would have much of an impact in such an already-developed area. "The science of what is the right solution [for cities] is not as clear as it is in less-developed areas, where you have forested environments," says Martin Baker, the Seattle delegate. "There's a tendency to take science models applied to forested environments and apply them to urban environments, and it's not a very good model." For example, he says, the chinook in the urban areas of Elliott Bay, Lake Washington and Lake Union are either juveniles preparing for their journey to the Pacific Ocean or adults on their way back to spawning grounds. Since the fish are simply rearing or passing through those bodies of water, he argues, they may not need the same purity of water or gravel beds as in areas where the fish spawn. So, instead of a buffer, the three cities are preparing to propose a set of alternatives. One main element would be for the cities to hire scientists to figure out what salmon need when they are rearing or migrating. Another would have developers or homeowners intent on building within 200 feet of a waterway in any of the three municipalities be required to consult with a city inspector, as part of the permitting process, says Mr. Baker. The inspector would survey the site, impose conditions for approval designed to limit harm to salmon habitat and then follow up with the owner once the building is complete. All 18 negotiating-committee members would have to endorse that approach, which seems unlikely. The urban trio has been "plumbing new depths of pseudo-science," says Eric Espenhorst, a negotiating-committee member and a policy associate for Friends of the Earth in Seattle. "They're still casting about for a miracle solution here when the science is clear," he says. Another negotiating-committee member, Terry Williams, the fisheries and natural-resources commissioner for the Tulalip Tribe outside Marysville, says he doubts that some of the proposals from the "urban caucus," as he calls the trio, would pass federal muster because it doesn't ensure that the salmon runs will be replenished. "These are not fisheries people," says Mr. Williams of the three. "They're business people, planning people." Mr. Williams says he has some sympathy for his city colleagues, who are under political pressure to protect both business and fish. But he notes that Native Americans and fishermen are under no less stress. The tribe's unemployment rate is 26%; it's even higher among fishermen in the tribe. "If the cities or counties were facing even 7% or 8%, they'd be screaming," Mr. Williams says. "There's a huge dependence upon these resources . . . Fishermen have families and children to support and school and house payments." For all the tribes in the tri-county area, he says, ensuring that chinook runs recover "is extremely critical." Mr. Baker disagrees that the trio is engaging in pseudo-science, and disputes that the science on salmon recovery is clear-cut. And all the urban representatives say they do want to help salmon recover. But they say they are also trying to be practical about where they will get the greatest effort for their dollars. Mr. Baker points out that Seattle has already committed about $5 million to efforts in the Cedar River watershed, outside of Seattle -- which, he argues, is a better place to try to restore the salmon population than in a heavily urban area. He adds that the trio are consulting with their own scientists and those from Bellingham and Vancouver ports. Mr. Sims, the King County executive, vows that the Tri-County Salmon Response Effort won't produce an unsound plan. "We have said it's going to be a science-based solution, not a politically based solution," he says, adding, "I don't believe Seattle politically wants to be sued by environmentalists or the tribes for failure to adopt rules for salmon." Federal scientists will review the cities' proposal before the full committee discusses it, perhaps later this month. "I think [the scientists] are trying to be realistic" about the political situation cities face, says Bob Turner, Washington-area director for NMFS and the agency's emissary on the committee. Still, "if science says [the salmon] need cold, clean water, then they need it both in the city and rural environments." Meanwhile, some state officials have asked NMFS to put off the chinook 4(d) rule. The agency hasn't made a decision. Curt Smitch, special assistant for natural resources to Gov. Gary Locke, says Olympia favors a delay by the fisheries service. To be sure, he says, not everyone would be unhappy if the tri-county effort were to fall apart, leaving NMFS to levy its prohibitions and paving the way for a spotted-owl-size battle. "There are some people on both sides of the issue who think a train wreck would be a good thing," Mr. Smitch says. "Some people would want to use ensuing battles as a tool to get rid of the Endangered Species Act. . . And there are some on the other side who [want to] start filing lawsuits." ---                     Working Together    Here are the entities that make up the Tri-County ESA Response Effort    -- City of Bellevue   -- City of Everett   -- City of Seattle   -- City of Tacoma   -- Port of Seattle   -- King County   -- Pierce County   -- Snohomish County   -- Muckleshoot Tribe   -- Nisqually Tribe   -- Puyallup Tribe   -- Stillaguamish Tribe   -- Tulalip Tribe   -- Local environmental community   -- Master Builders Association   -- Boeing Co.   -- Wash. Title: Ruling Near In Wash. Water Case
Text: Washington regulators say they are within days of deciding whether a golf course co-owned by Paul Allen is illegally drawing irrigation water from the Sammamish River.    The Department of Ecology demanded a year ago that Mr. Allen, the Microsoft Corp. co-founder, and his brother-in-law, Brian Patton, prove that their 294-acre Willows Run complex in Redmond was in compliance with state water-rights laws. The documentation Messrs. Allen and Patton produced was deemed "unsatisfactory," according to Mary Getchell, a department spokeswoman in Olympia, and the agency continued its investigation.    Now, under increasing pressure from environmentalists, the department is ready to rule in the high-profile case, according to Ms. Getchell. She says the agency will next week either issue a so-called relinquishment order to stop the pumping or allow Willows Run to continue pulling about 50 million gallons annually from the river, home to a threatened population of Puget Sound Chinook salmon.    If the latter route is taken, the environmental community will be "outraged," says Rob Caldwell, executive director of the nonprofit Center for Environmental Law & Policy in Seattle. "To not move forward with a relinquishment order at this stage is unconscionable."    Willows Run officials say they aren't unlawfully irrigating their two Scottish-style, 18-hole golf courses. For one thing, maintains Larry Martin, vice president of real estate for Mr. Allen's Seattle-based investment firm, Vulcan Ventures Inc., Willows Run isn't drawing directly from the river, though he says it has a legal right to do so. Instead, he says, the complex is irrigating from a well on Willows Run grounds. (A spokeswoman for Mr. Allen said he was unavailable to comment.)    The DOE's response is that pumping from the well is the same as pumping from the Sammamish, because the well taps an aquifer that feeds the river.    For their part, environmentalists -- along with the Muckleshoot Indian Tribe, which owns the river's fishing rights -- insist the complex's irrigation system imperils a run of salmon listed under the U.S. Endangered Species Act. And they've seized on the dispute as a test of the state's commitment to saving at-risk fish.    "Willows Run is one of the most glaring examples of the Department of Ecology's failure to come to grips with how low-water flows impact salmon," says Michael Rossotto, legal director for the Washington Environmental Council in Seattle. State surveys of the Sammamish suggest that low flows, which result in warmer water, are killing fish.    DOE Water Resources Manager Keith Phillips, who oversees the case, didn't return telephone calls. Ms. Getchell, the agency spokeswoman, defends the lengthy investigation against complaints from environmental organizations, saying the department has proceeded cautiously because it expects Messrs. Allen and Patton to aggressively appeal any relinquishment order, and wants to make sure it has a bulletproof case. She insists that doesn't mean the agency has decided on a crackdown.    Ms. Getchell also points out that DOE officials have worked -- so far without avail -- to find an irrigation source other than the Sammamish for Willows Run. Talks with officials from Willows Run, environmental groups, the Muckleshoot tribe and King County haven't gone anywhere yet. Among the proposals still under consideration: having the golf complex buy irrigation water from Redmond at an annual cost of about $150,000, or having it lease Sammamish water rights owned by King County for a yet-to-be-determined price.    The Center for Environmental Law & Policy initiated these talks, which Mr. Caldwell, the center's executive director, describes as aimed at avoiding "going to court and getting in a big fight." Now Mr. Caldwell says "the environmental community is fed up" because Willows Run officials have made it clear they have no intention of paying to buy water when they can get it free from the ground.    "We have bent over backward for Willows Run, offering solutions essentially as a courtesy," he says. "In return, we get the argument that they can't afford to buy water. Pardon me, Paul Allen, but that's ridiculous."    Mr. Martin, of Vulcan Ventures, says it's environmentalists who are being ridiculous. "The fact of the matter is that Willows Run has legal water rights," Mr. Martin says. "So it wouldn't be a prudent business decision to say, `Oh, well, I'll just go out and buy water anyway.' Water is expensive."    In fact, Mr. Martin says, Willows Run would welcome a relinquishment enforcement order from DOE. "That might be a good avenue to get this resolved," he says. "We will appeal such an order as far as we need to, and we strongly believe that the courts will rule in our favor."    Should the DOE next week issue such an order, it would most likely be years before the dispute would be settled. Messrs. Allen and Patton would be able to appeal the decision to the state Pollution Control Hearings Board. If the board upholds the order, the owners can then appeal to superior court, and ultimately to the state Supreme Court.    The squabble dates to August 1993. That's when Willows Run, which opened in 1994, applied to the DOE for permission to convert old surface-water rights to groundwater rights.    The application put Willows Run at the end of a long queue for rights conversions and permits, and by June of 1998, the course's owners were still waiting for an answer. A Willows Run engineer wrote to the agency that summer and threatened to start drawing water from the river if the application wasn't acted on soon. Three months later, department officials documented that the course was in fact being watered with surface-rights water from the river, possibly in violation of state law. But the agency didn't move to enforce the law, mostly because spending cuts enacted by the Legislature in 1994 had slashed about 40 positions from the department.    Then, last summer, the department was able to hire several new compliance investigators, and conducted a new field survey of Willows Run, during which it was noted that a portable pump was taking water from the Sammamish. The department demanded that Messrs. Allen and Patton provide documentation showing the irrigation was legal, setting an Aug. 9 deadline.    "We found that the golf course was putting an incredible burden on the river," Ms. Getchell says.    At the heart of the dispute is whether Willows Run has valid surface-water rights to convert. The rights were granted to the site's previous owners in the 1950s. The DOE notes that under a 1967 Washington law, rights revert to the state if they aren't exercised for a period of five continuous years.    According to Mr. Martin, Willows Run doesn't necessarily dispute that the rights went unused for that period of time. But he contends that doesn't matter. Mr. Martin says that the 1967 law establishing the "use it or lose it" rule exempted water rights granted before 1967. "We've had two law firms and a water-rights expert opine on this, and they absolutely agree that we are exempt from the forfeiture law," he says.    DOE officials have long maintained that the 1967 law applies to all water-rights certificates, regardless of when issued. That means that if the agency issues a relinquishment order and Willows Run gets that order overturned on appeal, "certain aspects of Washington's water-rights laws could be turned on their end," Ms. Getchell says.  Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: U.S. News: U.S. Scraps Rules In Bid for Savings
Text: The Obama administration's campaign against "dumb" federal rules yielded a raft of proposals to slash paperwork and scrap some outdated regulations, but didn't touch many much-larger administration initiatives that have drawn fire from business interests and Congress. The White House said Thursday that agencies are moving immediately to consign some regulations -- many of them obscure -- to the trash heap. The administration highlighted a move by the Environmental Protection Agency to exempt the dairy industry from rules that treat bulk milk containers as if they were bulk oil containers, subject to standards designed to prevent oil spills. The administration said the exemption would save the dairy industry $1.4 billion over a decade. The International Dairy Foods Association said it welcomed the exemption, but said the administration should have gone further to free the dairy industry from the oil-tank rules. However, the estimated savings of costs and time from rolling back rules are a fraction of the tabs likely to be generated by rules in other programs that will continue. Business groups complained the White House review hadn't gone far enough. "This is progress. This is also not nearly enough," Bill Kovacs, a senior vice president at the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, said in a blog post on the group's website Thursday. Manufacturers and groups that represent the coal and oil industries are particularly worried about the EPA's efforts to regulate carbon dioxide as a pollutant and set tougher standards for power-plant emissions -- multibillion-dollar initiatives that have drawn opposition from various business interests and many members of Congress. Cass Sunstein, administrator of the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs and the overseer of the regulatory review, said the administration's moves could save "hundreds of millions of dollars" in the near term, and billions of dollars over the next decades. The White House said that after four months of scouring their books, federal agencies had identified ways to eliminate tens of millions of hours a year in paperwork burdens on individuals, businesses, and state and local governments. The savings come through steps such as adopting electronic records, eliminating overlapping reporting requirements and revamping programs such as the Commerce Department's licensing requirements for exporters. The regulatory review was launched amid a debate over whether the cost of complying with federal rules is a root cause of the job market's slow recovery. Mr. Sunstein's initiative -- rolled out Thursday in a speech to the conservative-leaning American Enterprise Institute and an opinion piece in The Wall Street Journal -- was met with concern from groups that favor a stronger federal role in the economy and skepticism from business organizations that want a lighter government hand in the market. The White House's call to review burdensome rules isn't binding for agencies considered independent of the administration, such as the Federal Communications Commission and the Securities and Exchange Commission. Neither the FCC nor the SEC submitted suggestions to the White House. --- Melanie Trottman and Louise Radnofsky contributed to this article. --- Rewriting Rules Among federal regulations to be scrapped or overhauled: -- The Interior Department will streamline Endangered Species Act rules. -- The Occupational Safety and Health Administration will cut paperwork required of employers. -- The Environmental Protection Agency will stop requiring air pollution 'vapor recovery systems' at gas stations. Credit: By Stephen Power

Title: Legal beat: Justices show concern over smut on the Net in indecency-law case
Text: WASHINGTON -- The Supreme Court, hearing a challenge to Congress's first attempt to regulate the Internet, appeared deeply concerned about the presence of smut in cyberspace.    Although the justices gave little indication of how they will ultimately rule on the law, which makes it a crime to transmit "indecent" material to minors, they seemed open to the idea that Congress had legitimate motives in getting involved. Several justices suggested that, even if this law is too harsh, other restrictions on Internet pornography might not be. That would be a blow to some of the plaintiffs in the case, who have argued that any regulation of Internet content violates the First Amendment's free-speech protections.    The law, known as the Communications Decency Act, makes transmitting indecent material punishable by two years in prison and a $250,000 fine. On-line services could be found to violate the law if they promote or advertise discussion groups or World Wide Web sites that contain such material. Last year, a federal appeals court in Philadelphia struck down the act, calling it a "profoundly repugnant" violation of the First Amendment and arguing in strident terms that the global computer network must be free from government intrusion.    But in oral arguments at the Supreme Court yesterday, the justices took on a decidedly more even-tempered tone. Justice Anthony Kennedy worried about "protecting kids who don't have parents at home" to monitor their behavior. Chief Justice William Rehnquist compared the law to regulations of radio stations that have been held to be constitutional and indicated that he didn't see why the Internet should be treated differently.    Although some of the justices have admitted to discomfort in discussing the complex world of new media, the court had clearly boned up on cyberspace jargon and brandished it in repeated questions about Web technologies. Justices John Paul Stevens and Antonin Scalia seemed interested in ways to "tag" Web sites as improper for minors, much as the proposed "V-chip" for television would allow parents to block sexually explicit or violent programs. Justice Sandra Day O'Connor inquired about special software designed to help parents control what their children do on-line.    But much of the morning turned into a lively and somewhat informal conversation about the demands of the First Amendment and the rigors of child-rearing. Bruce J. Ennis, who represented the 50-odd companies and groups that are challenging the law, and Seth Waxman, the lawyer for the government, are both seasoned Supreme Court advocates, and the justices appeared to enjoy the give and take.    Justice Scalia, who has nine children, chided Mr. Ennis for being unrealistic about the amount of time parents can devote to policing their children's activities in cyberspace. "If I had to be present every time my 16-year-old is on the Internet, I would know less about this case than I do today," he said. Justice Stephen Breyer twice mused about the prospect of high-school students mischievously describing their sexual experiences to one another on the Web. "Are you saying that every high-school student who would do this would be guilty of a federal crime?" he asked Mr. Waxman.    Despite their concern about children, the justices were obviously troubled by the rigidity of the act and the possibility that its stiff punishments might deter other kinds of speech on the Internet that are perfectly legal. Justice Kennedy fretted that the law might ultimately lead to the imprisonment of some librarians or the owners of novelty cafes that provide both coffee and Internet access. Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg compared the law to archaic provisions once on the books in many states that made it a misdemeanor to use bad language around women and children.    Industry observers fighting the act were encouraged by the court's interest in the technology. "When you understand the technology and see how the Internet really works and how parental control tools really work, then you realize that the Communications Decency Act, as currently drafted, won't work," said William Burrington, director of law and public policy at America Online Inc. Mr. Burrington believed the best way to protect children from adult material is through the use of software tools that block access to certain corners of the Internet as well as various ratings systems that have been applied to thousands of Web sites.    A decision in the case is expected in late June. The court has also been asked to resolve a separate New York case that challenges the indecency law; its outcome will presumably be determined by the court's ruling in this case. (Reno vs. American Civil Liberties Union)    Separately, in a victory for business, the court ruled that property owners can sue under the Endangered Species Act to limit government conservation efforts.    The controversial 1973 species-protection act contains a provision that lets citizens sue the government or anyone else who is violating it. The government had argued that the provision was intended to allow suits only by people with an interest in protecting wildlife. But the justices, in a unanimous opinion by Justice Scalia, said it also lets business sue to block overly intrusive environmental regulations.    "There's going to be a surge of litigation under the Endangered Species Act as a result of this," predicted Patrick Parenteau, director the Environmental Law Center at Vermont Law School. Mr. Parenteau said the decision may also be used to expand the scope of other laws with similar "citizen suit" provisions.    The case was filed by ranchers and others who object to restrictions on how much water can be drawn from reservoirs in southern Oregon and northern California for irrigation. The limits are designed to protect the habitat of two kinds of endangered fish: the Lost River sucker and shortnose sucker. The ranchers' suit claims that federal officials failed to follow a provision of the species act that requires consideration of the "economic impact" of preservation efforts. The case now returns to the lower court for a trial. (Bennett vs. Spear)    ---    Jared Sandberg contributed to this article. Title: Speed Limits Await Infrastructure Spree --- Environmental, historical and other rules will likely delay Trump wish list
Text: Corrections & Amplifications The Natural Resources Defense Council was incorrectly identified as the National Resources Defense Council in a Page One article on Feb. 13 about constraints facing planned efforts to address U.S. infrastructure needs. (WSJ Fedbruary 24, 2017) Almost sixty years ago, officials at California's transportation department unveiled a plan to build a six-mile freeway extension in Los Angeles County. They are still working on it. During the 1960s, the road plan appeared on track. In the 1970s, new environmental laws required voluminous studies and sparked legal fights between the neighboring towns of South Pasadena and Alhambra, which lie along its intended path. The project remains under review. "I am totally for the national and statewide environmental laws," said Hasan Ikhrata, executive director of the Southern California Association of Governments, who supports the extension project. Still, "sometimes it gets to be ridiculous." Many lawmakers and economists agree with President Donald Trump that America needs to fix a backlog of infrastructure needs, which the Transportation Department pegs at $926 billion. There's a similar agreement that conservation and preservation laws have helped mitigate damage on neighborhoods and the environment. A tour through of the nation's thorniest infrastructure struggles shows how these two goals are often in conflict. As a result, long, costly reviews and legal battles will likely confront Mr. Trump's efforts, just as they delayed much of President Barack Obama's 2009 economic-stimulus efforts. "You would have to fix some of these issues" said McKinsey & Co. partner Tyler Duvall, a DOT assistant secretary for policy in the George W. Bush administration, "in order to get the money into the system in a productive way." The president has yet to reveal details of his plan. On Jan. 24, Mr. Trump issued an executive order calling for expedited reviews on "high priority" projects. Before signing, he said: "We can't be in an environmental process for 15 years if a bridge is going to be falling down or if a highway is crumbling." Any significant new infrastructure-spending package would have to clear Congress. And executive orders alone won't do much to change a well-entrenched four-decade-old regulatory process, said Philip Howard, chairman of Common Good, a think tank favoring looser federal regulation. The White House didn't respond to requests for comment. Presidents Obama and George W. Bush sought to accelerate projects with executive orders. The Obama administration was concerned prolonged reviews could hold back stimulus spending under the 2009 American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, said Gary Guzy, general counsel at the White House Council on Environmental Quality under Mr. Obama, now a lawyer for Covington & Burling LLP. The act devoted about $48 billion to transportation, with a priority on "shovel-ready" projects. Getting money out the door took longer than expected. By January 2012, about $33.5 billion had been spent. In 2015, Congress exempted some bridge replacements from environmental reviews. Economists say well-designed infrastructure investments could increase economic productivity in the long term by making it easier for businesses to ship products and for employees to get to work. In advanced economies, boosting infrastructure investment by 1% of gross domestic product can raise overall GDP by 1.5% four years later, an International Monetary Fund study found. It can take decades to bring such investments to fruition. Reviews under the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966, the National Environmental Policy Act of 1970, the Endangered Species Act of 1973 and other laws can involve multiple agencies before permits are issued. Completing the process took an average of almost 10 years for major highway projects that received their final review in 2015, up from about five years in 2005, according to a study by Piet and Carole A. deWitt, retired Interior Department officials who have compiled some of the most comprehensive and frequently cited data on infrastructure-project reviews. It took 16 years to get permits for the Army Corps of Engineers to dredge the harbor in Savannah, Ga. At least 10 federal and state agencies in Georgia and South Carolina weighed in. Work began in 2015. In Mobile, Ala., local officials say a state proposal to bridge the Mobile River could expand business. Now, more than 73,000 cars daily cram a tunnel built for 36,000. The Port of Mobile, on the bay's western side, opened a new container terminal in 2008. A less-congested crossing could entice businesses to use the port, said Brian Harold, managing director of APM Terminals, a port operator in Mobile, which runs the new facility. "When prospective companies look at the eastern side of Mobile Bay and into Florida, the tunnel is always a topic of concern for them." The proposed $850 million bridge would generate $173 million to $690 million annually in increased economic activity, the state estimates. After 14 years of reviews, it is years away from construction. It is hard to compare project timelines before and after the 1970 environmental law because earlier projects weren't subject to the same reporting requirements. Anecdotally, it appears projects before that year moved more quickly. Ten years after the Interstate Highway System's 1956 creation, the government had inaugurated 21,000 Interstate miles. That drove public capital spending to record levels and helped boost the country's productivity, according to research by John Fernald, a senior research adviser at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco. The postwar U.S. construction boom eventually faced backlash among people who objected to the impact on neighborhoods, sensitive environmental locations and historical sites. The 1970 National Environmental Policy Act, or NEPA, made planners issue environmental-impact statements for their most significant projects detailing how they would alter surroundings while offering ways to mitigate damage. NEPA gave environmentalists and conservationists a voice in planning, allowing them to sue if they believed developers weren't properly following the law. Today, the law has become so deeply ingrained that officials often spend years working through every detail to avoid suits, even if an environmental-impact statement isn't required. "There's a lot of defensive medicine built into it," said John D. Porcari, Maryland's former transportation secretary, who served in the Obama administration and is now an executive at Parsons Brinckerhoff Inc., an engineering and consulting firm. Environmental groups have found themselves making the same case, on the grounds that more efficient reviews would let planners devote more energy to mitigating damage, according to Deron Lovaas, senior policy adviser at the National Resources Defense Council, an environmental group "I don't think unnecessary delay serves anyone." Almost 100 NEPA-related lawsuits hit federal agencies every year. One, filed by North Carolina environmental groups, spent four years in court before a resolution last year let the state replace the deteriorating Herbert C. Bonner Bridge, which links Hatteras Island to the mainland. Since opening in 1963, the 2.7-mile bridge on the Outer Banks has been scoured by wind, water and hurricanes. State officials said it has reached the end of its life. Environmental groups challenging a $246 million replacement said the new bridge would illegally disturb a wildlife refuge. Construction, begun in 2016, is scheduled for 2019 completion. In 2014, Oklahoma discovered cracks on a 79-year-old bridge between Purcell and Lexington, about 45 minutes south of Oklahoma City. State officials launched an expedited effort to replace it. Because of the bridge's historical significance as a Depression-era project, they first needed to consult Oklahoma's historical-preservation office under the 1966 federal preservation act. Then officials needed to find a way to protect the Arkansas River shiner, a threatened minnow under the endangered-species act. The state plans to begin work in 2018. "It's hard to explain that to our constituency," said Mike Patterson, director of Oklahoma's transportation department, "because for them it's illogical." As an example of how things should work, Mr. Porcari, the former Maryland transportation chief, cites the renovation of the Woodrow Wilson Bridge connecting Maryland and Virginia. After years of lawsuits almost killed the project, officials revived it in 1999, inviting environmentalists and community groups to planning meetings to discuss how to offset the new bridge's effects. They agreed to restore the nearby Anacostia River, including cleaning up an illegal landfill. The revamped review was completed in 2000 and the new bridge opened in 2006. Today, the landfill is a wetland where wild rice and cattails thrive. Cormorants, herons and egrets populate the cleaner river. In Southern California, planning for the State Route 710 extension continues to divide South Pasadena and Alhambra. During the 1960s, the state prepared by buying homes along its proposed route. After the 1970 environmental law, South Pasadena sued to block construction, saying the state hadn't followed the act's review process. Residents feared the highway would split the town in two. Neighboring Alhambra argued the highway would ease congestion. The 1973 lawsuit touched off a 25-year effort to revise the proposal, which succumbed to another lawsuit in 1999 by South Pasadena. Planning efforts since have focused on a tunnel, which state officials estimate would generate up to $1.59 billion in net benefits over 20 years. The state is starting to sell the homes it bought 50 years ago for the roadway. Opponents in South Pasadena worry a tunnel could weaken the ground under its historic Craftsman houses. "This is something that can never be built," said Joanne Nuckols, 73, a board member of a local preservation group who has been fighting the road for 30 years. Alhambra Council member Barbara Messina, 76, has been advocating for the extension since 1978. "God forbid we had people like that when we had our major infrastructure projects done," she said. "We would never have gotten anything done." Credit: By David Harrison

Title: Feds to Ease Permit Delays For Coastal Construction
Text: Get set, Lake Washington: The hammering and nailing is about to resume.    Federal officials plan to ease some of the construction backlog created after the chinook salmon was listed as a threatened species.    Since the chinook was listed in the spring of 1999, plans to build new docks, repair sea walls and carry out other projects on the region's major shorelines have encountered lengthy delays as officials tried to balance urban development with the requirements of the federal Endangered Species Act. Waits of a year or more have been common.    Now, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, working with two other federal agencies, is finalizing plans to relieve the mess that has frustrated property owners, idled construction workers and left the agencies with a record backlog of permit applications.    "There is a light at the end of the tunnel," says Gail Terzi, environmental analyst for the Army Corps' regulatory branch in Seattle.    It's about time, say property owners.    "They've taken too long to come up with a process," says Jim Stanfill, a manager for consulting services at Redmond-based Microsoft Corp., who is frustrated with his relatively short three-month-wait. The delay was one more nuisance in an already lengthy permitting process, says Mr. Stanfill, who has been awaiting clearance to build a 5-by-30-foot dock off his Kenmore waterfront home.    "I thought we would have had it by now," he says, of the project he estimates will take two days. But Mr. Stanfill's patience was already worn thin by the long permitting and public-notice requirements by the city, county and state -- long before he even got to the Army Corps. "We should have done this five years ago," he says, "before salmon became an issue."    How does a private homeowner's plan to build a dock run into so much bureaucracy about salmon?    It starts with the Army Corps. Any project in navigable waterways or any filling of wetlands requires a permit from the agency, a process that used to take days or weeks, officials say.    But then came the Endangered Species Act. Under that law, any agency overseeing a project that receives federal funding or requires a federal permit -- including almost anything along the coast and major inland waterways -- must consult with the agencies overseeing the listed species. With salmon, that means the National Marine Fisheries Service; with the bull trout, it's the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.    The three agencies need to consider what kind of impact the project will have on the listed species and identify ways to prevent any adverse effects before they will approve a permit application.    Corps officials say that choreographing the process is extremely cumbersome and time-consuming -- and that they haven't gotten the staff they need to handle the extra work. "Our backlog has doubled, our workload is way up, and our staffing has remained constant," says Patricia Graesser, a spokeswoman for the Army Corps in Seattle. In her office, about 20 people process permit requests, with some handling up to 100 applications at a time.    As Ms. Terzi says, "If we can just get one thing off our desk, it's a joyous occasion."    Over the past several weeks, the Army Corps and the two fisheries services have been grouping together similar types of projects -- such as dock repairs -- to conduct one overarching study into the biological impacts of the projects, instead of studies for each individual project. The agencies then agree on how large an effect such projects will have on salmon and bull trout.    Under the new plan, which is being finalized by the three agencies' staffs, these projects would get the go-ahead rapidly if they follow certain standardized requirements.    Applicants wanting to build docks, for example, would have to follow restrictions on when they can build, how many pilings they can use and how much light they need to let filter through to the water, says Gordon Zillges, a fisheries biologist for the National Marine Fisheries Service in Lacey.    Ms. Terzi says roughly 25% of the Army Corps' current applications, mostly those proposing simple designs, would be able to use the new procedures.    This "programmatic" approach would speed up approval over the one-at-a-time process the agencies have been pursuing, Mr. Zillges says. Although programmatics for the most complicated projects, such as road construction, are possibly one or two years away, he says, the agencies expect to finish their requirements for the more-routine projects that don't have a big impact on salmon in the next couple months.    An end to the delays can come none to soon for homeowners. Many support restrictions to help salmon recover, but assail the red tape that has held up their projects.    Paul Song, chairman of Aris Corp. in Bellevue, Wash., has been watching part of the existing dock at his Medina home sink into Lake Washington over the past 16 months, as he has waited for approval on his application to replace creosote-treated pilings, drive new untreated wood supports and extend the dock. The bureaucracy "frustrates people who do want to see good government policies," says Mr. Song. "It's hard to believe that a homeowner on Lake Washington trying to repair an existing dock is really a true threat to salmon."    Property owners aren't the only ones frustrated. Companies that specialize in waterfront construction are especially bitter that the slow pace of permit approval has tied them up at the height of their construction season.    "It has created a vortex," says Steve Zuvela, permit-department supervisor for Waterfront Construction Inc. in Seattle, which is waiting on permits from a year ago for several projects. "You throw a permit in and it disappears."    Barges and excavators meant for pier repairs and other shoreline projects sit idle behind his offices, says Mr. Zuvela. The company now has 40 employees, when in a normal summer it would have more than 55 on its payroll. "We've had people quit, [and] we've had to lay some people off," he says.    Greg Ashley, permit coordinator for the marine division of Sierra Construction Inc. in Redmond, echoes those concerns.    "We've had lots of [customers] just say `The heck with it,'" he says. Even worse, he says, they find someone who will do the work without getting the necessary permits. He has told local authorities of three instances of major dock work being done without a permit. (Both the National Marine Fisheries Service and the Army Corps say they haven't received an increase in reports -- usually by neighbors -- of work being done without a permit.)    The company has nearly $500,000 of projects that have been on hold for months, says Mr. Ashley. Instead of nine employees during the summer, the company now has three.    "This is supposed to be our busy season," he says.  Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal
