Title: A Plucky Family Fights for Survival In a Montana Valley --- Strangers in a Strange Land Face Hostility and Death; The Lone Wolf Syndrome
Text: NINEMILE VALLEY, Mont. -- They were a perfect match. He was a loner seeking a companion. She was a drifter searching for a home. Together, the pair -- let's call them the Grays -- made a life for themselves on a hillside in this rural valley 20 miles west of Missoula. Soon they had a number of frisky children, and just keeping them fed was a chore. The parents relied on the federal government for help in a part of the country where mistrust of Uncle Sam runs deep. While certain neighbors were friendly, others hated the Grays. They were outsiders, and occasionally they would get rowdy. In early June, the mother of the Gray brood disappeared in the woods. Her body hasn't been found, but a fisherman found the neckband she wore, in a stream about two miles from her home. Investigators haven't found a killer. The father, suddenly the sole provider, was a "super-dad," says a federal official who kept track of the family. But now he, too, is gone. He was struck and killed by a hit-and-run driver as he crossed the Interstate Sept. 1. "Jiminy," exclaims Ed Bangs, the federal official. "You can't buy a lucky break sometimes." Now, the six Gray offspring are orphans. With further government help, they might make it. But, considering their family history, no one can be certain. The Grays are wolves. For the first time since 1930, when ranchers, hunters and the government had killed off the wolves in these parts, Northern Rocky Mountain gray wolves are making a comeback under the protection of the Endangered Species Act of 1973. Once plentiful throughout North America as far south as central Mexico, wolves all but disappeared except in Canada, Alaska and Minnesota. Since 1987, government officials have been trying to get the Northern Rocky Mountain gray wolf off the endangered species list by maintaining at least 10 breeding pairs in each of three locations for three consecutive years. In Montana, the Gray family advanced farther south from Canada than any other known Montana pack. Their saga, however, illustrates how difficult bringing wolves back to the American West is turning out to be. False notions about wolves are one major hurdle. Many ranchers and others still view the animal, a relative of the domestic dog, as a threat to their livelihood and lives. Actually, wolves prefer to make a meal of deer or elk, though they will kill sheep and cattle and, sometimes, pets. They aren't inclined to harm people. Still, "wolves are going to be nothing but controversial from now on," says Steven Fritts, Northern Rocky Mountain wolf coordinator for the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. The Gray family's travails began last year when the female was raising a litter of pups in the Pleasant Valley area of northwest Montana. In early September 1989, a federal animal-control official shot her from a helicopter with a tranquilizer dart. The wildlife service had decided that the wolves were too close to ranches and that a move 65 miles northeast to the "wolf recovery area" in and around Glacier National Park was in order. Instead of taking care of the pups after they were moved by helicopter and released into the wild, the mother took off. For wolves, the instinct to return home is even stronger than the instinct to care for their young. With their mother gone, wildlife officials hoped, the pups might hook up with another pack. But they starved to death. Their mother, meanwhile, had headed south. She crossed roads and forded rivers. She even swam the Hungry Horse reservoir, but failed to find home. Four months and hundreds of miles later, "she met a guy around Missoula," in the words of Mr. Bangs. "They had some pups." In some ways, the Ninemile area, the place they chose to live, was ideal for starting a new pack. The pair found an old coyote den that reached back five feet into a hillside. A quarter-mile away, a creek provided plenty of water for a nursing mother with six pups. The newborns also ate the regurgitated food of their parents. And later the family would gather at a rendezvous site, to share pieces of meat from the latest kill and howl a little. As their parents hunted, the pups played with bones and skulls leftover from previous meals. Studies of the Gray family's scat prove that they didn't kill any livestock. But the male did have one bad habit: He attacked dogs. Maybe he saw them as a threat to his territory and his pups. A collie named Keena got a bloody gash on the belly. Shadow, a Labrador retriever, was bitten on the ear. Such incidents strengthen the view among many ranchers and hunters that wolves are a menace. Their efficient answer to the stiff federal fines and jail terms for harming them: Shoot, shovel and shut up. A retired rancher was the last person known to have seen the mother alive. She was chasing gophers across a field. In early June, the radio collar the wildlife service had put on her stopped emitting signals. On July 4, a fisherman found the smashed collar in a trout stream. The father of the six motherless pups assumed their care. He would make a kill, then lead them to the meal. Mr. Bangs, the wildlife official monitoring the situation, expected that the wolf would soon be teaching the pups to hunt. But more trouble was looming. One night in early August, the father wolf crossed the valley and ran into a helpless, 13-year-old dog named Bear and cut his throat. His owners, Shirley and Fred Hager, saw the wolf in the headlights of their car as they returned home from a potluck dinner. They had urged others not to shoot the wolves, but the death of their dog brought them to this conclusion: Ninemile Valley is no place for Canis lupus. Three weeks later, a fisherman reported that a big dog had been killed by mile marker 81 of Interstate 90. It was actually a male wolf, hit by a speeding vehicle. The job of looking after the pups, who are now six months old, has fallen to Michael Jimenez, a biologist for the wildlife service. Soon after the pups were orphaned, he stood in a moonlit field and howled. His first call was a long, deep monotone: "Ooooooooo." The second started deep, then rose to a higher pitch: "Owwwww-oooooooo." Six pups jumped from the woods. But they quickly realized he was a fake and ran off. Mr. Jimenez feeds the young wolves deer, which they devour down to the bones. Sometimes they return for the bones. Once the pups are grown, wildlife officials expect they'll be doing their own hunting. Early one morning, Mr. Jimenez, a retired rancher named Ralph Thisted and a reporter peer through binoculars from the loft of an old barn, hoping to spot the young wolves. As dawn casts a dim light on the field, a pair of pups the size of collies emerge from the woods, soon to be joined by two others. They stop to frisk at the base of a cottonwood tree, then head for an open area. "Boy, I hope they don't do that in hunting season," whispers Mr. Jimenez. Hunting season for deer and elk began Oct. 21. When it ends in late November, nearly everyone expects that there will be fewer wolves alive in Ninemile Valley. Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: REVIEW & OUTLOOK (Editorial): Power to the People
Text: This begins with the admission that even we have to stifle a yawn when federalism is mentioned. The problem isn't the basic constitutional setup or the brilliance of the states as laboratories for innovation. The drowser is the first three syllables, "federal." The point to keep in mind is that federalism is the opposite of federal. A report on federalism recently submitted to the Domestic Policy Council at the White House is in fact a lively discussion of how the country went wrong in turning the states into "satrapies" of a "virtually omnipotent national government." The key idea is power: who's got it, how it got there and how to get it back to the states and localities. First, a quiz in the spirit of the bicentennial of the Constitution: In the Federalist Papers, Madison wrote, "the powers reserved to --- will extend to all objects which, in the ordinary course of affairs, concern the lives, liberties, and properties of the people." If you said "the federal government," guess again. The correct answer is "the several states." The 13 states agreed to a Constitution that enumerated the specific powers the federal government would have, but the 10th Amendment was included to make clear that everything not listed was left for the people and the states. The federal government was in no way supposed to be the major player in the political power game. Times changed with the New Deal, where the switch in time that saved the nine Supreme Court justices from FDR was that Congress could do whatever it wants. Congress has by now packed itself a kit bag of ways to foist itself on the states: There are direct orders, such as the requirements of the Davis-Bacon Act, Endangered Species Act and Occupational Safety and Health Act. There are "crosscutting" requirements, where grants are tied to social and economic policies of Congress, such as nondiscrimination under the Civil Rights Act and environmental rules under the Clean Air Act and Endangered Species Act. There are "crossover" sanctions, as where highway funding is conditioned on adhering to the 55-mph speed limit. Then there is "partial pre-emption," where the feds set the minimum or maximum standard for state rules; the Water Quality Act actually says, "if a state does not issue regulations acceptable to the U.S., then a federal agency or department will do so." Washington is not entirely to blame. The states were perfectly happy to apply for federal transportation aid when governors and mayors thought that they could get subways and bridges built for nothing. Many learned the hard way that with federal money comes federal mucking-up of these projects. The Reagan administration has tried to wean the states off Washington. Its welfare-reform proposals center on solving the problem at the state level. Thanks to Congress running out of money, we've reached the end of revenue sharing. The federalism report criticizes the administration's support, recently rescinded, for a national speed limit. It says much more needs to be done, including vetting proposed legislation for a "federalism assessment." The problem may be partly self-correcting. Federalism will get a boost by necessity. The spendthrifts in Congress no longer have as much pelf to throw to states in return for obeying their will. The states, many having required balanced budgets, are consequently in much better shape to go their own ways.

Title: Clinton Administration Plans to Remove Bald Eagles From 'Endangered' List
Text: The American bald eagle is likely to be taken off the federal list of endangered species next year, a move environmentalists hail as one of the great conservation success stories of the century. At the beginning of the Independence Day weekend Friday, President Clinton announced the administration's plan to remove the majestic bird from protection under the Endangered Species Act. Assuming no scientific evidence surfaces to undermine the decision during a final review, federal officials say, the bald eagle will lose its "threatened" status in approximately one year. "I can think of no better way to honor the birth of our nation than by celebrating the rebirth of our proudest living symbol," President Clinton said, in a Rose Garden ceremony at the White House, beside a domesticated eagle named Challenger. The action would cap a remarkable comeback for a bird whose mighty wingspan and proud visage prompted this country's founders to designate it as America's national symbol in 1782. Then, the eagle's population numbered as many as 100,000 nesting pairs, researchers estimate. But factors, including development of eagle habitat and widespread use of the insecticide DDT during the 20th century, reduced the eagle to as few as 417 nesting pairs by 1963. Yet the bird staged a rapid recovery after being listed as threatened when the Endangered Species Act was enacted in 1973. The recovery was helped by the Environmental Protection Agency's step in 1972 to ban DDT, which had caused the shells of eagle eggs to thin after females ingested it by eating contaminated fish. The act also prevented developers from encroaching on any eagle habitat, sparing nesting trees and a wide perimeter of foraging ground. As a result, the bald eagle has rebounded to nearly 6,000 nesting pairs in the lower 48 states and has even returned to the skies over big cities such as Seattle and Tampa, Fla. "This demonstrates that the Endangered Species Act actually does work," said John Flicker, president of the National Audubon Society, the big conservation group in New York. A number of other species have thrived under the act. The American alligator and Pacific gray whale, for instance, have regained enough numbers to be removed from the endangered-species list. Federal authorities are considering removing from the list two more species in the lower 48 states: the grizzly bear and the gray wolf. It is likely, however, that environmentalists will oppose such a move out of concern that animals would be subject to too much pressure from hunters. Some conservationists also continue to worry about the bald eagle. Although the bird would still be protected from hunting and nest destruction by the Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act and the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, they say developers will be free to destroy the surrounding habitat. This is especially a threat, they say, in heavily populated areas such as Maryland and Florida where populations of bald eagles have jumped. The bald eagle could be reclassified as endangered should numbers again decline. "We are basically putting the eagle out there, and it will be a little more vulnerable," said Al Louis Cecere, president of the National Foundation to Protect America's Eagles, a conservation group in Pigeon Forge, Tenn. "But you've got to let them spread their wings and hope for the best." Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: A Weekly Report From The Wall Street Journal's Capital Bureau
Text: CLINTON'S LIST of potential Supreme Court nominees grows longer. Former Virginia Gov. Baliles's name surfaces, given the president's desire for a "big" person with public experience. Another possible candidate is former ABA president Talbot D'Alemberte; Clinton aides also are looking at state Supreme Court Justice Shirley Abrahamson of Wisconsin. Hoping to refute charges that Solicitor General Days is too liberal, his backers point out that he has taken flak in civil-rights circles for expressing skepticism about some minority set-aside programs. Hispanic groups push hard for one of their own, but not necessarily moderate federal Judge Cabranes; the Latino Issues Forum urges Clinton to appoint Civil Rights Commission member Cruz Reynoso. Despite his reluctance last time around, Education Secretary Riley, a former governor, is seriously considered. THE U.S. LOOKS to Russia to bring the Serbs back to the table. Currently, the Serbs will talk only to Moscow's envoy. In Sarajevo, U.S. special emissary Redman and his Russian counterpart are coordinating their activities every couple of hours. To mollify Yeltsin, who was upset that he wasn't warned of the Gorazde airstrikes, the U.S. has told U.N. officials to do a better job of communicating with member states. As the Serbs grow more aggressive following the NATO airstrikes over Gorazde, Western officials get increasingly edgy about "nontraditional military responses," such as taking hostages or ambushing food convoys. A number of U.N. peacekeepers are already being detained. LOBBYISTS LINE UP to do battle over the GATT accord. Textile mogul Roger Milliken hires economist Pat Choate and former Labor Department official Steve Hofman to battle the trade pact's provisions for a new World Trade Organization; Hofman hires the law firm Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher to analyze the WTO's dispute-settlement mechanisms. Micron Technology, with Intel, Chrysler and others, seeks legislation toughening U.S. antidumping policies and uses former Commerce Department official Gilbert Kaplan. Others joining the cause include former U.S. trade negotiators Alan Wolff and Robert Lighthizer. But companies including Caterpillar, IBM and Cargill use former Commerce official Gary Horlick to fight the effort. SASSER EMERGES as the preferred candidate of some Southerners and senior lawmakers to succeed Senate Democratic leader Mitchell. They believe Daschle, the only declared candidate so far, is moving too fast. He was first elected only in 1986. But Daschle continues to gain supporters, including a couple who privately joined after their first choice, Ford, announced yesterday he won't seek the post. CLINTON ECONOMIST Alan Blinder pulls out of administration dealings with the Fed while he waits for his long-promised nomination to the central bank to clear the sluggish White House personnel machinery. Economic advisers interview four finalists for the other Fed vacancy, but Bentsen has yet to meet with the staff choice. CHANCES DIM for passage of Superfund legislation this year. Rep. Swift concludes that negotiations between industry and environmentalists are deadlocked over the bill's cleanup standards; General Electric is said to be particularly balky. EPA's Browner tries to broker a solution, but if she can't deliver quickly, the bill will probably die. TAX RECORDS released by the White House show that Hillary Rodham Clinton invested $473 in South Africa's De Beers Consolidated Mines Ltd. in 1979, at a time when civil-rights and student groups were calling for a boycott of South African stocks because of apartheid. She sold the shares in January 1980, for about $770. COMPROMISES ARE SOUGHT on universal coverage for health care. "There is a growing understanding that at some point we may need an employer mandate," Sen. Lieberman tells a forum of moderate and conservative Democrats. Some lawmakers discuss a trigger or "default" mandate that would go into effect at a designated time if universal coverage isn't achieved, but others say such a scheme would be too cumbersome. Sen. Packwood, the top Finance Committee Republican, makes a distinction between requiring employers to provide insurance and requiring them to pay for part of the insurance their workers buy. Bentsen suggests lengthening the phase-in period or scaling back the benefits package to help keep costs down. As Senate Democrats gather for their weekend issues-retreat, Mitchell's foregoing a Supreme Court seat "enhances his stature as a real broker of health reform," says Sen. Daschle. MINOR MEMOS: For a $100,000 contribution to the party, GOP fat cats meeting in New York later this month will get a briefing and photo opportunity with "special guest" Richard Nixon. . . . The Iowa City office of GOP Rep. Leach, the first couple's chief Whitewater tormentor, is located on South Clinton Street. . . . Justice Department auditors say the U.S. Marshals Service improperly donated $51,000 in seized furs to a thrift shop -- including a shabby jaguar coat that sold for $50 in violation of the Endangered Species Act.

Title: U.S. News: Bird Stays Off the Endangered List --- Conservation efforts are deemed enough for greater sage grouse in California and Nevada
Text: Voluntary conservation measures have been enough to keep a population of greater sage grouse in California and Nevada off the endangered species list, federal officials said Tuesday -- a decision that could have a broad impact on the West's economy. While the announcement by Interior Secretary Sally Jewell affects only an area of about two million acres straddling the two states, some see it as a signal her agency won't move to list the species as endangered in a habitat spanning 165 million acres in 11 Western states. Such a listing, many businesspeople in the West fear, would lock up land from mining, ranching and other activities and cripple the region's economy. Environmentalists sharply criticized Tuesday's decision, saying anything less than endangered-species protection would condemn the bird to a decline toward extinction. Throughout the West, the sage grouse population is thought to number up to 400,000. The area Ms. Jewell targeted is home to an estimated 9,000 of the birds living in isolation from larger groups. "The population is so small and the threats are so imminent that an ESA [Endangered Species Act listing] has to be triggered," said Erik Molvar, a wildlife biologist with WildEarth Guardians, a group that has pushed for the protection. Ms. Jewell said a key factor in the decision was what she called successful efforts by a bistate conservation program to remove threats against the greater sage grouse in that area. "Nice going everybody, nice going," Ms. Jewell said at a news briefing in Reno, Nev. "You are all part of an epic collaboration." Over the past 15 years, representatives from the states, local communities, tribes and businesses have worked to preserve the sage grouse. Efforts have included removing fences and invasive trees and improving livestock management. A ground-dwelling bird up to 30 inches tall, the greater sage grouse uses sage and other vegetation to hide from predators. Loss of sagebrush habitat has contributed to the bird's numbers' falling so low that the Fish and Wildlife Service in 2010 determined it was a candidate for protection under the Endangered Species Act. Fearful that an endangered listing would close off federal lands and cause economic hardship, as happened when the northern spotted owl was listed as threatened in 1990, many Westerners have been working to head off a similar designation for greater sage grouse. Ms. Jewell's agency has until Sept. 30 to determine if a listing is warranted for other parts of the West. Federal officials said they have been pleased with the extent of voluntary conservation measures outside California and Nevada as well. Credit: By Jim Carlton

Title: Oregon Dam Becomes Front Line In War Pitting Fish Against Power
Text: One of the smallest hydropower dams in the Northwest is the new battleground in the power struggle between fish and electricity. The U.S. Forest Service wants Portland-based PacifiCorp to remove the Soda Springs Dam on the North Umpqua River in Oregon as a precondition for the federal government's relicensing of seven of the utility's dams further upriver. The agency's insistence has so angered PacifiCorp that its negotiators recently walked out on relicensing talks that had been going on for seven years. According to PacifiCorp, the environmental benefits of dismantling Soda Springs, which would potentially return as much as eight miles of salmon spawning grounds to their natural state, simply wouldn't be worth the economic losses the company would suffer. What's more, the utility argues, yielding to the Forest Service's stipulation would set a dangerous precedent -- for PacifiCorp and every other utility in the region that relies on hydropower. "We took a look at what the Forest Service was saying and realized this could apply to a number of dams, ours and others, that are coming up for relicensing in the next decade," says Terry Flores, hydro-licensing director for PacifiCorp, a unit of Glasgow-based Scottish Power PLC. "We could not agree to a decision that would have such far-reaching consequences." The federal licenses for hundreds of dams in the region will expire over the next 10 years. Given that and the host of listings issued in the 1990s under the Endangered Species Act, power companies are preparing for pitched battles over relicensing. What took PacifiCorp by surprise was the Forest Service's involvement, and its citing of the Northwest Forest Plan as the basis for insisting that Soda Springs be torn down. The 1994 forest plan ended commercial logging on 80% of 24 million federally managed acres in Western Washington, Oregon and Northern California. Brokered by President Clinton, it resolved a host of lawsuits between timber companies and environmental organizations that were sparring over how to protect at-risk species on federal land. According to the Forest Service's reading of the plan, Soda Springs -- which is in the Umpqua National Forest -- must come down to increase prime salmon habitat in the 400,000-acre North Umpqua Watershed. As it is, the agency says, the dam blocks passage of fish through the river and its feeder streams. "We wouldn't have taken this position five years ago," says Jim Weiman, licensing coordinator for the Umpqua National Forest. "But the Northwest Forest Plan became the pivotal point in this decision." Mr. Weiman says utilities shouldn't be alarmed by the agency's position on PacifiCorp's relicensing application. "We are not out on a dam-removal agenda," he says. Some aren't so sure. Soda Springs is the first dam the Forest Service has insisted be removed, "but it won't be last," predicts Chris West, a spokesman for the Northwest Forestry Association in Portland. Soda Springs is one of eight dams on the North Umpqua built between 1947 and 1956. At 11 megawatts, it's the least powerful, but according to PacifiCorp serves an important function by keeping the entire eight-dam system operating at its peak output of 185 megawatts. Without Soda Springs, the company says, the system would be less efficient, losing between 24 and 43 megawatts of generating capacity. The Soda Springs reservoir collects water from the upper seven dams and acts as the main spigot for all of them by releasing water to regulate the flow of the river below. That allows the other seven dams to operate at capacity during periods of peak demand, says Dave Kvamme, a PacifiCorp spokesman. Because the North Umpqua dams had operated so smoothly, "we thought if ever there was a case to be made for relicensing a dam, the North Umpqua project was it," says Ms. Flores of PacifiCorp, adding that the company didn't foresee "a compelling environmental argument" against keeping Soda Springs in business. The company began work on its application early, five years before its license with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission expired in 1997. (The commission has been issuing temporary annual licenses for the past two years, waiting to see if the utility, federal agencies and citizen groups could reach an agreement that would pave the way for a 30-year license.) PacifiCorp officials clearly believe they have bent over backward. In 1996, the company paid $10 million for an analysis of the North Umpqua Watershed by Berkeley consulting firm Stillwater Ecosystem, Watershed & Riverine Sciences Inc., and invited representatives from environmental groups and government agencies to work with Stillwater on the study. Completed in March 1998, the analysis found that removing the dam would be the best way to return the salmon habitat to its pristine condition, but that good alternatives exist. "We specifically didn't make value judgments" on PacifiCorp's application, says Frank Lighon, senior aquatic ecologist for Stillwater. "We knew the final decision was a value judgment weighing science with economic factors." Then, this September, PacifiCorp became the second Northwest utility to voluntarily agree to remove a dam: It vowed to tear down its 9.6-megawatt Condit Dam on the White Salmon River in southern Washington to help restore fish runs there. "We honestly felt that we should have gained some credibility as a company trying to do the right thing," Ms. Flores says. PacifiCorp has offered to spend $35 million on projects around Soda Springs that it says would aid the migration of the endangered sea-run cut throat and coho salmon. (Dismantling Soda Springs would cost $50 million to $60 million.) Clearly, "for this small section of river, no dam is better than a dam," Ms. Flores acknowledges. "But we have agreed to do a number of things that we think would help the fish." Those include installing fish ladders, covering culverts that redirect water, building wildlife bridges and improving fish habitat on lower tributaries where other species of salmon are endangered. But the Forest Service won't back down, and it is supported by major environmental groups in the region. "Clearly, all the science points to that dam coming out as the best option," says Mr. Weiman. "Removing the dam, just one of eight the company has, will increase natural fish habitat in the North Umpqua Watershed by 5%." Mr. Weiman adds that under the Northwest Forest Plan, the agency has no choice but to take that position. The plan requires that the agency examine entire watersheds and work to smooth the flow between streams and rivers so that habitat for fish and other river critters, including salamanders and frogs, can be restored as much as possible to their pre-dam status. The plan's language is clear, he says: It states that the Forest Service must "implement actions to restore conditions" that occurred naturally and to restore "connectivity" between bodies of water so that fish and other creatures can move up and down the river freely. "There is no model for this," Mr. Weiman says. "Still, we firmly believe that the long-term environmental benefits outweigh" the costs of Soda Springs' removal. (It would not be necessary to remove other dams, he says, because fish wouldn't spawn that far upstream anyway.) Interestingly, the Forest Service condemned Soda Springs without the concurrence of the National Marine Fisheries Service, the federal agency in charge of caring for dwindling salmon populations. "This is a complex system of dams, and we do not think it so clear that dam removal is the best option at Soda Springs," says NMFS spokesman Brian Gorman in Seattle. "In contrast to other waterways in the region, things are fairly healthy for fish in the North Umpqua." Mr. Weiman says that "because these dams are located on Forest Service lands, we have a more pressing interest" than any other arm of the U.S. government. The NMFS has yet to demand the removal of a dam in the Northwest, though it has spent the past year examining four hydro projects on the Lower Snake River in Idaho for their impact on the endangered Snake River chinook. Those four dams are federally owned. The Soda Springs battle is being waged on one of the last remaining premier rivers for salmon, the signature fish in the Northwest. While steelhead trout and spring chinook, both salmon species, have been listed as endangered on rivers and streams across the region, they remain in strong supply on the North Umpqua. Underscoring the difficulty of the dam debate in the region, the Soda Spring controversy has split the two main fishing groups on the North Umpqua. The Steamboaters, a fly-fishing group with about 300 members based in Roseburg, about 60 miles downstream from Soda Springs, backs removal of the dam, says Ken Ferguson, conservation director for the group. But the Umpqua Fishermen Association, another group of 300 anglers based in Roseburg, says tearing out the dam could create a landslide of silt and rock. That "could kill everything downstream for 10 miles and take 10 years to recover," says Bob Hissong, president of the association. "We say, why take that risk?" Mr. Ferguson says the silt would likely kill only about 29% of the fish downriver, and only for a period of weeks or months. At PacifiCorp, officials are examining their legal options. But "we still very much favor a settlement" that keeps Soda Springs in action, Ms. Flores says. The utility has asked all federal agencies with a say in the relicensing -- the Forest Service, the NMFS, the Bureau of Land Management and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service -- to convene a "high-level policy committee to examine this decision and see if they agree it is right," she says. So far, no action has been taken on that request, says Rex Holloway, a spokesman for the Forest Service's regional office in Portland. "I don't really see us changing this decision," he says. Mr. Holloway notes that if the agency doesn't require the dam's removal, "we would almost certainly be sued" by the environmental groups supporting the Forest Service's decision. In the meantime, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, which will make the ultimate decision on relicensing PacifiCorp's dams, last month ordered the Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Oak Ridge, Tenn., to conduct a full environmental-impact statement on the entire system, says Celeste Miller, a spokeswoman for the commission in Washington, D.C. FERC hasn't taken an active role in the negotiations, other than to encourage all the parties to reach a consensus, says Ms. Miller. The impact statement will take one to five years to complete but will probably end up including the Forest Service's demand, she adds. PacifiCorp expects as much. "We wanted to create a new model to make this process work for everybody," Ms. Flores says. "Instead, we may end up as the poster child for how not to get a dam relicensed." ---                     Keeping Control    PacifiCorp facts:    -- Headquartered: Portland, Ore.   -- Parent: Scottish Power, Glasgow, Scotland   -- Service area: Oregon, Washington, Idaho, Wyoming, Utah and Northern California   -- Generation: 84,445 megawatts; 1,100 megawatts from hydropower and 7,345 megawatts from thermal, coal, gas and wind   -- Customers: 1.5 million    Source: PacifiCorp ---                      Power Sources    North Umpqua Hydroelectric Project   Built: 1947-1956   Location: 60 miles east of Roseburg on the North Umpqua National Forest, on the North Umpqua River, Clearwater River, and Slide and Fish creeks    Dams Power            Generation    Toketee ............. 42 megawatts   Lemolo No.2 ......... 33 megawatts   Lemolo No.1 ......... 29 megawatts   Clearwater No.2 ..... 26 megawatts   Slide Creek ......... 18 megawatts   Clearwater No.1 ..... 15 megawatts   Fish Creek .......... 11 megawatts   Soda Spring ......... 11 megawatts   Total Generation ... 185 megawatts    Source: PacifiCorp Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: A Logger's Story
Text: Defenders of the northern spotted owl jumped yesterday to criticize a government panel decision to override the Endangered Species Act and allow logging in some Oregon forests where it had been banned. The Sierra Club's Michael Fischer told the Associated Press that "the Bush administration's message to America's forests is 'drop dead.'" But the decision, a compromise, left many tracts safe for the nocturnal bird while protecting as many as 1,000 jobs for loggers. A report from one member of that (human) endangered species landed in our in-box recently. We print it below: My name is Donald Walker Jr. For 30 years, I was an Oregon logger. I have been out of work since August 1989, when the company I worked for closed out its operations near Oakridge, where my wife and I live. Times have been pretty tough since then, though I think we have been luckier than many woodworkers. We still have our home, where we raised our children. Many younger loggers, with small children at home, have lost everything as a result of the spotted owl controversy that has tied Congress in knots. My wife has an office job with the same company I worked for, but she had to accept a transfer to another office a four hour drive from home. Now we see each other only on weekends. It gets pretty lonely here without her, but our faith in God has kept us strong, and we continue to hope for better days when we can be together again like a family should be. After I lost my job I took some courses at a local community college, thinking that I might be able to make a new start in life. I figured my best hope was to learn enough to start some sort of small business that was related to my 30 years of woods experience. I took welding, some small business classes and a couple of courses in interpersonal communications. Can you imagine a logger in an interpersonal communications class! Community college helped me a lot personally, but starting over when you are 55 years old isn't easy. Since 1989 the only work I've been able to find is as a part-time caretaker on some private timber land near here. I've also worked seasonally as a yew bark collector for an outfit that has a contract with a big drug company that is searching for a cure for cancer. They think Taxol, which comes from yew bark, might be a miracle cancer cure. I also work on the family tree farm, and that is the other part of this story. My dad and my grandad bought this farm in 1932. Our family has been logging it for 60 years. We've replanted as we've gone along, or converted the land to fields where we graze a few cattle. Our land was burned badly in a fire in 1912, so we don't have any of the old growth timber Oregon is famous for. None of our trees are more than 80 years old. One of the hopes I have held on to since I lost my job is that I could supplement our income by continuing to manage our tree farm as my father and grandfather did for so many years. But it doesn't look like this is going to pan out either. Last November, I received a letter from an outfit called the Forest Conservation Council telling me that if I cut any more timber on our land it would sue me for violating the Endangered Species Act, which protects spotted owls, and makes it a crime to tamper with their habitat. I have never seen a spotted owl on our place, and I have never met anyone from the Forest Conservation Council. So far as I know, it's never even been on our farm. But I do have a typewritten, single-spaced four-page letter from their lawyer saying that what we have been doing on our tree farm for 60 years is no longer legal. I might have felt a little bit better about the letter if they had offered to buy the land, or at least pay the taxes, which we have also been doing for 60 years. But they didn't and I guess I'm not surprised. From what I've read about these people, they don't believe in private property rights. About 200 Oregon tree farmers got the same letter I got. There are actually many more tree farmers in Oregon, but for some reason we were singled out. It got me to thinking about how what has happened to us could happen to any private property owner. In fact, the newspapers are filled with stories like ours. It's happening to people all over the United States. There is even a Supreme Court case now, involving a fellow in South Carolina who paid almost a million dollars for a couple of beachfront lots he has been told he can't build on because somebody thinks the land should be left to nature. A lot of news reporters have visited our place since we got our letter from the Forest Conservation Council. I think they're impressed with the beauty of our farm, but I'm afraid they don't grasp the significance of what is happening to us, or to other private landowners across the country. Do they understand that the right of ownership of private property is fundamental to our democracy? I don't think so. I think they are too busy collecting what are called six-second sound bites, and that is not something I am very good at. Some people say we should cut down all our trees now, while we still can, before the Forest Conservation Council letter becomes a court case. But we don't want to. We're conservationists. This tree farm is our home, and the trees are a part of our way of life. We work with nature to grow a crop the nation needs. The crop is wood. It puts food on our tables. In 26 years of married life, we have never been late on a bill we owed. The pressure on us now is hard to describe. My wife won't even read the newspaper anymore, because it's filled with stories about loggers losing everything, and preservationists filing more lawsuits. Where does it all end? Do people count anymore? Do private property rights still have meaning in America? Who will compensate us for our loss? The public? The Forest Conservation Council? So far, I haven't heard from anyone except the property tax collector. The problem isn't the owl, or even old growth for that matter. The problem is an out-of-control preservationist movement that doesn't care about people or their rights. Our tree farm is our last hope. It is worth fighting for, and I intend to fight for it every way I know how.

Title: As Olympia Girds for Salmon War, The Battle Lines Are Taking Shape
Text: The Puget Sound wild Chinook salmon isn't an endangered species yet, but the first major land-use battle spawned by its imminent listing is already brewing. The front lines are on Cherry Point, at the northwestern tip of Washington, near the waters that are home to half of the state's herring, a staple in the salmon diet. The point has for years been Washington's biggest industrial zone, with two oil refineries and a smelter, and local civic leaders figured it would be fairly smooth sailing for a proposed addition: a 1,000-acre industrial park with a deep-water pier called Gateway Pacific Terminal. Gateway Pacific is popular in Whatcom County for the 50 to 60 jobs it would provide directly, and the several hundred more it could create indirectly. Gov. Gary Locke has touted the project -- along with several others on Cherry Point -- as just the kind of endeavor that is crucial to his rural economic-development program. In October, he predicted all state regulatory approvals would be granted within a month. But the governor didn't count on his old friend Jennifer Belcher, the powerful commissioner of public lands. She is refusing to grant Gateway Pacific a permit until its backers prepare an exacting environmental study never before required of a proposed development in the state. The reason: Juvenile salmon snack on Cherry Point herring during their migration, and the Puget Sound wild Chinook is to be listed next month under the U.S. Endangered Species Act. The herring population is shrinking, and Ms. Belcher wants to be sure that Gateway Pacific's heavy shipping traffic won't harm the species further. "Everyone says they want to save the salmon, but no one says, `I'll be the first to make a sacrifice,'" says Ms. Belcher, who also heads the Department of Natural Resources. "Cherry Point is a perfect example of how we're still in denial." Civic and business leaders are dumbfounded by the mixed messages out of Olympia. "Who is the real governor of Washington?" Fred Sexton, president of the Bellingham/Whatcom Economic-Development Council, asked in a recent speech. "Gary Locke or Jennifer Belcher?" Some in the capital are exasperated, too. "There are people who feel like this is state government not getting its act together," says Joan Pelley, a spokeswoman for the Department of Ecology, which says it's leaning toward endorsing the Gateway project. "These businesses get run through interminable bureaucracies with no end in sight. I think their frustration is justified." The fight over Cherry Point puts in stark relief the dilemma the Endangered Species Act presents: How can states save fish and wildlife without checking economic growth? With nearly 20 local fish species listed or expected to be, many fear proposed developments of all kinds will be put through a new level of regulatory hoops. But there is no agreement on how rigorous the new level should be. Gov. Locke doesn't necessarily think business should be let off the hook. His proposal for a $200 million salmon-recovery plan, made in anticipation of the listing, would impose new restrictions on water use and development on sensitive lands. "The listing of salmon in Puget Sound means a new day for land-use decisions," says Joe Dear, the governor's chief of staff. But Mr. Dear says his boss thinks Ms. Belcher is being a bit too hard on Gateway Pacific, and on three other Cherry Point projects whose petitions have been stalled by the Department of Natural Resources: a proposed new wing on the pier at a refinery of Arco Products Co., a unit of Atlantic Richfield Co. of Los Angeles, which needs a tidelands lease; and an Intalco Aluminum Corp. smelter and Tosco Oil Corp. refinery that want tidelands lease renewals. The bulk of these, Mr. Dear points out, were well into the planning stages long before it became known that the Puget Sound salmon was to be listed. It would be unfair, he says, to subject such projects to "all of the new enhanced reviews." Ms. Belcher doesn't buy that argument. Twice elected with broad support from environmentalists, she says she takes seriously her job as custodian of Washington's five million acres of state-managed land. "We've always been willing to err on the side of business," she says. "If we really want to save salmon, we cannot err on the side of development anymore." Until late last year, the $200 million Gateway project, including a pier stretching into the Strait of Georgia at the entrance to Puget Sound, had been essentially on track. A joint venture of Jim Pattison Group, a Vancouver, B.C., conglomerate, and Stevedoring Services of America Inc., Seattle, it had won approvals from Whatcom County and concluded 18 months of negotiations with the Ecology and Fish and Wildlife departments. With permits from those departments apparently imminent, developers, encouraged by Gov. Locke's enthusiasm, were confident they'd get a tidelands lease from the Department of Natural Resources. But they didn't count on Ms. Belcher, either. Scientists can't explain the shrinkage in herring schools, which spawn in the eel grass around Cherry Point and are the most important food for juvenile salmon on their way to the sound. Until scientists can explain the decline, Ms. Belcher says, the agency must "put on the brakes" and make sure new development poses no threat. It is doing that by requiring Gateway Pacific and the other projects to produce a "regional risk assessment," a demanding analysis that can take more than a year to complete. The Gateway project has been under review for several years, but that doesn't faze Ms. Belcher. "I don't think four or five years is too long to deliberate on something like this," she says. Naturally, Gateway developers disagree. "We're not willing to fund and participate in a bunch of studies to get to `maybe,'" says Wayne Schwandt, the project manager. "It would seem to be much better public policy if the state could speak as `the state' and have all its collective interests come from one point. As we talk with Fish and Wildlife about herring, we resolve the issues with them -- then we have to do it all over again with DNR." David Fordon, development manager for the Lummi Tribe, which has fishing rights off Cherry Point, says the tribe won't take a position on the project until all state permits and leases are granted. But Mr. Fordon complains that Ms. Belcher's opposition to Gateway Pacific at this late stage is "a little surprising." Gov. Locke is being heavily lobbied by representatives of Gateway Pacific, Arco, Intalco and Tosco. They want him to convince Ms. Belcher to relax her position. (They might figure he holds some sway, as he and Ms. Belcher were political allies when they served together in the House from 1983 to 1993, and friends, too: She was his landlord when he needed a place to crash in Olympia during one session.) The governor hopes for a compromise. "This is not some absolute trade-off between economic development and saving salmon -- new development can occur" even while local wildlife are protected, says Mr. Dear, Gov. Locke's chief of staff. "It might take longer while the state adjusts, but I think the state can adjust." Not everyone is so sure. Some say a bill introduced by a co-chairman of the House Agriculture Committee, Democrat Kelli Linville of Bellingham, could shift the balance of power toward the appointed director of the Department of Ecology and away from the elected public-lands commissioner. The bill proposes giving the Department of Ecology "primary responsibility" for cleaning up and preventing damage to certain public lands, a power that would be "binding on all other state agencies." Rep. Linville says the measure is neither a Cherry Point bill nor an "anti-Belcher bill," as some in Olympia call it. But Department of Natural Resources officials fear that if it is approved, it will usurp the agency's power, and they are lobbying against it. And some policy makers say that if Ms. Belcher continues to oppose Cherry Point projects, a stronger measure could emerge. For her part, Ms. Belcher says she and the governor have discussed Cherry Point on more than a dozen occasions, but haven't bridged the gap in their opinions. But that, she says, is a testament to democracy. "That's the reason we have separately elected officials," she says. "In the past, we've made quick decisions that have pushed our resources to the brink of extinction," she says. "Now, the reality is that fish listings are going to cause us to slow down our decision-making. This is the new reality." Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: City News: Greater New York Watch
Text: THE BRONX Baychester Shooting Leaves One Man Dead A man was killed and another wounded after were both shot while sitting inside a car in the Bronx early Sunday, police said. Jordan Jackwett, 23, and an 18-year-old man were in a vehicle parked at Ely and Adee avenues in the Baychester section of the Bronx when shots rang out just after 5 a.m., police said. The unknown shooter walked up to the vehicle and shot Mr. Jackwett in the head and the other victim in the leg, police said. Both were taken to Jacobi Medical Center, where Mr. Jackwett died a short time later. As of Sunday afternoon, no one had been arrested in connection with the shooting, police said. -- Mark Morales --- CONNECTICUT Two Men Are Killed In Accidents on I-91 Two men have died in separate accidents Saturday on Interstate 91 in central Connecticut. State police said 51-year-old David Sanchez of New Haven was killed when his car rear-ended a tractor-trailer, wedged underneath it, and caught fire at about 6:30 a.m. Saturday. The crash happened near southbound Exit 13 in Wallingford. The truck driver was taken to a hospital as a precaution. WTNH-TV reports police say 26-year-old Steven Baez of Bronx, New York, was killed in the same area at about 2:30 a.m., when the car he was riding in hit another car and overturned. The car's driver, 28-year-old Sean Brown of Ardsley, N.Y., and another passenger, 25-year-old Jasmine Clifford of Greenwich, were taken to the hospital as a precaution. -- Associated Press --- NEW JERSEY Police Seek a Motive In Shooting of Teen Authorities are seeking a motive for the fatal shooting of a man in northern New Jersey. Essex County prosecutors say East Orange police found 18-year-old city resident Sharod Jefferson around 9:40 p.m. Saturday on the lawn of a home in the 200 block of Dodd Street. The discovery came after they were flagged down by residents who told them someone had been shot. Further details on the shooting weren't disclosed, including what type of weapon was used. -- Associated Press --- NEW YORK Nabokov's Butterfly Makes a Comeback More than 20 years of habitat restoration and breeding programs have helped the endangered Karner blue butterfly make a comeback in the pine barrens of upstate New York, where it was discovered by Russian author Vladimir Nabokov decades ago. "This project has been unbelievably rewarding," said Neil Gifford, conservation director for the 3,200-acre Albany Pine Bush Preserve. "Getting to see an animal that was on the brink of extinction locally, now have a robust and healthy population, is just incredible." The silvery blue, postage-stamp-sized butterfly that was among the first species on the federal endangered list in 1973 is also making a comeback in parts of Ohio and New Hampshire, where it was thought to have been wiped out before 2000. Populations have persisted in Wisconsin and Michigan. The author of "Lolita" discovered Karner blue just west of Albany in the 1940s. Nabokov was also a notable butterfly expert who played a key role in establishing the relationship between the Karner blue and its dwindling pine barrens habitat. His research was at the heart of the discussion of habitat and restoration provisions of the Endangered Species Act passed by Congress in 1973. Recovery efforts focus on restoring the original pine barrens ecology by removing nonnative trees, and planting plenty of blue lupine, the only plant Karner blue larvae eat. -- Associated Press --- NEW YORK Commission to Meet On Attorney Discipline A new state panel examining how attorneys are disciplined in New York plans to hold its first public hearing next week. The Commission on Statewide Attorney Discipline is set to meet for two hours on Tuesday at the Court of Appeals in Albany. Issues before the commission appointed by Chief Judge Jonathan Lippman include whether disciplinary charges or findings should be made public earlier as a consumer-protection matter. -- Associated Press --- CONNECTICUT Public Hearing Is Set On Highway Widening The Department of Transportation hopes to hear from the public about the I-84 widening project in Waterbury. The agency has scheduled a "public listening session" on Aug. 1 at the Brooklyn Baking Co. in Waterbury. The event will run from 8 a.m. to 11 a.m. Members of DOT's public information team will be available to talk with residents. -- Associated Press

Title: Fisheries Service Supports Expansion of Interstate 405
Text: A federal agency has abruptly dropped its opposition to Olympia's plans to expand Interstate 405.    Amid pressure from Washington's congressional delegation to allow the expansion project to move forward, National Marine Fisheries Service officials told the Washington State Department of Transportation on Friday that they would sign off on the state's four congestion-relieving proposals. That's an about-face from earlier last week, when the agency insisted that the proposals were unacceptable because they would imperil the habitat of wild salmon.    In an eight-page letter to the DOT, Robert Turner, the fisheries service's Washington-area director, said his agency's refusal to assent to the proposals was based on a misunderstanding. He said his agency was under the impression that it either had to agree with the proposals in full or oppose them, and didn't realize it could give conditional approval.    The DOT "indicated the only available options for response . . . were to concur or not concur," Mr. Turner wrote. "NMFS now understands that participating agencies can concur with comments."    Agency Concerns    The Washington Department of Ecology and Washington State Department of Fish and Wildlife signed off on the proposals in August. Until last week, however, the fisheries agency refused. In a September letter to the state, the agency said each option would facilitate residential and commercial growth in the area bordering I-405. It feared that growth would imperil the habitat of Puget Sound Chinook, a salmon run listed by the U.S. government as threatened under the federal Endangered Species Act.    Although the fisheries service is allowing the project to continue, Mr. Turner noted in his current letter that the agency continues to have "serious concerns" about the expansion's potential impact on streams used by the Puget Sound Chinook during migration. Among other concerns, it believes that runoff from the highway would elevate stream temperatures and collapse stream banks, thus harming the fish.    The agency's reversal came days after U.S. Sen. Slade Gorton and U.S. Rep. Jennifer Dunn, who represents the region east of Seattle that I-405 serves, sent a letter to the fisheries service urging it to drop its opposition. Saying they were "deeply concerned," the two Republicans told the fisheries service it was overstepping its bounds, writing that "NMFS' demands regarding the I-405 project are another example of the expansion of the federal government's reach over responsibilities that have been traditionally and properly handled by the state."    The state transportation department needed the fisheries service's approval to proceed with the I-405 project, because without it the DOT wouldn't be able to get the permits it needs to start construction, and would find it difficult to obtain federal funding.    "It's good news that they've decided to back down," says Rob McKenna, a King County Councilman and a member of the 26-member I-405 planning committee, which is composed of representatives of city and county governments affected by the highway. "This is an important project, and I think the pressure from Washington's federal representatives helped the agency realize that its opposition was unfounded."    Brian Gorman, a fisheries service spokesman, says the reversal shouldn't be viewed as the agency bowing to the demands of Washington's congressional delegation. In fact, Mr. Gorman says the Oct. 16 letter from Sen. Gorton and Rep. Dunn irritated the agency. "There's no point of having a process of review if nobody is allowed to dissent," he says. "We're not going to just rubber-stamp the proposals."    The state DOT has spent nearly $6 million developing proposals for making traffic flow more swiftly on I-405. That highway is expected to see a 250% increase in traffic by 2020. A 36-mile stretch of asphalt from Tukwila to Lynwood, the expressway feeds traffic in and out of Bellevue and Redmond on the technology-rich east side of Lake Washington.    The I-405 planning committee gave its nod last summer to four congestion-relieving options costing between $2 billion and $6 billion each:    -- Build a light-rail or monorail system along the I-405 corridor, add an extra lane in each direction and complete limited improvements on feeder roads.    -- Expand bus service on the highway, build two extra lanes in each direction and improve feeder roads.    -- Add one lane in each direction and build a new four-lane toll expressway from Renton to Lynwood that would run parallel to I-405 and be elevated in some portions.    -- Build the light-rail or monorail system along the I-405 corridor, but add no new lanes.  Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Endangered Species Act receives a streamlining
Text: WASHINGTON -- Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt announced a series of policies aimed at streamlining administration of the Endangered Species Act.   The initiatives, unveiled by Mr. Babbitt and D. James Baker, undersecretary of commerce for oceans and atmosphere, are part of a Clinton administration effort to head off more-radical legislative changes in the endangered-species law, which over the years has stirred opposition from a variety of industries. Congress is considering ways to overhaul the law, and may act sometime next year.   Among the new policies is a requirement that at least three independent panels provide peer review of scientific data that form the basis of any decision to list a species as endangered. In the past, Mr. Babbitt said, "it's been done sometimes, but not every time."   In addition, Mr. Babbitt and Mr. Baker pledged to give businesses and other "stakeholders" more say in developing plans for preserving endangered species, and to more clearly state, when listing a species as endangered, what commercial activities will be affected.

Title: U.S. denies request of San Diego Zoo to import 2 pandas
Text: SAN DIEGO -- The San Diego Zoo's application to import two rare Chinese giant pandas for breeding purposes was denied by the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service.    The zoo, renowned for its work with endangered species, nonetheless had run into severe opposition from wildlife groups that suggested the zoo was being driven by the potential for the huge boost in revenue that comes with display of the popular animals. A 200-day panda exhibit in 1984 and 1985 in San Diego led to record attendance, and produced net merchandising revenue of $5.7 million.    In a letter denying San Diego's application, Fish & Wildlife Deputy Director Kenneth Stansell said the zoo had failed to meet requirements of the Endangered Species Act and a related agreement, which would provide that the proposed three-year breeding loan must "more than likely produce progeny and thus enhance the survivial of the species." He noted that the rules also prohibit importation "primarily for commercial purposes."    The Fish & Wildlife Service raised questions about the problems China has had breeding the male panda, Shi Shi, and a dangerous tumor on the female, Shun Shun. The agency of the Interior Department also raised a question about the circumstances of Shun Shun's removal from the wild. Fewer than 1,000 giant pandas are believed to exist in the wild.    The San Diego Zoo, which has 45 days to appeal the ruling to Marshall Jones, chief of the Fish & Wildlife Service's endangered-species authority, said zoo officials were "shocked, frustrated and concerned" by the denial. "We believe that this shortsighted decision is a tragedy in that it will further delay any positive efforts to bring the giant panda species back from the brink of extinction," Executive Director Doug Myers said.

Title: U.S. News: U.S. Watch
Text: WASHINGTON Court Lifts Barrier for Suits Against Police In a victory for people falsely accused by police of crimes, the Supreme Court removed a barrier Monday to lawsuits against law enforcement for malicious prosecution. The 6-3 ruling means some malicious prosecution lawsuits that had previously been thrown out at an early stage will instead be allowed to move forward. The ruling was joined by both liberal and conservative justices. Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote for the majority of the court that a person seeking to sue for malicious prosecution under a federal civil-rights law has to prove that the case brought against him "ended without a conviction." The justices rejected a higher bar that federal appeals courts in much of the country had adopted that said the person had to show their case ended because they were innocent. Justice Samuel Alito wrote in a dissent that his colleagues' decision "has no basis in the Constitution and is almost certain to lead to confusion." He was joined by two other conservatives, Justice Clarence Thomas and Justice Neil Gorsuch. The case before the justices involved the 2014 arrest of Brooklyn, N.Y., resident Larry Thompson, who sued for malicious prosecution after charges against him resulting from a scuffle with police were dropped. Mr. Thompson's lawyer Amir Ali said the court's decision was "welcome and needed," eliminating "completely unjust and really senseless barrier to bringing these lawsuits." -- Associated Press --- PENNSYLVANIA State to Speed Up Clemency Process The process for inmates and ex-convicts in Pennsylvania to apply for clemency should go fully online by the end of the year, an effort to improve access to an emerging cornerstone of the nation's criminal-justice movement and to reduce the wait by years, Lt. Gov. John Fetterman said Monday. Mr. Fetterman, a Democrat who is running for the U.S. Senate, said his goal is for the state Board of Pardons to use the online system to turn around an application for a pardon or commutation in a year or less. The process often takes several years currently under what Mr. Fetterman calls an ineffective and paper-based system. Mr. Fetterman as lieutenant governor chairs the five-member Board of Pardons, and has worked to transform the tiny agency into a bigger tool in a criminal-justice change movement working to undo laws and systems that inflated prison populations, disproportionately with racial minorities. The pardons system once required someone seeking an application to mail in a check or money order, wait to receive the application by mail and then to mail it back in, filled out, with documents from their criminal case -- and another payment. After taking office in 2019, Mr. Fetterman got rid of the fees, and applications can now be downloaded from online. -- Associated Press --- NEVADA Toad Is Declared Endangered In a rare emergency move, the U.S. government temporarily declared a northern Nevada toad endangered Monday, saying a geothermal power plant in the works could result in its extinction. The Fish and Wildlife Service announced it is formally proposing a rule to list the Dixie Valley toad as an endangered species subject to 60 days of public comment under the Endangered Species Act's normal rule-making process. But it said the emergency listing goes into effect immediately and will continue for eight months while more permanent protections are considered for the toad at the only place it is known to exist in the world. It marks only the second time in 20 years the service has listed a species as endangered on an emergency basis. It wasn't immediately clear how the toad's listing might affect construction of the power plant about 100 miles east of Reno. -- Associated Press

Title: Hampers's National Medical bid shows drive of founder used to having control
Text: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal  Financing for the bid remains uncertain, and Dr. Hampers didn't return calls seeking an interview.  In the past year, Dr. Hampers had clashed with J.P. Bolduc, Grace's chief executive until recently, over Mr. Bolduc's efforts to centralize National Medical's headquarters functions. Dr. Hampers even went so far as to tender his resignation last December, after deciding the company "was going the wrong way," according to Edmund G. Lowrie, National Medical's president. But that offer was apparently withdrawn after major changes shook W.R. Grace.  Mr. Bolduc had tussled with Grace's chairman, J. Peter Grace, over issues involving Grace family perquisites. When those issues came to the attention of major stockholders, Mr. Grace agreed under pressure to step down. He would have done so at next Wednesday's annual meeting, but he died last month at age 81.  Meanwhile, Mr. Bolduc was forced to resign on March 2 over unrelated allegations that he had sexually harassed female employees, charges he denies.  At one point, Dr. Hampers had hired the Kroll Associates detective agency to investigate Mr. Bolduc; he has contended publicly that he hired the firm only to find who was orchestrating an effort to impugn his reputation.  With Mr. Bolduc out of the picture, Dr. Hampers immediately began lobbying for the job of Grace CEO. He had been the chairman's choice as successor, but was opposed by many institutional holders. "I've never applied for a job in my life," he said in an interview in March, concerning his lobbying effort. "This is the first time."  But a week ago, the board tapped an outsider, Albert J. Costello, the 59-year-old former CEO of American Cyanamid Co., for the job. Days later, Dr. Hampers made his surprising $3.5 billion bid for Waltham, Mass.-based National Medical, which he runs as a Grace executive vice president.  Many observers were stunned by the move, but those who know the urbane, sometimes imperious 62-year-old weren't terribly surprised. "He's very competitive," says David McNeish, an investment banker who in the 1960s helped bring National Medical into being by raising $1.5 million through a private placement. "Gus wants to win."  Dr. Hampers's audacious bid for Grace's most profitable unit has raised eyebrows on Wall Street, in part because he has yet to demonstrate he can finance the deal. Friday, Dr. Hampers further mystified the Street by announcing that a little-known investment group, Quad-C Inc., Charlottesville, Va., will assist in his bid. Quad-C is led by Terrence D. Daniels, a former Grace vice chairman who was instrumental in Grace's purchase of National Medical.  But Dr. Hampers, a self-made millionaire, big-game hunter, Boston Celtics fan and a leading light in Boston's social and medical establishment, has raised eyebrows before.  For example, in 1988 he was indicted on 13 felony counts for allegedly violating a federal endangered species act by importing into the U.S. the hides of two jaguars and three ocelots that he bagged in a hunting trip in Mexico. The first trial ended with a hung jury. To avoid a second trial, Dr. Hampers plead guilty to a lesser charge and contributed $180,000 to a wildlife preservation fund.  National Medical is under pressure from the Food and Drug Administration to resolve long-standing quality-control problems at three plants. Moreover, Grace recently disclosed in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission that National Medical is the subject of two federal grand jury investigations. One is looking at whether National Medical sold defective products; the other is examining relationships between the company and third parties providing services to National Medical.  Trained at the University of Pittsburgh, Dr. Hampers served a hitch in the Navy before becoming an instructor at a Harvard-affiliated hospital in Boston. Out of a moonlighting job to supplement his instructor pay, he made an important discovery: Outpatient clinics can provide consistent, reliable kidney-dialysis treatment for less than hospitals charge.  With Dr. Edward B. Hager, another Harvard nephrologist, Dr. Hampers then co-founded what would become the nation's largest supplier of dialysis services and products. The two doctors began opening dialysis clinics around the country, but many insurance companies balked at picking up the tab.  Dr. Hampers brought stories of dying indigent patients to state and federal government officials, trying to get funding. National Medical grew rapidly, and the company went public in 1971. Soon afterward, U.S. lawmakers put the company's profit into liftoff by voting to guarantee payment for much of the cost of dialysis.  Dr. Hager left the company in 1980 for a fling at politics, leaving Dr. Hampers at the helm. By the early 1980s, the U.S. government began seeking to reduce its dialysis outlays, which run to billions of dollars. In that environment, National Medical shares softened. And W.R. Grace, looking for a diversification move, helped fund a buyout by which Dr. Hampers and others took National Medical private; Grace picked up a 49% stake in the process. By 1992, W.R. Grace had acquired 100% ownership in stages. Dr. Hampers has said he pocketed more than $100 million from selling his holdings to Grace.  Ever since he founded it in 1968, Constantine L. "Gus" Hampers has run National Medical Care Inc. the way he wanted -- no matter who owned it. Now, with his control over his kidney-dialysis company seriously threatened, he has moved to take it back.  Dr. Hampers called the shots at National Medical when it was closely held, when it was a publicly traded concern, and even after it was acquired by W.R. Grace & Co. in a staged process that began in the mid-1980s. Last week, he and some associates bid $3.5 billion to regain control.

Title: Endangered-Species Act, Itself Endangered, May Have Found the Political Backing to Survive
Text: When the weather is nice, Frank Yturria, a rancher near Brownsville, Texas, likes to prowl the marshy land on his 13,000-acre spread to watch his Aplomado Falcons hunt.    The dark, crow-sized bird can outfly and outwit most other birds. Just watching it maneuver gives Mr. Yturria what he calls "a good feeling" because a few years ago the once-plentiful species disappeared in the southwestern U.S. Now it is coming back.    The fact that Mr. Yturria and other ranchers in the area helped the bird's comeback may be the political key to the survival of another endangered species -- the Endangered Species Act, a 1973 law that has been under attack on Capitol Hill for most of the 1990s.    A coalition of Republicans and some Democrats, backed by developers, labor unions, farmers and the Clinton administration, may have finally assembled the critical political mass necessary to modify the law. They argue that its goals were noble, but that they have proved to be very difficult and expensive to carry out.    Of the 1,126 species listed as "endangered" under the law, only about 25 are no longer considered endangered, despite the fact that the U.S. government spends $227 million a year to carry it out. States and private landowners spend tens of millions more. Landowners found to have endangered species on their property are required to carry out costly "mitigation measures," a process that sometimes ties up their land for years and has driven some into bankruptcy.    The difficulties of the law may have spawned a contrary policy among landowners to "shoot, shovel and shut up," says Michael Bean, who has spent 20 years following the law for the Environmental Defense Fund. While there are no statistics on how much species destruction the law has influenced, he concedes, "the belief is widespread that this occurs to some degree."    It hasn't been a fun law to administer. "When I came into office we had gridlocks and train wrecks," recalls Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt, referring to the war over the spotted owl and other controversies in the West. Then Mr. Babbitt found the law was working better in the Southeast. Why? Because the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service had begun making deals that relaxed sections of the law.    The battle over the Red Cockaded Woodpecker, for example, was never fought because golf course developers in the Carolinas agreed to provide a habitat for the bird -- which likes the openness of golf courses -- as long as the government promised to do nothing legally to impair the future use of their land. It came to be known as a "safe-harbor agreement."    Mr. Yturria got his falcons through a similar deal. Peter Jenny, a zoologist with the private Peregrine Fund, who brokered the arrangement, assured the Texas rancher and his neighbors the government wouldn't later penalize them if the fledgling falcons, imported from Mexico, flourished on their land. "They said, gee, this doesn't sound like something the [Fish and Wildlife] Service would do," Mr. Jenny says. "It sounded way too logical."    Safe-harbor deals and a similar law softening policy called "no surprises," have been encouraged by Mr. Babbitt, who says there are about 200 deals with private land owners controlling more than five million acres. Now Mr. Babbitt wants to insure the policies' survival by writing them into a revised version of the law. He has found a powerful ally in Republican Sen. Dirk Kempthorne of Idaho.    Sen. Kempthorne earned his stripes in the endangered species wars trying to help farmers near tiny Bruneau, Idaho. They can't get bank loans on their land because of a tiny snail that lives in the springs that serve as the area's water supply. The farmers successfully sued to have the snail removed from the endangered-species list, only to have a federal appeals court put it back on.    The senator believes such fights will continue unless farmers and ranchers see incentives written into law that encourage them to protect species on private land, where between 50% and 80% of endangered species are believed to live. "Let's find a way to bring them forward."    Individual environmentalists, such as Mr. Bean, applaud Sen. Kempthorne's revision, but most environmental groups don't. They object to "no surprises" deals -- which can bar the government from taking future action in settled endangered-species cases for many years. Kim Delfino, an attorney for the U.S. Public Interest Research Group, thinks removing such liability is wrong. "The polluter should pay," she contends.    Property-rights groups, on the other hand, want the federal government to pay landowners for any changes required to keep their land as habitat for endangered species. "The fact that we're being shot at from both sides tells us we've found political balance," says the senator, who recently pushed the bill through the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee. The vote was 15-3.    It will be closer in the House, where opposing groups are more entrenched. "One of the main issues here is the protection of private property owners under the act," says Republican Rep. Richard Pombo, who has supported property-rights groups in battles involving the kit fox, the kangaroo rat and giant garter snakes in his central-valley district.    Rep. Pombo of California, who says he likes parts of the Kempthorne bill, isn't sure how it will play out. But he does sense some movement. "If there is a bill out of the Senate, there will definitely be one out of the House."    One wild card in the final debates could be House Speaker Newt Gingrich, who once wanted to be a zookeeper. "The speaker has always been a supporter for zoos and wild animals," says Andrew Weinstein, a spokesman. It's too early to tell what role, if any, the speaker might play, he added.    While the argument about incentives drones on in Washington, Mr. Yturria -- the Texas rancher who is thrilled by falcons -- has found some on his own. His neighbors who once worried about what endangered species might do to the value of their land have gone into the ecotourism business to show off their exotic wildlife.    "You take 10 tourists out a day at $50 to $100 a day and you can make $5,000 a week," says the rancher. "It's almost as much as you make from cattle."    (See related letter: "Letters to the Editor: Imperiled Species Law" -- WSJ March 27, 1998)  Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: U.S. News: U.S. Watch
Text: CENSUS Coalition Sues to Extend Head Count A day after the U.S. Census Bureau said that it has already taken steps to wind down operations for the 2020 census, a coalition of cities, counties and civil rights groups is trying to stop the statistical agency in its tracks. The coalition asked a federal judge in San Jose on Thursday to issue a temporary restraining order stopping the Census Bureau from taking any further actions toward ending the once-a-decade head count of every U.S. resident. The coalition is asking a judge in a lawsuit to make the Census Bureau restore its previous deadline for finishing the census to the end of October, instead of using a revised schedule to end operations at the end of September. Arguments aren't scheduled until the middle of the month. "More immediate relief is needed," said the court filing by the coalition. The door-knocking phase of the 2020 didn't start for most of the U.S. until the beginning of August, so winding down operations in September will lead to an inaccurate count that overlooks minority communities, the court filing said. During the door-knocking phase, census takers go to households that haven't yet answered the census questionnaire online, by phone or by mail. The lawsuit was brought by the National Urban League, the League of Women Voters, counties that are home to Houston and Seattle and the cities of Los Angeles, San Jose and Salinas, California. In an op-ed piece in USA Today, Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross, whose department oversees the Census Bureau, said Friday that almost 85% of households had been counted, between residents who self-responded and those who were counted by door-knocking census takers. -- Associated Press --- WHITE HOUSE Trump to Honor Football Coach Holtz President Trump said Friday he plans to award the Presidential Medal of Freedom to celebrated football coach Lou Holtz. "We've looked at Lou's life and his career and what he's done for charity and the football is obvious, he was a great coach, but what he's done beyond even coaching," Mr. Trump said. Mr. Holtz coached college teams at Notre Dame and the University of South Carolina and briefly coached the New York Jets of the National Football League.
