Mr. Holtz spoke at the Republican National Convention last month and praised the president for his antiabortion stance and suggested Democratic presidential candidate Joe Biden was a Catholic "in name only." In an MSNBC interview, Mr. Biden said he has been a practicing Catholic his entire life and called Mr. Holtz's attack "preposterous." -- Rebecca Ballhaus --- ENDANGERED SPECIES ACT Rule Change Carves Out Exemptions U.S. wildlife officials on Friday proposed making it easier to carve out exemptions from habitat protections meant to save imperiled species, by placing greater weight on the potential economic benefits of development when making decisions. Officials from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service described the proposal as giving more deference to local governments seeking to build things like schools and hospitals. But wildlife advocates said it could open up areas that are crucial for endangered species' survival to more drilling, mining, agriculture and logging. The proposal would require federal officials to consider factors such as economic or employment losses when making decisions. That includes decisions affecting federal land for which companies have permits or leases. -- Associated Press

Title: U.S. News: U.S. Watch
Text: ECONOMY Leading Indicators Rise In Latest Sign of Recovery The index of leading indicators rose for the fifth consecutive month in August, offering another sign of a recovering U.S. economy. The leading index, which is designed to predict the path of the economy, increased 0.6% last month, after a revised 0.9% gain in July, the Conference Board reported Monday. Data also showed that the coincident index, which measures current economic activity, had stopped falling. "These numbers are consistent with the view that after a very severe downturn, a recovery is very near," said Ken Goldstein, economist at the nonprofit business-research group. "But the intensity and pattern of that recovery is more uncertain." -- Deborah Lynn Blumberg --- CALIFORNIA Whitman to Announce Candidacy for Governor California Republican gubernatorial candidate Meg Whitman says she wants to cut state spending by another $15 billion and reduce the existing state work force by 17%. The former eBay chief executive will make those proposals in a speech Tuesday in Fullerton, where she will formally announce her bid for the Republican nomination in 2010. In excerpts of her speech provided to the Associated Press, Ms. Whitman reiterates her goal of creating two million private-sector jobs by 2015. -- Associated Press --- MONTANA Judge Orders Protections Restored for Grizzly Bears A federal judge in Montana says the government must restore protections for an estimated 600 grizzly bears in and around Yellowstone National Park, citing a decline in their food supply caused in part by climate change. Grizzlies lost their status as a threatened species under the Endangered Species Act in spring 2007. On Monday, U.S. District Judge Donald Molloy in Missoula, Mont., sided with environmental groups who argued in a lawsuit that the bear population remained at risk even after bouncing back from near-extermination last century. -- Associated Press --- WASHINGTON STATE Business Fined $100,000 For Undocumented Workers Two owners of a Bellingham company won't have to go to prison for hiring undocumented workers, but the business must pay a $100,000 fine. A guilty plea was entered Monday in U.S. District Court on behalf of Yamato Engine Specialists 1990 Ltd. The two owners -- Shafique Amirali Dhanani and his sister, Shirin Dhanani Makala -- pleaded guilty last month and were sentenced to a year of probation. Yamato was the first workplace to be raided by immigration agents after President Obama took office. Mr. Obama had called for less emphasis on prosecuting undocumented workers and more on prosecuting businesses that hire them. -- Associated Press --- FEDERAL RESERVE Central Bank to Miss Deadline For Submitting Review of Itself The Federal Reserve won't meet the U.S. Treasury's Oct. 1 deadline to prepare a broad review of the central bank's structure and governance, a Federal Reserve official said. The Treasury requested the study in June as part of its sweeping blueprint for revamping financial-system regulations, saying a review of the central bank was needed "to better align its structure and governance with its authorities and responsibilities." It isn't clear if the Fed will complete the study and, if so, when. A Fed official said it had become a low priority while other efforts are under way. -- Jon Hilsenrath

Title: One Company Treats A Butterfly Gruffly, Another Is Friendlier --- Endangered-Species Plan Has Defense Contractor Riled; Waste Firm Makes a Deal
Text: SAN JOSE, Calif. -- United Technologies Corp., the giant defense contractor, peered out over the rolling green hills near here and spotted the enemy. It was a butterfly. The company declared war. It implied that the butterfly was a menace to national defense because it might interfere with the company's building and testing of motors for missiles and rockets at its 5,200-acre facility here. Waste Management Inc., the big waste-disposal concern, gazed across its own green hills in adjacent Kirby Canyon and saw, in the same butterfly, an opportunity. The company set up a butterfly preserve and made the butterfly the mascot of its 800-acre local landfill. The butterfly also stars in a slick television commercial aimed at showing that Waste Management, whose garbage-disposal plans haven't always inspired public confidence, isn't an environmental lout. Herein lies a tale of how two corporations, faced with the same public-policy question, can see it a mite differently. The issue is whether "Euphydryas editha bayensis", commonly known as the Bay checkerspot, belongs on the federal endangered-species list. A decision by the Interior Department is due this summer, and most people who know anything about the subject think the checkerspot will make the list. Why should United Technologies or Waste Management care? Well, three years ago, federal officials proposed to designate their land here "critical habitat" for the checkerspot, which meant that if the butterfly finally made the endangered list, their use of the land might be restricted. United Technologies has waged an aggressive three-year campaign to derail the listing, largely by contending that the butterfly isn't so rare. The Connecticut-based contractor hired a biologist and sent him on a butterfly-sighting expedition by helicopter. He said he found the checkerspot population far larger than had been supposed. The company has also pressed its national-defense argument -- and rolled out some big guns in the process: The undersecretaries of the Navy and Air Force told the Interior Department that the listing of the butterfly could slow the delivery of Minuteman and Tomahawk missile propulsion systems. United Technologies has also retained Pillsbury, Madison & Sutro, a prestigious San Francisco law firm, to raise technical challenges to the listing. And not long ago the defense contractor further angered butterfly supporters by digging a water pipeline through a butterfly patch. The company says the pipeline didn't disturb more than 1% of the patch, and it uses the project as an example of the kind of thing it won't be able to do if the butterfly is listed. "What's stupid about this is that United Technologies has spent far more money fighting this listing than it would have ever cost them to accommodate the butterfly," says Dennis Murphy, a Stanford University associate professor of biology who is the butterfly's chief sponsor. "Now you understand why there are $600 toilet seats," he says. Besides, Mr. Murphy says, the company is still fighting as though its use of the entire 5,200 acres might be restricted, whereas the government now has determined that the checkerspots on United Technologies property largely inhabit only buffer lands that distance the company's rocket work from prying eyes. The company, for its part, says its defense work at the site is top secret, so Mr. Murphy can't possibly know how the butterfly's listing might interfere with company projects or how much a butterfly accommodation program would cost. The diminutive checkerspots seem harmless enough. Each March and April, millions of them flutter from cocoons in a billowing dance of yellow, black and orange. But sheer numbers can be misleading. The butterfly's world-wide permanent range, experts say, is largely confined to a handful of native grass and wildflower plots on the rocky slopes of the hills here. And without a plan to preserve and nurture that habitat, the Bay checkerspot's days are numbered, says Paul Ehrlich, a Stanford professor who has monitored the butterfly's dwindling population for 28 years. The checkerspot is also involved in long-term behavioral studies -- carried out by Mr. Ehrlich under National Science Foundation grants -- that hold promise of widening science's ability to control insect pests without poisons. For those reasons, Mr. Murphy sponsored the butterfly for protected status in 1980. Four years later, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, which administers the Endangered Species Act, recommended to its bosses at the Interior Department that the butterfly be put on the endangered-species list. If that happens, landowners would be barred from proceeding with development on checkerspot habitats until they assured federal authorities, in formal plans, that the species would be protected. At the time, Waste Management was still negotiating approval for its landfill, a $15 million garbage-disposal site for San Jose that is expected to generate hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue for the company over a 50-year period. So initially, Waste Management greeted the butterfly's emergence as an issue with the same glee it might muster upon finding Godzilla crawling out of a dumpster. But a company official, who had dealt with endangered species before, suggested summoning Mr. Murphy, who came over to take a look. What he found was that the checkerspots on the Waste Management land thrived largely on a 250-acre plot that sat on an upper slope well out of the reach of the prime garbage-disposal area. Wheels whirred and telephones rang in the upper echelons of Waste Management's Oak Brook, Ill., corporate offices. Soon Mr. Murphy had arranged a deal. Only the 250 acres would be designated critical habitat. Waste Management agreed to set aside that plot as a permanent Bay checkerspot preserve and to spend more than $1 million over the next 10 years in research and preservation efforts, including eventual reseeding of landfill slopes to make them habitable to new colonies of checkerspots outside the 250 acres. In exchange, Mr. Murphy vouched that the plan offered the butterfly adequate protection, a move that silenced critics who had vowed to stop the landfill. "It could have been a serious problem for us," says Phillip Rooney, Waste Management's president. Fighting the listing "was an alternative," he says, "but we chose preservation as the way to go." These days, huge "butterfly crossing" signs mark the entrance of the recently opened landfill, and Waste Management has sponsored a contest to name a caricature of the butterfly that will appear on logos for its San Jose garbage trucks. Mr. Murphy was so buoyed by the Waste Management response that he says he sought out United Technologies, offering them free consulting services and a chance, in essence, to join with Waste Management in a butterfly alliance. He says, and U.S. Fish and Wildlife officials concur, that the pact at most would have obligated United Technologies to do two things: alter grazing practices of cows that roam its property -- so as to leave more grass and flowers for the butterflies' breeding and feeding -- and perhaps to route future pipelines around butterfly habitats. United Technologies says it bid Mr. Murphy a polite thank you but had reached a different conclusion about its best interests. Most galling to the butterfly's supporters has been United Technologies' contention that the Bay checkerspot is "thriving and multiplying beyond belief." The claim is based on the findings of the biologist who undertook the helicopter expedition. He said his searches had uncovered enough new Bay checkerspot colonies to raise the insect's population 40% over previous estimates. The new estimates were unsettling enough to persuade the Fish and Wildlife Service last year to convene a blue-ribbon panel of biologists to determine whether checkerspot populations had indeed been seriously underestimated. Messrs. Murphy and Ehrlich dismissed the findings as "blinking light" colonies, temporary clusters of butterflies that may spring up in years of favorable weather but whose presence doesn't negate the need to protect the butterfly's known permanent breeder colonies. The agency panel, which had the power to scuttle the proposed listing, sided with the Stanford scientists. A senior Waste Management official who asked not to be identified observes: "I think United Technologies really believed they could beat this listing. But in this case they've been out-butterflied." Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Environmentalists Seek River Water for Wildlife
Text: Environmentalists from both sides of the U.S.-Mexican border have teamed up to pressure federal officials into allocating more water from the Colorado River for endangered species, a move that could trigger new legal battles over one of the West's most hotly contested resources. The 14 groups notified the Interior Department, chief overseer of the river, and eight other agencies of their intent to file suit within 60 days for allegedly violating provisions of the Endangered Species Act by not providing enough water for fish and other wildlife downstream in Arizona and Mexico. The suit would seek more water for conservation purposes. The advance notice is required under the act. As a result of most river water being diverted to farms and cities in the Southwest, environmentalists estimate three-quarters of the fish species in the Colorado River's Mexican delta have been either wiped out or are on their way to extinction. "There is absolutely no excuse for not balancing the needs of agriculture, urban areas and wildlife conservation," said David Hogan, rivers program director of the Center for Biological Diversity, an environmental group in Tucson, Ariz., which co-wrote the notice with another group, Washington-based Defenders of Wildlife. Other signatories include an array of U.S. environmental interests, including the Earth Island Institute, as well as four groups from Mexico, where environmental activism is far less visible. Federal officials declined to comment, pending their review of the petition. Independent observers say the environmentalists could present a strong case because even though extensive environmental damage is in Mexico, it has been caused by U.S. actions that could violate the Endangered Species Act. The action comes amid a growing outcry by environmentalists over economic globalization and its impact on dwindling natural resources, sentiment that boiled over in Seattle two weeks ago when environmental protesters disrupted the World Trade Organization summit. It also represents the latest skirmish in the fight over water rights. The Colorado River, which originates in the snowfields of the Rocky Mountains, wends 1,400 miles through six states and into Mexico's Sea of Cortez, providing water for power plants, farms and cities throughout the arid region. Mexico is last in line for water, with a set amount of 1.5 million square feet a year, or about 10% of the total allocated, as prescribed under a 1944 treaty with the U.S. Most of that water is used by farms and towns in Mexico, mainly around the big border city of Mexicali. However, environmentalists say the treaty didn't require any of that Mexican water be used for conservation purposes; nor, for that matter, any in the U.S. As a result, animals that depended on the river habitat of cottonwoods and willows have been pushed to extinction while the once-lush Colorado River delta has at times been dried to mud flats. Only 500 mating pairs of the endangered Southwestern willow flycatcher bird are believed to exist. Environmentalists say they have tried without success since 1995 to get federal officials to allocate more water for conservation. Heavy rain and snow in the past two years have given the lower Colorado River a reprieve, they say. "We have no more time to analyze, dawdle and research this issue," said Bill Snape, legal director of Defenders of Wildlife. He and the other environmentalists want to see at least 250,000 acre feet of annual river flow set aside. "We are at the point now that if we don't do something for the delta soon, it will be gone." Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Supreme Court prepares to decide if regulators have gone too far to aid endangered species
Text: WASHINGTON -- How far may federal regulators go to protect the habitats of the northern spotted owl, the red-cockaded woodpecker and the golden-cheeked warbler?    The Supreme Court is poised to decide whether, in their desire to protect endangered species, the feds have gone too far in curtailing logging and development on millions of acres of private land all across the country. The case, which will be argued on Monday, has set off a frenzy among business and property-rights groups. Dozens of trade associations, lobbyists and companies have joined "friend-of-the-court" briefs, urging the justices to rein in the regulators. On the other side, environmentalists warn that if the high court hinders preservation of fragile animal habitats, all manner of bugs, birds and rodents could face extinction.    "The issue in this case goes clearly to the heart of the Endangered Species Act's effectiveness when applied to private land," according to Prof. Denis Binder of Western New England College School of Law.    Although the case pits the timber industry against the government, many individual landowners are also watching avidly. Among them are Marj and Roger Krueger, who have been offered to the justices in a couple of briefs as typical victims of overzealous regulation. The Kruegers were blocked from building a house in Austin, Texas, on a one-and-a-half acre plot they bought for $40,000 in 1989. There weren't any endangered animals on the Krueger property, but golden-cheeked warblers had been sighted in nearby wooded canyons. The plot remains "useless and worthless," Ms. Krueger said in an interview. "The irony is that the lot itself has only one tree on it, and it's a scrub. We were going to cut that one down and put 20 trees up."    The unusual degree of excitement surrounding the case has been heightened by the Republican push in Congress to scale back the Endangered Species Act and expand the right of landowners to be compensated for regulation of their property. Backers of these legislative efforts hope to gain critical momentum from a Supreme Court victory. A win would "sort of be affirming what many people in Congress already believe: that the Endangered Species Act has gone too far, and that the bureaucrats are out of control," asserts Nancie Marzulla, president of the Defenders of Property Rights, a Washington, D.C.-based advocacy group.    Kevin Kirchner, an attorney with the Sierra Club Legal Defense Fund, counters that "there is no certainty that the folks in Congress who want to gut the [Endangered Species Act] will succeed" because "the public support isn't there for gutting the act." If the conservative legislative foray fizzles, the Supreme Court could end up setting the terms of engagement in what will undoubtedly be a continuing legal battle over imperiled animals. The high court's ruling is expected by summer.    The law, passed in 1973 to save animals in danger of disappearing, has evolved into a powerful tool for federal regulation of private land use. In recent years, it became one of the main catalysts of a nationwide property-rights movement propelled by corporate financial support and grass-roots anger over purported excesses of environmentalism.    As important as the Supreme Court case is for its potential practical effects, it also has tremendous symbolic resonance for conservatives, populists and business interests -- which helps explain the profusion of passionate friend-of-the-court briefs. Ms. Marzulla, an attorney, declares in her group's brief that "the backlash against the Endangered Species Act has fueled a property-rights movement the likes of which have not been seen in this country since the 1960s when black Americans marched on Washington in protest of the violation of their civil rights by a government that had all but forgotten its duty to uphold the constitutional rights of all of its citizens."    Vivid imagery abounds. The case is called "Sweet Home" because the lead plaintiff in the 1991 lawsuit from which the Supreme Court case stems is the Sweet Home Chapter of Communities for a Great Oregon, a citizens' group in the town of Sweet Home. But the real force behind the suit is the American Forest and Paper Association, which organized the plaintiff group of landowners and small timber companies from Oregon, Washington state and Georgia. The Washington, D.C.-based timber trade association also financed the litigation in federal court in the nation's capital.    The plaintiffs complained that they were financially hurt by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's curbs on logging to protect the spotted owl in the Pacific Northwest and the red-cockaded woodpecker in the Southeast. Specifically, the plaintiffs challenged the government's interpretation of a part of the Endangered Species Act that prohibits any action that would "harm" an animal that has been deemed endangered or threatened. The Fish and Wildlife Service reads "harm" to include "significant habitat modification or degredation where it actually kills or injures wildlife."    The timber industry lost in U.S. district court and in an initial appeal. But in a relatively rare occurrence, one member of a three-judge appellate panel flipped his position, handing the plaintiffs a 2-1 victory. The appellate panel said that the Endangered Species Act doesn't authorize the government to bar changes to animal habitats on private land. As used in the law, "harm" requires a "direct application of force" against the animals themselves, the panel concluded. (Another part of the act explicitly bars changing the habitats of endangered species on public land.)    Without the authority to prevent changes in endangered species' habitats on private property, regulators will lose crucial leverage in dealing with landowners, the Clinton administration stresses in its appeal to the Supreme Court. The Fish and Wildlife Service has relied on an expansive view of harm to negotiate a series of voluntary conservation plans with industry, including one in which developers in Southern California agreed to preserve vast tracts of privately owned land that is home to a threatened bird called the California gnatcatcher.    The Clinton administration, backed by a coalition of environmental groups, contends that Fish and Wildlife officials don't try to stop changes in habitat unless they will actually injure or kill animals. The environmentalists go so far as to note that the total number of reported court cases involving habitat-modification disputes is less than 15. "For 20 years, private and public landowners have adapted their behavior to conform to the Fish and Wildlife Service's `harm regulation' without dire consequences," maintains Patti Goldman, lead lawyer for the environmental groups.    Business and property-rights proponents look at the same two decades and don't see sweetness and light. Only under the threat of legal sanctions, including criminal penalties, have developers, logging companies and other landowners agreed to limit the use of their property, says William Murray, a lawyer with the American Forest and Paper Association. These situations may not produce lawsuits, but they leave many property owners furious. "A lot of times the animals aren't anywhere near the property, and it's just the Fish and Wildlife Service trying to get a free ride on private land," Mr. Murray charges.    One case pending in federal court in Washington state involves Anderson & Middleton Logging Co. The federal government sued the small Hoquiam, Wash., concern in 1993 to stop it from logging a 71-acre tract on the Olympic Peninsula. The government's concern: Timber harvesting on the company's land would harm a pair of northern spotted owls believed to be nesting some 1.6 miles away in the Olympic National Park. The company's lawyer, Mark Rutzik, responds that "the government has absolutely no evidence that logging this tract will have any effect on the owls 1.6 miles away."    ---                   Endangered Species Spat   Choosing sides in fight over habitat-protection rule:    ATTACKING THE RULE    -- Sweet Home Chapter of Communities for a Great Oregon    -- U. Title: THE WALL STREET JOURNAL / NORTHWEST --- Agency Fails To Inspect Well Water
Text: The Oregon Department of Environmental Quality has inspected groundwater in only one part of the state in the past 18 months, despite a state law that requires it to carry out "on-going" assessments where groundwater is vulnerable to pollutants. The inspections fall short of what the department promised the Legislature in 1997. Back then, it said it would perform tests on wells in four to six parts of the state in fiscal years 1997 and 1998. What's more, it hasn't done follow-up testing on contamination in the Coburg and Junction City areas north of Eugene, where tests earlier in the decade found that water in more than a quarter of residential wells contained nitrates at or above the safe-drinking limit. "I am disappointed to learn that is the case," says Bill Bradbury, who as a state senator in 1989 was one of the main proponents of the measure. The Democrat from Bandon has retired from politics and is now director of the Portland environmental group For the Sake of Salmon. Langdon Marsh, director of the DEQ, says funding for testing was discretionary within the budget, and the department had the authority to shift funds to more pressing salmon and clean-water programs. Spotty testing by the department in the early 1990s satisfies the law's requirements, he says, though he agrees that "it's disappointing that we have not been able to do the follow-up" in problem areas. He adds: "You wish you could do more, but you do the best with what you've got." Critics say the funding shift puts at risk the one-quarter of the state's three million residents who use private wells. "There is no one standing watch," says Maryann Helferty, coordinator for drinking-water protection at the Seattle office of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. The EPA monitors water quality only for systems serving 25 or more customers; it has no authority over private wells. Ms. Helferty notes that 90% of Oregonians in rural areas depend on groundwater for drinking. In 1989, when the state Groundwater Protection Act was enacted, the Legislature appropriated $1.9 million for the first two years of groundwater monitoring and management. "For a few years, we were testing a new area almost every month," says Greg Pettit, manager of water-quality monitoring at the DEQ's main laboratory in Portland. But then, says Mr. Pettit, who helped draft the law, the funding gradually dropped off. After the $1.9 million ran out, the program was paid for with general funds appropriated by the Legislature to the department. Specific budgets for groundwater protection were never accounted for in the state budget, he says. Mike Llewelyn, director of the water-quality program, says the agency has no choice but to cut down on groundwater testing. By 1996, money was so scarce -- and the demands of federally ordered clean-river initiatives and salmon-rescue endeavors so great -- that the department was forced to slash the groundwater budget, he says. At the same time, the agency had a budget shortfall, after revenue from fees -- for such services as sewer systems and permits, came in below projections. As a result, staff cuts were ordered. By the end of 1997, the water-quality program's total staff in Portland was reduced to five full-time employees and one part-time worker from 11 full-time employees at the start of 1996, says Mr. Llewelyn, who became director in May 1997. "We had to cut 15 positions out of 200" department-wide, he says. And the water-quality program, he adds, "was one of the few areas where we had some flexibility" to eliminate jobs, such as lab technicians and policy staff. That's because federal and state statutes mandate positions in other divisions, while the groundwater act didn't. To make matters worse, as the flow of money into the DEQ was declining, its obligations under the federal Clean Water and Endangered Species acts began to increase. According to Mr. Marsh, the DEQ devotes about 30 more staffers to meeting Clean Water and Endangered Species act requirements than it did two years ago. The groundwater law was enacted, says Mr. Pettit of the DEQ, after the department in 1985 and 1986 "discovered some pretty extensive contamination" in rural areas. He says the idea was to pinpoint potential pollution before it became dangerous. "By the time contaminants show up in the water table, it comes from activity on the surface that has been going on for 30 or 40 years," he says. That preventive approach, says the EPA's Ms. Helferty, made Oregon's law "one of the best in the nation." The law instructs the DEQ to locate areas where nitrates appear in well samples at seven milligrams per liter -- the federal safe drinking maximum is 10 milligrams per liter -- and where pesticides appear at 50% of the federal maximum. Those areas would be designated "groundwater management areas." For each management area, the agency is to form a committee of local farmers and other water users that will help develop a plan for eliminating the contaminants. Ultimately, the state has the power to condemn polluted wells if the contaminating activity continues. Between 1989 and 1996, the department conducted random tests in 45 areas of the state where farming or other industry led it to suspect that underground water supplies might be contaminated. Only two areas in three Eastern Oregon counties -- one in northern Malheur and one covering parts of Umatilla and Morrow -- have been designated as groundwater-management areas so far. Pollution had already been found in the groundwater in the areas in the mid-1980s, which led in part to the law. The two areas were designated for protection in 1989 and 1990, respectively, and are the only areas in the state today where routine testing continues. That's in an effort to determine how well the action plans devised by the local committees are working, says Mr. Pettit. Since 1991, the agency hasn't "been able to declare any new groundwater-management areas," due to lack of funds, says Amy Patton, who was the manager of the department's groundwater-protection section from 1990 to 1996 and is now a part-time senior groundwater policy analyst. The department has asked Gov. John Kitzhaber to include money for five to six more positions in the budget he sends to the Legislature in January, to restore the jobs cut from the groundwater-protection program. Gov. Kitzhaber's office says it hasn't reviewed the request yet, but Press Secretary Bob Applegate says the governor isn't optimistic revenue will support much new spending. "It is becoming harder and harder to fund programs that have been cut if they do not have a dedicated source of revenue," Mr. Applegate says Until more funding comes through, areas that need to be tested will go without. Ms. Helferty says that state test results indicate that some 17 areas might qualify as management areas and require follow-up testing. Preliminary tests early in the decade found that nitrate levels in those areas were at 70% of the safe standard. In Coburg, where the DEQ found nitrate contamination in 1994, Dave Downing, a groundwater technical specialist with the East Lane County Soil and Water Conservation District, says he didn't even know that the state groundwater program existed. "That would be a great program -- if we could get it," Mr. Downing says. State Sen. Kate Brown, a Democrat from Portland says the program all but disappeared without a whisper. "I don't even remember a stir about the groundwater program" during the 1997 Legislature, she says. One thing is certain, "This one's going come back and bite us in the butt." (See related letter: "Letters to the Editor: Protecting Well Water in Oregon" -- WSJ NWJ Nov. 25, 1998) Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Bush to Call for Greenhouse-Gas Curbs; Pressured for Years, President Warms To Broad Regulation
Text: WASHINGTON -- In a significant shift on global warming, President Bush will propose stopping growth in U.S. greenhouse-gas emissions by 2025 and signal that he is open to lawmakers reining in pollution from power companies. The stance, set to be unveiled Wednesday at a White House speech, indicates Mr. Bush's willingness to grapple with the growing legislative debate over global warming. It marks an acknowledgment by the Bush administration that the U.S. likely will adopt some sort of broad new legal system to curb greenhouse-gas emissions in coming years. Mr. Bush has opposed comprehensive legislation to curb emissions. But like an increasing number of utilities and manufacturers, he is aiming to join the discussions in hopes of shaping the debate and creating a system that won't be too costly to industry or consumers. Mr. Bush faces the challenge of attracting sympathetic Republicans to support concrete proposals in the waning days of his administration. The White House is under pressure from a growing number of big businesses to take more action this year to spare them from the prospect of still-tougher regulation. All three major presidential candidates, including Republican Sen. John McCain, have supported efforts to curb emissions that are more onerous than some industries would like. The Bush administration contends that one proposal, soon to be debated in the Senate, that seeks to halt emissions growth by 2012 is too costly. Mr. Bush's goals will likely face criticism from Democrats and environmental groups because they are less ambitious than other targets before U.S. lawmakers. They also will face hostility from conservatives who worry that showing flexibility now will mean giving up too much ground. Environmentalists and other groups already have gained ground without comprehensive emissions legislation. They have successfully pushed lawsuits and regulatory actions that would use the Clean Air Act, Endangered Species Act and National Environmental Policy Act to address the problem of global warming. The White House fears a regulatory train wreck that could create a bewildering and costly set of rules affecting not just major emitters but office buildings and schools. Overall U.S. emissions of greenhouse gases fell 1.1% in 2006 from the previous year. But the general trend has been one of growth, with emissions rising 14.7% from 1990 to 2006, according to the Environmental Protection Agency. In the most specific part of his speech, Mr. Bush will carve out a more ambitious goal for power generators, source of about 40% of U.S. emissions. He will call for a halt in the growth of greenhouse gases from electric power plants within 10 to 15 years. He won't propose specific legislation, but White House officials hope his goals could shape a growing congressional debate. The White House continues to oppose economywide caps on emissions, but it is not shutting the door to creative market-based approaches to particular sectors. That could include what's known as a cap-and-trade system, in which companies buy and sell what amount to permits to emit global-warming gases such as carbon dioxide. Proponents say such a system gives companies financial incentives to curb emissions. "We're not favoring one policy tool over another," said one senior official who provided a detailed preview of the remarks, noting the administration has supported market-based systems in several contexts. A spokesman for the Edison Electric Institute, a Washington-based group that represents U.S. utilities, declined to comment ahead of Mr. Bush's speech. The U.S. Energy Department has projected that carbon-dioxide emissions from power generation will rise 19% between 2007 and 2030 as a result of new or expanded coal-fired plants. In his remarks, President Bush is expected to focus less on sectors outside power. Instead, the remarks will be devoted to shaping the eventual debate rather than offering specific proposals. He will highlight the costs that the wrong approach on climate change would impose for U.S. businesses and consumers. Mr. Bush is expected to say the administration has made progress on several fronts, such as improving vehicle efficiency standards. He will make the case that elected lawmakers, not bureaucrats, should decide how to reshape the regulatory framework. He will also argue against legislation that raises taxes or makes demands that are technologically unattainable and could hurt the economy, such as by raising fuel costs. He will call for more emphasis on new technology rather than raising the price of old technology. The administration wants to make sure that coal, which currently provides about half of U.S. power needs and is a major source of greenhouse gases, isn't squeezed out of the U.S. power sector. It also will oppose placing tariffs on goods from other countries over global- warming concerns. That could set up what the official warned could become a "carbon-based global trade war." The White House wants to shift financial incentives to favor emissions-reducing energy sources, such as nuclear power and renewable fuels, in part to boost U.S. manufacturing. Carbon dioxide, considered the main man-made global warming gas, is emitted when fossil fuels are burned. Scientists say the gases collect in the atmosphere, forming a blanket that traps heat, raising global temperatures. A United Nations panel said earlier this year that human activity is "very likely" the cause of a global-warming trend in recent decades. The administration's goal of halting the growth of emissions by 2025 appears aimed at speeding up international negotiations over a replacement treaty for the Kyoto Protocol, which expires in 2012, and persuading developing giants such as China and India to enact potentially painful curbs to their own soaring emissions. The White House considers that crucial to achieving a follow-on agreement. Officials believe a pact that doesn't include China and India could put U.S. industry at a cost disadvantage and accelerate the flow of jobs to those countries, while failing to make any significant inroads on world-wide emissions. Previously, the administration has proposed only a short-term goal of slowing growth of greenhouse gases by 18%, as measured against economic output, by 2012 through piecemeal efforts such as the new vehicle efficiency rules, as well as renewable fuel increases and appliance and lighting efficiency. "The U.S. has a significant portion already in law of what we need," the official said. Mr. Bush's move comes as the U.S. Senate is preparing to take up legislation that calls for reducing U.S. greenhouse-gas emissions by as much as 25% below 2005 emissions levels in 2020 and by as much as 66% below 2005 emissions levels in 2050. The legislation, sponsored by Sens. Joseph Lieberman (I., Conn.) and John Warner (R., Va.), would allow companies that exceeded the limits to buy credits from other companies that met them with room to spare. Many large businesses now endorse the idea of setting caps on greenhouse-gas emissions, though few have publicly committed to supporting the Lieberman-Warner measure. At a meeting with House Republicans last week, White House officials warned that the EPA is on track to eventually regulate carbon-dioxide emissions through the Clean Air Act, according to a lawmaker who was present. "They [White House officials] were trying to get the temperature [of lawmakers] on climate-change legislation and trying to get engaged," said the lawmaker, Rep. John Shimkus (R., Ill.). Mr. Shimkus said the response from his fellow Republicans was "very skeptical." "It's a game of chicken. Do you do nothing during this Congress? . . . Or by doing that do you run the risk of really terrible legislation in the next Congress?" Mr. Shimkus said. "That's what we're trying to figure out." Environmentalists first petitioned the EPA to regulate greenhouse gases in 1999, and Mr. Bush, as a presidential candidate in 2000, vowed to regulate carbon-dioxide emissions if elected. He retreated from that pledge shortly into his first term, citing concern that such a move would lead to higher energy prices.

Title: Green Group Pitches Plan To Save Birds
Text: Environmentalists seeking to protect two high-profile endangered species in Central Texas are trying to breathe new life into a failed state effort that asks landowners to help save the birds. The Environmental Defense Fund is proposing a "safe harbor" program that would allow landowners whose lands contain habitat for golden-cheeked warblers and black-capped vireos to develop or otherwise alter some of their property with immunity from prosecution -- so long as they promise to preserve part of it for use by the birds. The plan, however, faces steep opposition from the people it would seem to help: landowners in the scenic Hill Country near Austin. Last year, ranchers, farmers and property-rights advocates killed a similar plan by the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department, and some already have signaled opposition to the new effort. Landowners and property-rights advocates fear the proposal could actually expose landowners to more regulation by giving environmentalists and the government more information about which properties have habitats. "Safe harbors are a fraud," says R.J. Smith, a senior environmental scholar at the Competitive Enterprise Institute in Washington, D.C., a private-property think tank that wrote anti-safe-harbor op-ed pieces for Texas newspapers and called landowners to ask them to oppose the Parks and Wildlife plan last year. He and others say landowners would be better off rejecting such programs and instead lobbying for more substantive changes to the Endangered Species Act. But EDF officials say their plan, which must be approved by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, will succeed where the past effort failed because they think landowners will be more willing to work with them than with a state agency. As evidence, they say, more than a dozen landowners have asked them for help in implementing land-management practices to help conserve the species. And besides, even if the state failed, they say, the project is too important not to give it another shot. The plan is "absolutely critical to [the species'] survival," says Melinda Taylor, a senior attorney in Austin for the New York-based environmental group. Under a draft version of the EDF plan, which was submitted to Fish and Wildlife last month, landowners would be asked to voluntarily notify the group that their land contains habitat for the birds. Then the landowner would negotiate a conservation agreement with the EDF that outlines the steps to maintain the habitat on a mutually agreed-upon portion of the land. For example, the landowner would promise not to clear-cut vegetation, or to steer cattle herds that eat vegetation to other areas. In return, the landowner would get immunity from fines or criminal prosecution from the federal government for destroying any habitat not covered by the agreement. For example, the landowner would be able to clear-cut his or her land for farming, livestock grazing, or the construction of a house or other building without threat of hassle from federal regulators -- so long as the original section of habitat is preserved. The landowner would even be able to alter the originally protected land, so long as he or she creates an equal amount of desirable habitat somewhere else, and no net loss of the birds occurs. The EDF also would be required by U.S. Fish and Wildlife to make sure that the safe-harbor agreements negotiated with individual landowners don't threaten other endangered species. An official with the Fish and Wildlife Service says the department is still working out details of the agreement with the EDF, but is likely to approve the plan. Such programs have been implemented in a handful of cases around the country; in Texas, safe-harbor programs are in place to protect the Attwater's prairie chicken along the Gulf Coast and the northern aplomado falcon in South Texas, as well as the red-cockaded woodpecker in East Texas. EDF officials argue the program is needed in the case of the warbler and vireo because most of the birds' habitat is on private lands, and something must be done to encourage more landowners to preserve it. Indeed, they point out, some landowners have actually destroyed vireo and warbler habitat out of fear that if the government finds out their land is amenable to the birds, they won't be able to use it as they please. The vireo, which was declared endangered in 1987, lives in shrubs and patchy woodlands, while the warbler, which was declared endangered in 1990, lives in oak and juniper trees. Both are threatened by the destruction of habitats that has come about with the growth of Austin and other Hill Country communities. EDF officials point out that 18 landowners have already agreed to conserve about 22,000 acres of land for vireos and warblers through an existing EDF conservation project, which doesn't include the promise of immunity. They say about a half-dozen of those landowners have expressed interest in participating in the safe-harbor program. And they're hoping that the promise of immunity will attract even more takers; the EDF aims to get 250,000 acres set aside for warblers and vireos through the program in the next three or four years. But landowners and the state's leading agricultural groups remain suspicious. Ned Meister, director of commodity and regulatory activities for the Texas Farm Bureau, says his organization supports the safe-harbor concept, but fears that federal regulators and environmentalists could renege on the deal at some future date, exposing those who volunteered information about their land to more regulation. "There's a worry that ... the rules could change in the middle of the game," he says. And, unfortunately, he says, "I don't know that there could ever be that guarantee" that the government won't later turn on the landowners and hassle them for altering lands that were offered immunity. Tobin Parker, a rancher in Kerr County, says he is all for protecting the two species, but the plan is "probably not something that a whole lot of people would want to take advantage of," he says. By participating, he says, "you're opening yourself up to regulation of some sort," and that is "inherently not good." The same concerns emerged in 1997 and 1998, when Texas Parks and Wildlife proposed its plan to set up safe harbors for the birds. The agency dropped the plan after landowners and agricultural groups signaled that they would be unlikely to participate. Backers of the new program admit it's possible individual safe-harbor agreements could be rescinded, but they say that would only happen in situations of extreme and immediate peril to the species. Otherwise, the Fish and Wildlife Service is bound by a recent "no surprises" policy it approved prohibiting the department from imposing new restrictions on landowners with safe-harbor agreements without their permission. Backers of the plan are also hoping that, as time passes, some of the antagonism created by the listing of the species is calming down. "There's still a strong current of suspicion of the federal government in Texas," says Ms. Taylor of the EDF. But now, she says, pointing to the handful of landowners that have expressed interest in participating, "there's a growing desire to help." Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: The Gulf Oil Spill: U.S. Debated Probe Announcement
Text: Attorney General Eric Holder disclosed the Justice Department's civil and criminal probes of the Gulf oil spill Tuesday after weeks of internal debate. The initial reluctance included some Justice officials who were sensitive about making the investigations public even as the government pressed BP PLC to plug the well. Still, Mr. Holder's decision to confirm the probes Tuesday, in a staged appearance on the Gulf Coast, appears to be in line with the department's guidelines in high-profile cases. Mr. Holder stressed that 11 people died in the April 20 rig accident that precipitated the spill and said there is "a wide range of possible violations." Facing growing criticism over its response as the leak drags on, the Obama administration has been pushing aggressively on several fronts to show it is in command of the situation and to keep pressure on BP. But it faces a tricky balance keeping up that pressure and showing the public it is taking action even as it depends heavily on the company, and its technical expertise, to stop the flow from the crippled well. Inside the department, some officials feared that the threat of agents of the Federal Bureau of Investigation looking over the shoulder of BP and others could hinder the work to plug the well, people familiar with the debate said. Mr. Holder sought to at least tacitly address those concerns Tuesday when he said the government's first priority was to stop the spill. The department usually doesn't discuss investigations until charges are filed. But Mr. Holder's defenders pointed to guidelines from the U.S. Attorney's Manual, the Justice Department's bible for handling prosecutions, which allows officials to confirm ongoing probes "in matters that have already received substantial publicity, or about which the community needs to be reassured that the appropriate law enforcement agency is investigating the incident." Most of these companies were aware that a Justice Department investigation was under way. For weeks, the department has been dropping hints that it was taking preliminary steps toward an investigation. Mr. Holder told reporters last month that he had dispatched senior prosecutors to the Gulf of Mexico region. More recently, the department sent letters to companies involved in the accident asking them to preserve all relevant documents. The question is what will come of it -- amid some very real hurdles. The very fact that there is oil in the water indicates a violation of federal environmental laws, one Justice Department official argued. Whether that leads to a criminal case for the companies involved in the Deepwater Horizon operation -- BP, rig owner Transocean Ltd. and other contractors -- may depend on whether the government concludes that willful violations of the law led to the rig explosion that led to the spill. The Justice Department's environmental section has been aggressive in pursuing cases against corporations -- though many end up with misdemeanor pleas and fines that are easily absorbed by big companies. BP didn't return requests for comment on its legal strategy for defending itself in a criminal investigation. Transocean's position is that it was following BP's orders and that the engineering of the well was BP's design and responsibility. It has hired outside lawyers and is seeking BP's engineering documents to review them for faults. The company would not comment other than to say through a spokesman: "Transocean has not been named in any criminal investigation. We will not speculate on actions the Justice Department may or may not take." Mr. Holder on Tuesday said investigators were reviewing environmental laws, such as the Clean Water Act, the Oil Pollution Act, the Migratory Bird Treaty Act and the Endangered Species Act, to see if there were violations. Some measures, such as the bird act, allow prosecutors to prove a violation without having to show that a company intended any wrongdoing, thereby lowering the bar to fine corporations. Mr. Holder said officials also were reviewing other statutes. Legal experts said those likely included fraud and obstruction of justice. Also, prosecutors will look at whether BP and others made any allegedly false statements to government officials at the Minerals Management Service, the U.S. Coast Guard or the Environmental Protection Agency, either before or after the explosion at the Deepwater Horizon oil rig. Last year, Exxon Mobil Corp. pleaded guilty to killing migratory birds in five states and paid roughly $7,000 for each bird killed, for a total of about $600,000. In 2007, Citgo Refining and Chemicals Co. went to trial and was found guilty of three misdemeanor criminal violations of the Migratory Bird Treaty Act by a judge in Corpus Christi, Texas. It could take months or even years before the Justice Department can build a case that is ready for a courtroom. BP and its contractors have hired multiple law firms to represent their interests, as have some individual officials at the various companies involved. They already have pointed fingers at each other in a series of public hearings before members of Congress, and before an investigative panel led by the Coast Guard and the Minerals Management Service. White-collar criminal defense attorneys said BP and other companies in the government's crosshairs likely will insist the event was an accident. On Tuesday, the Justice Department asked a Houston court to reject Transocean's effort to limit its liability for the oil spill to around $27 million by invoking a 159-year-old law. The Limitation of Liability Act of 1851 was previously invoked by the owners of the SS Titanic to avoid liability when the supposedly unsinkable ship sank. ---     Thomas Catan and Amir Efrati contributed to this article.            Credit: By Evan Perez and Dionne Searcey

Title: U.S. News: Texans Fight Over Birds, Water Rights --- Suit Claims River Managers Shortchange Endangered Cranes; Nuclear Project Is Issue
Text: DALLAS -- A coalition of environmentalists, bird lovers and Gulf Coast municipalities sued Texas regulators in federal court this past week, accusing them of mismanaging waters necessary for the survival of the biggest flock of endangered whooping cranes, which migrate to South Texas every winter. The group, called the Aransas Project, claims that officials from the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality violated the Endangered Species Act by not ensuring enough fresh water from the Guadalupe River flowed to the estuary where the cranes stay, causing the death of 23 birds in Texas last year. The lawsuit was filed late Wednesday in Corpus Christi. But state-designated water managers say the real goal of the suit is to block a potential nuclear-power project that would compete for the same water. The tallest bird in North America, the whooping crane is also the rarest crane species in the world. Less than 400 survive in the wild, according to U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. A report released Thursday by the Department of Interior found that climate change threatens to exacerbate current pressures on birds such as whooping cranes. "What we are trying to do with the litigation is put the whooping cranes into the water-rights process," said Jim Blackburn, the Aransas Project's lawyer. The Texas environmental commission countered that it was "far from certain" how reduced fresh-water inflows affected the cranes, adding that it was reviewing existing studies on the subject. Disputes over water that pit people and industry against wildlife are likely to emerge more frequently in Texas as the state's population continues to expand in regions where water supplies are already stretched and where water rights have long been a point of contention. Regulators have sold much of the state's surface water. In some basins, they have sold more than the rivers actually carry, even in wet years, though not all water rights are currently exercised. A severe drought that parched the state last year offered a glimpse of what would happen if more water owners made use of their permits. Guadalupe River managers cut deliveries to junior-rights holders who are subject to restrictions when flows are low. (Senior-rights holders, which have first priority, received their water.) Reduced fresh-water flows increased salinity levels in the marshes where the lanky white birds with black-tipped wings settle with their chicks after their trip from Canada. That reduced the availability of blue crabs and wolfberries, the cranes' preferred foods, and forced them to fly farther to find fresh water, said Tom Stehn, whooping-crane coordinator for the Fish and Wildlife Service. Almost 9% of the 270 birds that arrived last winter died. With the drought ended, the crane's population bounced back to 264 at the beginning of this season, and only one has died since. Still, Mr. Stehn worries that insufficient water flows in the future could shrink the size of the flock, by far the largest in the world and the only one left that migrates without human help. Charles Smith, a commissioner of Aransas County, which is a member of the plaintiff coalition, said bird-watching accounts for some 25% of the local economy, with the cranes the biggest stars. Bill West, the general manager of the Guadalupe-Blanco River Authority, which manages the river that feeds the crane habitat, said the Aransas Project's claims are off-base. His agency recently extended an agreement to reserve 75,000 acre-feet of water for a potential nuclear project by Exelon Corp. That amount is about seven times the yearly amount that is used by the nearby city of Victoria, according to calculations from the Aransas Project. Mr. West says the lawsuit -- which claims that more cranes will die if the nuclear project is built -- is primarily about the plant. "This is not about the whooping crane; it's a NIMBY situation" to kill the potential nuclear plant, he said, referring to the common phrase for Not In My Back Yard. But the main patron of the Aransas Project, a local ranching family named O'Connor, countered that they have been working to preserve water in the area for years. "The nuclear-power plant issue eventually was the last straw for the family," said Bill Jones, water-policy consultant for the O'Connor family. An Exelon spokesman says the company is not involved in the dispute and will not pursue the power-plant project if there is not enough water. The company said last year it was slowing development efforts on the Texas project after losing out on a request for a federal loan guarantee that would have dramatically reduced financing costs for the plant. Since then, the Obama administration has said it favored raising loan guarantees for nuclear plants to $54.5 billion from $18.5 billion. Another factor that will influence Exelon's decision whether to proceed is likely to be the nuclear development plans of its competitors. Credit: By Ana Campoy

Title: World-Wide
Text: The first lady announced the U.S. will provide $25 million for the emergency repair of homes in Bosnia. She said the funds would fix at least 2,500 houses. --- Dole is expected to lock up more than enough delegates to secure the Republican nomination in primaries in California, Washington and Nevada today. Buchanan, campaigning in California, hammered away at anti-immigration themes. GOP stands on that issue and affirmative action worry some in the party. --- The U.S. expressed relief as tensions eased between China and Taiwan. Beijing wound up its war games near Taiwan, and the U.S. prepared to withdraw an aircraft carrier from the area. In the U.S., a cabinet-level meeting is set for today to discuss possible sanctions against China for the sale of nuclear-weapons equipment to Pakistan. --- The Supreme Court agreed to rule in an Arizona case involving the issue of whether states may require civil servants to speak English on the job. A decision isn't due until next year. Justices also took a case in which they will decide whether landowners can use the Endangered Species Act to curb conservation efforts. --- Yeltsin said Russia has no intention of forming a single state with Belarus after a weekend agreement to tighten links provoked protests in the former Soviet republic. The Russian president also scheduled a weekend TV address to unveil a plan to end fighting in Chechnya. Troops there braced for an expected rebel assault on Grozny. --- A key Whitewater figure was sentenced to 28 months in prison for defrauding the U.S. of more than $2 million. The sentence, about half the term former Arkansas municipal-court judge David Hale could have received, is the result of a plea agreement. Hale is a major government witness in the trial of former Clinton business partners. --- AFL-CIO delegates approved a plan for a one-time surtax on union members to raise about $25 million to support Democratic candidates this year. The special Washington meeting called by the labor federation's new president also endorsed Clinton. Past endorsements have always followed the political conventions. --- A White House advisory panel made a series of recommendations on Social Security reforms, with the common theme being that investment of retirement funds in private equities should be allowed. The most controversial option would let workers put some of their taxes in accounts held outside the government. --- The EU agreed to ban British beef exports after a British government scientific advisory panel last week said a cattle disease was probably the cause of an incurable human brain disorder. London yesterday decided against slaughtering a large portion of the British herd. --- Indian troops surrounded a Muslim shrine in Kashmir and ordered separatist rebels holding it to surrender or face further attacks. The standoff followed fighting Sunday in which at least 14 people, possibly 26 according to the rebels, were killed. --- France, Britain and the U.S. signed a treaty to ban nuclear weapons from the South Pacific. The signing comes just two months after France completed a series of nuclear tests, and its signature is seen as an attempt to repair relations in the region. --- A military court in Lebanon ordered 15 Islamic militants to stand trial for the 1983 bombing of the U.S. Embassy in Beirut, which killed 62. A lower court in 1993 said the suspects were covered by an amnesty for crimes committed in Lebanon's civil war. --- A Japanese court ordered Okinawa's governor to renew leases of U.S. bases, saying a refusal would be overridden by Tokyo. American presence on Okinawa has drawn protests since the rape last year of a 12-year-old girl by three U.S. servicemen. NATO SAID its peacekeepers in Bosnia will take part in reconstruction efforts. A NATO spokesman said the force has been so successful in securing compliance with the military provisions of the Dayton peace accord that it could now turn to assisting civil authorities in rebuilding war-damaged infrastructure. Such a shift would be a significant expansion of the alliance's mandate. Meanwhile, Clinton visited U.S. peacekeeping troops at their posts around the main base at Tuzla.

Title: U.S. News -- Election 2012: A Big Play for Bigger Donors
Text: Newt Gingrich's rise to the front of the Republican presidential field is all the more surprising because he has done it without a national network of large-dollar fund-raisers or an army of elected officials touting his candidacy. The former House speaker is scrambling to capitalize on his surge in the polls by courting religious and conservative leaders while trying to assemble big-dollar donors to supplement the financial supporters he developed while building an advocacy group during his years away from government. The Gingrich campaign at this stage is in stark contrast to that of his top rival, former Massachusetts Gov. Mitt Romney, who spent much of the fall holding fund-raisers with some of the GOP's wealthiest donors and whose campaign trumpets new endorsements every day. The differences underscore a divide between the party's primary-election voters, who polls show are supporting Mr. Gingrich in substantial numbers, and the establishment figures who are rallying around Mr. Romney. In recent weeks, Mr. Gingrich has stepped up his outreach to conservative leaders who have been reluctant to support Mr. Romney. The former speaker sat for two hours of questioning last week by 50 or so conservative leaders in Northern Virginia. The assembled activists grilled him about his multiple marriages and his support for programs that conservatives generally dislike, including the Endangered Species Act, subsidies for alternative energy and the Medicare prescription-drug benefit signed into law by former President George W. Bush. "The questions that were put to him were tougher than any questions put to any candidate this year," said Brent Bozell, a conservative writer and activist who attended the session. "Newt's different than any other candidate: Newt came from the conservative family. And when you talk to a family member, you're more matter-of-fact in your questioning." Gingrich spokesman R.C. Hammond said, "The purpose of it was to reach out to conservative leaders who had been sitting on the sidelines. It was a reverse wake: We had people show up to show them that we aren't dead." The session was reported by the Los Angeles Times. At one point, someone in attendance asked Mr. Gingrich about his three marriages and his admitted extramarital affair, asserting that surrogates for President Barack Obama would raise these issues, according to people who attended the session. Mr. Gingrich told the group that he believes the American people are willing to forgive him for things he did years ago and that any attacks would backfire. At this point, many conservatives are willing to give Mr. Gingrich a second look because they trust him more than Mr. Romney, said Penny Nance, the president of Concerned Women for America, who attended the meeting. "Based just on policy, most conservatives are more comfortable with Newt Gingrich," she said. "He's just more believable as a conservative." Mr. Gingrich will need the activists' support to upend Mr. Romney in what could prove to be a protracted primary fight, because the former governor has far more money and a more sophisticated campaign infrastructure. Unlike those of other major White House contenders, Mr. Gingrich's campaign isn't financed by large donations, and he hasn't built a network of prominent fund-raising "bundlers," who gather donations from their circle of associates. Where some other candidates regularly hold fund-raisers that ask for the legal per-person maximum of $2,500 for primary elections, Mr. Gingrich has held few such events. "I don't know of any of the traditional sources of major support -- whether in Washington or elsewhere -- who are contributing to Gingrich," said Fred Malek, a major Republican fund-raiser with extensive ties to the national party, who is assisting Mr. Romney. The Gingrich campaign held a fund-raiser in Washington last week in which supporters were asked for $1,000 each, far less than the $2,500 that Mr. Romney often requests. Mr. Gingrich raised $60,000 at the time of an October debate in Las Vegas, and he raised about $25,000 in Naples, Fla., over Thanksgiving weekend, his campaign said. That's a far cry from Mr. Romney, who collected $1 million at a single event in Texas this month and the same amount at another event in Florida. Most major presidential candidates launch their campaigns with seed money from hundreds of wealthy donors. That usually means that in the early part of the campaign, top candidates are largely dependent on donations of $2,500 from wealthy backers. As the campaign wears on, successful candidates gradually build out their fund-raising operations and draw in a majority of their money from millions of smaller donors who contribute $100, $25 or less. Through Sept. 30, two-thirds of the $32.5 million raised by Mr. Romney from individuals came from people making donations of $2,500, according to a study by the nonpartisan Campaign Finance Institute. Mr. Gingrich received just 29% of his total individual donations from people contributing $2,500, according to the study. In all, more than 300 people each donated $2,500 to Mr. Gingrich's campaign -- accounting for $800,000. In total, he had raised $2.8 million for his campaign through Sept. 30, the close of the most recent finance filing period. Mr. Gingrich's reliance on smaller donors could give him an advantage because people who have already given can be asked to donate again without reaching the legal contribution limit. Mr. Hammond said Mr. Gingrich has raised $5.5 million in the past few months and hopes to bring in close to $10 million for October through December. Mr. Romney is expected to at least double that total. Credit: By Brody Mullins and Patrick O'Connor

Title: Bonneville Power Proposal Sparks Battle Among States
Text: Officials in Oregon and Washington are sparring over a Bonneville Power Administration plan to offer its favored customers lengthier contracts for low-cost electricity. The BPA, which sells power from federally owned dams at substantially below-market rates, wants to offer public utilities in the Northwest 10-year contracts, instead of five-year deals. Such an arrangement, the BPA argues, would help protect the power-marketing group's rates from federal action. Lately, a number of U.S. lawmakers have argued that the BPA should be forced to sell its power at market rates -- but, the BPA argues, if it locks up its rates in long-term pacts, the federal government will have no choice but to leave those rates alone. The conflict? Washington gets most of its power from public utilities, which by law get first dibs on BPA power. Oregon gets most of its power from investor-owned utilities, which get from the BPA whatever cheap energy is left over. Oregon Gov. John Kitzhaber argues that the deal perpetuates a structure that denies low rates to most Oregonians. And he says that tying up Bonneville power for 10 years would get in the way of plans for a regional takeover of the federal agency -- something he supports but that Washington Gov. Gary Locke doesn't. "It smacks of an agency trying to protect itself," Mr. Kitzhaber says. "This region needs a consensus around the BPA to keep the benefits in the long run. I don't see how you do that without addressing the preference issue in some fashion." For his part, Gov. Locke told BPA Administrator Judi Johansen in a recent letter that long-term contracts "will enhance future discussions of how to protect" the BPA from those in Congress who don't like the fact that hydrodams built with all taxpayers' money are subsidizing electricity costs for a few. Adds BPA spokesman Ed Mosey: "One reason to sign long-term contracts is to give the agency some protection. Gov. Kitzhaber just doesn't get it." The fight is brewing as Bonneville prepares to next month complete two years of work on how to allocate power among 137 utilities in Washington, Oregon, Idaho and western Montana, and how much to charge each class of customer starting in October 2001, when current contracts expire. BPA officials won't say exactly how much 10-year power they are thinking of offering to public utilities. They confirm only that that they have received longer-contract requests for 2,700 megawatts. That figure is more than half of the 5,000 megawatts that would be sold to public utilities each year after 2001. The proposed change of contract length is ruffling feathers throughout Oregon. "The politics around this issue are just explosive," says Jason Eisdorfer, a lawyer with the Portland-based Citizen's Utility Board, an advocacy group for residential customers. "We're near the end of a very public and contentious effort. Suddenly it appears that Bonneville is making critical policy decisions behind the closed doors of contract negotiations." The underlying problem -- according to many Oregonians and for-profit utilities, at least -- is in the federal law that created the BPA in 1937. It gave publicly owned utilities status as the preferred buyers of the agency's electricity, with any leftover power available for sale to for-profit utility companies. Today, 75% of Bonneville electricity goes to public utilities, which serve 40% of the consumers in the region. That effectively "denies six million people in the region their fair share of the region's cheap federal hydropower," says Bill Gaines, a vice president of energy supply for Puget Sound Energy Inc., a for-profit utility in Bellevue that has 907,000 electricity customers. Some in Congress don't like the arrangement, either, but for a different reason: They argue that, especially as the nation's electricity industry is deregulated, one part of the country shouldn't have singular access to low-cost power. Two U.S. representatives -- Republican Bob Franks of New Jersey and Massachusetts Democrat Mary Meehan -- and a senator -- Democrat Daniel Patrick Moynihan of New York -- are sponsoring legislation that would require Bonneville to charge all customers market rates for its power. The profit -- which they estimate would total $3.5 billion over the next five years -- would go to the federal treasury. The bill hasn't gone anywhere since it was introduced in April 1999, but many in the Northwest nonetheless see it as a real threat. Roy Hemmingway, Gov. Kitzhaber's policy adviser on salmon and energy, says that as the power industry moves toward the free market, "Bonneville's policy of serving the minority of residents in the regions is going to make it stick out like a sore thumb." Locking up a substantial amount of electricity for that minority for 10 years, he says, would just aggravate the situation. Many in Washington don't buy those arguments. Steve Johnson, executive director of the Washington Public Utility District Association, a Seattle-based group of 28 public utilities, says Oregonians are squawking about the 10-year pacts to squeeze more electricity out of Bonneville, which charges about 30% less than market rates for its power. "Some people just want a second or third bite out of the apple," Mr. Johnson says. Further, Tom Karier, an energy adviser to Gov. Locke who serves as the governor's appointee on the Northwest Power Planning Council, which monitors the BPA, argues that longer-term contracts would prove that Northwesterners are committed to doing whatever it will take to protect the 11 populations of salmon in the region classified as endangered or threatened under the Endangered Species Act. Congress is supposed to decide later this year whether to order the dismantling of four BPA dams on the lower Snake River in Washington as a way to help at-risk salmon runs thrive; the four dams supply about 5% of Bonneville's power. If the dams are dismantled, the BPA's prices will almost certainly rise. By signing long-term deals, Mr. Karier says, public utilities are showing that they're willing to shoulder higher costs for a long time. (Although the contracts will be negotiated before a decision is made, the rates will be up for renegotiation after five years -- and the price of the dams would be factored in then.) Gov. Kitzhaber believes there is a better way to demonstrate that commitment: The four states served by Bonneville should buy the BPA from the federal government and have the Northwest Power Planning Council operate it as a regional agency. "That gives the region some voice in how those dollars are spent for fish recovery," the governor says. According to Mr. Karier, the Washington governor doesn't necessarily object to the idea of regional ownership, but thinks that the timing is bad. Federal legislation would be required to transfer dam ownership, Mr. Karier notes, and any such bill "would just give forces in Congress looking to take the benefit away an opening." Last year, Oregon Senate majority leader Gene Derfler, a Salem Republican, formed the Legislative Council on River Governance, a bipartisan group of about 25 lawmakers from Oregon, Washington, Idaho and Montana, to begin talks about a regional buyout. The takeover would go like this: The legislative council would form a utility cooperative to execute the acquisition -- paying for it by floating bonds -- then sell the power from the dams and run the salmon-recovery program. Ms. Johansen thinks a regional effort is a good idea, says Mr. Mosley, but agrees with Gov. Locke that the timing is wrong. Mr. Kitzhaber says delay "just protects the status quo. It's a dangerous strategy when you have an agency that is an anachronism, some might say anticompetitive influence on the development of a free market." Sen. Derfler says the takeover campaign will continue regardless of the outcome of the contract-length debate, though he says longer contracts could delay any regional action. And "I truly believe if we don't make the move to take over the BPA in the next five years, we will lose it," he says. Many observers agree. The BPA is gradually paying down its debts -- it owes about $13.64 billion to the federal government and bondholders. The debt will be fully repaid by 2030, but half of it is tied to paying off one project, and that will be retired by 2018. And when the debt payments start dwindling, the theory goes, the Bonneville system will become an attractive target for a buyout. Sen. Derfler reasons that the region needs to act as quickly as possible with its own takeover to prevent Congress taking away the benefit. "It is going to be much harder to make the case to Congress to let the region have the system once the debt payments start dropping," says Mr. Eisdorfer, the Oregon residential customer advocate. A meeting of the legislative council is scheduled for next month in Montana. "We plan to sit down with the people from Washington and ask them what it takes in order for them to agree to get involved," Sen. Derfler says. "If they want a guarantee of 15 or 20 years with the same amount of power they get now, I'll deal with that and work from there." And if Washingtonians refuse to play? Sen. Derfler says he is crafting a backup plan -- a bill in the Oregon Legislature next year to create a statewide public-power agency that would give Oregon rights to lay claim to more Bonneville power. Essentially, the state would create a big public utility that would have the right to buy, and then re-sell, Bonneville energy. "I'd rather get their attention through persuasion," says Sen. Derfler. "But I'll use a baseball bat if I have to." Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Private Matter: The Push to Expand Property Rights Stirs Both Hopes and Fears --- Some California Farmers See Windfall in GOP Bills; Officials Fret About Costs --- Do Grazing Elk `Take' Grass?
Text: The new Republican-controlled Congress is on its way to passing the biggest expansion of property rights in U.S. history.
