In California, this could very well radically drive up the cost of saving salmon -- and add to the tide of litigation those rescue efforts have already spawned. Indeed, the Republican proposals, depending on their final form, promise a procession of policy zigzags and lawsuits at all levels of government, both critics and even some proponents agree. Consider the salmon example: Big agricultural corporations in California's arid Central Valley now get huge amounts of public water at subsidized rates to pour on crops. But some of the state's historic salmon streams are drying up; under previous congressional mandates, federal and state regulators want to divert some of this water to restore salmon runs. But, under "takings" legislation passed by the House last month, corporate farmers would have to be compensated for any diversion of their allotments. In fact, under some circumstances, the corporate farmers could claim reimbursement at market rates -- meaning reimbursement out of the federal treasury at rates 10 times the subsidized rate they now pay. "We have a right to that water, and if the government wants it for fish, they have to pay us," says Jason Peltier, a top California farm lobbyist. Until now, federal courts and the U.S. Supreme Court have, in a number of decisions, rejected this view. But the breadth and wording of the new Republican takings proposals would unquestionably give Central Valley farmers a potent new weapon; they are already preparing lawsuits in anticipation of passage of a generous takings law. Environmentalists are naturally alarmed. Says Hal Candee, an environmental lawyer with the Natural Resources Defense Council: "This is insane -- the public is already subsidizing irrigation that is devastating the environment, and now we have to pay even more to make it stop?" Moreover, the takings movement is being watched with growing concern by numerous state and local governments, which fear a huge hit on the public treasury -- or a sharp decline in their ability to enforce what they consider reasonable environmental, planning and other regulations. In Riverside, Calif., a fast-growing Southern California city bedeviled by numerous endangered species, traffic and open-space conflicts, city planner Stephen Whyld calls the new takings proposals "prescriptions for total gridlock." Nonsense, say proponents, who argue that such legislation is necessary to rein in overweening regulators. "It's obvious that bureaucracies from the federal level down to the local school board have come to believe that the Fifth Amendment just doesn't apply to them," says R.S. Radford, a property-law expert at the Pacific Legal Foundation, a conservative legal think tank that has handled many takings lawsuits on behalf of landowners. The takings movement, he says, confronts "terrible abuses by government against individuals." Central Valley farmers, for example, have long painted efforts to save salmon as an example of government "worrying more about fish than people." What is certain is that the takings campaign, both in Congress and in a number of states, seeks to significantly expand interpretation of the Constitution's so-called takings clause. This is a snippet of the Fifth Amendment that holds that government "shall not take private property for public use without just compensation." The recent House proposal also fulfills a promise in the "Contract With America" and is strongly supported by large industries such as mining, ranching, oil and agriculture. It requires the government to pay landowners full compensation when certain government actions to protect the environment trim the value of any portion of their property by 20% or more. The Senate is considering a proposal championed by presidential hopeful and Senate Majority Leader Robert Dole that lifts that threshold to 33% -- but it would apply to all federal regulations, not just environmental rules. Whatever its final form, such a bill, if passed, would be a populist rallying point that may be difficult for President Clinton to veto. Even if he does, the movement has plenty of steam at a state and local level. Colorado, Oregon, Texas and other states are considering their own expanded takings bills. In fact, some private-property interests have already begun to push novel legal theories under the current state of takings law -- theories that they clearly hope will be enshrined under the more expansive Republican bills. Wayne Hage, a Nevada rancher and a leader of the West's private-property movement, alleges in a lawsuit pending in the federal court of appeals in Washington that the government owes him compensation because fish and game agencies don't prevent elk herds from drinking from his streams and munching range on his 7,000-acre spread. That is a taking of his water and grass, he contends. Mr. Hage also is credited with devising another now-popular theory in the West: that ranchers have what amounts to a private-property right to graze on public range land. Thus, Mr. Hage and several other Western ranchers have sued the U.S. Forest Service and the Bureau of Land Management, claiming that they suffered takings when the agencies tried to restrict grazing on public range, which in many areas has been scalped by years of overgrazing. In Mr. Hage's case, the Forest Service confiscated some of his cows because he repeatedly defied the agency's orders to stop grazing on public land that federal range experts considered "trampled, compacted, gullied." For damage from regulators and elk, Mr. Hage seeks compensation of at least $28.4 million. Then there is the case of the Summitville Mine in south-central Colorado. Mining practices there have created a heap of cyanide-laced mine wastes; the Superfund cleanup is expected to cost taxpayers at least $120 million. The Canadian company that operated the mine for its owners has declared bankruptcy and left the country. Now, the mine owners, Aztec Minerals Corp., Gray Eagle Mining Corp. and South Mountain Minerals Corp., have sued Colorado's governor and main environmental agencies. Their claim: Because regulators did as the companies wished and permitted mining that earned them substantial profits but polluted their property, their land has been devalued by regulatory action -- a taking under the Colorado constitution. The mine owners also say their property values have been hurt because regulators' emergency cleanup of Summitville, undertaken to prevent further poisoning of their land, has closed down mining, possibly for good. "Let me get this straight: It's a taking when you're allowed to mine, and a taking when you're prevented from mining?" scoffs Roger Flynn, an environmental attorney with the Western Mining Action Project. Just so, says Tim Gablehouse, the mine owners' attorney: "Government action and inaction have damaged the value of private property, and we have a constitutional right to compensation." Colorado is one of many states considering local takings legislation modeled on the new congressional proposals, and indeed, it is at the state and local level, where planning commissions make numerous decisions on a daily basis, that such measures could really open the floodgates. For example, local governments often deny permission for landowners to subdivide lots or undertake high-density development, on the theory that approval would aggravate congestion or traffic. Yet such decisions often diminish land values by as much as one-third. Jennifer Moulton, Denver's planning director, predicts that takings legislation pending in the Colorado state legislature would mean "a nightmare of dueling appraisers and dueling lawyers." The Colorado proposal says that any diminution of property values whatsoever requires compensation but leaves it to appraisers to determine how much. "Property owners will have their appraisers, and we'll have ours, and we'll all go around and around and around," Ms. Moulton says. Other recent federal takings claims have featured coal companies alleging that they must be compensated because federal law requires them to pay money into a fund for miners stricken with black lung. And a company owned by Texas oil millionaire Clayton Williams has sued Wyoming wildlife agencies over limits and licensing requirements for hunting deer, elk and antelope. Mr. Williams's theory: He owns the wildlife on his 90,000-acre Wyoming hideaway, and state hunting restrictions are a taking of his private wildlife for which he must be compensated. Mr. Williams lost the first legal round in federal court, but he has appealed. Not all the recent federal cases deal with environmental matters. International House of Pancakes Inc. has claimed that modifications to restaurants required by a 1990 handicap-access law are a taking for which it should be paid. IHOP made the claim in defense of a lawsuit brought by Theodore Pinnock, a San Diego attorney with cerebral palsy who sued after he allegedly couldn't get his wheelchair through a narrow restroom door and had to crawl into the men's room. Last summer, the U.S. Supreme Court refused to review a lower court decision against IHOP's takings claim. But many lawyers say IHOP probably would have prevailed under some of the new takings theories being pushed in Congress. It is that kind of scenario that concerns people like Jerold S. Kayden, a Harvard University property-law scholar. In his view, the Republican takings bills would "vastly expand" the opportunities for claiming compensable takings -- and would likely trigger a blizzard of such claims that will force a cash-strapped government to choose between enforcing regulations in the public interest or paying huge sums to landowners. More fundamentally, the new takings proposals mark a drastic departure from how courts and policy makers have historically interpreted the Fifth Amendment's taking clause. In general, courts have allowed the government significant latitude to make regulations impinging upon private property in the interest of protecting public health and safety, building highways, limiting growth and the like, particularly when the regulation didn't wipe out all economic value of the private land. The Supreme Court twice in recent terms has taken up major takings claims; both times the court ruled narrowly in favor of landowners, strengthening private-property rights without fundamentally altering past property-law concepts. The court is currently hearing another potential landmark private-property case involving how far regulators can go to enforce the federal Endangered Species Act on private land. Mr. Kayden also posits another question: If property owners are going to be paid by the public when a regulation decreases property values, he asks, why shouldn't they have to repay the public when regulatory action -- flood control, for example -- enhances property values? Takings proponents, however, contend that the Republican bills aim merely to put common sense back in government's attitude about private property, and they have their own list of abuses that they believe shows the need for a radical change in the takings law. There is the case of a Washington man who was barred from cutting down a few trees on his land because a spotted-owl nest had been discovered some five miles away. There is the South Carolina developer whose $1 million investment in residential property was totally wiped out by subsequent erosion-control rules, even though his lots were a football-field distance away from the beach. There are the various landowners who have been thrown in jail for dumping clean sand on slivers of their property that were classified as wetlands; in some cases, the "wetlands" had been dry for decades. Backers also accuse their critics of fear-mongering when they suggest the bills invite landowners to raid the environment and the national treasury. Critics "have propounded the myth that private property and environmental protection are inconsistent," says Rep. Lamar Smith, a Texas Republican and a House leader on property rights. The House takings proposal, for example, wouldn't apply to any activity that runs afoul of state nuisance laws; that, he and other supporters say, will prevent landowners from "getting paid not to pollute." (See related letters: "Letters to the Editor: The Government Doesn't Own Us" -- WSJ May 4, 1995) 950404-0086 YY95 MM05 Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: U.S. News: California Island Fox Bounces Back --- Revival led to fastest removal of a mammal from the endangered species list
Text: Three subspecies of island fox that nearly became extinct in California two decades ago have recovered so fully that federal officials Thursday announced their removal from protection under the Endangered Species Act. The foxes had fallen from about 4,000 on three of the Channel Islands -- Santa Cruz, Santa Rosa and San Miguel -- in 1994 to fewer than 100 by 1999, due in part to a proliferation of nonnative feral pigs that attracted legions of predatory golden eagles, say federal and conservation biologists who assisted in their recovery. But after the cat-sized island foxes were listed as endangered in 2004, the National Park Service, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and Nature Conservancy, among others, ramped up an eradication of the pigs and capture and removal of the eagles. That allowed the foxes to rebound to their old levels, prompting the Fish and Wildlife Service to issue its fastest delisting of a mammal -- which can take 25 years or more to recover -- since the Endangered Species Act was passed in 1973. "At the core of this was a bunch of people coming together and deciding they wouldn't let a species go extinct on their watch," said Scott Morrison, California science director for Arlington, Va.-based Nature Conservancy, which owns three-quarters of Santa Cruz Island off the coast of Ventura, Calif. The rest of the island, along with Santa Rosa and San Miguel, are part of Channel Islands National Park. The recovery comes as the Endangered Species Act in recent years has come under assault from many Republican lawmakers on Capitol Hill, who say so few species ever leave protected status that it needs to be overhauled. Supporters of the act point to other successes, including the recoveries of the bald eagle, Yellowstone grizzly and Northern Rocky Mountain gray wolf. Critics say the act often impinges on other land uses, such as when a 1990 listing of the northern spotted owl led to a shutdown of logging on many national forests in the Pacific Northwest. "Certain species require additional management in order to prevent extinction. But the Endangered Species Act is too often used as a political weapon to lock up land or deter economic activity," said Rep. Jason Chaffetz (R., Utah), a critic of the law. Even some conservation groups don't agree on it. A San Rafael, Calif.,-based group called In Defense of Animals unsuccessfully sued the federal government to try to block the slaughter of about 5,000 feral pigs as part of the fox recovery project. Federal biologists say they had to euthanize the pigs, which they said were causing other damage to Santa Cruz Island. Descendants of domestic pigs brought in by settlers during the mid-19th century, the dead and young of the herds began attracting flocks of golden eagles in the 1990s, said Tim Coonan, a retired biologist at Channel Islands National Park. The birds started invading the islands then, he said, partly because bald eagles, which used to inhabit the area and kept out most other predatory fowl, had disappeared due to DDT poisoning, among other past threats. With no historic predators on the islands, the foxes didn't stand a chance against the golden eagles, which unlike bald eagles prey on land-based animals rather than marine ones. "They were sitting ducks out there," Mr. Coonan said. Credit: By Jim Carlton

Title: REVIEW & OUTLOOK (Editorial): Science Fights Back
Text: Scientists, who claim to have above-average powers of insight, probably should have seen what they were in for on that first Earth Day in 1970. When people started to chant and sway at gatherings dedicated to "saving" everything from water to whales and the air, one might have assumed that the scientific method was going to come under a bit of pressure. After 20 years of much silliness, many lawsuits by Jeremy Rifkin, the degradation of science in liability suits, and too many TV shows calling apples a public-health catastrophe, serious scientists are finally starting to fight back. This nonunion of concerned scientists doesn't object to environmentalism. Frankly, no one does. But they do object to slipshod science and apocalyptic science. They object to "studies" that in fact don't prove what they say they prove. They object to an intellectual absolutism that tries to close out reassessments of available data. We also suspect that you are seeing more rigorous scientific minds entering the policy debates simply because restoring balance is in their self-interest. If "scientific" studies are the reason that ever-larger slices of the tax base get dedicated to grandiose and oversold environmental goals, less money will be left to support serious scientific research. There is also the matter of the credibility of science. If the public comes to believe that "science" is responsible for school budgets destroyed by asbestos mandates, or for property values lowered by radon studies, or the higher living costs passed along by firms complying with the Clean Air Act, or jobs destroyed because "science" ordered the rescue of the spotted owl, then the public may become less sympathetic to the research community's pleas for ever more financial support. Besides, can all this bad news possibly be true? The answer in most cases is that there may be a kernel of truth in the warnings but there's often an undisclosed reservoir of mitigating details that deserve to be aired. After a large survey of the literature on greenhouse warming last year, most of the scientists on a panel of the National Academy of Sciences said that the probable rise in global temperatures wouldn't be dire. Moreover, the panel drew attention to a truth that both environmentalists and most of the reporters who cover these subjects ignore: Humanity's record of technological innovation and adaptation in the face of challenges such as global warming is excellent. We're still here, aren't we? Dioxin. Two efforts -- a study published in the New England Journal of Medicine last January and a symposium at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory -- acknowledged that dioxin is a carcinogen but concluded that regulation of the chemical needs to incorporate data suggesting its effects are not necessarily dangerous under all circumstances. Endangered Species. The Endangered Species Act is up for reauthorization this year. The battle between loggers' jobs and advocates of the spotted owl in the Northwest makes it clear that current enforcement practices have implications for people, property and jobs. As with global warming, this highly publicized issue is drawing the attention of scientists who know something about the complex subject of species survival and differentiation. Some of their caveats were discussed in the August 16 issue of Science ("Extinction: Are Ecologists Crying Wolf?"). The reauthorization debate should shed further light. Other examples accumulate of a richer scientific debate over public policy. In May, the Chronicle of Higher Education described scientists at the last meeting of the American Physical Society who have serious doubts about the widely publicized claim that electrical power-transmission lines pose a significant cancer risk. A July 6 article in the New England Journal of Medicine by three physicians from Columbia University, "Physicians and the Animal-Rights Movement," concluded: "Having seen the lives of the sick and their families savaged by illness, doctors must help prevent ideology from blocking medical progress." For all of this interest, Elizabeth Whelan, an epidemiologist who heads the New York-based American Council on Science and Health and who has been a leader in the effort to involve working scientists in these subjects, has made an intriguing observation about the behavior of scientists. She notes that while it's often easy to get scientists mobilized against the misuse of their own disciplines, they can be as flaky as a flower child over some airy cause that is undermining an unrelated discipline. Scientists need to appreciate that they're all in this together. They have a common interest in stepping back from the workbench long enough to support colleagues who've stepped forward to examine publicly the nightmarish claims made in the name of science. The good news is that more scientists are doing just that.

Title: REVIEW & OUTLOOK (Editorial): Species Act, Endangered
Text: If you want to miss the recession, go to green land. Take up with one of the environmental lobbies. You'd never know that the economy was hurting. When barely a building can get built, a job offered or a loan financed in much of America, the environmental politics of delays, limits and injunctions has rarely seemed better: -- Congress appears ready to add 18 million acres to the 94 million already in the nation's wilderness reserves, eight million of the increment coming in the form of California desert. -- The Alaskan wilderness, more than half the country's total, has been put off-limits to oil drilling a mere six months after the U.S. fought a war to preserve such access in the Persian Gulf. Virtually the whole California coastline has been similarly blocked out. -- The new Clean Air Act kicks in, with surprises all around. California leads the way: Instead of taking off the road the 10% of autos that cause 80% of the pollution, it mandates new gasoline formulas that will cost 16 cents more a gallon. -- The timber industry of Oregon is decimated by restrictions on "old growth" harvesting in the interest of the lawsuit-protected spotted owl. Northward in Washington -- where the bum economy arrived with sudden force -- hydroelectric-power rates are hostage to a subspecies of salmon. -- The insatiable litigation maw known as Superfund continues to eat up millions of dollars that long ago could have cleaned up much of the country's truly toxic waste. -- And the terraqueous treasure known as wetlands is somehow discovered wherever the bulldozers roam, as policy makers seek to inscribe in bedrock a commitment to "no net loss" of what we never knew we had. The fact that much of the human species is hurting economically may not count for much with crusading ecologists, for whom they are not the favorite fauna anyway. But these Homo sapiens do sometimes cast ballots, and we suspect the last word hasn't been heard yet on environmental overreaching. Consider the new dynamics around the interesting race next year for the U.S. Senate in Oregon. Incumbent Bob Packwood, once green to the toes of his boots, says he'll campaign on behalf of loggers and other resource users, and against the excesses of the Endangered Species Act. Some say this is a cynical pose by a desperate politician, but Oregon elections aren't usually won by romancing the roughnecks. It's a place, as Mr. Packwood noted not long ago, where stocking lake trout was attacked as a form of pollution. As that pivotal campaign unfolds, the hallowed Endangered Species Act itself comes up for renewal in Congress. Mr. Packwood's senior colleague, Mark Hatfield, predicts a waning of support for the law as its effects spread beyond the Northwest timber industry. The Oregonian newspaper notes that Mr. Hatfield was one of the legislation's original sponsors. But now that teary-eyed federal judges have gotten hold of it, he thinks "it is being applied far beyond the scope of what any of us who helped adopt it intended." The act has moved from outlawing the wanton killing off of a species to barring the disturbance of vast habitats. A pair of judges has brought to a standstill the old-forest cut in Oregon, while a tangle of other procedures pits the spotted owl against the loggers. When the issue is at least partially settled, 30,000 to 60,000 jobs by conservative estimate stand to be lost (add to that the loggers' families). There are likely to be more such cases. In addition to about 700 species already listed, an additional 3,500 are in line for protection. According to a skeptical cover article about the species act in the January issue of the Atlantic -- another sign of a countercurrent -- 100 million species may exist, with barely 1% of them yet having a name. World-wide, we may be losing 50,000 a year, with perhaps 4,000 at risk of extinction in the U.S. by the end of the century. The potential costs of enforcing the act are enormous. Most of the direct outlays are being eaten up by hyped species such as the spotted owl, but "recovery" of all those listed is estimated to run nearly $5 billion over 10 years, and that doesn't take into account the economic losses suffered when private and public projects must be stopped. In California, an attorney for developers claims that more than $6 billion is at stake in the listing of a bird called the gnatcatcher, and notes, "In the nearly two decades of the act's operation, the Fish and Wildlife Service has never made an offer of compensation for the destruction of property rights. . . ." The gnatcatcher is a vexing obstacle, builders maintain, because Fish and Wildlife says the creature has only 54,000 acres of habitat left -- but won't identify where exactly that turf is supposed to be. And while it is saving the gnatcatchers, California must look out for the Sacramento Delta smelt, at an estimated $12 billion recovery cost. The point that Oregon's Senators and the Atlantic magazine's authors would make is that priorities need to be established, both among endangered species and between those species and man. Moreover, environmental scientists have sometimes been proved wrong in insisting that particular habitats were irreplaceable. Remember the snail darter, later found far away from the Tellico Dam? The Supreme Court has ruled "the plain intent of Congress" in passing the 1973 law was that extinction be stopped in all cases, regardless of cost. And it's true that the environmental movement has had a good long run through a political system willing to indulge its disdain of costs. But in a functioning political system there are limits to costs. The movement's willingness to sacrifice tens of thousands of loggers for an owl may have been the symbolic break point. When House Speaker Tom Foley (from Washington state) asked congressional scientific committees last fall to review the act with its economic effects in mind, it was yet another indication that the ground had shifted. The defeat in 1990 of major environmental initiatives in California and Washington registered politically, just as science and sometimes the media reflect intellectual questioning. If the Bush administration doesn't flinch, the reauthorization of the Endangered Species Act will become the focus of this debate. The pendulum still has quite a ways to swing back. The greens remain a powerful force. But at any number of field-study sites, word processors and precinct meetings, the ecosystem of human decision-making is undergoing change. A more balanced order cannot come soon enough.

Title: World-Wide
Text: CHRISTOPHER PLAYED DOWN prospects for a Mideast breakthrough. The secretary of state, who leaves tonight on his first overseas mission, said he doesn't expect to get an immediate green light for resumption of stalled Arab-Israeli talks. Even with U.N. endorsement of a U.S. compromise with Israel over Palestinian deportations, Christopher voiced limited expectations as he met in Washington with Israeli Foreign Minister Peres. "I hope that subsequently the peace process can be restarted," Christopher said. But he added, "I would not expect that to happen during the course of my trip." Christopher plans to stop in Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Israel. He will then meet in Geneva with Russia's foreign minister and go on to Brussels for NATO talks. --- U.N. mediator Vance is expected to quit peace talks on the former Yugoslavia once negotiations on Bosnia are completed in New York, diplomats said. In Bosnia, Serbs battered Sarajevo and blocked an airport road. On the border with Yugoslavia, Serbs halted a U.N. convoy for a third day, but a second convoy passed into Bosnia. Kosovo's president pressed for U.S. and international action -- including immediate deployment of U.N. peacekeepers -- to prevent the Balkan war from spreading to his semiautonomous province. Rugova, on a trip to Washington, said a U.S. threat to use force in response to Serb aggression would help protect Kosovo. --- Defense Secretary Aspin has delayed release of a report on the Navy's Tailhook sex abuse scandal until the appointment of a new Navy secretary. A Pentagon spokesman said politics had nothing to do with delaying the report on the sexual harassment of women at a 1991 aviators' convention. The report was to have been issued this month. --- Yeltsin requested an urgent session of Russia's legislature aimed at ending a power struggle that could derail his reforms. A statement issued after Kremlin talks between the president and his conservative rival Khasbulatov suggested the Congress of People's Deputies could meet in early March to ratify a power-sharing accord. --- Men who have vasectomies may run a higher risk of developing prostate cancer, two studies indicated. Both studies, done by Boston researchers, indicated that men who had vasectomies over 20 years ago might have an 85% to 90% higher risk of developing prostate cancer than men who didn't have the operation. --- Interior Secretary Babbitt appealed for a broad new approach to the Endangered Species Act that seeks to protect entire ecosystems instead of focusing on individual plants and animals. Babbitt also told a House committee that the administration would boost national park funding. He endorsed mining law reforms. --- Iran is working with North Korea on developing a long-range missile, military sources said. The sources, speaking on condition of anonymity at an arms show in the United Arab Emirates, said the North Korean system could be ready for production within three years. --- U.N. chief Boutros-Ghali asked Japan to play a bigger role in world peacekeeping, saying this would help counter complaints that the U.N. was dominated by the U.S. But Prime Minister Miyazawa, facing domestic opposition to expanded responsibilities for Japan's army, responded cautiously during a meeting in Tokyo with the U.N. chief. --- The U.N. plans to send more weapons inspectors to Baghdad and conduct aerial surveys of two sites where it suspects Saddam Hussein's government designed nuclear arms, U.N. officials said. The decision to challenge an Iraqi ban on flights over Baghdad will test Iraq's compliance with U.N. terms for ending the Gulf War. --- The House urged that the U.S. remain opposed to resumption of commercial whaling despite pressure from Norway and other whaling nations. The nonbinding resolution, passed 382-0, also said the U.S. should work toward a moratorium on the direct commercial harvest of dolphins and porpoises. The measure was sent to the Senate. --- China's agriculture minister criticized local officials for levying excessive taxes and fees on farmers. Senior officials in Beijing are said to be concerned about recent public protests by angry farmers.

Title: House vote for regulatory moratorium presages passage of cost-benefits bill
Text: WASHINGTON -- The House's strong vote in favor of a regulatory moratorium presages likely swift passage this week of a separate bill requiring extensive cost-benefit analysis before new regulations can be issued.    Both bills are opposed by the Clinton administration, which contends that they would halt necessary regulatory activity. After the moratorium bill cleared the House 276-146 on Friday, Environmental Protection Administration chief Carol Browner predicted its passage would mean "we'd have to stop rules to control dioxin from incinerators, lead poisoning, and bacterial contamination of drinking water." The bill passed with a margin slightly short of the two-thirds majority needed to override a presidential veto.    But the moratorium bill, which was supported by 51 Democrats, will likely accelerate the momentum for passage of the cost-benefit bill. The cost-benefit measure, which has more widespread business support, largely supersedes the moratorium bill. Rep. David McIntosh (R., Ind.), the freshman member and former Bush administration aide who sponsored the moratorium, termed it "a link between the election last fall" and the cost-benefit bill, "which is the more permanent change."    The moratorium would stop most federal regulations issued since Nov. 20 from taking effect. An amendment to extend the ban another year in the case of regulations under the Endangered Species Act -- even if the cost-benefit bill is passed -- was easily adopted Thursday. By comparison, Democratic proposals to exempt food or aircraft-safety regulations, for example, were repeatedly rejected.    In the two days of debate, most of the major changes adopted were business oriented, including exempting regulatory actions related to textile imports and extending the moratorium for an extra six months in the case of small employers with 100 or fewer workers.    Debate begins today on the cost-benefit-analysis bill, which would require all regulations that cost the economy in excess of $25 million to be subject to cost-benefit analyses. In many cases, the analyses would be peer-reviewed by scientific panels that could include representatives of affected industries. The Clinton administration currently requires cost-benefit analysis for regulations that cost the economy more than $100 million; a Senate bill sponsored by Majority Leader Robert Dole proposes a threshold of $50 million.    The House will then take up a bill requiring monetary compensation to owners of private property that loses more than 10% of its value as a result of regulatory action. Because this so-called takings bill could involve costly new expenditures for the government, its fate is more uncertain, and there is some movement afoot by moderate Republicans to restrict its scope.  Credit: Staff Reporters of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Lawsuit Is Filed to Curb Cattle Grazing Across Vast Expanse of Rocky Mountains
Text: A coalition of 10 environmental and hunting groups filed suit to sharply restrict the decades-old practice of livestock grazing on millions of acres of national forest land in the Rocky Mountains, in an action that vastly expands the war over use of the West's public lands.    The suit was filed in U.S. District Court in Tucson, Ariz., against the U.S. Forest Service, targeting 11 national forests in Arizona and New Mexico that cover 18 million acres. It alleges the forest service has failed to halt grazing damage in the forests under a 1996 plan to protect the threatened Mexican spotted owl, and it asks a federal judge to make the agency comply.    The litigation has broader implications as a growing number of environmentalists are embracing the antigrazing movement with the same passion they brought to successful efforts to curtail logging in the Pacific Northwest. The Sierra Club is considering a policy advocating an all-out ban against grazing on public lands, and several other groups support such a hard-line stance. Backers of this suit hope it will become a precedent for limiting grazing elsewhere by elevating public and judicial concern about grazing lands.    "This case has the potential to fundamentally change the way grazing is managed in the Southwest and hopefully set a trend for the rest of the West," said John Horning, a director of the Forest Guardians environmental group in Santa Fe, N.M., one of the entities that brought the suit.    Forest Service officials declined to comment. Cattlemen's associations denied ranchers were abusing the lands. "These folks have made it clear their intent is to remove livestock from the West, and they are using the litigation process to do that," says Caren Cowan, executive secretary of the New Mexico Cattle Growers' Association, which represents about 5,000 ranchers whose livestock roam on public lands.    At issue is what the environmentalists say is mounting scientific evidence that the cows are ruining the land by trampling streambeds and munching away at grass and trees that support the habitat for the Mexican spotted owl and other species designated as threatened under federal law. The Mexican spotted owl is related to the northern spotted owl, whose threatened status triggered the logging wars a decade ago in the Northwest. The environmentalists argue the grazing is subsidized by the federal government in the same way the logging of public forests is, since access to the land is gained at much lower prices than if the businesses had to buy the land.    But cattlemen say the lower land cost is offset by the higher cost of complying with federal management rules. They also assert the cattle operations have proved beneficial for the Western ecology. "Water improvements, private pastures and feed supplies are ranchers' contributions that have helped big-game populations on federal lands increase dramatically," says Jason Campbell, director of federal lands for the National Cattlemen's Beef Association, an industry trade group in Washington, D.C.    While grazing has been the subject of litigation in the West in recent years, this is by far the largest suit in terms of acreage that could be affected. It was filed after the Forest Guardians group obtained data that, the group says, show the forest service has violated the Endangered Species Act by failing to monitor and limit cattle grazing in 75% of the grazing allotments issued for the national forests in Arizona and New Mexico. According to the suit, the Forest Service had agreed to undertake those actions under standards of a Mexican-spotted-owl protection plan it framed in 1996.    "All we are asking for is the agency to comply with its own guidelines," says Jim Angell, an attorney for the Earthjustice Legal Defense Fund, a San Francisco environmental group that is representing the plaintiffs in the suit.  Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Pentagon Is Seeking Exemptions To Some Environmental Laws
Text: WASHINGTON -- The Pentagon is asking Congress for exemptions to some of the nation's environmental laws, asserting that they are needed to improve military readiness and to make the training at military bases and bombing ranges more realistic.   In a statement released yesterday, the Department of Defense said the legislative request has "great significance" for military capabilities and said the resulting changes would have either "neutral" or "strongly positive" effects on the environment.   Officials of state agencies, which enforce many federal environmental laws, and environmental groups opposed the exemptions, which the House Armed Services Committee may take up tomorro. "The federal government should act as an example to private industry. It should have to comply with the same laws that everybody else does," said Sandra Schubert, a lawyer for Earthjustice, an environmental group based here.   Ken Salazar, attorney general of Colorado and head of a national committee of state attorneys general, complained in a letter to the House committee that the exemptions could have "adverse impacts on human health and the environment." Currently, the Defense Department, he said, has a poorer record complying with the Clean Water Act than other federal agencies or private industry.   According to the Pentagon's statement, the Endangered Species Act and pending lawsuits brought under it by environmental groups to protect birds and animals could restrict training on substantial portions of the bases it uses for training operations, including 65% of Camp Pendleton, a Marine Base near San Diego, and 72% of Fort Lewis, an Army base on the coast of Washington state.   The Pentagon wants more flexibility under the Clean Air Act because new aircraft engines produce nitrogen oxides, a smog-causing pollutant. Restrictions about to be phased in, it stated, "could be a significant obstacle" to basing military jets in "any Southern California location."   James Van Ness, an associate general counsel for the Defense Department, said: "This goes to whether or not the young men and women we put in harms way are properly trained."   The measure also seeks relief from the strictures of the Migratory Bird Treaty Act. A recent federal-court decision that halts bombing exercises on Farallon de Medinilla, an island in the Western Pacific, where birds were being killed, he said, could affect other ranges where live firing and bombing is used for training. "That would be a very unfortunate thing," he said.   While the legislation is being considered as part of this year's budget request by the House Armed Services Committee, it has provoked jurisdictional complaints because the environmental laws involved are overseen by at least two other committees. "DOD should concentrate on complying with the law and cleaning up the environment instead of seeking special preference to continue as the nation's greatest polluter," said Rep. John Dingell of Michigan, the ranking Democrat on the House Energy and Commerce Committee.   The Pentagon wants hazardous waste to be redefined under state and federal Superfund laws to exclude the need to clean up munitions as long as they are on operational military bases. The exemption wouldn't apply to previously used bases.

Title: Court Enjoins Maxaam's Lumber Unit From Cutting Trees in California Tract
Text: SAN FRANCISCO -- A state judge has enjoined Pacific Lumber Co. from harvesting a large stand of ancient redwoods in Northern California, amid allegations the company may have violated state and federal laws by logging there during the Thanksgiving holidays without clearance from wildlife officials. The trees are part of a 237-acre company-owned tract of old growth redwoods in a larger grove known as Owl Creek, an environmental battleground in recent years. Since 1990, the company has been trying to log the 237-acre tract, but has been largely blocked by lawsuits from environmentalists and objections from wildlife officials. The tract sits in the middle of an area that's widely acknowledged as one of the last remaining habitats for the marbled murrelet, a rare coastal seabird that nests in tall trees and is protected under both state and federal Endangered Species Acts. Pacific Lumber has been fighting with the federal Fish and Wildlife Service and the state's Department of Fish and Game about whether its plans to log the Owl Creek area would harm the bird. Both agencies say they have agreements with the company that would prevent any logging on the site unless wildlife officials give the go ahead. However, during the Thanksgiving weekend, unknown to wildlife officials, the company sent teams of loggers into Owl Creek and felled dozens of huge trees. Mark Harris, an environmental attorney who has led the legal fight against many Pacific Lumber logging plans, learned of the logging and obtained an injunction from the state appeals court here Tuesday that blocks any further cutting in the area. "This was pirate logging at its most heinous," Mr. Harris said. "At one point, they were dropping one huge tree every six minutes." In letters to Mr. Harris, Fish and Wildlife Field Supervisor Wayne White said Pacific Lumber had assured agency officials it would not log in the area without consulting with federal biologists and had led them to believe no logging was imminent. Mr. White said that the weekend logging "may place Pacific Lumber . . . in violation" of the Endangered Species Act. In the case of the murrelet, the act prevents any activity that damages the bird's habitat to a degree that jeapordizes its survival. Mr. White couldn't be reached to comment. Pacific Lumber chief executive John Campbell denied any wrongdoing and said the company's "private property and perhaps civil rights are now being violated" by the logging ban. The company maintains that its operations won't hurt murrelets and that it doesn't need approval from wildlife officials to log in Owl Creek. The Owl Creek incident is the latest in a long line of disputes involving Pacific Lumber's logging practices since the company was bought by Texas financier Charles Hurwitz in a 1986 hostile takeover. To pay off junk bonds used to finance the deal, Mr. Hurwitz, chairman and chief executive of Maxxam Corp., Houston, immediately doubled the rate at which Pacific Lumber logged its lands. That angered environmentalists, who have been fighting to brake the Pacific Lumber's heavy cutting ever since. In June, Pacific Lumber cut down 25 acres in Owl Creek during a weekend, also without approval of regulators. State wildlife officials wanted to pursue charges against the company at that time, but dropped the matter after they found that Pacific Lumber's logging trucks and bulldozers had obliterated potential evidence at the logging site, according to state biologists. Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Playing Chicken in Oil-Patch Politics
Text: The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service recently announced that it will formally consider listing the Lesser Prairie Chicken -- whose habitat includes some of the nation's major energy fields -- as a threatened species under the Endangered Species Act. This clearly is another desperate ploy by the Obama administration to further its campaign against oil and gas drilling. Such egregious overreach has been a specialty of the Environmental Protection Agency in the past. The administration has now found another agency to do its bidding. The Lesser Prairie Chicken is a ground-nesting bird native to portions of Texas, Colorado, Kansas, New Mexico and Oklahoma. In Texas, it is found primarily in the Texas Panhandle and the Permian Basin. Listing the bird as threatened or endangered would make drilling all but impossible in these economically thriving regions. The Permian Basin alone produces more than one million barrels of oil a day, accounting for almost 70% of Texas' total production and 20% of the nation's oil production. It also supports thousands of jobs and provides millions of dollars in state revenue. Several groups, including the Panhandle Producers and Royalty Owners Association and the Permian Basin Petroleum Association, have drafted something called a "Candidate Conservation Agreement With Assurances" in the hope that Fish and Wildlife will approve the plan and forgo listing the bird. The agreement describes oil and gas companies' involvement in habitat-conservation efforts and ideally will be merged with similar documents being developed in other states. Operators who choose not to participate in the voluntary conservation process will be held responsible for any reduction in wildlife or habitat and could be subject to penalties or even jail. The Lesser Prairie Chicken matter isn't the first time the federal government has tried to use the Endangered Species Act as a tool in the war on drilling. Not that it is always successful. This summer, after months of research, Fish and Wildlife conceded that listing the Dunes Sagebrush Lizard as threatened or endangered wasn't warranted. The agency reviewed some 800 written comments and 147 comments from individuals or organizations at a two-day public hearing. Only 30 supported listing the lizard. As it happens, the habitat of the Lesser Prairie Chicken largely overlaps that of the Dunes Sagebrush Lizard. Since Texas was able to produce a plan for the lizard that would work for environmentalists and operators alike, there is reason to hope that a similar plan being drafted for the Lesser Prairie Chicken will work. Yet another issue of concern is the funding behind these efforts to list certain animals as endangered. Texas Land Commissioner Jerry Patterson testified to Congress in June that taxpayer money is being spent in litigation over these listings. For instance, the petition to list the Dunes Sagebrush Lizard was originally filed by a radical environmental group, the Wild Earth Guardians. Interestingly, this group collected $680,492 in tax money (as grants and the like) from Fish and Wildlife between 2007 and 2011. During that time the group sued the federal agency 76 times over alleged environmental violations. The Wild Earth Guardians are also behind the petition to list the Spot-Tailed Earless Lizard under the Endangered Species Act. Not coincidentally, the range of this particular lizard includes portions of the Eagle Ford Shale in Texas, which is emerging as one of the top oil- and gas-producing regions in the country. Production in the nine-field formation is steadily increasing, reporting 310,370 barrels of oil a day in July of this year, compared with 120,532 barrels a day in July 2011. By filing an outlandish number of lawsuits, groups like the Wild Earth Guardians are trying to overwhelm Fish and Wildlife resources and force settlements that the groups can dictate, instead of letting the courts decide. Such groups are willing to use extreme tactics to pursue their goal of shutting down the oil and gas industry with blatant disregard to how their actions will affect the economy or the power supply on which we all depend. We must not allow the Obama administration to use the Endangered Species Act as a weapon against the oil and gas industry. The federal government needs to learn that we here in Texas best understand our unique geological, economical and regulatory environment -- and to stop wasting taxpayers' money on frivolous lawsuits. One-size-fits-all regulation doesn't work, and thinly veiled attempts to control energy production masquerading as environmentalism don't fool anyone. --- Mr. Porter is a member of the Texas Railroad Commission, which is the state's primary regulator of energy production and exploration. (See related letter: "Letters to the Editor: There's Lots of Oil but Few Chickens" -- WSJ Dec. 17, 2012) Subscribe to WSJ: Credit: By David Porter

Title: Environmental Groups Sue Over Spotted Owl Decision
Text: SAN FRANCISCO -- Environmental groups launched their legal assault on the Bush administration's decision to waive protection of northern spotted owls in certain logging regions.    The Sierra Club Legal Defense and several other environmental groups filed suit in federal appeals court here, challenging the decision made last month by a rarely convened panel of cabinet members and federal officials that can exempt troubled species from protection under the Endangered Species Act. The panel ruled that protecting owls on 13 tracts of timberland in Oregon would be too economically disruptive; the move opens up the acreage for logging, even if it harms owls.    The lawsuit was expected. It opens a new chapter in the battle over owls and the Northwest's remaining ancient forests. It is likely to be the most important legal test to date of the government's power to limit the reach of the Endangered Species Act and other conservation laws, which have come under attack from critics who assert that environmental protection is hurting economic growth.

Title: U.S. News: Tiny Fish Makes Big Comeback In Oregon
Text: PORTLAND, Ore. -- The Oregon chub made history Tuesday, as the minnow became the first fish proposed for removal from the federal endangered-species list thanks to its recovery. "This is a huge compliment to Oregonians and our history of conservation leadership," said Gov. John Kitzhaber, a Democrat. "I'm proud that the first fish species proposed to be delisted under the Endangered Species Act is an Oregon native." The chub, whose formal name is Oregonichthys crameri, joins the bald eagle, the gray wolf and American alligator, among some 30 species that have recovered sufficiently to be dropped from the roster of plants, animals and insects compiled since the Endangered Species Act was passed in 1973. The chub was listed as "endangered" in 1993 and a recovery plan was published in 1998. In 2010, its classification on the endangered list improved to "threatened." Fish have been removed from the endangered list before, but it was because they were improperly classified or became extinct. The latter category includes the blue pike and Tecopa pupfish. Oregon officials praised the work of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and local farmers who joined forces to save the chub. Since 1995, when $1.3 million of federal funding became available to restore its habitat along the Willamette River, farmers have put land aside on their properties to help protect the fish. "We set aside some pastureland," said Karen Finley, whose Queen Bee Honey Co. sits on a creek feeding into the Willamette. Her family raises sheep on the land, but agreed to allow a strip along the creek to return to natural conditions. The 100 fish that wildlife officials introduced there a few years ago now number close to 1,000, she estimates. Paul Henson, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's Oregon director, said the chub are breeding in at least 80 pools, up from nine in 1995. He said farmers who agreed to host chub colonies don't have to submit to a slew of regulations, as long they maintain water levels and keep an eye out for nonnative species that prey on chub, such as bullfrogs and bass. The chub's delisting now awaits a 60-day public-comment period during which objections to the proposal can be raised. That can happen, environmental officials say, especially when groups working in support of a species feel its delisting might be premature. "There was one recently, the Hawaiian hawk," said Gavin Shire, a Fish and Wildlife spokesman in Washington, D.C. A proposal for delisting the bird in 2008 was later withdrawn. Credit: By Joel Millman

Title: Medicine: Taxol Receives Endorsement of FDA Panel
Text: WASHINGTON -- A Food and Drug Administration advisory committee recommended that taxol, the controversial drug derived from the Pacific yew tree, be approved for treating ovarian cancer.    The FDA is likely to accept the panel's recommendation of the drug, which has the potential to prolong the lives of thousands of women in the advanced stages of the disease. It also offers a major boost for Bristol-Myers Squibb Co., the maker of the drug.    At a crowded hearing yesterday, the agency's oncology drugs advisory panel voted 11-0 to recommend that the company be allowed to market taxol for treating people with advanced ovarian cancer who have failed to respond to at least one other chemotherapy treatment. The FDA generally follows the recommendations of its advisory panels, but isn't required to.    A Bristol-Myers spokesman praised the panel's decision and the agency's quick action on the company's application, which was submitted last summer. The spokesman said yesterday that the company hasn't yet set a price for taxol, but that it intends to price the drug "fairly and responsibly." The drug's development was largely paid for by the government's National Cancer Institute, and questions have arisen over how much the company should charge for it.    The committee chose the broadest of several proposed alternatives, rejecting choices that would have authorized a more limited use of taxol, such as restricting its use to patients who had relapsed or to those who had failed to respond to several treatments. The company would be allowed to market the drug only for ovarian cancer, but FDA officials said physicians probably would start prescribing taxol for breast and other cancers as well, once it becomes available and they become familiar with it.    The recommendation was based primarily on five pivotal studies involving 192 women at various stages of the disease. Taxol shrank tumors by at least one-half in 20% to 30% of the patients treated. The lives of those who responded to the treatment were prolonged by a median of five months. Grant Williams, an FDA oncologist, called the drug's apparent effectiveness where other drugs have failed "the biggest selling point for taxol."    Moreover, he said in an interview after the session, the response rates for taxol as a later-stage treatment suggest that it holds promise for eventual use as an initial treatment.    Ovarian cancer is the leading cause of gynecologic cancer deaths in the U.S., with about 21,000 new cases diagnosed annually. About 80% of patients respond to non-taxol chemotherapy, but tumors begin growing again in 60% to 80% of those cases.    Taxol is made from the bark of the Pacific yew tree, which is found in the old growth forests of the Northwest. Environmental groups have clashed with cancer researchers over access to the forests, which are also home to the northern spotted owl, a protected species under the Endangered Species Act. Bristol-Myers said yesterday that it would be able to provide adequate supplies to meet anticipated demand.    An Interior Department spokeswoman said a recently completed inventory of trees found more bark than the government originally expected, despite legal restrictions on logging. In addition, work is under way on finding alternative sources of the drug.    Yesterday, the advisory panel also voted 10-1 to recommend that the FDA authorize the lower of two proposed doses for taxol. And it called for additional studies of the proper dosage.    Like other chemotherapy, taxol produces toxic side effects, including hair loss, numbness of fingers and toes and a decrease in white blood cells, which can lead to infection.  Credit: Staff Reporters of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Once They Chased Guerrillas, but This Is a Different Animal --- Peruvian Army Gets Lessons On Protecting the Vicuna, A Woolly National Treasure
Text: PAMPA GALERAS, Peru -- In a windswept outpost here in the Andean highlands, 25 men stand at attention, hands on hearts, before a strutting drill sergeant. "Some of your comrades dropped out of our camp, lacking courage to fight for the cause," the sergeant barks. "But you have passed the test." A rifle shot cracks out in the air. And a raucous cheer goes up from the ranks: "For God, for country, for the vicuna!" Battle-tested in Peru's long war against fanatical leftist guerrillas, this "Elite Group" of infantry reservists is now embarking on a new defense mission: guarding the vicuna, a graceful, woolly animal that is an ancient symbol of Peruvian identity. A cuddly cousin of the llama, the vicuna is celebrated in Peruvian literature and memorialized on the national seal. But to the marauding Maoist guerrilla group known as Shining Path, the vicuna has stood as a hated emblem of a decadent capitalist state. The subversives launched waves of relentless, scorched-earth raids on the Pampa Galeras reserve, the main vicuna refuge. And with police and the military busy fighting the insurgents, poachers slaughtered vicunas by the thousands, brazenly trafficking in the highly prized fur of this endangered species. By the early 1990s, Peru, home to about two-thirds of the world's vicuna population, had less than 50,000 of the animals left. Now, in an unusual case in which a counterinsurgency campaign has coincided with a conservationist one, the vicuna is making a big comeback. The Peruvian army's smashing reduction of guerrilla ranks, and its all-out campaign against poaching, has kindled a population boom among vicunas, which now number about 90,000. The thriving vicuna packs are even becoming a part of Peru's economic reconstruction effort, as war-ravaged mountain communities earn income by processing vicuna wool for luxury-apparel designers. "The vicuna is our ally in the next war, the one against poverty," says Alfonso Martinez, the Agricultural Ministry's top vicuna man. Peruvians have always been extremely serious about the animal known to science as vicugna vicugna. In the days of the Inca empire, cloaks made from vicuna fur were reserved exclusively for the royal family. Killing a vicuna was a capital offense. Ancient power brokers weren't the only ones who coveted vicuna clothing. In a U.S. political scandal of the 1950s, Sherman Adams resigned as President Eisenhower's chief of staff following revelations that he accepted a vicuna overcoat from favor-seeking textile interests. Other vicuna lovers have derived a purely aesthetic pleasure from watching this elegant animal roam the wilds. The legendary Latin American liberator Simon Bolivar so admired the vicuna that he decreed poachers serve a four-month jail sentence for each animal they bagged. "Agile, silken and delicate," wrote the Peruvian novelist Mario Vargas Llosa, of the vicuna. "His great, intelligent eyes observe the visitor with haughtiness." But all of the vicuna's cunning didn't save it from being a casualty of Peru's guerrilla wars. In Ayacucho, the mountainous province that has been the main breeding ground for both the vicuna and Shining Path, the population of about 30,000 vicunas fell to less than half that during the course of the 1980s. The early 1990s, though, marked a turning point in the war to save the Peruvian state -- and the vicuna. The military nabbed the leaders of the Shining Path and, at the same time, the government turned over ownership of the vicuna to the Andean villages. "Privatizing the vicuna was the first step toward creating a renewable vicuna industry," says Mr. Martinez, of the Agricultural Ministry. War-torn mountain communities certainly needed a spark to bring them back to life again. "This town had never recovered from the Day of the Dead," says Salustian Roberto Arias, deputy mayor of Lucanas. He is referring to Nov. 2, 1987, the All Souls holiday when a raiding party of 20 Shining Path guerrillas burned down the municipal hall and half a dozen stores. The Maoists then dragged a local political leader and seven merchants out of their homes and stoned them to death. "They might as well have killed the whole village," says Mr. Arias, one of the minority of townsfolk who didn't leave after the attack. Now, with the guerrilla threat diminished, villagers are returning to Lucanas -- and rediscovering ancient rites involving the vicuna. Since 1994, Lucanas and neighboring Andean communities have revived an Incan tradition called the Chaku, in which peasants corral vicuna herds by forming a mile-long human chain. Amid drinking and laughter, the villagers pin down the animals and clip their wool. The vicunas are turned loose again, shorn of their thick coats, but unharmed. Lucanas is swapping part of its wool harvest with the government in exchange for a new electrical station. Processing the remainder of the fur provides desperately needed jobs for 55 Lucanas residents like teenager Ana Senovia. "I would have moved to the city by now if it weren't for the vicuna," says Ms. Senovia, dressed in the sombrero and long braids that are the Andean fashion. When woven into cloth by a Peruvian and Italian textile consortium, vicuna wool sells for about $800 a line yard, five times as much as cashmere. Top continental designers such as Armani, Lagerfeld and Versace have begun to produce clothing made of the vicuna fabric -- though it isn't made for everyone's budget. In Rome, a vicuna coat retails for as much as $10,000; a man's scarf for $1,000. Don't bother shopping for vicuna fashions in the U.S., though. Under the U.S. Endangered Species Act, it is still illegal to sell, or even to wear, vicuna clothing in the states. Peru's government is currently petitioning the U.S. Interior Department to allow the sale of vicuna wool, so long as it is taken from live animals. The Peruvians point out that restrictions on selling vicuna clothing have already been liberalized in a global treaty governing the wildlife trade. However, Interior Department officials say they are still studying the Peruvian program to make sure it adequately protects the vicuna. Some conservationists accuse the Interior Department of bureaucratic foot-dragging, and say it ought to hurry up and get with the Peruvian program. "This is a positive conservation story that offers a happy ending for everyone," says Andrea Gaski, a vicuna specialist at the World Wildlife Fund. "The Peruvian communities get income, the vicunas get protection and consumers can still get a luxury coat." Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Beastly Burdens
Text: Is the Earth in the midst of a massive wave of extinctions? Environmental alarmists such as Norman Myers estimate that 150 human-caused extinctions occur each day. On a prorated basis, this suggests that the U.S. has seen 72,000 extinctions since 1973, when the Endangered Species Act was adopted. Yet only seven actual extinctions have been confirmed. Globally, the World Conservation Monitoring Centre lists 1,237 species as having gone extinct since 1600 -- just one-thousandth of the 1.2 million species that Mr. Myers calculates should have disappeared in just the past 22 years. The alarmists have indeed overstated the case. Even so, it is quite true that humanity's activities are transforming wildlife habitats and thus imperiling many species. What should we do? In "Noah's Choice: The Future of Endangered Species" (Knopf, 302 pages, $24), Charles C. Mann and Mark L. Plummer highlight the failings of America's current species-protection efforts and suggest ways to balance the legitimate interests of human beings with the needs of wildlife. However, they explicitly reject the Noah Principle, enunciated by ecologist David Ehrenfeld, that all species should be protected -- always and everywhere, no matter what the cost -- simply because they exist. Unfortunately, this absolutist principle has guided U.S. species-protection efforts. Under the ESA, people are prohibited from "taking" any endangered species; to take is defined as "to harass, harm, pursue, hunt, shoot, wound, kill, trap, capture, or collect or to attempt to engage in any such conduct." In a major expansion of bureaucratic power, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has broadly defined "harm" and "harass" to include the destruction of the habitat of any endangered species. Problems begin with this broad definition. If a city wants to build a school or a hospital on your land, government officials can't just move in and start construction. They must pay you. Most people agree that it's only fair that the public pay for projects that are in the public interest. But what if the government decides that your land is part of the "critical habitat" of an endangered bird or beetle? Under the ESA, the Fish and Wildlife Service can simply stop you from using your land. The ESA stipulates that species conservation comes first regardless of social and economic costs. Thus, as "Noah's Choice" documents, "the present system forces the burden of saving biodiversity on whoever happens to live near endangered species, automatically imposing costs on a few to generate benefits for many." This basic unfairness is driving a growing grass-roots movement to reform the ESA. "Noah's Choice" looks at the hardships being imposed on people in the name of protecting species such as the Karner blue butterfly in upstate New York, the American burying beetle in Oklahoma, the Kretschmarr Cave mold beetle and the golden-cheeked warbler in Texas. Protecting the warbler would stop development on tens of thousands of acres of private land around Austin. One landowner, Margaret Rector, says the value of her land has plummeted to $30,000 from $830,000 because it might contain warbler habitat. Another, Fred Purcell is prohibited from building a parking lot in order to protect the Kretschmarr Cave mold beetle. Mr. Purcell says that the ESA is "telling me -- one person in Austin, Texas -- to foot the bill for preserving things that supposedly benefit the whole country. Well, if they're so good, then why doesn't the whole country pay me to protect them? Why should I get stuck with the bill for it all?" The ESA, the authors note, has "ended up turning landowners into the enemies of species on their land and wildlife biologists into ecological mandarins, deciding the fate of resentful communities." Under the act property owners have strong disincentives against harboring endangered species on their land. These disincentives have led to some sad situations. Just 10 days after the Fish and Wildlife Service announced its intention to list the golden-cheeked warbler, Hillwood Development in Austin chopped down oak and juniper trees in order to deny habitat to the bird. The slogan "Shoot, shovel and shut up" aptly describes the way increasing numbers of landowners feel about endangered-species protection. "It is time to stop pretending that the country's natural endowment can be protected for free, without hurting anyone," write Messrs. Mann and Plummer. They recommend that we scale back the broad definition of "taking" an endangered species -- perhaps limiting it to the "intentional direct harm of an individual member of a listed species" and excluding harm caused by habitat modification. More important, they argue that "public coffers should bear a significant proportion of the costs of saving species." If saving endangered species is a public good, then the public should pay for it. In practice, government could pay landowners for conservation easements, or buy land outright. The authors make it crystal clear that the environmentalists' demand that humanity save every species is a fantasy. We live in a world of trade-offs and we must choose which species we will protect and which we will let go. Environmentalists, landowners and their representatives in Congress would do well to take their advice. --- Mr. Bailey, the producer of the national weekly public TV series "Think Tank," is the editor of "The True State of the Planet," just published by Free Press.

Title: Norton Faces Tough Scrutiny of Her Words, Activities at Hearing
Text: WASHINGTON -- Opponents of Interior Secretary-designate Gale A. Norton are readying some strong ammunition to fire at confirmation hearings that begin today: her own words.    In a spate of legal articles, court briefs and speeches, the 47-year-old Colorado lawyer has argued for tighter limits on federal power: She challenges the constitutionality of some of the 19 major laws she would be required to enforce at the Interior Department, in a post that would make her the protector of 681 million acres of parks, monuments and vacant lands that comprise roughly one-fifth of the U.S.    "In order to run this agency, you have to have a fundamental belief in its mission," says Gregory Wetstone, director of programs for the Natural Resources Defense Council. By arguing that some laws, including the Endangered Species Act and the law that regulates strip mining, are unconstitutional, Ms. Norton has shown a "limited vision" of her role, he says.    Despite the opposition of most of the nation's environmental groups as well as labor and civil-rights groups, Ms. Norton is expected to win Senate confirmation. But her words and her record as a protege of James Watt, the conservative interior secretary in the Reagan administration, have made her President-elect George W. Bush's most controversial cabinet pick after Attorney General-designate John Ashcroft. Her record also provides clues to how she may apply market-based approaches as chief steward of U.S. land and mineral assets.    Even some Republicans are troubled by that record. Martha Marks, the head of Republicans for Environmental Protection, says that a rival group, created by Ms. Norton and others in 1997, was financed by mining, timber, chemical, oil and coal companies. The group, called Coalition of Republican Environmental Activists, staged a fund-raiser here in 1998 to show, as one of its press releases stated, that the Republican "common sense approach to environmental issues is well balanced."    David Wright, a Republican businessman and former member of the planning commission in Chaffee County, Colo., remembers Ms. Norton as the high-powered Denver lawyer who overturned the county's "smart growth" plan on behalf of a real-estate developer. A scenic rural area the county wanted to preserve as open space and a pasture for elk, he says, is now being turned into a subdivision for modular homes.    "She literally bullied her way through the legal process. I found her attitude one that I would hate to see on a national level. If it's all for the money, then God help us," says Mr. Wright. A colleague of Ms. Norton responds that part of her effort was to preserve 30% of the land as elk habitat.    The vehemence of the attacks on Ms. Norton has stunned some of her supporters. "She's being depicted as James Watt in a skirt," says Fred Smith, a Norton confidant who heads the Competitive Enterprise Institute, a conservative think tank here. "She's not that. Watt was a much harsher individual," he says. "Gale's a better communicator. And I think she'll try harder to reach out and even cross party lines."    But Ms. Norton's critics aren't swayed. "Her views are outside the mainstream of even conservative political thinking," contends Doug Kendall of Community Rights Counsel, an environmental group.    Ms. Norton may find the comparison to James Watt hard to shake off. After graduating from the University of Denver Law School, she spent four years in Mr. Watt's Mountain States Legal Foundation, starting in 1979. Then she went to Washington to serve in Interior's legal department, where she helped prepare a plan to explore for oil on part of Alaska's Arctic National Wildlife Refuge.    Later she returned to Colorado where, in 1991, she was elected attorney general. According to her biography, one of the highlights of her tenure, which expired in 1999, was a lawsuit that forced the U.S. Department of Energy to develop tougher standards to clean up nuclear wastes at its Rocky Flats facility, which once processed plutonium for nuclear weapons.    After leaving state government, she joined a Denver law firm, Brownstein Hyatt & Farber, where she represented a number of clients facing environmental actions from federal, state, and local governments. She was a lobbyist for NL Industries Inc., a Houston company formerly known as National Lead Co. The company has been involved in federal Superfund cases and other legal disputes charging it with toxic dumping.    Some of Ms. Norton's more vociferous attacks on federal power stem from fellowships she has had with conservative or libertarian-oriented think tanks, such as the Political Economy Research Center in Bozeman, Mont. Terry Anderson, its executive director, acknowledges that Ms. Norton's return to Washington will be jarring to some.    "She will pursue achieving environmental quality in ways that the typical top-down-oriented national environmental groups don't like," he says. "But in the end, her bottom-up approaches will be aimed at good resource stewardship in Interior."    Mr. Anderson, who is on the Bush administration's transition team at the Interior Department, predicts market-based innovations will help Ms. Norton develop an effective political base to help her run the department. One he has in mind is a plan that would allow ranchers to sell their grazing rights to environmental groups, who could then retire them in perpetuity and take more cattle off of federal land.    At the moment, federal law requires the Interior Department to decide such matters by land-use planning, which doesn't permit such market-based moves to determine grazing practices. "We would get out of all this political rhetoric of should there be cows out there by saying here are the rules, you guys figure it out," explains Mr. Anderson.    A market-based approach outlined by Ms. Norton in her writing would be to require the Interior Department to pay for habitat required to help preserve endangered species.    Under current law, the agency forces landowners to maintain habitat. The change, she writes, would force the government to develop spending priorities: "Government officials could find themselves subject to public pressure to save a scenic coastline instead of a little known, but endangered, black-spored quillwort." (The quillwort, a small, fern-like plant, is on the endangered species list).    Her friends have more market-based ideas. Mr. Smith of the Competitive Enterprise Institute wants Ms. Norton to turn over federal land for management experiments by states and private groups to help solve chronic staffing shortages in the Bureau of Land Management. Spelunking groups could help run scenic caves. Mountain-climbing groups, he thinks, could take over the management of certain designated ridge tops. Off-road motorcyclists could be assigned some areas, horse riders and hikers some others, he says.    "It would be a way to enlist more of the energy and genius of various people in this country rather than trying to find formulas that everyone can agree to," explains Mr. Smith. He concedes that environmental groups might not like this change. "You've got a bunch of purists out there, but this is a big country."  Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Squaring Off: Question: Should hydropower dams on the Snake River be breached to save the salmon?
Text: In the Northwest, it's hard to find a question that evokes such passionate responses: Should four Snake River dams be breached to help revive endangered salmon? Even biologists can't agree on whether dismantling the dams -- the Ice Harbor, Lower Monumental, Little Goose and Lower Granite -- would make a significant difference to the fish that swim in the Snake. In the end, because the dams are federally maintained, Washington, D.C. will decide their fate. Whatever the outcome, there will be emotional objections. Here, Buzz Ramsey, president of the Northwest Sportsfishing Industry Assocation in Hood River, Ore., and Roger Koller, a wheat farmer in Pomeroy, Wash., argue the case. YES -- Buzz Ramsey At least $2 billion has been spent on barges, trucks and elaborate collection-and-bypass systems to help young fish get around hydropower dams on the Lower Snake and Columbia rivers. Everything has been tried except retiring a few dams. The result has been a costly failure. Every wild Snake River salmon and steelhead stock, along with several Columbia River runs, is either extinct or listed under the Endangered Species Act. It's time to stop throwing good money after bad. Sure, dams aren't the only reason the fish are disappearing, just the biggest. Most Northwest fishery biologists agree that dams cause 80% of all human-related salmon deaths on the Columbia and Snake rivers. A team of internationally recognized scientists has concluded that continuing to barge salmon around the dams is unlikely to lead to their recovery. What is virtually certain to restore wild Snake River salmon to pre-dam levels, they say, is dismantling the earthen parts of four Lower Snake dams, letting the river flow around the remaining concrete sections. Industries dependent on these dams cite other possible causes for the general decline of salmon populations, and they advocate spending taxpayer and ratepayer money on ineffective, short-sighted recovery measures, including continued fish barging and bans on fishing.
