It's time for industries that have benefited from these federally subsidized dams to pay their fair share for salmon recovery. Bypassing the dams would have an economic impact, but less than one might think. And the sport-fishing industry supports a federal plan to help businesses through the transition -- despite the fact that many fishing businesses have gone under with little compensation. Barge shipping on the Lower Snake would cease. But, with new investment in infrastructure, local economies could go back to using trucks and railroads, which carried goods for over a century before the Snake dams were finished in 1975. There's no question that grain exports are important to the region. But if the government can subsidize river traffic, by building and maintaining dams, it can subsidize shipping by truck and rail. It's just a matter of where your priorities lie. Maintain the dams, at the expense of the salmon, or upgrade highways and railroads -- if need be. The four dams were built primarily to make Lewiston, Idaho, a seaport. Indeed, they provide no flood control, and only one provides water for crop irrigation, supplying just 13 farms. The average 1,200-megawatt flow of electricity they produce could be replaced through conservation and by using clean, renewable energy resources, such as wind and geothermal. If the dams are discontinued, domestic electricity customers in the area would see their average monthly electricity bills rise only about $3 a month. At the same time, eliminating the dams would end expensive fish-barging programs, and the need to spend several hundred million dollars of taxpayer money for scheduled repairs at the dams, or the tens of millions in annual operating costs. There is no investment that will bring back the salmon if they become extinct. The decline in salmon runs already has had a tremendous impact on the local economy. Fishing sustains sport and commercial fishers, fish markets, guides, tackle shops, hotels, stores and makers of boats, trailers, lifejackets, clothes, anchors, tackle, motors and bait. An estimated 10,000 jobs have been lost in the sport-fishing industry alone in the past 10 years, due largely to declining salmon runs. When we restore healthy salmon runs, the Northwest will again become a destination for anglers from around the world, rather than an exporter of fishing jobs to Canada and Alaska. When the fish come back, so will fishermen, fishing businesses and thousands of jobs. According to a preliminary report produced for the Army Corps of Engineers, dam breaching could contribute $1 billion a year in increased sportfishing and recreation on the Snake River alone. What does it say about us if we are willing to kill off these magnificent fish, the soul of the Northwest? As Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt has pointed out, dams are not timeless monuments like Egypt's pyramids; they are tools. Some have simply become too expensive and deadly to keep. NO -- Roger Koller I treasure many memories of the Snake River from the time I was a boy growing up in Garfield County: picnics, beach parties and trips to my aunt and uncle's fruit ranch for peaches, cherries and the sweetest tomatoes one could imagine. The construction of dams and the deep, slow-moving waters that would result were distant concepts during those days. Progress, however, was marching forward. Society had deemed that the greater good lay in harnessing the river. When slack waters did arrive, it was not without some shock and disappointment. The river and the fruit ranch were gone forever, buried under a reservoir of water. But in return, a new river sprang to life, bearing new benefits for our region. Suddenly, the river provided power, transportation, irrigation and expanded opportunities for recreation. Do I miss the river of my youth? Yes. Would I turn back the clock? No! Today the river churns with activity transporting grain, wood chips and containers to the ocean, while providing enough electricity to power a population base the size of Seattle. Fishermen troll the river for chinook and steelhead. Yet there are those who propose breaching the dams in order to restore fish runs to levels of the early 1900s. The question is, will this restore the runs to past levels, and at what cost? Fish runs have diminished. But are the Snake River dams solely culpable? A recent National Marine Fisheries Service report stated there are more juvenile Snake River salmon surviving their migration to the Pacific today than there were in the early 1960s. Between 50% and 60% of the fish migrating in the river survive the trip, and evidence points to more than 90% surviving individual dam passages. This suggests other factors are at work in the salmon's decline. Since 1977, ocean conditions have not been favorable to salmon. Salmon are a cold-water fish, and the North Pacific has warmed noticeably. Commercial ocean fishing has grown, and net fishing is still allowed on the Columbia. Gill-netting of an endangered species is no way to save fish. Predators such as Caspian terns and sea lions snare millions of fish a year. Even if the dams are breached, much of the spawning grounds these fish once used is now under water behind dams without fish ladders in Idaho. Yet there has been no focus on breaching any of these dams. Those who would breach the Lower Snake dams fail to appreciate the huge role the rivers play in the region's economy. The Columbia-Snake river system is the largest grain gateway in the U.S. and the second-largest wheat corridor in the world. Some 43% of wheat exported from the U.S. is ferried down the Columbia, and 40% of that grain comes down the Snake. Moreover, no viable alternative for transporting our agricultural products to market currently exists. Rural roads and bridges are in dire need of repair at a time when less funding is available for their maintenance. Rural rail lines are disappearing as railroads drop lines and consolidate. What short-line rail operations remain often are undercapitalized and run on tracks 65 to 100 years old. Without barges, exports would decline and transportation costs from my region would at least double. In today's fiercely competitive global economy, if our grain cannot reach export markets in a timely, reliable fashion, our buyers will soon take their business elsewhere. Yes, some jobs are lost because of a decline in salmon. But if the dams are lost, communities throughout eastern Washington, northern Idaho and western Montana will suffer. The goal of this debate should be finding a way to sustain fish and dams. Fish runs are dynamic, not static. Their migrations have ebbed and flowed through time. In today's world, surely we can find a way to elevate fish populations while maintaining the current multiple-use river system. I will always love and miss the river of my youth. I was fascinated by the drawdown of the Lower Granite reservoir a few years ago. It was a chance to see the old river once again. The river, however, that reappeared from beneath the slack water was not the river of my childhood. It was a river of mud flats and devastation. A river nowhere near my memories. Perhaps Thomas Wolfe wrote it best: "You can't go home again." (See related letter: "THE WALL STREET JOURNAL / NORTHWEST --- Letters to the Editor: House Republican Caucus Just the Dam Facts " -- WSJ April 21, 1999)

Title: Election 2012: GOP Race Tightens in South
Text: BILOXI, Miss. -- Mitt Romney on Monday urged Alabama voters to help him bag a surprise win, while Rick Santorum downplayed his chances in the region, in yet more signs of how the Republican race has taken an unexpected turn in the Deep South. Mississippi and Alabama, which both hold polls on Tuesday, have been considered difficult terrain for Mr. Romney with their plentiful evangelical and conservative voters. In prior contests, those types of voters have resisted Mr. Romney, and last week he called the region "a bit of an away game" for him. But polling and voter interviews show the former Massachusetts governor running even with Mr. Santorum and Newt Gingrich, suggesting that Tuesday's balloting may wind up strengthening Mr. Romney. "We're going to get this thing won," Mr. Romney told a rain-soaked crowd in Mobile, Ala. His brief appearance in Mobile on Monday was scheduled only late last week, part of a last-minute push to score an upset in Alabama. It reflected a change of strategy from Mr. Romney's initial efforts to damp expectations for victory in the state. Mr. Santorum, a former U.S. senator from Pennsylvania, talked to reporters here not about winning the state's primary but about trying to "show some strength." Texas Rep. Ron Paul has trailed in polling and has little presence in the region. Messrs. Santorum and Gingrich also signaled Monday that they intended to remain in the presidential race after Tuesday, pushing back against expectation that a poor showing by either would create pressure to withdraw. Conservative leaders are eager for one of the two to have a chance to go head-to-head against Mr. Romney. "If this race continues on its current path, it's going to be very difficult for anyone to get the majority of the delegates before the convention," Mr. Santorum said. Messrs. Santorum and Gingrich appeared at an energy-policy summit here, hosted by groups friendly to their pro-drilling policies. Mr. Santorum portrayed Mr. Gingrich as a false conservative who had embraced global-warming science. Mr. Santorum also said the former House speaker's support while in Congress for the Endangered Species Act amounted to putting "critters above people." He spoke to the group after Mr. Gingrich, who trained his fire on President Barack Obama's policies rather than on GOP rivals. --- Ryan Tracy contributed to this article. Credit: By Janet Hook and Patrick O'Connor

Title: U.S. News: U.S. Watch
Text: LAW ENFORCEMENT DEA Is Faulted Over Seizures of Assets The Drug Enforcement Administration regularly seizes money or goods it believes are related to criminal activity, but in a sample of 100 such cases, more than half didn't aid investigations or produce arrests or prosecutions, a Justice Department watchdog said on Wednesday. The report, by the department's inspector general, could provide fuel to critics who say authorities have too much latitude, and an improper financial incentive, to seize property suspected of ties to criminal activity. Such "asset forfeiture" has long been a contentious subject among criminal-justice experts. The DEA seized $4.15 billion in assets in the 2007-16 fiscal years, according to the report. The sample in the report was from the 2012 fiscal year. The Justice Department's criminal division responded that the sample was small and outdated, and that it found 81 of the sampled forfeitures were "likely tied" to a criminal investigation or prosecution. -- Aruna Viswanatha --- ENDANGERED SPECIES ACT Federal Protections Bolstered by Ruling Utah prairie dogs and environmentalists scored a legal win Wednesday in an appeals court ruling that affirmed the federal government has broad power to protect threatened species. The 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Denver wiped out a Utah judge's ruling from 2014 that restricted use of the Endangered Species Act for species located only in one state, handing a loss to landowners who say the animal is a nuisance. The trial court's decision had been the first of its kind. The Pacific Legal Foundation, a conservative legal organization that advocates for property rights, represented the landowners. Damien Schiff, a lawyer with the organization, said the challengers would appeal to the Supreme Court. -- Brent Kendall

Title: Water Rights Sold Illegally, Judge Rules
Text: The state of Washington for the past year has been illegally allowing cities and developers to buy coveted water rights from farmers and divert them to nonagricultural uses, according to a state judge.    The ruling last month by Thurston County Superior Court Judge Daniel J. Berschauer cheered environmentalists, but it stunned real-estate developers, at least one town and the state Department of Ecology. And it threw into turmoil, at least temporarily, the Legislature's solution to a 38-year backlog in water-rights applications.    Redmond-based Trendwest Resorts Inc., which needs more than two million gallons a day for a planned 6,225-acre resort in Kittitas County, has filed an emergency petition asking to intervene in the lawsuit and urging Judge Berschauer to reconsider. A similar emergency petition was filed by Warden, a water-strapped town in Central Washington.    "If this ruling is upheld, our city will become a ghost town," says Mike Thompson, city administrator for Warden, population 2,500. "We need to be able to buy agricultural water rights and use them to supplement our municipal water supply, and we need to do it immediately if we're going to survive."    The Sept. 8 ruling came in a lawsuit filed against the state in January by environmental groups. The lawsuit claimed that too much power had been given to so-called water conservancy boards, which were authorized by the Legislature in 1997 to help the state ecology agency process its staggering backlog of applications for new water rights and for adjustments to existing permits.    According to Robert Caldwell, director for the nonprofit Center for Environmental Law & Policy in Seattle, his group decided to sue because the state Department of Ecology had handed complex decisions over to "a bunch of lay volunteers who have little or no experience in water management and who have no understanding of the environmental implications tied to their decisions."    Judge Berschauer agreed that the state agency had allowed the boards to make decisions not envisioned by the legislation signed by Gov. Gary Locke. Ruling from the bench on Sept. 8, he said that the state's water conservancy boards don't have the authority to decide whether an existing water right can be used for another purpose, the type of adjustment on which the boards have spent most of their time since they went into business last summer.    However, the judge said the boards are perfectly qualified to process other applications, such as those made by farmers seeking permission to irrigate plots of land not designated in their rights when originally granted.    Environmentalists herald the ruling as a major victory. "We've closed a loophole that developers can use to get water without proper scrutiny," says Mr. Caldwell, whose group is one of the two plaintiffs. The other is the Seattle-based Washington Environmental Council.    But Mary Getchell, a spokeswoman for the DOE in Olympia, says the state "firmly supports how the boards function" and "strongly believes local governments should be involved in water management."    Still unclear is exactly how the state might move to change its current procedures for dealing with water rights. With demand for water growing, supplies increasingly restricted by the Endangered Species Act, and the agency chronically underfunded, the queue of candidates for permit adjustments and new water rights is 7,000 applicants long.    The Legislature tried to break the logjam in 1997, by authorizing the creation of county-level committees called water conservancy boards. The idea was to give applicants who were requesting adjustments to existing water rights a way of getting answers in months instead of decades.    In 1999, the agency adopted administrative rules that gave the boards the right to approve or deny adjustments to existing rights, including deciding whether developers and cities can buy rights from farmers and use them to provide drinking water. Since then, the agency has established boards in 17 of Washington's 39 counties.    Board rulings are forwarded to the Department of Ecology, which has 45 days to review them. Decisions can be appealed to the Pollution Control Hearings Board.    Because Judge Berschauer ruled from the bench, the Department of Ecology and the plaintiffs must submit a document summarizing their understanding of his decision. Judge Berschauer will then formulate a formal, written decision from that material, or -- if the DOE and the environmental groups submit drastically different opinions -- schedule a hearing. No firm deadlines have been set for such steps.    First, the judge must deal with the emergency petitions filed by Warden, Trendwest and four landowners. Lawyers for the six petitioners are scheduled to appear before Judge Berschauer Friday, when they will ask him to allow them to argue that his decision was wrong. If the judge agrees, Warden, Trendwest and the four landowners would gain the right to appeal if they don't like his final decision.    Environmentalists are furious that the six parties want to intervene. "Letting them come in now will complicate the case and prolong it," says Mr. Caldwell of the Center for Environmental Law & Policy.    If Judge Berschauer denies the bids to intervene and issues a written decision consistent with his oral ruling, the Department of Ecology will have several options: comply with the court by changing how the water conservancy boards operate; appeal the ruling to a higher court; or ask the Legislature to pass a new law giving the boards broader powers.    Already, however, the DOE "has advised us that we would be smart to move slowly and cautiously," says Henry Johnson, a former farmer who is chairman of the Franklin County Water Conservancy Board in Pasco.    Ms. Getchell, the spokeswoman, says the department has asked the boards to stop processing noncritical applications until the department "can figure out what to do." Officials, she says, are still "analyzing what direction the judge gave."    The lawyer representing the state, Assistant Attorney General Kathryn Gerla, says it's unclear whether the judge really meant to prohibit the boards from deciding what are called purpose-of-use applications; for example, Warden's request for permission to buy agricultural water rights and use them for its municipal supply. The plaintiffs counter that Judge Berschauer clearly issued such a prohibition when he at one point said, "Purpose-of-use, I think, is clearly not allowed by my interpretation."    Meanwhile, both Warden and Trendwest say they are counting on a reversal from Judge Berschauer. Mr. Thompson, the Warden city administrator, says the town needs at least 50 million more gallons of water a year for of its growing population and for two potato-processing plants that are the town's main employers. Trendwest's lawyer, Joe Mentor Jr. of Seattle, says the developer's plans to start building the MountainStar resort later this year could be threatened if the project has to wait in line at the DOE: "We can't wait 40 years for an answer."  Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Avoiding ESA's Perverse Incentives
Text: Terry Anderson correctly pinpoints the fundamental problem with the Endangered Species Act in "When the Endangered Species Act Threatens Wildlife" (op-ed, Oct. 21): The act's penalty-based approach is counterproductive by creating disincentives for landowners to harbor species. Private landowners are the linchpin for successful endangered species conservation because nearly 80% of endangered species have some or all of their habitat on private land, compared with 50% for federal land. Most landowners, such as those mentioned by Mr. Anderson, are superb conservationists and happy to harbor endangered species so long as they are not punished for doing so. Yet by penalizing landowners the Endangered Species Act goes about achieving its purpose in exactly the wrong way. That is why the ratio of declining to improving species on private land is an abysmal 9 to 1, but on federal land it is a much better 1.5 to 1. While Mr. Anderson is also correct that incentives are needed to encourage landowners to conserve endangered species, the most significant incentive would be to remove the harmful disincentives. Federally approved habitat conservation agreements are a step in the right direction, but they ameliorate, not eliminate, the Endangered Species Act's disincentives. All those serious about conserving endangered species should seek to harness the talent and energy of America's true conservationists, its increasingly beleaguered landowners, by charting a new path that doesn't punish them, respects their property rights and compensates them for costs incurred conserving endangered species. Brian Seasholes Reason Foundation Los Angeles

Title: California, U.S. set water plan affecting farmers
Text: California and the federal government agreed on a historic new water plan that helps wildlife, mainly at the expense of farmers.    The pact for the moment ends almost-decades of bitter wrangling between state agencies, environmentalists, farmers, urban water districts and federal regulators. It calls for farmers and cities to relinquish water equal to about 10% of the water drawn from the San Francisco Bay delta each year. Most of the surrendered water will come from agriculture.    About 20 million people get their drinking water from the delta, but agriculture historically has used about 75% of water drawn from the delta.    Agriculture's heavy pumping -- even in periods of drought -- has caused extensive environmental damage in the delta, destroying habitat for such now-protected species as the Sacramento River winter run chinook salmon and the delta smelt. Much of the water -- for which farmers have paid little because of federal subsidies -- has been used to irrigate desert acreage for cotton and rice, crops that also are subsidized because of chronic oversupply. The policy has been attacked by courts, Congress and environmentalists for decades, but farmers generally have been able to keep their stranglehold on California's water.    Yesterday's agreement was hailed by the White House. The federal government praised it as the kind of cooperative approach to balancing environmental and economic concerns that the Clinton administration has been talking about -- but having some difficulty achieving -- since it took office.    "This historic agreement is good for economic growth, good for the environment and good for California and the nation," President Bill Clinton said.    The pact was good political news for defenders of the Endangered Species Act, which include Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt. He and other supporters of the act are bracing for a likely Republican-led effort to gut the statute, which critics say costs too many jobs in the name of saving wildlife. The water agreement is likely to join the recovery of the bald eagle as Mr. Babbitt's chief evidence that the act is flexible enough to balance economics and conservation without major revisions.    Under the agreement, farmers and cities will surrender about 450,000 acre feet of water each year in order to meet new state and Environmental Protection Agency water quality standards and to meet federal Endangered Species Act requirements. The water will be left in the delta system to bring water levels back up and to decrease water salinity, two key factors for wildlife survival. In dry years, farmers and cities would be required to yield as much as 1.1 million acre feet of water. (An acre foot is 326,000 gallons.)    Typically, about 4.5 million acre feet of water are drawn from the delta, the vast majority for irrigation.    Environmentalists had hoped to free up more water for wildlife, but were satisfied with the pact nonetheless.    "The bottom line is this agreement will help wildlife -- and soon," said Tom Graff, an attorney for the Environmental Defense Fund, which has battled water interests over the issue for years. Under the agreement, the additional water for wildlife likely will start becoming available in February.    (See related letters: "Letters to the Editor: California Water Woes: Don't Blame the Farmer" -- WSJ Feb. 7, 1995)    941216-0072    YY95 MM02  Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Government Officials Work on a Plan To Boost Populations of Wild Salmon
Text: SEATTLE -- Federal, state and local officials convened at a "salmon summit" to begin hammering out a plan to restore depleted populations of wild salmon rather than have the federal government issue a mandate. The gathering was organized by two lawmakers from Washington state, Republican Sen. Slade Gorton and Rep. Norm Dicks, a Democrat, after federal agencies last month added nine species of wild salmon to the Endangered Species Act. The listings pose potentially onerous development restrictions for millions of people, since the species are dispersed throughout the waterways of greater Seattle, much of the rest of Washington and parts of Oregon, including Portland. Enforcement of the act is being deferred for several months until the National Marine Fisheries Service, which oversees salmon, can review proposals by state and local agencies to spearhead a regional effort to boost the numbers of fish to a healthy level. The alternative would be for a federal court to take matters into its own hands, a prospect few here want, given the effect on the local timber industry following court-issued logging bans designed to protect the northern spotted owl listed as endangered about a decade ago. "Only one issue counts for the state -- local control," Washington State Rep. Jim Buck, one of two dozen witnesses appearing before the hearing yesterday, said in his statement. "We must persuade federal authorities that we can handle this problem ourselves." On that point, most of the more than 200 people attending the summit were in agreement, including a congressional delegation that also included Alaska Sen. Ted Stevens, a Republican and chairman of the Senate Appropriations Committee, and Patty Murray, the other U.S. senator from Washington. "We need to pool all of our resources in the recovery of this fish," said Mr. Dicks, the ranking Democrat on the House interior subcommittee. Indeed, the Clinton administration has proposed to allot $100 million toward initial recovery efforts in the Northwest, with states putting up matching amounts. Sen. Gorton, chairman of the Senate's interior subcommittee, wants three times that amount. Meanwhile, Washington Gov. Gary Locke told the panel his legislature is considering setting aside as much as an additional $100 million. Passage of the federal funding is expected this fall, while the state funding is expected to be approved by the end of this month. "I'm very optimistic that we will have a decent funding package," the governor said in an interview. It's far less clear, however, exactly how that money will be used. Reflecting the diverse and sometimes conflicting interests of the Northwest, groups ranging from farmers and fishermen to builders and environmentalists offered a plethora of suggestions that are bound to offend some if implemented. Officials of the Washington State Farm Bureau, for instance, advocated an all-out ban on wild salmon fishing for 15 years, a proposal considered overly severe by many fishermen. Tim Stearns, chairman of Save Our Wild Salmon, an environmental group in Seattle, suggested tearing down some dams, a move that would hurt the electric utilities. "Salmon recovery is not rocket science," Mr. Stearns testified, as other Save Our Salmon members held banners and appeared in fish costumes. To appease the various factions, William Ruckleshaus, a former secretary of the Environmental Protection Agency, proposed that President Clinton and Gov. Locke jointly appoint a regional coordinator to head the recovery plan. Mr. Ruckleshaus, who lives in the Seattle area, also has been negotiating with Canada for a long-term treaty with the U.S. to better safeguard the salmon as they travel through ocean waters off British Columbia on their way to the Northwest. Whatever comes out of all these salmon efforts, few predict a quick resolution to the problem. "It will take 12 to 40 years to demonstrate whether or not we have been successful," said Mr. Buck. Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: U.S. Set to Unveil Plan in Bid to Save Songbird and Jobs
Text: The federal government is set to unveil a new approach to the stormy conflict between wildlife protection and jobs. Environmental and government sources said the Interior Department will announce today that it intends to list the California gnatcatcher, a tiny songbird that lives in the arid sage and scrub along the Southern California coastline, as threatened under the Endangered Species Act. But in an unprecedented move, the government will essentially exempt owners of the bird's habitat -- mostly real estate developers -- from the law's absolute prohibitions on killing any members of a protected species, as long as the landowners agree to preserve substantial parts of their gnatcatcher habitat. The gnatcatcher has been a closely watched test case of the Clinton administration's theories on how to balance conservation and economy. The bird is in trouble because 90% of its habitat has been plowed under for housing tracts over the past few decades. Much of what's left is prime Southern California real estate owned by major developers. Environmentalists have argued that the gnatcatcher will disappear if not protected, but developers say the usual Endangered Species Act procedures for saving the bird would cost tens of thousands of jobs and billions of dollars in economic activity. The Interior Department's plan for the bird is an attempt to defuse that clash by preventing the bird's extinction without totally shutting down building along the California coast. It is meant to promote a concept known as ecosystem planning; this approach changes the focus of wildlife protection from saving individual species to one that seeks to preserve enough habitat to guarantee the survival of all species that depend on that habitat. The gnatcatcher plan is specifically aimed at encouraging a two-year-old effort coordinated by California's Department of Resources to apply ecosystem planning to the gnatcatcher battle. Under the state plan, developers have voluntarily put about 200,000 acres off limits while scientists map out crucial gnatcatcher habitat. Developers will be allowed to build in some gnatcatcher habitat, as long as they agree to preserve crucial areas; developers that don't cooperate will still be subject to the full array of Endangered Species Act bans on damaging habitat. Some environmentalists worry that the California plan doesn't have enough teeth, largely because it relies on local authorities -- such as county planning commissions -- to enforce it. But Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt has said that ecosystem planning could serve as a model for resolving other bitter conservation battles. Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: U.S. Proposes Protection For Another Western Bird
Text: The federal government has nominated another Western bird for protected status, giving environmentalists a new victory in their challenges to logging practices in the Pacific Northwest. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service recommended that the marbled murrelet be listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act, the same status given the northwestern spotted owl. The service found that logging and other practices have destroyed much murrelet habitat, putting its survival at risk. The murrelet, a robin-sized coastal seabird, nests in the same type of ancient forest as the owl does. The listing may add to pressure from some in Congress and the Bush administration for reform of the Endangered Species Act. The Fish and Wildlife Service proposed listing the murrelet as threatened in California, Oregon and Washington. The decision means that forest managers in those states, primarily federal agencies such as the Forest Service, must come up with a plan to protect the murrelet, just as they have been struggling to do for the owl for almost two years. Environmentalists hailed the decision as further proof that timber-cutting in old forests is ravaging many species. Logging interests decried it and called anew for congressional action to save jobs they say are being sacrificed to birds, fish and trees.

Title: Suit Challenges Columbia River Water Rights
Text: Communities along the Columbia River are preparing to help fight a lawsuit that seeks to stop a farm from drawing irrigation water from the river. Local governments and business interests in Oregon and Washington say that economies dependent on the Columbia are threatened by the federal lawsuit against the Morrow County, Ore., farm. The fear is that if the plaintiffs prevail, generations-old water rights held by farmers and others on both sides of the river will be jeopardized, and a state's ability to set its own water policy could be compromised. "This is the biggest challenge to Western water law... since the West was won," says Tom Gilleese, president of Hermiston Development Corp., a nonprofit economic-development organization in Oregon that belongs to the recently formed Public and Private Water Users Association. The association has hired a lawyer to prepare a petition to intervene in the suit. If the court allows the intervention, the association would essentially become a party in the lawsuit, able to put forth its own evidence. Kim Puzey, general manager of the Port of Umatilla, says the port and other association members are willing to spend resources to prevent a "draconian" ruling that could decimate the Columbia River Basin economy. The suit objects to irrigation plans for the farm, which owns water-rights permits granted by the state of Oregon more than 20 years ago. The Oregon Water Resources Department in May issued a preliminary ruling that those permits allow Inland Land Co. of Hermiston, which manages the farm, to pump roughly 50,000 acre feet of water a year from the river to irrigate 18,500 acres where it wants to plant potatoes, wheat, alfalfa and other crops. Environmentalists were outraged, saying the removal of such a large amount of water might harm several salmon runs, including the spring and summer Chinook. In May, they challenged the state's preliminary ruling. A hearings officer will issue a proposed order in the fall, which becomes final if no one appeals it. Then, in June, three environmental groups -- WaterWatch of Oregon, Trout Unlimited and the Northwest Environmental Defense Center -- filed the current lawsuit in U.S. District Court. The defendant isn't Inland or the state, but the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. The claim: The agency violated the U.S. Endangered Species Act when it failed to stop Inland from using an Army Corps pumping permit to draw the extra water from the river. Army Corps officials respond that they had no legal authority to step in, because Inland didn't apply for a new permit and agency rules don't prohibit Inland from using its existing permit to pump more water. But the plaintiffs argue that, under the Endangered Species Act, federal agencies must take action when a threatened or endangered species might be at risk, even if their regulations don't specifically instruct them to do so. The Army Corps, the suit says, should have consulted with the National Marine Fisheries Service when it learned of Inland's plan -- and the suit asks the court to rule that the fisheries service be consulted whenever the Army Corps is involved with water withdrawals along the Columbia River. And that could bring a sea change to water law, observers say. James Karr, a professor of fisheries and zoology at the University of Washington, says the suit "has the potential to set precedent" because it questions whether in the era of the Endangered Species Act, a state has the authority to control the allocation of the water within its own boundaries. The lawsuits' opponents say if the plaintiffs win, it would spell disaster -- inviting a federal bureaucracy to interfere with the allocation of a resource that for more than a century has been the province of the state. "You're talking about shutting down the river if this lawsuit is successful," says Mr. Gilleese of Hermiston Development. "If so, this place is a desert. We're done for." The concern is as great in Benton County in Washington, where the County Commission has asked its legal staff to file a friend-of-the-court brief on behalf of the Army Crops of Engineers. "The water rights that have been allocated from the Columbia ... have helped build the diverse economic industry that we have here in the county," says Benton County Commissioner Max Benitz. "I do not believe it is in the best interest to reverse that process." The environmental groups say their goal isn't to call a halt to withdrawals from the Columbia. But, they say, sacrifices must be made in order to save the salmon population. "That's what happens when you have an Endangered Species Act," says Kristen Boyles, a lawyer for Seattle-based Earthjustice Legal Defense Fund Inc., which is representing the plaintiffs. "State water rights is not all that controls use. Now we've got a new player in state water rights." Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: U.S. Urges Declaring Three Species of Northwestern Salmon Threatened
Text: The federal government recommended declaring three species of Northwestern salmon threatened species, heightening a preservation battle that could reshape the region's economy.    The National Marine Fisheries Service, an arm of the Commerce Department,Friday proposed listing as threatened the fall run of the Snake River chinook. The agency also lumped the spring and summer runs of Snake River chinook together and proposed it for threatened status. Another species, the lower Columbia River coho, wasn't given threatened status because the agency determined that no distinct wild population of those fish exists any more.    Another species, the Snake River sockeye, was proposed for listing as an endangered species earlier this year. Under the Endangered Species Act, listing the fish as either endangered or threatened will require broad measures to restore habitat and save what's left of their populations.    The agency's move Friday went further than most business interests had hoped and not far enough for many environmental groups, increasing the likelihood that the salmon issue will eventually end up in court. For example, fish groups attacked the agency's ruling on the coho and its combining of the spring and summer chinook runs. "The salmon issue isn't going to get solved without litigation," said Rick Braun, legal counsel for Oregon Trout, a fish advocacy group.    The salmon fight has higher stakes than the bruising battle over the Northwest spotted owl. Salmon are in trouble primarily because of eight huge federal dams on the Columbia and Snake rivers, which kill millions of salmon each year by sweeping them into their turbines or by hindering their march up and down the river.    But the dams, built beginning in the 1930s, produce cheap power and irrigation water and make the rivers navigable. Saving the salmon will almost certainly require substantial changes in the way the dams operate; business groups in the region have predicted economic disaster, with electric rates rising, shipping slowing down and water for farms drying up.    Under the Endangered Species Act, the proposed listings can be debated for as much as a year before becoming official. In hopes of avoiding the polarization that has marked the owl fight, water users and fish advocates have been negotiating for months on potential compromises. Those plans have run into numeorus snags. On Friday, Idaho Gov. Cecil Andrus, an influential voice in the salmon debate, blasted the Army Corps of Engineers and the federal Bonneville Power Administration, for encouraging "doomsday fears" of the econmic impacts of salmon protection. The corps operates the dams, while the power administration, a federal agency, markets the power they produce.    Mr. Andrus couldn't be reached to elaborate. He was salmon fishing in Alaska. "He has to go a long way from Idaho to find salmon any more," observed Scott Peyron, an aide to the governor.  Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Babbitt Proposes Reforms to Ease Conservation Law
Text: WASHINGTON -- Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt proposed a series of legislative reforms for minimizing the impact of the Endangered Species Act on small landowners and others. At a news conference, Mr. Babbitt described 10 principles that he said should guide Congress as it rewrites the act. Although his remarks were a departure from his oft-repeated claim that the species-conservation law doesn't need to be amended, the Republican congressional victory last November greatly increased the likelihood that the 1973 act will be overhauled this year. Congress hasn't moved very far toward changing the species-protection statute. But the House, in a blunt expression of its displeasure with the law, recently amended its proposed regulatory moratorium so that any rules specifically connected to the Endangered Species Act would be blocked for an additional year. Mr. Babbitt insisted yesterday that "we've always recognized that this act would be up for reauthorization," adding he never thought the law was engraved "in bronze." An aide said that Mr. Babbitt doesn't intend to submit a formal bill to Congress. An aide to Sen. John Chafee (R., R.I.), a strong environmental ally who is chairman of the Senate Environment and Public Works committee, said of the Babbitt proposal: "We think that it holds a great deal of promise for resolving some of the problems we're hearing about." But Rep. Don Young (R., Ala.), who as chairman of the House Natural Resources committee is more likely to clash with Mr. Babbitt, said in a statement that while he was "encouraged" by the proposal, "We now have to see how far the administration is willing to go toward addressing all of the problems associated with the act." The interior secretary's proposed changes are of a piece with various administrative actions he has taken during the past two years to minimize the endangered-species law's impact on landowners and businesses. For example, the Interior Department just last month said small landowners in California and Washington state with fewer than 80 forest acres would be exempted from the agency's efforts to protect the northern spotted owl. Mr. Babbitt said the law's provisions allowing for such exemptions are "cumbersome," however, and should be broadened. Mr. Babbitt's other proposed reforms include shifting more enforcement to the states, improving the scientific basis of decisions, and minimizing the law's "social and economic impacts." But the secretary conceded that the proposed changes stop short of allowing certain species to be judged sufficiently minor -- and the social or economic costs of saving them sufficiently great -- that their extinction requires no federal action. This option has been attracting growing numbers of adherents, and is advanced in a new book entitled "Noah's Choice: The Future of Endangered Species," by Charles C. Mann and Mark L. Plummer. Mr. Babbitt said that the law currently allows appointed "God squads" to suspend species protection in individual cases, but that this mechanism has gone virtually unused because there are generally "ways of working out processes that provide a chance for recovery." Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Columbia Dam Issue to Push Into Election Year
Text: WASHINGTON -- Ten federal agencies studying ways to protect some species of salmon and trout from extinction in the Columbia River system will issue environmental-impact statements and other reports today on the nation's options. Some of them suggest the removal of four hydroelectric dams on the Snake River, which flows into the Columbia, may be the best way to save the fish. The move will push a politically contentious and potentially expensive issue into the election year. Farmers and businessmen in the area have mounted a campaign to save the dams, which provide clean, cheap electricity, irrigation water and a placid waterway to ship farm goods to market. Environmentalists, some Indian tribes, fishermen and outdoors groups have been pushing to remove the dams -- all of which are in eastern Washington -- to save some species of fish and promote tourism along the scenic river. "This is the first time that the science has clearly concluded that dam removal must be part of our salmon recovery strategy," said Scott Faber, policy director for American Rivers, a national conservation group. He referred to a scientific report by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service that concludes that removing the four dams would provide the most benefits for the fish and wildlife in the river and on the land that surrounds the dam reservoirs. Bill Shake, assistant regional director for the Fish and Wildlife Service in Portland, Ore., cautioned the agency's recommendation isn't a final political decision, but a preliminary scientific conclusion reached after studying the evidence. "Our recommendation should in no way be construed as Fish and Wildlife policy decision on whether or not to remove them." The Army Corps of Engineers, the agency leading the trout and salmon study, has estimated that it would cost $1 billion to remove the dams and more than $400 million a year to replace electric power, shift transportation patterns, obtain new irrigation water sources, and to compensate for what it estimates to be an expected slump in tourism and recreational business provided by the dams. But the studies also say it may be expensive to improve the chance of fish survival without breaching the dams. That could involve moves by federal agencies to increase restrictions on logging, irrigation and commercial fishing to meet requirements of the Endangered Species Act. The Clinton administration has attempted to reduce the dams' impact on endangered species by hauling young fish in barges and trucks around the dams. The Department of Energy is also sponsoring research on more fish-friendly types of turbine blades, which the mature fish must swim through on their way to spawning grounds upstream. The dams being considered for removal supply a total of about 1,200 megawatts of power. They are the Lower Granite Dam, Little Goose Dam, Lower Monumental Dam and Ice Harbor Dam. Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: U.S. News: Hunters Take a Hit to Preserve Grouse
Text: Ken Jafek, a hunting guide from Idaho, has been chasing greater sage grouse for roughly half of his 79 years. But with federal officials weighing whether to protect the chicken-like bird under the Endangered Species Act, Mr. Jafek is dialing back his hunting to just one kill during Idaho's annual seven-day hunt, which started Saturday. "One is enough," he said. "I don't want to see them listed." As eight states across the West hold what could be one of the last sage-grouse hunting seasons this month, many hunters are cutting back on the traditional pastime, either by choice or because they are being forced to do so by wildlife managers. Montana severely curtailed hunting this year because of low sage-grouse numbers, and several states, including Idaho and California, closed some hunting areas. The curbs come as states seek to demonstrate to federal officials that they can preserve the bird's population without Washington interference. Despite the cutbacks, oil companies and ranchers, who also are trying to manage the grouse's population without federal oversight, argue that killing the birds for sport no longer makes sense. "I have a hard time accepting the fact that if a bird is that close to being endangered that we still have a hunting season," said David Galt, executive director of the Montana Petroleum Association. Meanwhile, some hunters are critical of the restrictions, saying land development and cattle grazing are responsible for the bird's dwindling numbers, not the short seasonal hunts. For some environmentalists, the debate about hunting is moot. The grouse, they say, would still be in trouble if the whole season were canceled. "We spend all of our energy on the top threats," said Brian Rutledge, who oversees sage-grouse preservation at the National Audubon Society. Hunting, he added, has "not been on my list of things to really go after." The tension over the hunts comes as the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service is set to determine next year whether the sage grouse, the largest native grouse species in North America, should be considered threatened or endangered. Once abundant in the West, greater-sage-grouse populations are estimated to be between 200,000 and 500,000. Its historic range has shrunk by more than half. A listing of the species would restrict activities that harm the bird's habitat, an area nearly the size of Texas stretching across 11 states from Colorado to Washington. The U.S. agency has said hunting isn't among the chief risks to the grouse's long-term survival, pointing instead to habitat loss from farms and subdivisions, increased oil-and-gas drilling, invasive species and wildfires. The potential listing has spurred a widespread campaign by federal and state regulators, ranchers, oil companies, environmentalists and sportsmen to safeguard the bird. In Idaho, the state Department of Fish and Game's decision to close a small area to hunting this season was backed by more than 60% of the 146 participants in a poll conducted by the agency this summer. Some hunters among them advocated for a statewide ban. Virgil Moore, the Idaho agency's director, said that if the grouse is listed and hunting is prohibited, research on the bird will take a hit, because it is funded by game licenses, as well as by gun and ammunition taxes. Amid all the friction surrounding the bird's future, some hunters are opting to put down their firearms, for now. Ken Miracle grew up hunting sage grouse with his grandfather. But this year, he will only be shooting sage grouse with a camera. After killing a prize specimen that hangs over his fireplace a few years ago, he mostly goes out to the sagebrush to document and preserve the birds. He still has sage-grouse cravings, though. "The big toms, they make extraordinary chili," Mr. Miracle said. Credit: By Ana Campoy

Title: U.S. News: Drilling Plan Would Undo Bird Protections
Text: Corrections & Amplifications Rep. Raul Grijalva is a Democrat from Arizona. A U.S. News article Friday about sage-grouse policy incorrectly said he is from New Mexico. (WSJ Dec. 8, 2018) The Trump administration on Thursday moved to open millions of acres of public lands in the West to new oil and gas drilling and increased grazing by easing restrictions meant to protect a native bird. The action could undo a 2015 compromise crafted by government officials and some environmental and business groups to avoid listing the greater sage grouse, a chicken-like bird, as threatened, which would have triggered even more severe restrictions. Some Republicans and energy and ranching businesses said the Obama-era deal unnecessarily locked out vast parts of the West to development The Bureau of Land Management, which unveiled the long-expected changes in a public notice, is expected to complete the proposal early next year. Experts consider the decline of the sage grouse across most of the Western states to be a barometer of the overall health of the region's vast sagebrush ecosystem, which has been identified by the U.S. Forest Service as among the most endangered in North America. Environmental groups and some congressional Democrats assailed Interior Secretary Ryan Zinke on Thursday. "President Trump and Secretary Zinke are leaving no stone unturned in their race to trash our public lands and give polluting industries whatever they want," said New Mexico Rep. Raul Grijalva, ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee. "An assertion that this is a giveaway to the oil and gas industry can only be made if you haven't read the proposal," said Faith Vander Voort, an Interior Department spokeswoman. In 2015, then-Interior Secretary Sally Jewell praised the sage-grouse plan as a compromise that staved off the need to list the bird as endangered. But many ranchers have said they were unfairly forced out of grazing allotments that were deemed as too close to sage-grouse territory. Energy industry officials said any new drilling would be done so as not to disturb the sage grouse Critics predicted the issue would end up in the courts -- possibly triggering a listing under the Endangered Species Act that almost all sides had sought to avoid because of its more severe economic implications.   Credit: By Jim Carlton

Title: Judge Throws Out Bush Plan For Northwest's Klamath River
Text: In a blow to the Bush administration, a U.S. district judge in Oakland, Calif., has thrown out a 10-year federal management plan for the Northwest's Klamath River on grounds it doesn't adequately protect endangered salmon. The judge, Saundra B. Armstrong, ordered the government to revamp the plan after finding that it violates the Endangered Species Act. The judge allowed the government to divert water as planned this year. But she said the National Marine Fisheries Service plan relies too heavily on state and local entities to supply water for endangered coho salmon on the Klamath, which begins in Oregon, passes through northern California and empties into the Pacific Ocean. Environmentalists said the decision, made public yesterday, repudiates the Bush administration on a hotly contested environmental issue and gives the Democrats more ammunition in their bid to unseat President Bush. But the fish may benefit the most, environmentalists said. "This is a step toward getting the Klamath River basin back into balance," said Kristen Boyles, a Seattle attorney for Earthjustice, which filed the suit on behalf of commercial fishermen and others. Justice Department officials said they were pleased the judge didn't interfere with Klamath flows this year and added they are confident the National Marine Fisheries Service can modify the river plan. Under the plan devised last year, the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation was responsible for supplying 57% of the water needed for the fish, with the rest divvied up among nonfederal parties. At issue is whether water from the upper reaches of the Klamath should be used more to irrigate numerous farms or to help restore depleted runs of salmon and other species on the river. Tensions have run so high that two years ago farmers pried open spigots closed by federal officials to give more water to the fish.

Title: Plan to Give Wolves New Home May Be A Howling Success --- Six of Endangered Red Type Are to Be Released in Test On Carolina Outer Banks
Text: EAST LAKE, N.C. -- Is the wolf at the door? No, says Warren Parker. What's more, it won't be, even if he is allowed to release six red wolves into the swampy thickets of North Carolina's Outer Banks next spring. Mr. Parker is a biologist for the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. For several years, he has been searching for a new home for the endangered species, and he thinks he has found it here. Now, the main problem is convincing local residents that -- contrary to popular belief -- the wolf can be a good neighbor. "What we've got to overcome," he says, "is that preconceived notion that these animals will blow the door down and eat little Red Riding Hood." Public opinion isn't to be taken lightly. Two years ago, the government proposed releasing the wolves into a rural area along the Kentucky-Tennessee border. But the plan was howled down. Small farmers and hunters feared livestock losses and hunting restrictions. Environmentalists complained about plans to trap coyotes so they wouldn't interfere with the project. Public hearings turned hostile: One woman said she recalled tales of wolves carrying off children, and a man warned that they would dig up graves. "It was devastating," Mr. Parker recalls. "We got a real education out there." And the wolves remained homeless. The irony is that to hear the experts tell it, the wolf is largely the victim of bad press. David Mech, a Minnesota-based researcher for the Fish and Wildlife Service, says that with the exception of a few cases of rabies, there isn't a single documented case of a wolf attacking human beings in North America. The animals are too frightened of people, he says. Moreover, the red wolf is a different species from the gray wolf, which in northern climates has even been known to down moose. Red wolves are only about half the size of gray wolves, stay well clear of people, generally eat small mammals and don't even hunt in packs. Once common in the Southeast, they no longer are seen outside of zoos. Not that red wolves are just sheep in wolves' clothing. Mr. Parker does concede that "they'll occasionally take a deer." But, standing on the stage of the East Lake Community Center, speaking to a group of flannel-shirted locals gathered around a wood stove, he insists that people around here will probably never see more of them than their tracks. This piece of the Carolinas was chosen for the project as much for the people as for the terrain. Most residents of the peninsula's four tiny communities live off commercial fishing and don't keep livestock. They are hunters and trappers, used to the notion of bobcats and black bears nearby, and most aren't very worried about wolves. "Turn 'em loose," says Louis Basnight, a local resident. "As long as I can dog-hunt I don't care if they turn a rhinoceros loose." Another man suggested releasing the animals near his mother-in-law's house. But some are still concerned, fearing the wolves could eventually kill the deer or quickly overpopulate the area. "I don't see any good in it," grumbles Don Perry, a heavy-set man in a quilted jacket and baseball cap. To assuage local fears and help manage the wolves, the government plans to outfit them with space-age dog collars. The collars emit radio signals that would enable satellite telemetry to identify each animal's precise location instantaneously. The collar could also hold a microcomputer to store information about the animal's health or habits. And it could hold a remote-controlled tranquilizer dart for emergencies and an explosive bolt to remove the collar when the experiment ends. "It would work well on kids, too," suggests Mr. Parker. The gear is costly, but this project is a high priority for the Fish and Wildlife Service. The government says that never before in North America -- and perhaps never before in the world -- has a predator extinct in its natural habitat been reintroduced to the wild. Success here might accelerate government plans to release Rocky Mountain wolves in Yellowstone National Park, Mexican wolves in New Mexico, panthers in Florida and more. If, on the other hand, the red wolf project fails, funds for such programs might dry up. "Canis rufus," the only purely American species of wolf, once ranged from the Delaware Bay to the eastern Gulf of Mexico. Today, only about 65 red wolves remain in zoos and at a Mount Rainier, Wash., breeding facility. Time continually raises the risk that new generations will lose the ability to hunt; Mr. Parker recalls visiting the breeding facility and having wolves trot up and lick his hand. The last wild ones disappeared about a decade ago as development ravaged their last refuge in thick cane brakes of southeast Louisiana and east Texas. But in a 1978 experiment, two of them flourished in the wild on Bulls Island, S.C., for 11 months without even being seen by hunters and birdwatchers. Mr. Parker says the creatures can "hide behind a blade of grass." When the time came to end the experiment, officials had to use a dart gun fired from a helicopter to help recapture the two wolves. The Bulls Island experience makes experts think the Alligator River National Wildlife Refuge here will be a great place for the shy creatures to hide. Its 118,000 swampy acres teem with rabbits, opossums, raccoons and other small game. The area is so nearly impassable that the preferred deer-hunting technique is to loose a pack of dogs on one dirt road and string out hunters on another where deer might be flushed out. The refuge shares a peninsula with a 46,000-acre Air Force bombing range and only 20,000 acres of private land, mostly farms. The government hopes that the half-dozen wolves it releases will multiply to 25 or more before any stray afield. So far, unlike the Tennessee and Kentucky residents who cried wolf, local officials and environmental groups here seem to support the project. So, if all goes well, Mr. Parker plans to install his wolves in the woods here next fall in 50-foot-square pens. They will be held in the pens for about six months and fed local game to acclimate them before being set free. Roaming on the wildlife refuge, they would be protected by law. But provisions of the Endangered Species Act would be waived when they wandered off the refuge, and they could be shot if they threatened people's safety or property. Mr. Parker calls that concession crucial to gaining local approval for any such project. Ultimately, he says, the wolves "are going to have to make it on their own." Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: What's news: Northwest
Text: Great Idea. Now How Are You Going to Pay for It? Oregon Gov. John Kitzhaber laid out an ambitious agenda in his state-of-the-state speech, saying he wants to make Oregon the first in the nation with universal health insurance. How? Well, the former emergency-room doctor was vague on the details. He did say subsidies could make insurance available to everyone, but that struck observers of the Republican-controlled, tight-fisted Legislature as an unpromising approach. Much better received, by the Portland City Club audience at least, was the governor's description of Bill Sizemore's latest ballot initiative -- which would allow Oregonians to deduct from their state income taxes everything they pay in federal income taxes -- as "madness." Mr. Sizemore didn't much like that. He wasn't pleased either that Mr. Kitzhaber praised the state's public-beach, environmental and land-use laws, and then pointed out that nearly one-third of current residents have arrived one way or another since 1970, "after all these things we cherish and point to had been put in place." Said Mr. Sizemore, who moved to Oregon in 1972 and failed to unseat Mr. Kitzhaber in 1998: "He found a way to insult at least a third of us." Rough Waters The Washington Transportation Commission gave state ferry-system operators permission to take a stab at convincing voters that fares should go up by as much as 56% to keep commuter boats afloat in the wake of Initiative 695. Corporate Tax Relief, Take 2 One year and an imminent tax increase later, lawmakers in Olympia declared they were moving in on sealing a deal to give businesses a $575 million break over the next five years on unemployment-insurance payroll taxes. The measure heading for possible approval also would extend $140 million in benefits to laid-off workers enrolled in retraining programs, but that's probably not what's propelling things. Instead, it just might be the 23% boost in the unemployment-insurance levy due in April. Even liberal Democrats said that with the Unemployment Insurance Trust Fund flush with $1.7 billion, the tax increase -- triggered by current state law -- is unnecessary. There wasn't such urgency in 1999, when negotiations ended a bitter stalemate. No Gold in Those Hills. Yet. The Washington Pollution Control Hearings Board reversed a Department of Ecology ruling granting water-rights and water-quality permits to the proposed Crown Jewel open-pit gold mine on Buckhorn Mountain in Okanogan County. Coal in Their Stockings Calling the diversion unconstitutional, the Montana Supreme Court gave the boot to a 1999 law that would have put $20 million in state coal-tax collections into economic-development endeavors this year. Some lawmakers called for a special session to rewrite the law. But wouldn't it be easier to just dig into the surplus? The state budget director said in a speech that, thanks to surges in capital gains and taxable personal income, the surplus now totals $111 million and might grow to $140 million by June 2001. Budget Tricks Idaho lawmakers scratched their heads over Gov. Dirk Kempthorne's spending blueprint for the next fiscal year: It includes $873 million for public schools -- up 6.88% from the current fiscal year -- but doesn't reflect the annual escalation in revenue losses from a bill passed in 1995 that capped property-tax levels. Instead, the proposed budget states that "additional state support for property-tax replacement" should come from the $56.2 million in extra school funding. How is that again? The governor's office called it "an accounting argument," but legislators complained that Mr. Kempthorne was playing fast and loose with money that, basically, doesn't exist. Temporary Help The Washington Department of Labor and Industries issued a finding regarding the access temporary workers at Microsoft Corp. should have to their personnel files. Calling Microsoft at least a "co-employer" of the temps, who are provided by staffing agencies, the department said either Microsoft or the agencies must hand over personnel information to workers. What happens next? That's up to Microsoft. ---   The Buzz    The number of stories mentioning the following words in a representative selection of newspapers in the region and the Associated Press:                        JAN. 18 -- JAN. 25    Taxes                               122   Initiative 695                       58   Microsoft                            57   Rain                                 46   State of the State                   41   Semiconductor                        17   Amazon.com                           11   Budget Surplus                       11   Endangered Species Act                9

Title: Delta Smelt Is Placed On Endangered List By Wildlife Service --- Move Is a Blow to Agriculture In the Arid California Area Which Is This Fish's Home
Text: The tiny delta smelt has been declared a threatened species, dealing another blow to farming's historic lock on water in California. The U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service ruled yesterday that the smelt, a three-inch, blue-green fish that only lives in one zone of the brackish water near where California's big Sacramento and San Joaquin rivers join forces and flow to the sea, is in danger of extinction. The creature has been threatened by the combination of heavy water irrigation by farmers, the runoff of pesticides and a prolonged drought. The agency said the smelt's population, which once numbered in the many millions, has dropped 90% over the past 20 years. "No apparent recovery is occurring," said Marvin Plenert, the agency's pacific regional director. Under the Endangered Species Act, designation of a species as threatened requires that any practices that harm the species must be eliminated or altered so that it no longer menaces the creature's long-term survival. In the case of the smelt, protections are sure to mean agriculture will have less access to delta water in the future. The action has little immediate impact because recent heavy rains and earlier agreements by water deliverers to retain some water for smelt protection have alleviated the threat in the short term. Still, it is another blow to traditional water practices in California and by implication the rest of the West, where farmers have long guzzled a disproportionate amount of the arid region's water, despite their diminishing role in the regional economy. Because of the threat it posed to California's large, politically potent population of growers, the effort to grant the smelt protections provoked one of the fiercest attacks ever seen on federal wildlife regulators' plan to consider a species for protection. Since 1991, when federal biologists turned their attention to smelt, farm interests have spent millions of dollars trying to debunk studies indicating its problems and on lobbying federal officials and Congress. Growers enlisted former Vice President Dan Quayle's Council on Competitiveness, an instrument of attacks on government regulation, in the fight, too. Growers maintain that protecting the smelt will cause huge economic losses for farmers, a claim disputed by environmentalists and many economists. Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Green Groups Ask for Halt On Logging for Owls' Sake
Text: Six years ago, the Clinton administration unveiled the Northwest Timber Plan, a landmark compromise intended to preserve both jobs for loggers and a fragile inhabitant of the trees they fell: the northern spotted owl. The plan covered 24.4 million acres in the three Pacific Coast states, including six million acres in California's sparsely populated northern third. Today, according to a U.S. Forest Service report issued in April, the owl population -- now estimated at 8,000 pair -- is declining at 3.9% a year. For the Forest Service and the timber industry, it's a clear sign that the federal plan is working: The rate of decline is lower than it was earlier in the decade. But two environmental groups -- including the Pasadena-based John Muir Project and the Native Forest Council in Eugene, Ore. -- think the plan is failing. So much so that they have gone to Seattle federal district court, where they've asked Judge William Dwyer to issue a temporary injunction barring any further logging in the zone until more research is done into the owl's disappearance. Why? While the owls' decline rate has gone down, it's still four times greater than the Clinton administration predicted it would be under the compact -- 1% a year. "The plan is not working," says Tim Hermack, executive director of the Native Forest Council. The timber industry is quick to argue otherwise. "We can't help but question the need for a moratorium when the statistics suggest otherwise," says Chris Nance, a spokesman for the California Forestry Association in Sacramento. A moratorium "would clearly have an impact on our profession as we know it." The stakes certainly are high for the rugged -- and economically distressed -- region that the owl shares with loggers. While statewide unemployment in April averaged 5.5%, the timber-rich counties of Humboldt and Trinity, for example, had a combined jobless rate of 7.9%, according to the California Employment Development Department. And, claims the Independent Forest Products Association, an industry group in Beaverton, Ore., residents of Humboldt and Trinity counties would lose $24 million in income if all logging on federal lands there were halted. The Forest Service has not officially responded to the legal petition, and officials at the agency say they can't comment on pending litigation. But more broadly, they say, environmentalists are missing the good news: the report's conclusion that the threatened species is on a path toward recovery. "What we see now is that the rate of decline is dropping," says Rex Holloway, a spokesman for the Forest Service's regional office in Portland, Ore. "We cannot expect overnight results. This is a long-term plan, and to make a difference, it is going to take some time." Nevertheless, the owl's decline has been particularly pronounced in California. Wildlife experts don't have exact figures for the drop, but they suggest that differences between the owl's inland habitat in California and its coastal nesting areas in Oregon and Washington are to blame. The "cold, wet springs of Northern California exacerbate the pressures logging puts on the bird," says Alan Franklin, who teaches wildlife population biology at Arcata's Humboldt State University and studied the California owls up close for the Forest Service. Mr. Franklin is quick to add that the accelerating decline of California's spotted owl population is still unexplained and that the trend could disappear in three years. But that doesn't satisfy the owl's defenders, whose stunning victory in Judge Dwyer's court eight years ago gave rise to the Northwest Timber Plan. In 1991, the judge found that the Forest Service had failed to produce a plan to protect the northern spotted owl, which had been listed as threatened in 1990 under the Endangered Species Act. The owl lives in the top branches of mature fir trees; clear-cutting, the judge found, had destroyed 90% of the bird's habitat, leading to steep declines in the population. Judge Dwyer enjoined all timber sales in the owl's region until the agency adopted a management plan as required by the National Environmental Policy Act. But the plan, issued in March 1992, failed to assuage environmentalists. They contended that the Forest Service had ignored a study by its own researchers showing that the owl population was declining by 7.5% a year. The judge continued the logging ban until further research was conducted. The resulting reassessment led to the Northwest Forest Plan, which settled the lawsuits before Judge Dwyer. It covered the 24.4 million acres in the three states, and set aside some 10 million of them as spotted-owl habitat that could never be logged. Of the total acreage, 30% was already off-limits to logging because it encompasses national parks, wilderness areas or scenic rivers. The result: Timber harvests on the federal land were reduced to 20% of their 1980s levels. In their new motion, the John Muir Project and the Native Forest Council argue that Judge Dwyer should once again prohibit logging while the Forest Service conducts yet another spotted-owl evaluation, which the groups say is required because of the "significant new circumstances or information" contained in the agency's recent spotted-owl report. Mr. Nance of the California Forestry Association says that the environmental movement may be missing the forest for the trees by focusing solely on the owl -- and not on the overall state of the far north's economy and ecology. "We are one of the 10 largest employers in the state," says Mr. Nance. But "aside from jobs, the number one concern of ours is the state of our forests," he adds. "Three times more trees are dying than are being harvested in our national forests." But Chad Hanson, executive director of the John Muir Project, has little sympathy for those who rely on the timber industry. "It's good for those people to get away from the boom and bust of logging." (See related letter: "THE WALL STREET JOURNAL / CALIFORNIA --- Letters to the Editor: Helping the Timber Workers" -- WSJ CAJ June 16, 1999) (See related letter: "THE WALL STREET JOURNAL / CALIFORNIA --- Letters to the Editor: Owls and Biological Armageddon" -- WSJ CAJ July 28, 1999) Credit: Staff Reporters of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Easy Being Green: Pick a Name Bearing The Sounds of Nature --- Anti-Environmentalist Groups Choose Pleasant Monikers; The Forest's Many Friends
Text: Which of the following is an environmental group? The National Wilderness Institute, the Conservation Coalition, the Evergreen Foundation or the Alliance for Environment and Resources? If you guessed all of them, you're wrong. If you guessed even one of them, you're wrong. It just goes to show what's in a name -- or in this case, what's not. Consider also the Sustainable Development Coalition. Created this past summer by property-rights activists in Maine, it sounds like a classic green alliance. After all, sustainable development -- as opposed to the unsustainable kind -- is an environmental mantra. But this group's goal is to scuttle a global treaty to protect biological diversity, which it claims is part of an international plot to "create a centrally controlled, planned society" built around nature worship. "We wanted something catchy," explains spokesman Robert Voight, "and people already know the term sustainable development." Similarly, the Abundant Wildlife Society of North America works to convince people that wildlife is already so plentiful there is no reason not to kill some of it. This is a pro-hunting group. The Wilderness Impact Research Foundation, of Elko, Nev., fights efforts to designate new areas as protected wilderness. The Environmental Conservation Organization -- ECO for short -- is a group of land developers in Hollow Rock, Tenn., that fights environmental rules. The National Wetlands Coalition, in Washington, D.C., represents people who want to narrow the government's definition of wetlands, so they can build things on them. Environmentalists aren't amused. "I hate to see them confusing people," says Bennett Beach, a spokesman for the Washington-based Wilderness Society, which actually does work to preserve wilderness. People hearing the views of such groups might assume they are coming from an environmental group, he says, adding murkiness to already complicated debates. Some people do jump to conclusions based on a group's benevolent-sounding name. The Abundant Wildlife Society, of Gillette, Wyo., recently got a letter from a young man who plans to become a wildlife biologist and wanted to find out how he could help them save wolves. "Of course, he couldn't spell worth beans," says Troy Mader, the group's research director, who handled the letter. Mr. Mader sent back a packet stuffed with materials explaining why wolves should be exterminated. "We didn't hear from him again," he says, chuckling. Mr. Mader says the question of what is an appropriate name depends on one's perspective. His group, which uses the slogan "Fighting for North American Wildlife," contends the best way to promote wildlife coveted by hunters, such as deer and elk, is to kill predators, especially wolves. "We take our name from the fact that it's been through man's management that we have the abundant wildlife we have today," he says. The pattern extends to publications. The National Hardwood Lumber Association puts out a newsletter called "GreenSpeak," on cream-colored recycled paper. "We send it out to members of Congress, and we didn't want them to automatically toss it in the trash -- so the name had to be eye-catching," says editor Elizabeth Pease, who concedes the name is a takeoff on the big environmental group Greenpeace. "But we're not lying to anybody," she says. "And besides, we're talking about green issues, too -- it's just in a different context." Even some of the groups' logos are "green." The National Wilderness Institute, a Washington, D.C., group that fights the Endangered Species Act, uses the shadow of a wolf howling against a full moon as its symbol, even though wolves are protected under that law in the lower 48 states. Henry Lamb, the executive vice president of the Environmental Conservation Organization, says it is the greens who are guilty of playing name games. "They're the ones deliberately trying to co-opt words like `conservation,' when what they really are after is `preservation,'" he says. The difference is that conservationists "believe in responsible stewardship and wise use of resources," he says, while preservationists "want to lock everything away." Groups such as Mr. Lamb's are acknowledging what public-opinion polls consistently show -- that most people, regardless of their politics, favor protecting the environment. So the groups have to tread carefully, picking names that emphasize positive aspects of their work. "But it makes you kind of wonder," says Lani Sinclair, an environmental consultant in Washington.
