"If we are going to be able to do business and make money, we've got to be prepared to accommodate the public's view, and special-interest groups that represent that public," says Lee Thomas, a former Environmental Protection Agency administrator who now runs Georgia-Pacific's environmental unit. Setting aside tens of thousands of acres gives the company much freer rein to log elsewhere on its nearly six million U.S. acres. But the reasons for the change run deeper. Southerners view land differently than do people in other parts of the U.S., says Charles Bassett, regional director of the Nature Conservancy in Chapel Hill, N.C. "They observe things more holistically than in the North," he says. Land is to steward rather than to own. Conservationists, meanwhile, began to see their strategies weren't working all that well, either. A major one, buying land in small blocks, didn't provide enough habitat to protect wildlife. Without funding for bigger blocks, they needed other approaches. "What we're seeing is more of a way to try to preserve the system, rather than save a single species like the spotted owl," says James Stokes, chairman of the environmental practice group at the Atlanta law firm Alston & Bird. That doesn't mean the sides always agree. In water quality, disagreements still broadly outnumber accords; many pulp and paper mills in Georgia, for example, are battling conservationists over ground-water use. And developers in the fast-growing region, seeking open spaces for suburban expansion, face constant battles over land use. Still, "what we're finding out is there are a lot more agreements than disagreements," says Bob Izlar, executive director of the Georgia Forestry Association. Indeed, signs of Southern environmentalism are popping up all over the region. -- The number of "land trusts," in which nonprofit groups manage land that is donated or offered for easement, more than doubled in the South in the past four years. About 366,000 acres in the region are now covered by such trusts, according to the Land Trust Alliance in Washington, D.C. -- In Alabama, International Paper Co. has agreed to set aside 4,500 acres to protect the Red Hills salamander. -- And in Plymouth, N.C., Weyerhaeuser Co. in March startled environmental groups by calling them in advance to discuss a planned switch in disposal of wood waste ash. The mill owner had never before consulted environmentalists prior to changing a corporate strategy. "There had been a lot of misunderstanding about a lot of things we had been doing," says Keith Hundley, Weyerhaeuser's government-affairs manager in North Carolina. "So, rather than have somebody call and say, `Hey, did you know Weyerhaeuser is putting boiler ash on trees and we don't know what's in it,' we decided, why not just tell them up front?" Bill Holman, a Sierra Club lobbyist, says, "Five years ago, the only contact would have been if we were complaining about something, or if we were proposing some legislation and they wanted to be exempted." One result: Weyerhauser got a friendly write-up in the Sierra Club newsletter, a first for the paper company. It would be tough to find a company that has come so far so fast as Georgia-Pacific. Just two years ago, the Council on Economic Priorities, a New York research group, labeled the company one of the nation's eight worst corporate polluters. Among the sins cited by the organization: releases of toxic material; a weak recycling effort; and a record of overharvesting huge patches of timber, leaving scars on the land. Most companies that make the list complain about methodology or the government data behind the ratings, says the council's president, Alice Tepper Marlin. Not Georgia-Pacific. With Mr. Correll preparing to take the helm, and chastened by the industry's experience in the Northwest, the company was changing. The philosophy, in Mr. Thomas's words, had emerged: "Let's find a solution before someone dictates a solution for us." So, the company sat down with the council. It explained its forest-management principles and showed how it was changing its recycling program, among other things. "They were extraordinarily responsive to our recommendations," Ms. Marlin recalls. "In fact, they thanked us for making them." Georgia-Pacific was then taken off the polluter list. Mr. Correll, looking to further improve the company's environmental standing, tapped Mr. Thomas last year to help map conservation strategy. Environmental groups wondered how the move would play out. Mr. Thomas's tenure as head of the EPA had come under President Reagan, who drew fire from conservationists. They didn't have to wait long for a sign. A month after Mr. Thomas's hiring, Georgia-Pacific teamed up with the federal Fish and Wildlife Service to protect the rare red-cockaded woodpecker in four Southern states. Following a detailed survey, the company's foresters had begun to worry that they might be in violation of the Endangered Species Act. There were no federal guidelines on how to cut timberland and comply with the law. So, Georgia-Pacific and federal officials worked out a deal to locate the woodpeckers' nesting areas and provide at least 80 acres of foraging habitat for each woodpecker colony. In all, nearly 60,000 acres of land were affected. The agreement, and Mr. Correll's ascension, encouraged John Sawhill, the Nature Conservancy's president, to visit the company's Atlanta headquarters to plead the case for conservation. The two men agreed to build a closer relationship. Returning to the group's headquarters in Arlington, Va., Mr. Sawhill searched the conservancy's list of 75 "last great places" for matches with Georgia-Pacific holdings. Up popped the Roanoke property with the no-deal history. Mr. Sawhill went for broke: He asked for a donation. But Mr. Correll knew the conservancy bought land, so he offered to sell it. It looked like the same stalemate. From lower down the power chain, however, came a middle ground. Georgia-Pacific's forest-resources group recommended that the company retain ownership and the right to harvest trees, while at the same time safeguarding the habitat. Now, a board will determine environmental policy on the site. The company (which could apply for a property-tax break on the deal, but doesn't plan to) and the conservancy will have equal voting rights; in cases of deadlock, arbitration is possible, though both sides doubt disputes will get that far. The link certainly leads to some odd scenes. Walking through the site, Frederick Annand, the Nature Conservancy's North Carolina associate director, talks of profits: "We'll have G-P come in, find patches they can cut and make some money on, and then study to see whether that actually works," he says. Minutes later, Georgia-Pacific forester Mason Lilley, a member of the site's management board, pauses and wonders about the value of a 30-plus-foot ash. It's an $80 to $100 tree, he figures. But the ash stands too close to the water, in a protected area. So the tree will survive. And Georgia-Pacific will make money elsewhere. As Carolyn Hatcher, president of the Georgia Conservancy, an independent group, says, "Anybody who was enlightened could see we should be able to avoid the conflict of the Pacific Northwest. We in the East learned from their mistakes." ---        Georgia-Pacific focuses on the environment:  1992: -- Council on Economic Priorities names Georgia-Pacific "one of U.S.'s worst corporate polluters," a list of eight companies.   1993:   -- A.D. "Pete" Correll tapped as chief executive officer. -- Former Environmental Protection Agency head Lee Thomas hired to run environmental efforts. -- Georgia-Pacific agrees to change management of Southern land to create habitat for red-cockaded woodpecker. -- Council on Economic Priorities, calling Georgia-Pacific a "turnaround," takes company off polluter list.   1994: -- Georgia-Pacific agrees with National Wild Turkey Federation to combine timber-management land with wild-turkey habitat management. -- Company reaches pact with Nature Conservancy on Roanoke River area the group calls one of the "last great places." --- Key provisions of Georgia-Pacific/Nature Conservancy accord over the lower section of the Roanoke River in North Carolina -- Company retains ownership of the property. -- Any trees cut on 15,000 protected acres must be removed by helicopter. No roads allowed on site. -- No trees may be cut on additional 6,500 acres of particularly sensitive land. -- Land will be team-managed by the company and the environmental group, with academics and government officials on team but not voting. -- In case of dispute, arbitration will be used. Title: Environmentalists Threaten to Sue Feds Over the Bull Trout
Text: Environmentalists are threatening to sue the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service over its failure to declare the Coastal-Puget Sound bull trout a threatened species. In an intent-to-sue notice sent to the wildlife service earlier this week, three environmental groups say they will file suit if the service doesn't within 60 days give the trout threatened status, which would require governments to protect its habitats in some of the most densely populated areas of Washington. "We have a great focus on salmon in this region, but there are other native fish like bull trout which are equally in trouble and deserve equal attention," says Kristen Boyles, an attorney in the Seattle office of San Francisco-based Earthjustice Legal Defense Fund, which represents the three environmental groups: the Bellingham-based Northwest Ecosystem Alliance, the Seattle-based Washington Environmental Council and Friends of the Earth of Washington, D.C. The wildlife service in June 1998 proposed that the Coastal-Puget Sound bull trout be protected under the Endangered Species Act. According to the law, within one year of such a proposal, the agency must either list the species, withdraw the proposal or formally extend the proposal. "As of the date of this letter, the FWS has not complied with the law," the intent-to-sue notice says. Agency officials, pledging a decision soon, say they missed the deadline because they're preparing for the impact the listing would have on residents and businesses, according to Carol Schuler, regional ecological services and fisheries supervisor in Portland. Given that bull trout have highly specific habitat requirements -- they require much colder water temperatures for spawning, for instance, than salmon -- habitat-protection restrictions on activities such as logging, farming and real-estate development are likely to be quite stringent, environmentalists say. The Fish and Wildlife Service is working on rules outlining what types of activities would be allowed if the trout was listed. Ms. Schuler says the rules would "relax the restrictions" on certain activities as long as the individual or company responsible for the activity -- the building of a house, for example -- agreed to take certain agency-approved steps that would mitigate the damage, or work to protect the species elsewhere. Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: REVIEW & OUTLOOK (Editorial) -- Asides: Bruneau Snail Revisited
Text: For the first time, a federal judge has removed a species from the federal government's Endangered Species list. At issue was the Bruneau Hot Springs snail, a tiny creature the size of a pencil point. Its listing had itself endangered hundreds of agricultural jobs in Idaho's Bruneau Valley. This week U.S. District Judge Harold Ryan ruled that the snail's listing by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service was "arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, and otherwise not in accordance with law." Sounds about right to us. The judge noted that Washington hadn't even allowed the public to review the controversial scientific study that led to the snail's listing. Snail advocates vow to appeal the ruling. The good news here is that public and legal opinion is finally showing some skepticism toward the save-at-all-costs mentality that has guided enforcement of the Endangered Species Act.

Title: In Senate, Endangered Species Act Faces an Overhaul
Text: WASHINGTON -- After years of effort, landowners, developers and other business interests might see changes in the Endangered Species Act, a landmark environmental law that has itself become endangered owing to growing dissatisfaction among supporters and critics. The 1973 law, which grants federal protection to species threatened with extinction, hasn't been significantly updated since 1988. While it is widely seen as in need of reworking, though, there is little consensus over how to revise a central provision that restricts use and development of land considered essential to preserving a listed animal or plant species. In September, that began to change. The House approved revisions that would eliminate the so-called critical habitat program, which restricts encroachment in areas containing physical or biological features essential to the conservation of an endangered species. That change would relieve builders and loggers, among others, of the lengthy development permitting process and the costs of complying with critical habitats and make the government pay for economic losses owners suffer when use of their property is restricted. But the vote was close -- 229-193 -- and there was considerable support for a less-sweeping alternative. Now a showdown is brewing in the Senate, which will begin debating the law's future when Congress reconvenes next month. Congress added critical habitat restrictions to the law in 1978 to better protect species. Landowners say that forces them to pay for the program by denying them the full use of their property. Rep. Richard Pombo (R., Calif.) has used his post as chairman of the House Resources Committee to remove this onus. Legislation he drafted and pushed through the House would, among other changes, eliminate the critical habitat designation and adopt a new approach that involves landowners in planning ways to protect a listed species on their property and compensates them for any resulting economic loss. Mr. Pombo said he is willing to consider changes as the bill proceeds through the Senate. "Sure, none of this is written in stone," he said. But the seven-term congressman and cattle rancher -- who has made changing the ESA one of his top legislative priorities -- added he is confident the Senate will come back with a bill that also calls for a sweeping overhaul. "They've got to come to the same conclusion as the House -- that the current system is broken and needs to be fixed." The critical habitat provision affects a variety of industries, including developers, paper companies and agriculture. In the Pacific Northwest, for example, critical habitats have resulted in forest lands being protected, restricting lumber company harvests and driving up lumber prices. Business groups have pushed for changes in the law for more than 15 years. One, the National Endangered Species Act Reform Coalition, has grown to about 150 member organizations ranging from county governments to ranchers to utilities. They have pressed their case with lobbying and congressional testimony to advocate overhaul of the ESA. One of the ESA's most-vocal critics is the National Association of Home Builders, which says the law restricts development and drives up home prices. Jason Lynn, the group's legislative director, also contends that it isn't even effective in its primary mission. Only 10 of the 1,304 species listed since the law's inception have been "recovered," or saved to the point the species can be removed from the list, Mr. Lynn said. "The critical habitats cause tremendous delays and don't provide additional protection for endangered species." Environmentalists and other supporters of the law say the House bill turns the ESA on its head. Under current law, builders and others with plans for an area listed as a critical habitat can't proceed until the government determines the project doesn't threaten the species in question. Mr. Pombo's proposal would let development proceed if, after a limited consultation period, the government couldn't prove the project poses a threat. "The whole consultation section is what makes the ESA effective," said Bob Irvin of the Defenders of Wildlife. The House bill "would undermine the essential element of protecting species, which is protecting these habitats." Mr. Irvin also denies the law fails to protect endangered species, noting that only nine listed species have become extinct. Species with protected critical habitats have been shown to recover at twice the rate as those without, he added. Both sides, however, agree something must be done. The critical habitat dispute has spawned hundreds of lawsuits filed by environmentalists charging that the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service -- the agency that administers the law -- is slow to designate habitats, and by business interests arguing that the designations are government "takings" for which they should be compensated. Renne Lohoefener, who heads the endangered species program, says the cost of defending the government in all the lawsuits eats up much of the agency's time and budget, hindering new listings. "If our money wasn't tied up in litigation, we would be able to work on more species," he said. As the issue heads to the Senate, direction for updating the law passes to one of Congress's most-ardent environmentalists. Sen. Lincoln Chafee (R., R.I.) chairs the subcommittee on Fisheries, Wildlife and Water, and is skeptical of the House's far-reaching changes. A Chafee spokesman said the senator hopes to reinstate the critical habitat program, but with other senators he has asked a Colorado-based nonprofit group that specializes in collaborative problem solving to work with representatives of different business and environmental interests to come up with an acceptable compromise. While environmentalists have an ally in Mr. Chafee, Sens. Mike Crapo (R., Idaho) and Blanche Lincoln (D., Ark.) recently introduced an ESA bill that could attract considerable business support. The bill would prioritize species for recovery and provide incentives, including tax credits, for landowners who aid in species recovery. Cost, however, will be an issue if a compromise ever makes it to President Bush's desk. Running for re-election last year, Mr. Bush called for rewriting the ESA, and officials say he supports many provisions in the House bill. Money to run the program this fiscal year will total $379 million, and the Congressional Budget Office estimates that could balloon to more than $600 million a year to implement landowner-compensation measures and other provisions in the bill. Mr. Crapo's bill, which provides tax credits instead of compensation, may be more appealing to the White House. --- Jim Carlton in San Francisco contributed to this article.

Title: Builders Say Regulations Hammer Their Business
Text: Home builders say governmental regulation run amok is forcing them to pack up their hammers. Here's one example builders point to: For decades, they say, builders simply placed a $10 concrete slab beneath gutter downspouts to manage water runoff on a new single-family house. Now, due to strict rules spurred by concerns about flooding and damage to streams and wildlife, builders must engineer an intricate subterranean maze of pipes and storm-water vaults to capture roof runoff that once simply percolated through the soil. The price tag: roughly $15,000 per house. And that's only the start of it. With higher costs brought on by a multitude of environmental rules, as well as growth-management laws, some builders say they are unable to construct what they consider to be affordable single-family dwellings in King County. So they are liquidating their businesses, selling off land and dumping their inventories of houses. Some are forsaking the single-family market to concentrate on high-end custom building, where price is less of an issue. Others are abandoning King County altogether in search of greener, more easily-developed pastures. "When the federal government is going against you with the Endangered Species Act, and when regional governments are going against you [with the Growth Management Act], the deck is stacked against you," says Jeff Wright, a fourth-generation builder in Bellevue who owns Parkwood Homes Inc. "It's time to get out." And he is. Mr. Wright recently sold to a competitor a project in Bothell on which he was about to start construction. Once he sells off the last of his inventory of homes already erected, he plans to refocus his efforts in Pierce County, "where there is a lot of land not sensitive to all of these issues." But Mr. Wright and others in the business acknowledge that regulation isn't the only force at play. The Northwest, and the Seattle area in particular, has become a Mecca for out-of-state migrants seeking a better quality of life and the perks of high-paying jobs the region has been spawning this decade. And it doesn't help that technology companies such as Microsoft Corp. continue to mint millionaires who exert additional upward pressure on home prices. This influx of residents has increased the demand for housing, which, in turn, has bumped up home and land prices. And while that higher demand offers lots of opportunities for builders, the influx of people is also creating a strong push for new regulations and environmental controls. Government officials say this is the new reality the building industry must learn to handle. Builders "can't sit back and say growth management and environmental regulation is the bad guy," says Jean Carpenter, King County's regional governmental relations manager and the former housing liaison to County Executive Ron Sims. "We have agreed as a community to preserve our mountains and streams. This is the developing consciousness" that builders must work with. Tracy Burrows, executive director of 1000 Friends of Washington, an antisprawl nonprofit group in Seattle, says the industry's argument that regulation is increasing housing costs is an excuse. Some builders, she says, just aren't adapting to the wants of today's home buyers. Downtown rejuvenation in the likes of Renton, Bellevue and Seattle, Ms. Burrows adds, "shows the market for housing is shifting from sprawling [detached home] developments to more compact urban forms." Building-permit statistics tell the story. The city of Bellevue, for instance, has so far this year issued 30% fewer permits for single-family homes than a year earlier. Meantime, permits for multifamily units, particularly around downtown, are surging. The city has issued building permits for 531 multifamily units this year and it has another 2,469 in active review. Last year, the city issued just 752. Similar examples abound across King County, "indicative of a massive chilling effect on single-family home building by all the regulatory red-tape," says Trent Matson, tax and housing analyst for the Building Industry Association of Washington. "Many builders just can't face the costs.'' The building industry warned of pricing problems when the state Legislature passed in 1990 the Growth Management Act, a sweeping set of rules designed to slow growth by restricting land use. The act favors high-density apartments and condominiums built around urban cores; it frowns on low-density, single-family neighborhoods that carve into undeveloped tracts and put more cars on more roads. While builders say the law's intention is noble, the unintended consequence has been to drive land prices upward. Demand for housing continues to rise, but the supply of available land "has been artificially limited by regulations," says Mr. Matson. Priscilla Call, Seattle's manager of affordable housing and home ownership, says land-use rules "do indirectly create a land shortage" that, for average home buyers, "prices them out of detached homes." Slow-growth proponents scoff at that notion. The land supply is there, says Ms. Burrows at 1000 Friends of Washington. The problem "is that job growth is bringing more people to the market," increasing competition for homes and land. "That's driving the price, not a lack of land." Whatever the reason, Ron Smith, a partner in Kirkland Building Co., says he "can't even look at a lot these days for less than $200,000." Add material and labor costs -- up to $125 a square foot -- and the average starter home can run more than $400,000. Such high prices for new homes push prices higher for existing homes. The median home price in the county is $279,950, up 42% from five years ago. At the same time, the region's median family income is $57,700 a year. So a person earning that salary who puts down 10% would qualify for a loan to buy a house valued at roughly $208,000, according to Real Vision Research Inc., a Kirkland real-estate consulting firm. "You're aiming at a middle-class market, but you're forced to build homes that are" beyond their means, says Michael Paine, a senior planner for the city of Bellevue. And it could get worse. The U.S. government listed nine Washington and Oregon runs of salmon as either threatened or endangered this spring, and the recovery plans that will be established by federal, state and local agencies mean "there is the potential for builders to find considerable additional obstacles," Mr. Paine says. For example, builders expect that storm-water drain vaults will be required to grow in size to better handle the silt, dirt and oil that run off lawns and driveways. That, builders and city planners say, would further increase engineering and materials costs. Bellevue has already begun requiring builders to complete a checklist of development-activity items so the city can disclose to residents potential environmental impacts that could affect salmon streams. Though a minor hurdle, city staff reviewing the checklist could require builders "to perform additional, more comprehensive" environmental and biological evaluation studies, Mr. Paine says. Moreover, the National Marine Fisheries Service is considering policies that would triple to as much as 300 feet the distance a development must be from a body of water, including streams and drainage ditches as narrow as two feet. "That's going to take a lot of otherwise developable land off the table," says Charlie Conner, president of Conner Development Co., a big home builder in Bellevue with projects around King and Snohomish counties. The result: further escalating land costs. Meantime, anticipated changes in seasonal-work rules would prohibit ground work between November and April to keep rainfall from washing dirt and debris into storm sewers. That would force builders to lay as many foundations as possible during the summer -- increasing borrowing costs or requiring them to dip into savings. The building industry has already begun tallying some of the costs imposed by what Mike Nykrem, Mr. Smith's partner at Kirkland homes, calls "a regulatory landslide." For that reason, the two men are vacating the single-family-home market for high-end custom building and remodeling. On a Vancouver, Wash., home built by Taseca Homes Inc. in August, the base price of $183,114 was pushed up by $40,486, or more than 22%, due to governmental fees and taxes, according to Taseca. The company breaks out these added charges on a form labeled "Government Costs of New Home Construction" that it now gives to each home buyer. "Every time you turn around," says Faith Ivie, Taseca's general manager, "it's another regulation and another charge -- big and small -- that we have to cover." But perhaps most annoying to builders is the fact that it's taking ever longer to navigate the regulatory web, which increases the risks of holding land for development. Despite a state law requiring that home-building permits be processed within 120 days, Mr. Conner says two years is now the minimum, and three years isn't unheard of. A decade ago "all of this could be done in less than a year," he says. At Parkwood Homes, Mr. Wright complains that he recently heard back from King County on his request for approval of a 50-lot project just east of Bellevue. He had expected to hear back within two years. It took four. And the county "sliced the number of lots to 29," messing up the economics of the planned development. "The gamble," Mr. Wright says, "just isn't worth it any more." ---                     Raising the Roof    Some builders are quitting the single-family home market, citing increasing governmental and environmental rules that are driving up the cost of doing business    Some governmental fees charged on a new home in Vancouver, Wash.:   Fee                         Cost   Off-site improvements      $4,577  Building permits            2,235  Sidewalk paving permit      2,018  Processing permits          2,000  Utility hook up             1,507  Park impact                 1,461   Fee                         Cost   Transportation impact      $1,291  City/county administration  1,117  and application fees  Meter costs                 1,105  School impact                 931  Tree preservation             539  Erosion control                63   ---                     License to Build    Number of permits issued monthly for single-family homes  Location               JAN. Title: Acreage Marked for Desert Tortoise Includes Disputed California Dump Site
Text: Federal wildlife regulators have designated 6.4 million acres of southwestern desert -- including the proposed site of a bitterly-contested nuclear waste dump in California -- as critical habitat for the desert tortoise. The action by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service is certain to reverberate in the debate over conflicts between wildlife and commerce, which is intensifying as Congress takes up reauthorization of the nation's principal wildlife protection law, the Endangered Species Act. The agency's move sets aside nearly as much land for desert tortoises as the government did for spotted owls. Most of the land is in California, but three other states are also affected. Some 80% of the land is federally owned, with the remainder owned by states, Indian tribes and private interests. Protected under federal law, the tortoises have been in steady decline because of disease and habitat destruction caused by mining, off-road vehicles and other human encroachment on the desert, many scientists agree. Under the Endangered Species Act, human activities on land designated as critical habitat for protected species can be strictly limited. Thus, the agency's move casts further doubt over the future of the low-level nuclear dump project, known as Ward Valley. Business interests and California state officials say the facility is crucial to the health of California's burgeoning biotech, medical and research industries, which, in addition to many jobs, generate much low-level nuclear waste. The state has issued a license to U.S. Ecology Inc. to build and operate the dump. U.S. Ecology officials say they've invested about $40 million to date in engineering and environmental studies and other preconstruction costs. But antinuclear activists and environmentalists have fought the dump project fiercely for nearly 10 years, asserting that it threatens the nearby Colorado River, as well as desert animals such as the tortoise. Moreover, Ward Valley is on federal land, and the Clinton administration to date has declined to transfer the land to the state -- a prerequisite for dump construction -- while lawsuits challenging the dump wend their way through the courts. Although the critical habitat designation theoretically doesn't doom the Ward Valley project, since federal agencies can permit activities in prime habitat areas under certain circumstances, dump opponents were nonetheless jubilant. "It should be the final blow against this ill-advised project," said Philip Klansky, co-coordinator of the Bay Area Nuclear Waste Coalition. But Steve Romano, a U.S. Ecology vice president, said the company thinks it can still build the dump without harming tortoises if the Clinton administration transfers the land to the state. If it doesn't, Mr. Romano said, "our company would have little alternative but to sue" to recover its investment so far in the project. The Ward Valley debate is part of a larger national problem of coping with low-level nuclear leftovers. In the 1980s, Congress passed laws requiring states to have low-level dumps up and running by 1993. That process has melted down: Plagued by design and environmental problems and beset by environmental protests, not a single new low-level waste dump has been built.
