Title: REVIEW & OUTLOOK (Editorial): The Endangered Gremlins Act
Text: Like the critters it purports to save, the Endangered Species Act is one of those pieces of federal legislation that sounds so warm and cuddly that no right thinking person could possibly question it. Well, it turns out this law isn't the Discovery Channel, with Ranger Bob and a few Land Rovers rounding up some turtles for safekeeping. The Endangered Species Act is about spending megabucks -- and infuriating a lot of law abiding humans who now find themselves accused of crimes against the animal kingdom. Sold to Congress in 1973 as the only way to protect such rare creatures as the bald eagle and the manatee, the Endangered Species Act has become a regulatory straitjacket that mandates Herculean steps be taken to protect a total of 853 species, ranging from the Dudly Bluffs Bladder Pod to the Arkansas Fatmucket. Some 4,000 other plants and animals are official candidates for future listing. The ESA is up for reauthorization this year, and there's a growing call in Congress to get control of a wide-eyed law that has metastasized into a regulatory version of the horrorpic "Gremlins." Democratic Senator Richard Shelby says "lax scientific requirements" for listing species must be tightened and some priorities for protection set. Advocates of ESA reform were helped recently by the remarkable study done by the National Wilderness Institute of Alexandria, Virginia. It went through 25,000 pages of U.S. Fish & Wildlife Department "recovery" plans for 388 endangered species and found that the minimum cost of trying to protect all of them is $884 million. The actual cost will be far higher, adding in local government compliance and lost tax revenues from reduced business activity. Take the Florida Scrub Jay, a relative of the common blue jay. Federal officials said its "recovery" should cost only $65,000. But the recovery plan noted that didn't include habitat acquisition costs, which it notes "are in areas of high real estate values." The recovery plan also notes that "because of the extreme usefulness of the Act in this case, it is not desirable to remove the scrub jay from protection" and that "it may never be feasible to delist this species." Never? In the Pacific Northwest, their efforts to save the Spotted Owl have cost 30,000 jobs and reduced lumber harvests to 1.1 billion board feet a year from 5 billion. Since about one-third of lumber for home construction comes from the Northwest, the restrictions have sent the price of lumber skyrocketing. The cost of building a 2,000-square-foot house has increased by at least $4,000 since 1992, pricing at least 80,000 potential buyers out of the market. Many scientists say incentives and tax breaks for private landowners to protect key species and a relocation of some species to park lands would work much better than the ESA's threats of jail or fines. Right now, property owners often react in perverse ways. Rep. Charles Taylor of North Carolina tells us of a farmer who found that a Red-Cockaded Woodpecker had moved on to his land. What a disaster. To protect it, he was required to suspend economic activity on 1,000 surrounding acres, costing him $1.8 million in profits. "Now he is clear-cutting everything around it because if he doesn't, he fears the spread of the woodpecker will take up the total use of all his land," says Rep. Taylor. Take the Iowa Pleistocene Snail. The author of its recovery plan notes that "its major long-term cause of decline is cyclic climatic change." In other words: the Ice Age ended. But "with a return to glacial conditions it will be resuscitated over the major part of the upper Midwest, provided its relictual areas are preserved." No time estimates are given. The Socorro Isopod also appears to have a limited future. Its species habitat consists of a farmer's "1m x 2m x 0.03m cement-lined animal watering tank, a smaller pool and approximately 40 meters of open irrigation pipe." The bizarre abuses of the Endangered Species Act make it almost certain Congress will try to amend it this year. But the environmental community, sensing the public outrage against the ESA, has decided to go for the Big Stall. A March 4 memo to six leaders of environmental groups from their lobbyists recommended reauthorization of the Endangered Species Act "be taken off the table" for 1994. If their stall works, Congress will have to renew ESA without any changes year after year. That's probably just fine with the Blunt-Nosed Leopard Lizard, illustrated crawling through our chart and holding down the third most expensive recovery at $70 million. But it surely can't be good for the rest of us. ---                      Expensive Species   The 10 most expensive recovery plans for endangered species.  1  Atlantic Green Turtle                      $88,236,000  2  Loggerhead Turtle                          $85,947,000  3  Blunt-Nosed Leopard Lizard                 $70,252,000  4  Kemp's Ridley Sea Turtle                   $63,600,000  5  Colorado Squawfish                         $57,770,000   6  Humpback Chub   7  Bonytail Chub   8  Razorback Sucker  9  Black-Capped Vireo                         $53,538,000 10  Swamp Pink                                 $29,026,000   Source: National Wilderness Institute

Title: The Morning Brief: Death, and Legacy, Of President Ford
Text: The Wall Street Journal Online The Morning Brief, a look at the day's biggest news, is emailed to subscribers by 7 a.m. every business day. Sign up for the e-mail here. Former President Gerald Ford died last night at the age of 93, leaving behind a legacy as a healer during a time of national crisis and dissent over an unpopular war that resonated through the five presidencies that followed his brief time in the Oval Office. The unique nature of Mr. Ford's assumption of power at the White House -- replacing first a disgraced vice president and then the only president to quit in dishonor -- makes unavoidable the historical focus on his succession and pardon of President Nixon. But Mr. Ford tackled his fair share of international and domestic issues and seemed to have a strength of character that built -- rather than simply stood as -- the bridge from a troubled era to relative normalcy. "I have not sought this enormous responsibility, but I will not shirk it," he said on taking office. "My fellow Americans, our long national nightmare is over." Less than a month later, when Mr. Ford issued the pardon to Mr. Nixon now widely seen as a means for letting the country move on though it help sink Mr. Ford's chance for election, he showed a prescient understanding of his role in history: "Theirs is an American tragedy in which we all have played a part," he said, referring to the Nixon family. "It could go on and on and on, or someone must write the end to it. I have concluded that only I can do that, and if I can, I must." The decision brought widespread vilification. But looking back, the Detroit Free Press says the Michigan-raised athlete, lawyer and longtime Republican congressman brought an "old-fashioned, Midwestern stability [that] was what the country needed after two years of Watergate investigations, lies and resignations." Following a decade of division over the Vietnam War and the Watergate trauma, Mr. Ford offered "a soothing familiarity," the New York Times says. "He might have been the nice guy down the street suddenly put in charge of the nation, and if he seemed a bit predictable, he was also safe, reliable and reassuring." He resisted the trappings of the imperial presidency, even appearing before a House subcommittee to address Democrats' suggestion that the pardon came in exchange for his appointment by Mr. Nixon as vice president, averring: "There was no deal, period, under no circumstances." During his 2 1/2-year presidency, Mr. Ford ended American involvement in the war in Vietnam, helped work out a Middle East cease-fire, and reached arms-limitations and far-reaching human-rights protocols with the Soviet Union, the Washington Post notes. On the home front, in addition to dealing with a crippling gas shortage, he made inflation "public enemy No. 1" with his "Whip Inflation Now" campaign, only to reverse course a short time later to take on a deepening recession. The Nixon pardon was far from his only tough decision, as the famous New York Daily News headline: "Ford to City: Drop Dead" attested following his veto of funding measure for the Big Apple. In announcing the Nixon pardon, Mr. Ford said his customary policy "is to try and get all the facts and to consider the opinions of my countrymen and to take counsel with my most valued friends. But these seldom agree, and in the end, the decision is mine." And he then offered what might be considered a prescription for White House decision making: "To procrastinate, to agonize, and to wait for a more favorable turn of events that may never come or more compelling external pressures that may as well be wrong as right, is itself a decision of sorts and a weak and potentially dangerous course for a President to follow." --- SEC Changes Course on Compensation Reporting On a day before Christmas, when all through D.C., not a person was watching the SEC . . . Chairman Christopher Cox and fellow commissioners decided to backtrack on a much-ballyhooed move in July to require more upfront disclosure of compensation for executives and company directors. The decision, announced Friday, the last pre- holiday business day, would change Securities and Exchange Commission rules to allow the reporting of stock and options compensation over several years in tables required by the agency instead of as an aggregate figure for the year the grant is made, the San Jose Mercury News reports. In essence, the new rule would let a lot of companies report what the New York Times describes as significantly lower total compensation for top executives, and it marks a defeat for institutional investors that backed the original rule issued in July. "It was a holiday present to corporate America," Ann Yerger, the executive director of the Council of Institutional Investors, tells the Times. "It will certainly make the numbers look smaller in 2007 than they would otherwise have looked." In July, Mr. Cox said the stronger rule would let shareholders "make better decisions about the appropriate amount to pay the men and women entrusted with running their companies." Yesterday, he called Friday's change "a relative technicality." --- Hussein Approaches the Gallows A day after an Iraqi appeals court upheld the death sentence of Saddam Hussein, a spokesman for President Jalal Talabani said today that the head of state might not be required to approve the decision and is waiting on a court's ruling on that question. The war-crimes tribunal that tried Mr. Hussein has said its own rules make Mr. Talabani's unnecessary. And since the appeals court ordered that Mr. Hussein be executed within 30 days, it seems increasingly likely that he will be hanged despite the allegations of crimes against humanity he has yet to stand trial for. Elsewhere in Iraq, seven more American service members were killed, the U.S. military announced, making December the second-deadliest month of the year for troops, as the Washington Post reports. In Washington, Sen. Joseph Biden, the incoming Democratic chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and a possible candidate for president in 2008, said no new U.S. troops should be sent to Iraq -- a stance that sets up what The Wall Street Journal calls "a potential political battle over President Bush's tentative plan to deploy tens of thousands of additional forces to try to stabilize the country." But in a revelation that will likely bolster the administration's case against seeking Iran's help with Iraq, the American military said it has credible evidence linking detained Iranians and their Iraqi associates to attacks against American forces, the New York Times reports. --- China's Currency Reserves and Its Resources China plans to use its more than $1 trillion in foreign reserves to step up the acquisition of strategic resources that include oil, gas and minerals, according to state media, but it wasn't immediately clear how that would work. Vice Prime Minister Zeng Peiyan, who announced the plans, also decried China's relatively weak resource base compared with its huge population of 1.3 billion people, according to the state media, as cited by the Associated Press. And he noted that China ranks third -- behind the U.S. and Russia -- with 12% of the world's known mineral reserves. Mr. Zeng made a similar suggestion earlier this year, but the news could potentially have large repercussions for the global and U.S. economies, since such a move provides an intersection for two major economic roles played by China. The compilation of foreign reserves is in part due to China's massive purchase of U.S. debt, which has helped to pay for the giant American trade deficit -- and which in turn raised fears about what China will do with its dollars, especially since they have been diminishing in value against a host of other currencies. And China's voracious appetite for petroleum and metals has been one of the most important factors in commodity prices over recent years, as well a key influence on strategic alliances China has built with Iran and other countries around the world. --- Also of Note. . . Associated Press: A strong earthquake off Taiwan's southern coast damaged undersea cables, cutting off phone and Internet service today to parts of China, South Korea, Japan, Southeast Asia and the U.S., and the damage could take up to three weeks to fully repair. Women's Wear Daily: Stores across the country unleashed a barrage of price cuts, adding even steeper discounts on top of previously reduced goods in a rush to clear coats, sweaters, gloves, scarves, denim and Christmas ornaments to make space for resort and spring merchandise -- and in a move that represents an attempt by many chains to get back on track, after what many have acknowledged has been a disappointing holiday period so far, and raises questions about fourth-quarter profitability and margins. Financial Times: Texas Pacific Group has beaten Blackstone and Kohlberg Kravis Roberts to become the world's most prolific buyout group in 2006, notching up 17 deals with an aggregate value of just over $101 billion, a figure that reflects an extraordinary year for private equity in which the value of announced deals has risen to a record $700 billion. Bloomberg: For growing numbers of international business travelers, visa and customs regulations are making trips to the U.S. a thing of the past, with companies saying U.S. rules have become so onerous in the wake of 9/11 that it's often simpler to meet customers, business partners and employees elsewhere. BusinessWeek: Reports that Ford Motor CEO Alan Mulally and Toyota Motor Chairman Fujio Cho met last week in Japan are contributing to speculation the ailing U.S. auto maker and its thriving Japanese counterpart could form some kind of partnership. New York Times: Israel announced plans to construct a Jewish settlement in the occupied West Bank for the first time in 10 years, prompting Palestinian anger and American concern. Washington Post: The Bush administration has decided to propose listing the polar bear as threatened under the Endangered Species Act, putting the U.S. government on record as saying that global warming could drive one of the world's most recognizable animals out of existence. Wall Street Journal: McClatchy, one of the biggest believers in the newspaper field, agreed to sell the Minneapolis Star Tribune, its largest paper, to private-equity firm Avista Capital Partners for $530 million -- less than half of what McClatchy paid for the paper in 1998 and at a time when the value of papers has fallen as they face declining readership and a fragmented media environment. Los Angeles Times: California's largest physician organization asked to join patients in a class-action lawsuit alleging that Blue Cross illegally dumps policyholders after authorizing expensive medical treatment and then refuses to pay the bills. Miami Herald: Fidel Castro has suffered a "series of complications from a benign" illness, but doesn't have cancer and is undergoing a "slow but progressive" recovery, the Spanish surgeon who treated him said at a press conference in Madrid. BBC: At least 260 people seeking free fuel were killed by the explosion of a oil pipeline punctured by thieves outside Lagos. Some 2,000 people have died in similar incidents in recent years in Nigeria, which suffers frequent fuel shortages. --- Quote of the Day "Unfortunately, the talks with our Belarusian colleagues ended without result, despite the fact that Gazprom took several major steps to meet the Belarusian side. In the absence of a contract, there is not and cannot be a basis for the delivery of gas," said Alexander Medvedev, the head of state-owned Russian gas monopoly Gazprom's export division, after talks broke off between the Belarusian government and the company, which demanded a doubling of what Belarus pays for gas. Gazprom, which threatens to cut off delivery on New Year's Day, wants both more cash and shares in Belarus's natural-gas pipeline network, the Associated Press reports. --- Write to Joseph Schuman at joseph.schuman@wsj.com --- Some links in this column are to sites that require a subscription or registration.

Title: Plum Creek, U.S. Reach Agreement Involving Logging
Text: Plum Creek Timber Co. has reached an agreement with federal regulators under which it will be allowed to log in sensitive habitat in exchange for its commitment to employ more eco-friendly cutting practices. The company and Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt and other federal officials will announce the pact today in Seattle, Plum Creek's headquarters, people familiar with the agreement said. The accord is one of the largest so-called habitat conservation plans to be struck between federal regulators and private companies whose activities have been held up by the Endangered Species Act and other federal environmental laws. The Clinton administration will hail it as proof that those laws -- targets of Republican critics who want to weaken them -- are flexible enough to accommodate both wildlife protection and economic pursuits. In addition, Plum Creek has agreed to swap, under certain conditions, some 30,000 acres of roadless wilderness to the U.S. Forest Service in exchange for other federally owned land. That swap would theoretically increase the chances that the land would be preserved rather than eventually logged. Under the Plum Creek habitat conservation plan, the company would place 170,000 of its 1.7 million acres of private timberlands under special management practices designed to lessen the impact of logging on such protected or troubled species as the Northern Spotted owl. The land, in Washington state, would be lumped in with acreage currently owned in the same area by federal and state agencies and smaller private landowners, bringing the total area under the special management techniques to 418,000 acres. In addition to owls, the acreage is home to gray wolves, marbeled murrelets and grizzly bears. The plan is designed to minimize the impact of logging on those species and their habitat, while still enabling Plum Creek to do business in the forest. Plum Creek would defer cutting in certain old-growth groves, prime habitat for owls and some other species; the plan projects that old-growth habitat in the area would increase by the year 2045 from current levels, and that owl populations would decrease no more than 8%, to 80 nesting pairs from today's 87 known pairs. The company will also increase buffer zones along streams and take other steps to protect habitat. Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Pro-Environment Farm Sows Seeds of Success --- Agricultural Development And Recycling Meld At Threemile Canyon
Text: A LAND DEAL in a dusty corner of eastern Oregon has yielded one of the rarest of occurrences: almost total harmony between environmentalists and farmers.   The venture, called Threemile Canyon Farms, near Boardman, Ore., recently began operating one of the country's biggest agricultural operations: milking up to 15,000 dairy cows, growing enough potatoes to feed seven million people and harvesting a bushel basket of other crops including alfalfa, corn and wheat -- all across a 100-square-mile patch of desert.   And environmentalists love the project because it's being carried out to follow an emerging trend in the West called sustainable development. Under the concept, logging, ranching, farming and other traditional economic pastimes in the region are being modified to minimize the impacts on the land.   Here at Threemile Canyon, that has resulted in what environmentalists call one of the industry's most ambitious recycling systems. Potato skins and other crop waste are fed to the cows. Liquid and solid waste from the cows is harnessed for its methane gas, generating enough electricity to run the whole farm plus sell more to meet other power needs around the region. Whatever manure is left is used as crop fertilizer.   Meanwhile, about one-quarter of the farm -- 23,000 acres -- is being left untouched. It represents one of the last undisturbed expanses of juniper and sage terrain that explorers Lewis and Clark saw when they passed through this Columbia River basin nearly two centuries ago.   In the process, Threemile Canyon has succeeded so far on two disparate fronts: pacifying environmentalists who for years have fought farming efforts; and persuading Oregon's largest and most famous cheesery -- Tillamook County Creamery Association -- to keep a major expansion in Oregon. Tillamook recently began producing cheese from the Threemile Canyon dairy under the expansion plan.   "This project is helping our agricultural economy and the environment, too," Mark Simmons, speaker of the Oregon House of Representatives, said during a recent tour of the facility for dignitaries.   It wasn't always so blissful here. About 40 years ago, the space that is now Threemile Canyon was leased by the state of Oregon to Boeing Corp. for what the company initially planned as an aerospace industrial park but instead ended up subleasing to farmers. Battles broke out with environmental groups over what they considered the excessive volumes of water drawn out of the nearby Columbia River, contributing, they said, to the decline of several threatened salmon species in the region.   In 1999, the environmentalists filed suit against Boeing in U.S. district court in Portland, alleging the water use was violating terms of the 1973 Endangered Species Act under which the Columbia River salmon had been listed for protection.   Then along came R.D. Offutt Co., a big potato producer based in Fargo, N.D., which wanted the 93,000-acre property to expand its farming operations. Offutt officials bought Boeing's farming subsidiary for an undisclosed price in March 2000 and immediately embarked on stamping out the environmental fires.   "We wanted to get rid of the uncertainty so we could finance this operation properly," says Marty Myers, general manager of Threemile Canyon, a $185 million project that was formed as a joint venture in early 2000 between Offutt and Bos Family Oregon Farms, a dairy company based in Bakersfield, Calif.   Mr. Myers says Threemile Canyon managed to persuade environmentalists to settle their suit after agreeing to use only about half the amount of Columbia River water to which the lease entitled the operation. The lesser amount totals about 120,000 acre-feet of water annually, or roughly enough water to serve 120,000 households for one year. Another concession was agreeing to set aside a big tract of land for conservation. Although Threemile Canyon adopted the recycling practices as part of its own effort to be efficient as possible, environmentalists were pleased.   "This is one of the most threatened ecosystems in Oregon," says Berta Youtie, a local representative of the Nature Conservancy environmental group, "so all their actions here have been positive so far."   But Threemile Canyon had another hurdle to cross: coming up with a business plan that would help avoid the frequent downturns in the farming business. The farm needed, in particular, a big cheese customer to buy milk to provide a steady flow of revenue when other crops declined.   As luck would have it, officials at Tillamook in western Oregon were faced with their own conundrum: how to keep pace with expanding demand from supermarket customers around the U.S. when their cooperative was already close to capacity on how much milk it could produce in its home base of Tillamook County on the Oregon coast.   Not wanting to arouse a likely environmental battle by trying to set up new farms in the populated areas west of the Cascades, Tillamook began looking out of state, including California and Idaho.   Then Mr. Myers came calling. "Marty told us he had a piece of ground in eastern Oregon which had everything we needed -- irrigation, cattle feed, proximity to shipping on the Columbia River," recalls Harold Schild, president and chief executive officer of the Tillamook association, which is a cooperative of about 150 dairies. "It looked to us like they had all the pieces of the puzzle together."   Oregon state officials assisted by issuing $15 million of tax-exempt bonds for some of the farm's work, such as its plant to convert cow waste into electricity. They also are in the process of selling the 93,000 acres to Threemile Canyon for an appraised value of $7.6 million. Earlier this year, the farm brought in about half the 15,000 dairy cows that will eventually be housed on the place, herding them into half-mile long open barns between milkings at a high-tech carousel that can handle 500 cows at a time.   Besides proving a local boon -- employing as many as 600 people seasonally and expected to infuse as much as $250 million a year into the area economy -- the farm is greatly helping Tillamook. The company expects to produce as much as 58 million pounds of cheese annually when the project is completed by the end of next year, or as much as it can now make in Tillamook County.   "I think," says Mr. Myers," we have laid the foundation for success all around on this project."   ---   Journal Link: For the latest news and trends in commercial real estate, in addition to property listings, visit RealEstateJournal.com  Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Foresters Fight Feds Over Salamander
Text: Tree farmers in Florida, Georgia and South Carolina have got the shivers over the five-inch-long flatwoods salamander. Their fear: If the federal government protects the little-known, chocolate-brown amphibian under the Endangered Species Act, the farmers' livelihood could be more endangered than the salamander. Farmers argue that proposed curbs on their most common timbering practices -- which have destroyed the salamander's habitat or altered it so it can no longer prosper there -- will kill their business. The government's proposal "would essentially mean the end of forestry practices within those zones" where salamanders are thought to live, says Phil Gornicki, who handles environmental issues for the Tallahassee-based Florida Forestry Association, an industry group. This is no high-profile battle between well-heeled industry titans and TV-savvy environmentalists staging demonstrations on behalf of the likes of the spotted owl. But as both federal regulators and the region's big timber companies try to ease tensions with conciliatory statements, to some tree growers and environmentalists, the salamander has become a big deal. Consider a hearing in Tallahassee last month on a U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service proposal to list the salamander as a "threatened" species -- a status that is less severe than "endangered." "What you are proposing to do is going to completely destroy the present state of our lifestyle as we know it," Bob Roquemore, a timber manager on 6,000 acres in Lakeland, Ga., told officials. "It's this kind of mindless foolishness that makes people want to blow up federal buildings, send pipe bombs through the mail to judges, [and] be scared of what the government is going to do to them next week." But Bruce Means, president of the Coastal Plains Institute, a Tallahassee nonprofit environmental research group, says, "I don't know what they are crying about. It is patently untrue that this particular animal, when it gets listed, is going to affect very many people at all." The salamander was first discovered in Jasper County, S.C., in 1867. Females lay eggs for about two months of the year in ponds or wetlands found in open flatwood pine forests. For the rest of the year, the critters hide underground, sometimes borrowing crayfish dens. The Fish and Wildlife Service first took notice earlier this decade when biologists discovered that the creature's numbers had significantly declined in the Southeast. In 1992, the Biodiversity Legal Foundation, a Boulder, Colo., conservation group, filed a petition to list the salamander under the Endangered Species Act. The 25-year-old act, which has been used to protect nearly 1,150 plants and animals, makes it illegal to harass, harm or kill listed animals, collect protected plants or conduct land-use activities that could result in death or harm to the species. When the federal agency denied Biodiversity's request, the conservation group sued. In 1994, the Fish and Wildlife Service settled and agreed to accelerate a decision on whether to list the species, based on currently available information. Published information indicated that about 88% of the salamander's habitat has disappeared, replaced by agricultural operations, urban development and the activities of the timber industry, which converted naturally growing forests to dense, intensively cultivated tree plantations and began using herbicides to control unwanted growth. By 1997, studies showed, only 47 clumps of salamanders -- or evidence of their existence -- could be found in Florida, Georgia and South Carolina. So last December, the Fish and Wildlife Service proposed that the forestry industry curtail practices such as dense planting, clear-cut harvesting and intensive use of herbicides within a one-mile radius buffer zone around breeding ponds. And that sparked the ruckus among small timber farmers. "Why should I personally have to finance [the protection of the species] because I'm one of the unlucky few" with land that harbors the species, asks Joe Hopkins, president of family-owned Toledo Manufacturing Co., which grows pine trees on about 46,000 acres in Folkston, Ga. The federal agency's recommendations, landowners say, could be devastating to small farmers. Take, for example, a farmer who may have planted trees to finance his children's college tuition, says Chris Barneycastle, executive director of the Georgia Forestry Association, Norcross, Ga. If evidence of a salamander is found in the area, the farmer might be "unable to harvest any of the timber." But Sidney Maddock, a Buxton, N.C., environmental analyst who works for the Biodiversity Legal Foundation, argues that the forecasts of "economic doom and horrible impacts . . . are made up." Moreover, he says, the federal agency goes out of its way to accommodate industry concerns with habitat-conservation plans, which allow land owners to offset potentially harmful land uses with other protective measures for listed species. According to the Fish and Wildlife Service, the agency has signed 225 such plans across the country and has 200 more in the pipeline. To Fish and Wildlife Service officials, the fervor of the salamander debate came as a surprise. They extended a deadline for comments from the end of February to June 1 and are working with timber-industry representatives to come up with changes to the proposed listing. One change could be a reduction in the size of the buffer zone, says Linda LaClaire, wildlife biologist at the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's field office in Jackson, Miss., which is administering the salamander listing. Ms. LaClaire adds that the agency isn't currently trying to bring back the salamander to areas that "have already been altered" by urban development or forestry practices. The bottom line, she says: "We can protect the salamander and people can do what they need to do to make money." Indeed, representatives from 10 of the largest timber companies with Southeastern land holdings say the salamander needs some protection. "We want to work with the [Fish and Wildlife] Service on developing guidelines that we feel would protect the species," says Jim Sweeney, chairman of the timber group, "but also give some management flexibility" for timber companies. Mr. Sweeney also is manager of wildlife issues at Stamford, Conn.-based Champion International Corp., which has 1.07 million acres of forest land in Florida, Georgia and South Carolina. In Florida, meanwhile, state officials are considering a compromise. Because nearly 80% of the critters in the state have been found on public lands like national wildlife refuges and military bases, Florida wants to sign an agreement between land managers on the public property and the Fish and Wildlife Service. It would impose mandatory protection measures on public lands but make the provisions voluntary for private landowners. But to Elwood Geiger, a tree farmer and consulting forester with 600 acres near Jacksonville, Fla., such compromises miss the point. The Fish and Wildlife Service, he says, "is making this salamander more important than the people who have worked a lifetime protecting their land." Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Feud Flares Up Over Plan to Shut Down Washington Dam System to Save Fish
Text: LOWER GRANITE DAM, Wash. -- To the farmers, power companies, barge operators, irrigators and others across the Pacific Northwest, the Lower Granite Dam is a reassuring sight.    The dam and seven more that span the 465-mile Snake and Columbia river system below here, have turned nearby Lewiston, Idaho, into an inland port. Each year, 50 million bushels of grain are loaded on barges at Lewiston and sent down river, most of it headed for Asia. The hydroelectric plants, which light homes and offices from Washington to Montana, produce 11% of their power here.    "You take that dam away and it would be like taking Boeing out of Seattle," says David Doeringsfeld, manager of the port of Lewiston. "We'd lose our economy."    But if environmentalists have their way, the Lower Granite and its three sister dams on the lower Snake -- Little Goose, Lower Monumental and Ice Harbor -- will indeed be taken out.    The dams were built by the Army Corps of Engineers in the 1960s and 1970s to bring hydroelectric power to the region. But the Clinton administration has decided that the need for the dams has been superseded by the need to restore salmon runs. The Corps also is studying an even more far-reaching move: tearing down the huge dams that span the Columbia and block fish runs there. So far, however, no one has proposed breaching those dams.    By demolishing the dams on the lower Snake river, 130 miles of the currently dammed river would become free-flowing water where salmon -- an endangered species in these parts -- can once again thrive, a goal that has driven environmentalists for decades.    Federal biologists estimate removing the four dams would allow at least 30,000 Chinook and Sockeye salmon to return to the Snake to spawn. That would still be below predam spawning runs of 50,000 or more fish, but far more than recent runs. So few fish make it up the Snake these days that jubilant Idaho officials called a news conference in August when a single Sockeye salmon made it back to its spawning bed in central Idaho's Stanley Basin. Just four male salmon completed the trip to the spawning area this year.    Such enthusiasm for the beleaguered salmon on the one hand, and anxiety over the cost to save them on the other hand, explain why the economics of dam busting has become one of the most hotly debated topics in the Pacific Northwest. The issue is pitting potential winners -- environmentalists, trucking companies and highway construction firms -- against potential losers -- farmers, barge operators and electric utilities.    Congress is expected to make the final decision on whether to approve and fund breaching the dams next year, after the Army Corps of Engineers releases in December the findings of an economic study that compares the costs and benefits of saving salmon.    But groups on both sides of the issue are busy cranking out their own impact studies and, as is typical in economic studies, the findings are mixed.    On the one hand, for the Bonneville Power Administration, which distributes power across the Northwest from 30 dams on the Snake and Columbia river system, breaching the dams means it will lose 11% of its total power supply. That is 1,231 megawatts of electricity -- enough to light Seattle with about 200 megawatts left over. Audrey Perino, a BPA economist, says it will cost about $250 million annually to buy or produce the lost power. The BPA also must continue to pay $864 million it owes for the dams' construction.    Those costs will push electric bills in the Northwest up by $3.20 to $6.50 a month, the BPA estimates. Ms. Perino's agency hasn't taken a position on the dam-breaching controversy. "We think we have a good idea of the cost," she says, "but the benefits are pretty squishy."    Breaching the dams also would remove 35,000 acres of irrigated farmland, because alternative water-delivery systems aren't cost-effective. Cost: about $10 million, according to some estimates.    Alex McGregor, a third-generation, dry-land grain grower, calculates that breaching the dams would add $35,000 annually to the cost of running his 5,000-acre farm in Hooper, Wash. Most of that would be in increased shipping costs, he says. Like most of the region's farmers Mr. McGregor sends his wheat and barley down the Snake and Columbia river system by barge. About 43% of the nation's grain crop makes its way to Asia this way with enough grain passing through the locks at John Day dam on the Columbia to fill Seattle's Kingdome every two weeks. Shifting that grain to trucks and trains would cost farmers about $35 million annually in extra charges, says Dennis Wagner, a senior Corps economist.    In addition, Washington state officials calculate it will cost as much as $406 million to upgrade the region's local road and rail systems to handle the increased load.    Perhaps the community with the most at stake is Lewiston. Breaching the dams will lower the Snake to 7 feet from 14 feet at Lewiston, making it virtually impassable for barge traffic. When the city did its own study of the impact of breaching the dams, it found it would lose $117 million annually in river-related business and about 4,500 jobs.    Some opponents to breaching even question the notion that salmon will return to the rivers at all. Bruce Lovelin, executive director of the Columbia River Alliance in Portland, Ore., says his group estimates only 2,000 fish will make it back upstream if the dams are breached, too small a number to justify the economic pain that will fall on workers, consumers and farmers. "Those fish will cost $500,000 each," says Mr. Lovelin, who calls the spawners "gold fish."    Environmental advocates concede that breaching the four lower Snake River dams will cause some financial stress in the near term, but they say breaching will bring the region a number of long-term economic benefits.    Increased tourism from sport fishermen and increased commercial fishing activity would add about $390 million annually to the Northwest's economy, says Scott Faber, an attorney for American Rivers, a Washington, D.C., environmental group that favors breaching the dams.    Mr. Faber says removing the dams would bring 10,000 construction jobs, plus additional jobs created to mitigate the related economic impacts. "I don't think anyone can presume we can remove those dams and walk away," he says.    In any event, the economic impact of not removing the dams also would be substantial, breaching proponents say. Edward Whitelaw, a Eugene, Ore., economist with ECONorthwest, a private company working for environmental groups, says with the dams in place it could cost at least an additional $460 million to comply with requirements of the federal Clean Water Act.    The choice, says Mr. Faber, isn't just between paying to remove the dams or paying nothing to retain the status quo. Federal officials, he says, are required to come up with a plan by year end to comply with the federal Endangered Species Act and save the Snake River salmon. Without dam removal, he says, that could mean sharp limitations on timber cutting, irrigation, grazing and ocean fishing in the Northwest. Compared with another proposal before Congress to spend $7.8 billion to restore the ecology of the Everglades, breaching dams is "not too expensive."    (See related letters: "Letters to the Editor: Does Dam Removal Translate to More Fish?" -- WSJ Oct. 25, 1999)  Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: U.S. News: U.S. Watch
Text: WASHINGTON Housing Secretary Carson Has Virus Housing and Urban Development Secretary Ben Carson tested positive for Covid-19 on Monday morning, his office said, making him the latest person in President Trump's orbit to contract the virus. White House chief of staff Mark Meadows tested positive last week, as did the Trump campaign's director of battleground strategy, Nick Trainer. Coalter Baker, Mr. Carson's deputy chief of staff, said the secretary was "in good spirits and feels fortunate to have access to effective therapeutics which aid and markedly speed his recovery." Mr. Carson, a retired neurosurgeon, went to Walter Reed National Military Medical Center Monday morning but has since left, a person familiar with the matter said. Mr. Carson was among more than 100 people who attended an indoor party the White House hosted on election night, the person said. Mr. Meadows attended the party and, like many other officials, didn't wear a mask. The White House saw an outbreak of Covid-19 following a Sept. 26 Rose Garden ceremony and indoor reception the president hosted to announce his Supreme Court nominee. -- Rebecca Ballhaus --- UNIVERSITY OF NOTRE DAME School Cracks Down After Celebration The University of Notre Dame has implemented mandatory coronavirus testing for students and strict penalties for those who don't comply after students rushed the school's football field to celebrate a double-overtime upset over Clemson and held numerous weekend parties. Students, players and coaches crammed close together on the field in the minutes following the Fighting Irish's 47-40 win Saturday night in South Bend, Ind., over then-No. 1 Clemson. Many of the thousands who stormed the field weren't wearing masks or had their masks pulled down. Now, all Notre Dame students are required to undergo coronavirus testing before they leave South Bend for the extended winter break, Notre Dame President the Rev. John Jenkins said. If a student is exposed or tests positive, they will be required to quarantine on campus for two weeks. If students don't complete the mandatory coronavirus test -- or if they leave the campus area before they receive the results of their exit test -- they will be prevented from registering for classes, university officials said. -- Associated Press --- MASSACHUSETTS October Rains Ease Drought Conditions Drought conditions improved across Massachusetts thanks to rainfall in October, state officials said Monday. Precipitation totals for last month were at or above normal levels, ranging from 5 to 6 inches, with higher totals in parts of the southern and northeastern regions. As a result, State Energy and Environmental Affairs Secretary Kathleen Theoharides said officials have downgraded southeastern Massachusetts from a Level 3 "Critical Drought" to a Level 2 "Significant Drought." Cape Cod remains at Level 2 -- unchanged from last month -- and conditions have improved to a Level 1 "Mild Drought" elsewhere, Ms. Theoharides said. Conditions in the northern reaches of central Massachusetts worsened, however. The Nashua River basin now stands at Level 2. -- Associated Press --- MONTANA Removal of Gray Wolf Protection Challenged Wildlife advocates and environmental groups are challenging the removal of federal protections for gray wolves across most of the U.S. Two coalitions of groups filed formal notices over the past several days that they plan to sue the U.S. Interior Department in federal court unless protections are restored. The notices are required as a precursor to lawsuits brought under the Endangered Species Act. The Trump administration last week completed a decision that ends longstanding federal safeguards for gray wolves in the Lower 48 states except for a small population of Mexican gray wolves in the Southwest. The move puts states and tribes in charge of overseeing the predators and could allow hunting to resume in Michigan, Minnesota and Wisconsin. Gray wolves have recovered from near extinction in parts of the country with thousands now roaming the northern Rocky Mountains and western Great Lakes region and growing numbers of the animals in the Pacific Northwest. But they remain absent from much of their historical range and wildlife advocates have said protections still are needed. -- Associated Press

Title: Feds Sued Over Fishing Permits For Tribes
Text: A coalition of real-estate and agriculture interests claims the federal government is violating the Endangered Species Act by allowing Indian tribes to exercise their treaty fishing rights in Puget Sound and the Columbia River. The coalition, called Common Sense Salmon Recovery, charges in court documents that by giving tribes so-called incidental-take permits, the National Marine Fisheries Service is jeopardizing runs of salmon that are classified as threatened or endangered. "Politics is dictating these actions," says Jim Johnson, an Olympia lawyer representing the coalition, whose members are the Building Industry Association of Washington, the Washington Association of Realtors, the Washington Farm Bureau and the Washington Cattlemen's Association. "The tribes are politically powerful." The fisheries service denies the charge. And Native Americans say their limited takes of salmon -- which they are allowed to harvest under an 1855 treaty and a 1974 federal court decision -- have a minor impact on the health of the species. "We could stop fishing everywhere today, and some runs of salmon are still going to go extinct because there aren't habitats for them," says Tony Meyer, a spokesman for the Olympia-based Northwest Indian Fisheries Commission. But some experts say that tribes should be aware of the potential impact the legal argument could have. "This is one of the first cases where the effect of the ESA on treaty fishing rights has been at issue," says Phil Katzen, a Seattle attorney who has worked on tribal-fishing issues for 20 years. "This could have a major impact on tribes' abilities to conduct their fisheries." The coalition's claims are made in a recent addendum to its federal lawsuit against the national fisheries service. Filed in April in federal court in Washington, D.C., the suit accuses the agency of so poorly managing the Northwest's salmon resources that it essentially broke the law when it listed the Puget Sound run of wild Chinook salmon as threatened in March. The plaintiffs aren't seeking damages, but want the court to rule that the fisheries service must stringently enforce the laws that the suit alleges it is breaking. The suit contends the fisheries service failed to regulate commercial and tribal salmon fishing in ocean waters rigorously enough, and also didn't appropriately control the activities of salmon predators such as seals and sea lions. The suit also claims the agency didn't count hatchery-produced salmon when it determined that certain runs were in danger of extinction. Now the plaintiffs say the fisheries service is compounding its alleged transgressions by permitting the Muckleshoot tribe, among others, to catch salmon in Puget Sound this summer, and by not moving to stop four other tribes -- the Yakama, Nez Perce, Umatilla and Warm Springs -- from fishing in the Columbia this fall. "NMFS should not be authorizing harvest that takes anything from these {listed} species," Mr. Johnston says. Agency officials respond that tribes have special rights. In a landmark ruling in 1974, U.S. District Judge George Boldt in Seattle ruled that Native Americans are entitled to one-half of the harvestable salmon in the tribes' ancestral lands, including Puget Sound and the Columbia River. Judge Boldt based his decision on the terms of an 1855 treaty that promised tribal access to "usual and accustomed" fishing sites in western Washington. The tribes that will be angling for up-river bright Chinook in the Columbia this fall were issued federal permits for the accidental catch of listed fish, including the endangered upper Columbia River steelhead and the threatened Snake River basin steelhead. Incidental-take permits -- which allow tribes and others to accidentally catch and keep listed species while pursuing other fish -- are awarded at the discretion of the fisheries agency, says Brian Gorman, a spokesman for the agency in Seattle. The agency, he says, didn't break any law in awarding them to the tribes. The Muckleshoot tribe began fishing for Green River Chinook with gill nets in the Sound earlier this month. Although the Green River Chinook isn't listed as threatened or endangered, it swims in the same area as Puget Sound wild Chinook, which was listed as threatened in March. Mr. Gorman says that when the Puget Sound wild Chinook listing is fully implemented next year, the Muckleshoot tribe will be required to get an incidental-take permit from the federal government. In its addendum to its lawsuit, the coalition asks the court to order the government to more aggressively enforce the Endangered Species Act as it relates to tribal, commercial and recreational harvests of salmon. The group hasn't asked for a temporary restraining order stopping the tribes from fishing. "That is something we have to consider," says Mr. Johnson, the coalition's lawyer. Mr. Meyer of the Indian fisheries commission calls the coalition's suit "little more than a self-serving effort to allow continued degradation of salmon habitat" by developers and farmers. But Mr. Johnson says if the federal government had properly followed the Endangered Species Act and a host of federal fish-management laws, he says, salmon wouldn't be in danger of extinction today. "We're trying to solve the problem for the long term," he says. Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: House Defense Bill Could Ease Laws on Endangered Species
Text: Provisions tacked onto the House version of the defense appropriations bill would weaken the nation's laws protecting endangered species by giving new discretion to the interior secretary in enforcing them and exempting the military from following them.   The proposals, which, for instance, would make it easier for the Navy to conduct noisy underwater testing near endangered whales, are the latest of several recent attempts by conservative lawmakers to push against two 30-year-old laws protecting endangered animals.   They also come after the Bush administration had unsuccessfully sought broad exemptions for the military from federal antipollution laws, as the Defense Department faces potentially large liabilities for perchlorate contamination of drinking-water supplies.   Lawmakers in both houses of Congress rejected the antipollution exemption for the military. But the House bill allows the military an exemption to the 1973 Endangered Species Act and the 1972 Marine Mammal Protection Act. The Senate version grants a military exemption only to the 1973 act.   The House also added new discretion for the interior secretary to override the act, removing the legal requirement that the federal government set aside federal wildlife zones as essential feeding and roaming areas for threatened animals. Instead, it would be up to the secretary to decide.   "This is an attempt by the Department of Defense to use the victory in Iraq and high popularity of our military to completely dissemble and degrade our existing environmental laws," said Rep.Ellen Tauscher of California, a Democratic member of the House Armed Services Committee. She noted the military already is exempt from environmental rules in cases of national security.   The Pentagon's supporters in Congress say the bill's provisions would strengthen environmental protections by making them easier for the military and others to implement. Instead of being required to set up multiple "critical habitat" zones to protect various species on a single base, for example, military commanders could more easily use a more comprehensive approach and manage the base as an ecosystem, they say.   "We just want to streamline the way the military has to deal with environmental issues," said Brian Kennedy, spokesman for California Rep. Richard Pombo, the Republican who offered the provisions as chairman of the House Resources Committee.   There is considerable debate even within the administration over whether military operations actually are impaired by environmental restrictions. In testimony before the Senate a few months ago, Christine Whitman, administrator for the Environmental Protection Agency, said she didn't believe any military training missions were being held up because of environmental regulations.   But Deputy Defense Secretary Paul Wolfowitz recently ordered military commanders to report instances in which their preparedness is being threatened, writing in a March 7 memo to them: "As you know, in a growing number of cases environmental regulation and litigation threaten to limit our continued ability to use these lands and airspace for necessary military training and testing."   Separately, another controversial issue in the $400 billion defense authorization bill is a proposal to allow the Pentagon to begin studying the development of low-yield nuclear weapons. Such weapons could conceivably be used to destroy deeply buried targets.   Senate Democrats have charged that lifting the decade-old ban on studying the weapons could precipitate a new arms race. Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld said such complaints were groundless and argued that the "idea that we should not be allowed to study such a weapon is not a good idea." He said low-yield nuclear weapons could also be used on storage areas for chemical or biological weapons to mitigate the dispersal of those deadly agents that might be caused by a conventional warhead.   ---   Greg Jaffe contributed to this article.

Title: Roberts Threatens to Divide Democrats; Reactions to Supreme Court Nomination Suggest Minority Won't Muster United Front
Text: Washington -- ANY POLITICAL TACTICIAN'S goal is to unite his side while dividing the opposition. In nominating Judge John G. Roberts Jr. to the U.S. Supreme Court, President Bush stands a strong chance of doing just that. The affable conservative nominee has received near-universal acclaim from Mr. Bush's fellow Republicans, who hold a 55-seat majority in the Senate. That means Democrats have no chance of blocking his confirmation without maintaining unity in their own ranks. Initial reviews suggest that will be a challenge. While liberal Sen. Richard Durbin of Illinois chided Mr. Bush for a "controversial" nomination that won't "unite the country," his moderate counterpart Ben Nelson of Nebraska found nothing "alarming" or "disqualifying" about the choice so far, as a spokesman put it. The distance between those initial reactions reflects the diverse interests within a Democratic caucus that, so far this year, has stuck together against the White House on Social Security overhaul and other issues. With his pleasant demeanor and friendships across the political divide in Washington's legal establishment, Judge Roberts, who sits on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, offers a more elusive subject for attack. For Mr. Durbin and colleagues representing left-leaning constituencies such as Edward Kennedy of Massachusetts and Barbara Boxer of California, there are ready targets in Mr. Roberts's past statement questioning the court decision that legalized abortion or his judicial ruling casting doubt about the application of the Endangered Species Act. Cheering them on will be outside activist groups such as MoveOn.org, which already has labeled Judge Roberts a "right-wing corporate lawyer and ideologue." Democratic moderates, some of whom are up for re-election next year in so-called red states carried by Mr. Bush, face different calculations. Aside from Mr. Nelson of Nebraska, they include Sens. Bill Nelson of Florida and Kent Conrad of North Dakota. Even before the selection, Sen. Joseph Lieberman, a Connecticut Democrat, had labeled Judge Roberts "in the ball park" of acceptable nominees, though a spokesman says he remains noncommittal. Still, just 24 hours after Mr. Bush announced his nominee, many Democratic strategists privately concede Mr. Bush's choice of Judge Roberts is likely to split Democrats sufficiently to win confirmation. "Bush won" by picking a likable nominee with a solid intellectual record and scant paper trail, shrugged one Democratic staffer on Capitol Hill. "A lot of people are feeling that this is probably a guy who gets confirmed." One wild card in the debate is the reaction of the bloc of Democratic senators interested in their party's 2008 presidential nomination. The 2004 Democratic nominee, John Kerry of Massachusetts, quickly called Judge Roberts "no Sandra Day O'Connor" and raised expected questions about the judge's views on civil rights and abortion. For other possible White House aspirants, the choice is more complicated. Sen. Evan Bayh of Indiana has cultivated a moderate reputation, and Judge Roberts is a fellow Hoosier. But Mr. Bayh would have to appeal in the 2008 nomination contest to left-leaning primary voters and donors, many of whom are expected to line up against Judge Roberts's nomination. Sen. Hillary Rodham Clinton of New York could face the opposite kind of strategic dilemma. An icon among liberals, Ms. Clinton has spent recent years burnishing her moderate credentials on issues like national security. Acquiescing in Judge Roberts's nomination could offer another opportunity to do the same thing. Her initial reaction called for a "thoughtful and deliberate" confirmation process without indicating either support or opposition. Ranking Judiciary Committee Democrat Patrick Leahy of Vermont and Democratic campaign committee chairman Charles Schumer of New York quickly identified one ideologically neutral reason for slowing down the nomination. They demanded that the White House turn over confidential legal memorandums Judge Roberts wrote when he was a counsel in the U.S. Solicitor General's Office. Last year, Messrs. Schumer and Leahy blocked the nomination of Miguel Estrada to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, where Judge Roberts serves, because Mr. Estrada declined to turn over similar information from his time as a Department of Justice solicitor. The demand for documents -- and for answers to questions on abortion and other issues at confirmation hearings later this summer -- could yet pull diverse Democratic senators together. Similar tactics have kept Democrats together in blocking Mr. Bush's nomination of John Bolton for Ambassador to the United Nations. "The one thing that we are quite united on is the nominee needs to answer questions and provide information" to the Senate, Mr. Schumer told reporters yesterday. "I'm making a plea to Judge Roberts to answer the questions fully and openly." Whether the American public will rally behind that cause in a high- profile nomination fight remains unclear. In the latest Wall Street Journal-NBC News poll, respondents said by 53% to 43% that high-court nominees shouldn't have to answer questions about their views on issues that could come before the court. If Judge Roberts ducks questions about abortion, the Democrats' powerful abortion-rights constituency may try to fill in the blanks by raising questions about the past work of his wife as executive vice president of Feminists for Life, an antiabortion group in Washington. Whether that could galvanize broad opposition is uncertain. The organization generally has steered clear of advocating that the Supreme Court abandon its Roe v. Wade decision legalizing abortion, focusing instead on reducing the incidence of abortion while distancing itself from antiabortion extremists who commit acts of violence. Some Democrats may find political payback as a motivation to criticize the nominee. In the Bush-Gore Florida battle of 2000, Mr. Roberts assisted then-candidate Bush by briefing his brother, Gov. Jeb Bush, on election law as state Republicans worked to stymie Democratic recount efforts. Judge Roberts, who met with Mr. Leahy yesterday, will continue today to try to disarm resistance on Capitol Hill -- and potentially divide the Democratic caucus. He will meet in the morning with Sen. Herb Kohl, a moderate Wisconsin Democrat facing re-election in 2006, and in the afternoon with Mr. Schumer.

Title: ESA Has Saved Thousands of Species From Extinction
Text: In their manifesto about the Endangered Species Act, Damien Schiff and Julie MacDonald omit the fact that the ESA has prevented the extinction of 99% of the more than 1,500 plants and animals it protects, along the way preserving the health of the irreplaceable forests, waterways and ecosystems we all share ("The Endangered Species Act Turns 40 -- Hold the Applause," op-ed, Dec. 28). The act has put hundreds of species on the path to recovery. To its credit, the ESA has done a superb job of helping us balance our short-term economic needs with the long-term environmental and economic concerns that are in the best interest of our children and grandchildren. Noah Greenwald Endangered Species Director Center for Biological Diversity Portland, Ore. --- The authors correctly identify a number of problems with the ESA, such as using shoddy science to list species. But their prescriptions for change, which amount to procedural tweaks, focus on symptoms and so would do little to solve the root causes -- the ESA's severe penalties that violate landowners' property rights by not compensating them when property is devalued by species protection requirements. As a result, the act perversely and counterproductively causes landowners to make their property inhospitable to species. That is why the ratio of declining to improving species on private land is 9 to 1, whereas on federal lands it is 1.5 to 1. The Endangered Species Act needs a completely new approach that removes the penalties and replaces them with positive incentives. One model is the Agriculture Department's highly successful Conservation Reserve Program, which pays farmers who voluntarily agree to remove from production land considered "environmentally sensitive." Politically, this new approach -- call it the endangered species reserve program -- has significant potential because it would do what most members of Congress and the American people want: It would conserve endangered species more effectively. Brian Seasholes Research Fellow The Reason Foundation Los Angeles --- The ESA also has been used by animal-rights groups in ways never intended by the act. Feld Entertainment, the parent company of Ringling Bros. and Barnum & Bailey Circus, has been the target of philosophically motivated litigation that had nothing to do with actually saving an endangered species. Specifically, Ringling Bros. cares for the largest herd of endangered Asian elephants in the Western Hemisphere. We are very proud of the outstanding care provided these animals, and the company has made a commitment through its Center for Elephant Conservation to ensuring these magnificent animals survive for future generations. However, animal-rights groups tried for over a decade to use the law as their basis for removing the elephants from the circus and to deny millions of Americans the chance to appreciate them up close in a way available nowhere else but with Ringling Bros. Though Feld Entertainment eventually prevailed in what the court found to be frivolous litigation based on the testimony of a paid plaintiff with no credibility, it took 12 years, thousands of hours and millions in attorneys' fees. No individual or company should be forced to fight this level of extremism for so long based on the animal-rights groups' beliefs that they, and they alone, know what is best for animals. In addition to the common-sense changes to the law advocated by Mr. Schiff and Ms. MacDonald, reinstating the different regulations for endangered versus threatened species as well as requiring scientific documentation of the threats and consequences to each listed species, the administration would also be wise to rein in the ability of animal-rights groups and their allies to use the ESA to legally torment law-abiding companies who actually care for endangered animals. Stephen Payne Feld Entertainment Vienna, Va.

Title: World-Wide
Text: A BUSH PANEL VOTED to allow logging in forests vital to the spotted owl. For only the second time in two decades, a government committee overrode the Endangered Species Act by permitting limited logging in some of Oregon's old-growth forest. But logging won't begin immediately, because two court injunctions protect the owl, and environmentalists are expected to sue the government to appeal the override. The Bush administration also introduced a long-term compromise plan to preserve logging jobs. The spotted owl was named an endangered species in 1990. Since then, Northwest logging has declined as the government has curtailed timber sales. --- Serb irregulars fought artillery duels and house-to-house battles with Muslims in Sarajevo. An official in the Bosnian capital said nearly the entire city was bombarded, and at least four people were killed. Shells crashed into the presidential building and the headquarters of U.N. peacekeepers. --- The House approved $822 million in emergency aid and loans to help Los Angeles and Chicago recover from recent disasters. The measure, which goes to the Senate, has been endorsed by Bush, yet Republicans voted by more than a 2-1 margin against the bill. --- German public-sector workers rejected a wage settlement that ended a crippling 11-day strike last week. But it didn't appear that the workers would resume their walkout. The giant metalworkers union, meanwhile, is threatening work stoppages next week. --- A federal grand jury has subpoenaed six years of office records of three House members, including Rostenkowski. The grand jury appears to be looking into whether clerks at the House Post Office may have manipulated cash vouchers for personal gain. --- Gorbachev urged the U.S. Congress to pass a bill aiding the Soviet people, saying the assistance is crucial in a time of crisis. The former Soviet president, addressing about 300 members of the House and Senate, told the lawmakers they should regard the request as a "historic opportunity." --- Kuwaiti oil-well fires have caused an insignificant amount of global environmental damage, according to a study in the journal Science. The conclusions concerning damage from the fires, ignited by the Iraqi army during the Gulf War, contradict forecasts that the smoke would spread worldwide. --- South Africa's white leadership failed to reach an accord with the African National Congress on an interim government. ANC leader Mandela accused Pretoria officials of waging a "silent war" against his backers. Meanwhile, Zulu leader Buthelezi said he wouldn't attend a convention of black and white politicians that opens today. --- Rioters and looters rampaged through Nigeria's capital in a second day of violence by youths enraged by severe economic hardships. Police in Lagos clashed with the bands of anti-government protesters and fired tear gas to disperse them. --- A detained Nobel Peace laureate issued her first public statement since Burmese officials placed her under house arrest in July 1989. In the statement, released in Washington, opposition leader Aung San Suu Kyi expressed hope for reconciliation in military-ruled Burma. --- Philippine troops rushed to guard election offices in several towns after angry mobs stormed them to protest alleged vote fraud in this week's national election. Three days after the presidential balloting, anticorruption crusader Santiago was locked in a tight race with ex-defense chief Ramos, who was backed by President Aquino. --- Azerbaijan's Parliament restored ex-Communist Party leader Mutalibov as president, and he vowed to regain ground lost to Armenian forces in the disputed enclave of Nagorno-Karabakh, officials said. Mutalibov immediately declared a state of emergency in the Azerbaijani capital. --- Russia's foreign minister visited Afghanistan's new rebel government in Kabul but flew home without a promised prisoner of war. The interim government, which intends to free the soldier as a goodwill gesture, said transportation problems delayed his arrival from a rebel camp.

Title: Rural Land Owners Say Pain Goes Beyond Data
Text: Are endangered plants and animals dangerous to rural property owners? Choose a side. According to a new study by the Texas and Southwestern Cattle Raisers Association, the answer is "yes, very." By analyzing property-tax rolls around the state, the study attempts to show that land values in 33 environmentally sensitive counties have fallen much faster than the state average over the past four years, due in part to enforcement of the federal Endangered Species Act. Not surprisingly, the association's conclusions are drawing fire from environmentalists. And a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology has weighed in to say that the study actually proves the opposite of what ranchers claim. If nothing else, the flap about the study shows just how tough it can be to apply hard numbers to the highly emotional battle between property-rights advocates and environmentalists. "It's difficult to get your hands on something that will isolate that effect {on property values} conclusively," says Charles Gilliland, an associate research economist at Texas A&M's Real Estate Center. Steve Munday, a spokesman for the Cattle Raisers Association, says looking at the study purely from a statistical point of view misses the bigger picture. The association bolstered its examination of tax records with a survey of statements made by real-estate professionals, rural landowners and local government officials citing the Endangered Species Act's negative impact on land values. "If the real-estate experts say it's a problem, and local elected officials say it's a problem, and we know from first-person reports that it's a problem, then there's more here than just smoke," Mr. Munday says. The group's effort came after federal authorities caused a near-panic among landowners earlier this year when they considered designating 33 Central Texas counties as "critical habitat" for the endangered golden-cheeked warbler, a songbird that nests in the region. That plan -- which mainly would have placed additional restrictions on some uses of the land -- was later shelved under heavy political fire. But even without the special designation, those counties are already grappling with restrictions because they are home to 19 other endangered species. Property owners who play host to such plants and animals face strict limits on what they can do with their land, including any new developments that might imperil their endangered guests. To see whether those restrictions translate into lower land values in the countryside, the Cattle Raisers Association took a look at property-tax rolls across the state. The study found that average rural land values in the 33 counties declined 25.3% between 1989 and 1993 -- significantly more than the statewide drop of 22.2%. But Stephen Meyer at MIT, who directs the school's Project on Environmental Politics & Policy, says the association made a basic analytical error. The problem, he says, is that the 33 counties include Bexar and Travis counties, by far the most populous in the study. Because of the proximity to urban areas (Austin is located in Travis County, while San Antonio is in Bexar County), rural land in those counties was much more valuable to begin with, and represented a disproportionate amount of the value in the 33-county sample. It's likely that values dropped much more in Bexar and Travis counties than in the others when the speculative bubble burst in the late 1980s, Mr. Meyer maintains. Minus the two big counties, average values in the remaining 31 fell just 17.8%, far less than the state average. In fact, land values in 22 of the 33 counties did better than the state average, Mr. Meyer says. In some cases, the endangered species might have actually helped land values, says Mr. Meyer. He says it makes sense when you consider that species-free land might command a higher price when some land with endangered species habitat becomes undesirable. That's little comfort to residents of habitat-sensitive land. And the cattle association and real-estate market specialists point out that some problems faced by landowners when trying to sell their property within a suspected habitat area aren't necessarily reflected in tax records. For instance, property that's encumbered by endangered species might be impossible to sell at any price. And landowners whose property doesn't have such problems often must pay for expensive and time-consuming biological surveys to prove it before a prospect will agree to buy or a bank will finance the sale. Such surveys can cost anywhere from $10,000 to $50,000, depending on the size of the tract. Steve Paulson, director of the Texas office of SWCA Inc., an environmental consultant that provides such services, says business is booming. Without a survey, there is uncertainty, he says. "And wherever there's uncertainty, there's volatility in the market." That's something George Foote knows about firsthand. Back in 1961, Mr. Foote invested in 50 acres of land outside Austin with the idea that he could sell it in his retirement years. Now, Mr. Foote, 74 years old, can't find a buyer because wildlife officials believe it's a habitat for the golden-cheeked warbler. Several buyers have expressed interest, but they quickly lose it when warblers are mentioned, says Mr. Foote. If it's warbler habitat, then it can't be cleared to build a house or road -- the most marketable use for the property, he says. Title: Taste: Tony & Tacky
Text: GRIN AND BEAR IT: Among the last-minute efforts of the Clinton administration was a bid to use the Endangered Species Act to introduce grizzly bears to Idaho -- even though grizzlies are not an endangered species. Writing in USA Today, Idaho Gov. Dirk Kempthorne said that the Clintonites pushed for the experiment even though it was opposed by two Idaho governors, the state's entire congressional delegation, the Idaho Legislature and the Idaho Fish and Game Commission. What's more, says Gov. Kempthorne, the Clinton folks even calculated that this federal experiment would cost the U.S. Treasury between $4 million and $10 million for each human killed, "and the plan even amortized the annual costs at $80,000-$200,000." Who says liberals are blind to costs?    TOP GRADE: Most universities are delighted when the Princeton Review's annual college guide gives them a top ranking. But not the University of Tennessee at Knoxville. Maybe that's because the crown it won was for America's best party school. (It also took first place for most beer consumed.) According to the Chronicle of Higher Education, UT Knoxville's honors were based on ratings supplied by 65,000 students at 331 campuses across the country. At the other end of the spectrum, meanwhile, Brigham Young University again topped the list of "stone cold sober schools."

Title: U.S. News: Former Power Broker Is Now the Underdog
Text: TURLOCK, Calif. -- Former Rep. Richard Pombo, the onetime Washington power broker, is counting on anger over federal water policies in California's Central Valley to propel him back into office in November. But first, the former chairman of the House Resources Committee must confront a surprisingly strong challenge from two fellow conservatives in Tuesday's Republican primary. Mr. Pombo served for seven terms in the neighboring 11th Congressional District in what had been a safely Republican seat, until redistricting in 2002 opened it to more San Francisco Bay area Democrats and he was ousted in 2006. When incumbent George Radanovich announced his retirement earlier this year from the more conservative 19th district here, Mr. Pombo jumped back in the ring with little fear of having to face the Democrats or environmentalists who hounded him before. Instead, the 49-year-old is facing competition from two veteran politicians: state Sen. Jeff Denham, 42, who has attacked Mr. Pombo for alleged misuse of his old office, and former Fresno Mayor Jim Patterson, 62, whose wide name recognition in the more urbanized southern part of the district has boosted his profile. Mr. Pombo now stands as an underdog in essentially a three-man race. According to a mid-May nonpartisan Survey USA poll of likely GOP voters, Messrs. Denham and Patterson are running almost neck and neck, with 28% and 29% of support, while Mr. Pombo comes in at 18%. With roughly a fifth of the electorate still undecided, Mr. Pombo said it is too early to count anyone in or out. Given that the district of about 600,000 people is predominantly Republican, whoever wins on Tuesday will likely go on to Congress after the November general election. "It's a wide-open race at this point," Mr. Pombo told about 50 attendees at a "Pasta for Pombo" dinner Wednesday in this windblown Stanislaus County city. "In all honesty, anyone can win." One thing hindering Mr. Pombo is his record. Mr. Denham has attacked the former congressman for engaging in allegedly unethical behavior while in office, such as billing taxpayers for using a recreational vehicle to tour national parks with his family in 2003. That has put Mr. Pombo on the defensive. At the pasta event, he again defended his use of the RV as a cheaper alternative than flying to each of the 13 parks he oversaw as resources chairman in a jet. He also reiterated that he paid for his family's meals and other incidentals. Over breakfast Thursday morning at a Turlock diner, Mr. Denham suggested Mr. Pombo's campaign has been behind unsubstantiated "rumors" against him, such as that he backed an environmental group's ad hitting Mr. Pombo on ethics. Mr. Pombo denies that. "This is the ugliest campaign I have ever been involved with," said Mr. Denham, who is also an almond farmer.
