Mr. Patterson has mostly stayed out of the fray, focusing on issues all three men largely agree on, such as the need to free up more federal water supplies for Central Valley farmers, whose allotments have been sharply reduced amid drought and court-imposed environmental restrictions. Lacking the financial resources of Messrs. Pombo and Denham, who have raised more than $500,000 apiece, Mr. Patterson has largely relied on face-to-face meetings with voters who he hopes will be ready for an outsider to government. "I am the farthest one in this race removed from being an incumbent or sitting politician," said Mr. Patterson, a radio talk-show host whose final term as Fresno mayor ended in 2001. For his part, Mr. Pombo said he initially didn't want to re-enter the fray after his 2006 defeat. After returning to his family's ranch outside Tracy, Calif., he said, he was content to remain in private life. But when federal environmental regulations tightened under Washington's Democratic control, Mr. Pombo said, he felt "an obligation" to try and get back into office. Mr. Pombo's chief selling point is that he would return to Washington with his old seniority, putting him in a leadership role to resume efforts such as trying to overhaul the Endangered Species Act. "My record in office shows I am actually willing to fight to make something happen," he said in an interview. That resonates with some supporters. "I want to put someone in who can help us immediately," said Jim Walls, 56, a farmer who lost almost all his federal water allotment last year before federal officials increased the supply in March. Mr. Pombo "is a proven commodity, and has fought for us before." Political analysts say Mr. Pombo faces an uphill battle. Still, "I don't discount Pombo, because he has raised an awful lot of money," said Thomas Holyoke, an associate political science professor at California State University in Fresno. Credit: By Jim Carlton

Title: U.S. Will Designate 11.6 Million Acres in Northwest to Protect Owls, Tall Trees
Text: Score one for tall trees and spotted owls.    The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service confirmed Friday that its long-awaited proposal for protecting spotted owls and the towering Pacific Northwest forests where they live would designate some 11.6 million acres of woods as prime owl habitat.    That means that the government could put much -- perhaps all -- of that acreage off limits to loggers. More than three million acres is already off limits for other owl-related reasons, bringing the total acreage potentially affected by logging limits to about 14.8 million acres, an area the size of Massachusetts and Vermont. That would be by far the largest amount of land ever placed off limits to industry in order to save an animal under the Endangered Species Act or other preservation laws.    The announcement was short on details, more of which should come today when the agency releases its full report. The proposal was attacked by timber interests and even some environmentalists, and both sides warned that the seemingly endless fight over the owl issue and the timber policies it threatens is far from over. Nonetheless, the proposal augurs logging limits that are potentially far more restrictive than timber interests had anticipated when the agency's review of owl habitat began in February in response to a court order. And, with the owl fight now shifting into a new phase, the birds and the trees have gained a clear advantage.    "It's good news for owls," said Todd True, a senior attorney with the Sierra Club Legal Defense Fund. Mark Rey, a leading timber industry lobbyist, reluctantly agreed. "With this insane proposal, the government has placed the interest of owls above the interest of thousands of logging families and communities."    Timber is a multibillion dollar business in the Northwest, and the economic impact of the proposal remains difficult to sort out. Timber groups predicted economic catastrophe, estimating that more than 100,000 jobs could be lost; the government puts the figure at about 30,000. Environmentalists say both estimates are wild exaggerations, maintaining that many timber jobs are doomed anyway because of changing timber techniques and markets.    But the owl's edge could be short-lived. Timber interests have already begun hacking away at the Fish and Wildlife proposal, as rumors about its contents leaked out. Over the weekend, they denounced the proposal and vowed to carry the fight to Congress, the Bush administration and the courts.    "The proposal is mind-boggling and we will fight it every way we can," said Keven Brett, vice president of the American Forest Resource Alliance, a trade group.    The first attacks will come in Congress, where timber groups have a ready audience among Northwestern legislators concerned about the impact of the proposal on the economies of Oregon, Washington and Northern California. Indeed, several legislators, including Sen. Slade Gorton (R., Wash.), Rep. Norm Dicks (D., Wash.) and Rep. Les AuCoin (D., Ore.), lambasted the proposal and the process by which it was produced.    Timber interests also will attempt to persuade Interior Secretary Manuel Lujan to intervene on their behalf. Mr. Lujan has substantial authority under various natural resource and wildlife laws to shape the details of proposals relating to the protection of threatened and endangered species. Suits are also expected, adding to the thicket of litigation already surrounding the owl.    So far, though, timber groups haven't fared particularly well in the courts on the owl issue. Moreover, a federal judge in Seattle is to begin hearings tomorrow on a suit brought by environmentalists that could effectively halt virtually all logging in the Northwest for months.    In disclosing its proposal Friday, the Fish and Wildlife Service emphasized that many details remain to be worked out. John Turner, the service's director, noted that designating an area as prime owl habitat doesn't necessarily mean that loggers won't be allowed to operate there. He said he will appoint a team of economists to analyze the impact of the service's proposal on the Pacific Northwest's economy. Since the Interior Department can relax protections if they are considered too economically disruptive, that study will be crucial in determining how far timber-cutting curbs will eventually go.  Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: U.S. News: Nixon Library Hopes to Upgrade Legacy --- A $15 million overhaul of the center aims to challenge perceptions of the 37th president
Text: YORBA LINDA, Calif. -- As voters ponder which presidential aspirant they like better -- or dislike less -- Jim Byron hopes they will take a fresh look at a name from the past: Richard Milhous Nixon. Mr. Nixon, who died in 1994, "cared about a lot of the issues we care about today," said 23-year-old Mr. Byron, the director of strategic planning for the Richard Nixon Foundation. The foundation helps operate Mr. Nixon's presidential library and museum, which is having a reopening ceremony Friday after a $15 million overhaul. Along with sleek interactive displays -- including one that allows visitors to decide whether they favor launching bombing raids in connection with the Vietnam War -- supporters are hoping the museum also offers something of an image makeover for a widely criticized chief executive. "People don't know all he did. It's our job to tell them," said Mr. Byron, who started as a 14-year-old volunteer at the Orange County complex, which opened in 1990. Much of Mr. Nixon's legacy has been shaped by the Watergate scandal, where the president's efforts against his political opponents led to misdeeds that ranged from breaking into offices to attempting to block federal investigations. In August 1974, as he faced likely impeachment, President Nixon resigned less than two years after being re-elected in one of the most one-sided victories in presidential history. For Watergate, "he was punished and he should have been," said Fred Malek, a former Nixon White House aide and chair of the library fundraising effort. Besides Mr. Malek, major donors include George Argyros, a real-estate investor and former U.S. ambassador to Spain during the George W. Bush administration, and James Cavanaugh, a health-care industry executive who worked in the Nixon administration. The $15 million fundraising effort has faced some unusual challenges for a presidential library, said Mr. Malek. Most such efforts are undertaken on behalf of former presidents who "have a bevy of rich people who are core supporters," he said. But given how much time has passed, many of the wealthy Nixonites are dead. The new version of the museum will include a large Watergate exhibit, said William Baribault, president of the Nixon Foundation, which helps the National Archives operate the library. The new Watergate exhibit is essentially the same as the one that was revamped in 2011 and replaced with what critics said was a decidedly pro-Nixon view of the scandal. Mr. Nixon's admirers argue that he should be measured by his entire, remarkable career. During his five-plus years in the White House, Mr. Nixon created the Environmental Protection Agency and signed into law the 1970 Clean Air Act, the National Environmental Policy Act and the Endangered Species Act. His administration helped integrate public schools in several Southern states. He signed an education law that helped open intercollegiate athletics to women. He ended the Vietnam War, using sometimes controversial tactics, as well as the military draft. He moved to open relations with Communist China and improve them with the Soviet Union. The China exhibit will include an interactive station that allows visitors to read through the yellow-pad notes Mr. Nixon wrote in preparation for meeting China's top leaders in 1972. There will also be a re-creation of Mr. Nixon arriving in China with statues of him and Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai shaking hands. Nixon supporters hope to impress visitors, particularly younger ones who weren't alive during a political career where critics described Mr. Nixon as "Tricky Dick." The makeover will "really give people a chance to take a fresh look at his legacy and get a new appreciation of his accomplishments," said the former president's grandson Christopher Nixon Cox. As time passes, Watergate "will become less and less important" in people's evaluation of Mr. Nixon, said Mr. Cox, who is co-chair of the library's reopening committee. Nixon historians are split on his rehab chances. Douglas Schoen, an author and pollster whose clients have included Bill Clinton, said the need for a reassessment pushed him to write the 2016 book "The Nixon Effect," which calls Mr. Nixon's tenure "one of the most consequential and even salutary American presidencies of the 20th century." As for the idea of Mr. Nixon appealing to millennials, "let the record show that a historian laughed," said Rick Perlstein, who wrote the 2008 book "Nixonland: The Rise of a President and the Fracturing of America." Credit: By John R. Emshwiller

Title: Minnow Suit Raises Fears Over Water
Text: LUBBOCK -- High Plains residents fear a federal lawsuit by environmentalists seeking protection of a silvery, two-inch minnow will lead to restrictions on access to the region's two key water sources. The lawsuit, filed last month in U.S. district court in Albuquerque by the Sierra Club and the Southwest Center for Biological Diversity in Tucson, seeks to force the U.S. Interior Department to follow through with a four-year-old proposal to declare the Arkansas River shiner endangered. Locals fear such a designation would be a big step toward restricting access to the Ogallala Aquifer and Lake Meredith, which feed some shiner habitats. That, says Wayne Wyatt, manager of the High Plains Underground Water Conservation District in Lubbock, would "put everyone into the water-rationing business." Federal officials insist that, even if the shiner is declared endangered, they will not curb water use. Indeed, in a 1997 agreement with the state, they pledged not to regulate pumping from the aquifer or releases from the lake. But people in the High Plains, home to the 20 or so counties most concerned, know a successful lawsuit could force the government's hand. In the early 1990s, for example, environmental lawsuits spurred state legislators to limit pumping from the Edwards Aquifer. The shiner became an issue in 1994, when the Interior Department recommended declaring it endangered. Under the Endangered Species Act, such a declaration would allow the federal government to regulate land use in the shiner's habitat. The Interior Department was given a year either to declare the shiner endangered or let the recommendation lapse. Before the one-year period was up, though, Congress imposed a moratorium on endangered-species listings as it considered amending the Endangered Species Act. It ended the moratorium in 1996, but didn't set a new deadline for the shiner. In their lawsuit, the Southwest Center and the Sierra Club contend that the delay in deciding whether to declare the shiner endangered is illegal because Interior has taken more than a year, even accounting for the moratorium period. The plaintiffs want the court to order action by Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt. Fish and Wildlife officials say Director Jamie Clark plans to decide by May 31 whether to list the shiner as endangered. "It's most likely going to be added," says Ken Collins, a biologist in charge of shiner research at the agency's Tulsa office. But officials insist the agency, which is under the auspices of the Department of Interior, isn't reacting to the lawsuit, and that because the case falls into a statutory gray area they're under no formal deadline. The director's decision wouldn't require approval by Mr. Babbitt, who is the target of the suit only for procedural reasons. An endangered declaration would render moot only part of the lawsuit, that which seeks a decision on declaring the shiner itself endangered. The plaintiffs could still pursue a second part, seeking a decision on protecting the fish's habitat. Though their suit doesn't say so, the plaintiffs acknowledge that their object is "to see changes in the way the Arkansas River basin is managed," in the words of Peter Galvin, a biologist for the Southwest Center. That could mean restricting use of either the Ogallala Aquifer or Lake Meredith. Though most Texans know the shiner as a fishing-bait lookalike, environmentalists and the Fish and Wildlife Service say it's crucial to the ecosystem, and that it now inhabits only 20% of its original territory due partly to man-made intrusions such as the 1965 creation of Lake Meredith. Locals thought the long-running dispute had been resolved by the 1997 agreement struck by the Texas Parks & Wildlife Department and the Fish and Wildlife Service. The pact implied the federal government would grant the shiner "threatened" status -- a category less critical than "endangered" -- and Washington pledged not to limit access to water from either the aquifer or the lake. Meanwhile, Texas and federal officials would implement a "conservation strategy" that ultimately could have imposed land-use rules on areas near the shiner's waters. But federal officials say the agreement was merely a stopgap measure always subject to revision, or, if the shiner were declared endangered, to outright nullification. Federal officials never actually signed the pact, and now they say it indeed needs revision in light of new data showing the influence of the Ogallala Aquifer on shiner habitats is greater than previously believed. They insist the lawsuit has nothing to do with their change of heart, and that neither the revisions nor an endangered declaration would reverse their commitment not to restrict water access. That doesn't assuage concerns on the High Plains. "Water is our most important resource up here," says Jerry Glover, executive director of the Texas Corn Producers Board. "When someone starts playing with it, we start getting touchy." Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: State Brokers Local Solution To Protect Fish
Text: Texas wildlife officials are scrambling to avert a showdown between landowners and the federal government -- all over a 2-inch-long fish. Minuscule as it is, the striped Devils River minnow is no small matter to landowners in Val Verde County or to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. The fish, which lives in the Devils River and in nearby San Felipe and Sycamore creeks, is a candidate for federal protection as an endangered or threatened species. But ranchers along the paths of the waterways, fearing the impact of such a designation, won't let federal agents onto their property to collect samples of the minnow, which the agency needs to determine whether the fish is, in fact, in danger of extinction. Now the state is stepping in to help broker a compromise. Last week, a group of ranchers agreed to give biologists from the Texas Department of Parks and Wildlife access to their property to conduct studies on the fish. They are also negotiating with the agency on whether to accept the state's own minnow-preservation plan. For now, federal officials are willing to let the state initiative proceed. But it is not yet known whether a final agreement with ranchers would satisfy the requirements of the U.S. Endangered Species Act -- or, as the ranchers want, persuade the federal government to leave them alone. "It's going to be controversial," says Steve Spangle, listing coordinator for the federal agency's regional office in Albuquerque, N.M. "We're dealing with West Texas, after all." Indeed, rural Texans' loathing of Washington is the stuff of legend, and Val Verde ranchers hardly shy away from that image. "The federal government is the enemy," declares Todd Simpson, who lives along the Devils River, which flows for more than three miles through and beside the Rocker U Ranch, his 4,400-acre sheep and goat ranch about 50 miles northwest of Del Rio. "I don't think any landowners would cooperate with any federal people." State officials, too, are resistant to a federally imposed solution. During a meeting last week at Mr. Simpson's ranch, about 40 Val Verde County residents and Parks and Wildlife officials discussed the broad outline of a conservation plan for the minnow that would be administered by the state with help from ranchers. The plan, which has since been discussed with federal officials, would remove the U.S. government from the enforcement picture. Mr. Spangle of the Fish and Wildlife Service acknowledges that the idea has merit. If nothing else, he says, it's practical: Nearly all the land along the minnow habitat is privately owned, which would make any federal blueprint difficult for the government to enforce. "Our goal is very simple: It's to secure the future of that species," Mr. Spangle says. And simply listing the fish as endangered "wouldn't help it as much as a cooperative effort." But such state-led initiatives aren't guaranteed to survive, even if they initially pass muster with the federal government. Last year, a similar state-sponsored compromise that would have kept the Barton Springs salamander off the proposed list of endangered species won approval from U.S. Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt. But in March, after an Austin environmental group, the Save Our Springs Alliance, successfully challenged the compromise in federal court, Mr. Babbitt reversed his decision and declared the salamander threatened. The declaration, he warned, would lead to restrictions on development in the 350-square-mile Barton Springs watershed in Travis and Hays counties. One possible alternative that the Parks and Wildlife Department has used in the past: monetary incentives. Earlier this year, the agency introduced a program to pay landowners who help protect rare and endangered animals. So far two grants have been given out under the program. The designation of the Devils River minnow as a threatened or endangered species has been debated since the late 1970s, and even the current dispute dates back to a 1992 lawsuit by the New York-based Fund for Animals against the Fish and Wildlife Service. In the suit, filed in federal court in Washington, the group charged that the agency had wrongly delayed its review of 430 species. The judge in the case responded by ordering that all 430 be listed as candidates for protection. The minnow is one of 41 high-priority candidates whose fates have yet to be decided. Gary Graham, chief of the endangered-resources branch at the Parks and Wildlife Department in Austin, says that because there hasn't been a published study of the Devils River minnow since 1992, it is quite possible that the minnow is no longer in short supply. Under the plan his agency is discussing with ranchers, a new study would be conducted. If the minnow turns out to be scarce, Mr. Graham says, the agency would examine everything from water flow in minnow habitats to the effect that stocked fish such as some bass have had on its population. Then the state, with cooperation from ranchers, would probably try to develop a captively bred minnow population to be reintroduced into streams. Such a plan might be just what ranchers are looking for. "It's a welcome thing to have the state of Texas bring some rational and scientific effort to bear upon problems that endangered creatures present," says Mr. Simpson, at Rocker U. What ranchers say they don't want is any federal interference. Claudia Abbey Ball, who lives on a 15,000-acre ranch bisected by the river, says she worries that if the minnow is listed as endangered or threatened, federal officials may bar her cows and goats from drinking from the river or grazing along its banks. The city of Del Rio, 154 miles west of San Antonio, is also taking an interest, because San Felipe Creek runs through town. Among the concerns, says Assistant City Manager Beth Eby, is whether herbicide use at a city-owned golf course along the creek would be affected. Mr. Spangle says most fears of federal overreaching are unwarranted. Even if the minnow were listed, he says, land-use practices probably wouldn't be affected, because the agency would have to show a direct link between a rancher's actions -- negligent or intentional -- and the death of a protected fish before it could take action under the Endangered Species Act. "We're not going to go on people's lands" and tell them how to run their business, Mr. Spangle says. "It's just not workable." The Fish and Wildlife Service has until April 1, 1998, to decide whether to formally propose that the minnow be listed, and another year to make a final decision. The Fund for Animals, for one, thinks there's no room for a compromise. Listing the minnow "is supposed to be a purely biological decision," says Eric Glitzenstein, a Washington attorney for the fund in the 1992 suit. "Biologists have looked at this particular species and said it's facing the most imminent threat of extinction. The process is not supposed to take into account economic and political factors." But to rural Texans, those are fighting words. "To meet the conservation demands of an urban public, we have to generate solutions that work for the rural landscapes," says Dr. Graham, the state Parks and Wildlife official. "The urban environmental groups take a command-and-control approach, and that doesn't work in rural Texas." Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Redwoods war is grinding on in latest suit
Text: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal In its lawsuit, filed May 7 in Federal Claims Court in Washington, D.C., Pacific Lumber charged that the application of the Endangered Species Act to the Headwaters caused a de facto "taking" of the grove, closing it to logging. Mr. Hurwitz acquired the Headwaters -- the largest intact stand of ancient redwoods still in private hands -- in Maxxam's 1986 takeover of Pacific Lumber. On May 8, a federal Appeals Court in San Francisco upheld a ruling banning logging on 137 acres of redwoods near Headwaters because of the presence of the marbled murrelet, which is on the federal endangered-species list. A similar decision on the Headwaters itself is expected soon. The redwood grove has become a symbol of environmentalists' opposition to Mr. Hurwitz and Pacific Lumber, which greatly increased its logging rates after the takeover to pay down junk bonds used to finance the deal. Government officials have been talking with Mr. Hurwitz about a land swap or other transaction that would make the Headwaters publicly owned property, but they haven't been able to value the grove. The lawsuit charges that by blocking logging in the Headwaters the government violated the constitutional prohibition against "taking" private property without compensation. "It has gotten to the point where it's apparent Pacific Lumber won't be able to use this land," Michael Berger, the company's attorney, said Friday. "We are saying the government can have the property and pay us for it." But senior federal resource managers said the lawsuit is a bargaining ploy by Mr. Hurwitz to pressure the government to either cut a deal with him -- at a price close to the roughly $500 million he believes he could generate if he converted the Headwaters into lumber -- or let him log. Federal officials say Headwaters should be valued at several hundred million dollars less than Mr. Hurwitz's valuation, partly because environmental laws and public pressure may make it impossible to ever log the forest. A victory for Mr. Hurwitz would be a windfall; he paid only about $900 million for all of Pacific Lumber, and the Headwaters' 3,800 acres are a small fraction of the company's total timberlands, sawmills and other assets. James S. Gilliland, general counsel of the Agriculture Department, who has been involved in the Headwaters talks, declined to comment on Mr. Hurwitz's motives or the status of those negotiations, but he did say: "This is a lawsuit that we will win, I can tell you that." Mr. Berger denied Mr. Hurwitz's personal motives are behind the lawsuit. "We're dealing with the frustration of Pacific Lumber Co., regardless of who has stock in the company," he said. In a statement, Pacific Lumber said the government's use of the Endangered Species Act to protect the marbled murrelet has turned the forest into a public "murrelet sanctuary." "Takings" lawsuits have historically been difficult for property owners to win. Mr. Hurwitz's claim is one of the largest to date, but his chances could get a boost from Republican efforts to greatly expand the concept of regulatory takings, making it easier for property owners to collect when federal regulations impinge on plans to use their land. Sen. Bob Dole, the presumptive Republican presidential candidate, is sponsoring such legislation in the Senate, and similar legislation has strong support in the House of Representatives. Mr. Hurwitz could also get a boost from Republican efforts to water down the federal Endangered Species Act and other environmental laws. Those laws are the main tools that have been used by environmentalists to block logging in the Headwaters and in several other Pacific Lumber old-growth groves for several years. Texas financier Charles Hurwitz's $500 million lawsuit alleging the federal government has illegally prevented the company he controls from logging ancient redwoods is the latest shot in a long war over who will eventually determine the fate of a rare patch of old-growth forest -- Mr. Hurwitz or the public. Pacific Lumber Co., a unit of Maxxam Inc., Houston, sued the government alleging its use of the Environmental Protection Act prevented the company from proceeding with long-delayed and lucrative plans to log in its 3,800-acre old-growth stand in Northern California known as the Headwaters Forest. Mr. Hurwitz is Maxxam's chairman and chief executive and owns 60% of its voting stock. Corrections & Amplifications A LAWSUIT brought by Maxxam Inc. units against the federal government, alleging that logging restrictions on the Headwaters Forest and other assets amount to a regulatory "taking" of the units' private property, does not specify damages. An article May 13 incorrectly reported that the suit was brought by Charles Hurwitz, Maxxam's controlling shareholder and chairman, and indicated that the suit sought $500 million in damages. (WSJ May 24, 1996)

Title: Politics & Economics -- Washington Wire: A Special Weekly Report From The Wall Street Journal's Capital Bureau
Text: REPUBLICANS LEAD in most House races that remain undecided. Narrow margins for some candidates, such as Buchanan in Florida and incumbent Rep. Hayes in North Carolina, make recounts likely. But "it's very unusual for recounts to alter races," says Carl Forti of House Republican campaign committee, which hopes to keep Democratic gains below 30 seats. Women gain in Congress. Female senators number 16 with wins by Klobuchar in Minnesota and McCaskill in Missouri. House increase hinges partly on undecided races in Washington, where Darcy Burner hopes to unseat Rep. Reichert. Three undecided races feature female opponents, including Republican Rep. Wilson vs. Patricia Madrid in New Mexico. GINGRICH EMERGES as top conservative prospect for Republican 2008 field. Ebbing fortunes of Santorum, Allen and Frist leave opening for architect of Republicans' 1994 sweep. Gingrich faults Bush for "very disturbing" post-election news conference, saying earlier replacement of Rumsfeld might have saved control of the Senate and 10 House seats. "He can win some primaries," says Bush ad-maker Mark McKinnon, now with 2008 front-runner McCain. Anti-Washington mood helps departing Arkansas Gov. Huckabee compete with Kansas Sen. Brownback in wooing religious right. ECONOMIC CONSERVATIVES court incoming Democratic tax chief Rangel. The American Council on Capital Formation invites Rangel to breakfast next week. Despite campaign attacks labeling the New York Democrat a tax-raising liberal, the council's Mark Bloomfield predicts he'll be "a centrist legislator" who "understands the importance of economic growth." Democratic and Republican strategists predict Congress will reauthorize the Clinton-era State Children's Health Insurance Program in 2007. Some states have tightened enrollment standards, and in 2005, the number of uninsured children rose for the first time since 1998. Joseph Antos of American Enterprise Institute says Republicans won't want to look "hard-hearted" on the issue. TURNOUT RISES to highest midterm election level since 1982. Curtis Gans of American University's Center for the Study of the American Electorate estimates that 40.4% of those eligible to vote did so, up from 39.7% four years ago. STARTING GUN: Departing Iowa Gov. Vilsack's entry into Democratic presidential race creates early obstacle for 2008 rivals. "What we have to do is win Iowa," says an adviser to former vice presidential nominee Edwards. In 1992, Democrats generally sidestepped Iowa because of favorite son candidacy of Sen. Harkin. HOOSIER POWER: Democratic strategist Steve Elmendorf calls Indiana Sen. Bayh "the front-runner" for conservative slot vacated by ex- Virginia Gov. Warner's departure from 2008 field. Bayh touts Democratic pickup of three Indiana House seats; he had also dispatched staffers to help campaigns in Iowa and New Hampshire. OBAMA COULD cite opposition to Iraq war in a 2008 race, but one potential competitor for that constituency looms. Liberal strategist Bob Borosage says Gore would capture antiwar left "immediately" by entering. ACTIVISTS SEEKING end to Cuban trade embargo say Democratic control of Congress improves chances. Twelve groups seeking new policy write Rangel and Sen. Baucus, incoming chairman of Senate Finance Committee. ENVIRONMENTALISTS CLAIM big win with defeat of Rep. Pombo. As House Resources Committee chairman, Pombo sought to overhaul Endangered Species Act. Green groups poured more than $1 million into the Republican's California district. Wind-energy consultant Jerry McNerney, once written off, won with 53%. "We have the political strength to . . . defeat extreme anti- environmental politicians," says Rodger Schlickeisen of the Defenders of Wildlife Action Fund. Pombo cited the role of "outside groups" in his defeat. MINOR MEMOS: Blaming "arrogant Republicanism" for losses, one former Bush administration official says "I'm ticked off, too." . . . Republican Rep. Tom Cole, seeking support to run House campaign committee for 2008, reminds colleagues, "The most important election is not the last one -- it's the next one." --- Washington Wire is updated each weekday at www.washwire.com.

Title: Cross Country: It's Fish Versus Farmers in the San Joaquin Valley
Text: San Joaquin Valley, Calif. -- In 1931, a severe drought began that within a few years engulfed the Oklahoma panhandle and a third of the Great Plains in a "Dust Bowl." Tens of thousands of people fled the region -- many traveling to California along Route 66, which John Steinbeck called "the mother road, the road of flight" in "The Grapes of Wrath." A lot of the "Okies" settled in the San Joaquin Valley. In the decades that followed, state and federal officials built dams and other irrigation projects that helped turn the valley into some of the world's richest farmland. But today the San Joaquin Valley is being transformed into a dust bowl. Hundreds of thousands of acres are fallow, while almond and plum trees are being left to die in the scorching sun. Tens of thousands of people have been tossed out of work -- the town of Mendota alone has an unemployment rate of about 40% -- and the lines for food donations stretch down streets. The reason? There isn't enough water to go around this year, and the Obama administration is drawing up new reasons to divert more of it from farms and people and into the San Francisco Bay. The valley has traditionally been a place where someone with few belongings, little education and even no ability to speak English could prosper by picking grapes, milking cows, or hoeing cotton fields. The hearty people who came here were Portuguese, Mexican, Armenian, Italian, Basque and Dutch, along with westward-traveling Americans and Okies. More recent arrivals are from El Salvador, Vietnam and India. I am the product of a Portuguese family that came decades ago. California has the largest water storage and transportation system in the world. With 1,200 miles of canals and nearly 50 reservoirs, the system captures enough water to irrigate about four million acres and provide water to 23 million people. In many cases, as with the San Joaquin Valley, water in this system is sold to communities by the federal government. Some claim that California is facing a three-year-old drought. But, according to the state's Department of Water Resources, California reservoirs have received 80% of their normal amount of water and precipitation in the northern Sierras has been 95% of its yearly average this year. So why isn't there more water for farms? Because theirs is a regulatory-mandated drought. The 1973 Endangered Species Act requires that the government take steps to save endangered species. In California, that's meant diverting vast sums of water into rivers and streams to protect fish. Those diversions this year have forced federal authorities to decide who to serve -- fish or farmers. On Dec. 15, 2008, the Bush administration's Fish and Wildlife Service chose fish, a decision driven by a lawsuit filed in federal court in 2006 by the Natural Resources Defense Council and other environmental groups. To settle the suit, the Fish and Wildlife Service agreed to divert more than 150 billion gallons of water this year away from farmers south of San Francisco in hopes of protecting the Delta smelt -- a three-inch bait fish. The water is now flowing underneath the Golden Gate Bridge and out into the Pacific Ocean. Of course, the Delta smelt isn't a particularly attractive species to protect when it means throwing Americans out of work. On June 4, the National Marine Fisheries Service declared that delivering water to farms in the San Joaquin Valley would harm killer whales in the Pacific. And to save the whales, the Obama administration is now demanding even greater water restrictions beyond what has been diverted for the smelt. There are 130 animal species in California on the federal endangered list, including five salmon species, five steelhead species, four trout species and the North American green sturgeon. To date, not a single fish within the California water system has been removed from the Endangered Species List over the past 35 years. Despite massive amounts of water diverted to help them, the "protected" smelt, sturgeon and salmon populations have continued to decline. It is hardly unreasonable to ask why farmers should continue to suffer if diverting water hasn't even helped the fish. Congress has the power to solve this crisis. In 2003, a fish-versus-families debate erupted in New Mexico after water deliveries to Albuquerque from the Rio Grande River were cut off to protect habitat for the silvery minnow -- another three-inch bait fish. Congress temporarily suspended portions of the Endangered Species Act and guaranteed that water would be provided to Albuquerque. The situation in California is virtually identical and repeating what was done in New Mexico would do wonders for San Joaquin Valley farmers. It would also accomplish more than what the administration currently has in mind. Next month Interior Secretary Ken Salazar is planning to hold a hearing on the situation in California, following up on a visit he made to the valley in June. A spokesman for the Interior Department recently declared that San Joaquin Valley's water problems are a top priority for the Obama administration and that the river that flows through the valley and eventually to the ocean to form the San Joaquin Delta is as precious a natural resource as Florida's Everglades. What is precious and what President Barack Obama should come to see for himself are the 40,000 people in the valley who are desperate for water so they can get back to work. If it doesn't start flowing any time soon, perhaps he can tell them where they should go. Back to Oklahoma? --- Mr. Nunes is a Republican congressman representing California's 21st district. (See related letter: "Letters to the Editor: Government Agencies At Cross-Purposes" -- WSJ August 24, 2009) Credit: By Devin Nunes

Title: U.S. News: Gray Wolves Rebound, To Neighbors' Unease --- Close Encounters, Animal Killings Worry Wisconsin Town; Federal Government Pushes to Allow Hunting, Trapping
Text: HARRISON, Wis. -- David Schoone, a farmer in this lush region of northern Wisconsin, says a lone gray wolf sneaked up on his school-age daughter three years ago as she bounced on a trampoline in his backyard. More recently, Mr. Schoone was chased into his pickup truck by a wolf, and his cousin's wife had to run from two wolves that descended on her from opposite sides of a shed. This month, he lost two young steer to wolves. "We gotta watch all the time," said Mr. Schoone, 43 years old, who carries a loaded rifle when he works in his fields or goes for a walk, even though he can only legally shoot a wolf in the act of attacking a human. "They don't show any fear of us." Gray wolves, which resemble tall, lean huskies and can weigh more than 100 pounds, were hunted to near extinction in the lower 48 states by 1950. Since being placed under the protection of the Endangered Species Act in 1974, they have made a dramatic comeback, with some 4,000 in Minnesota, Wisconsin and Michigan and nearly 1,700 in Wyoming, Idaho and Montana. While there have been no reported killings of humans by healthy wolves in the contiguous U.S. in 100 years, they inspire fear in people wherever they roam. As their numbers increased, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has tried to have them removed from the endangered list so states can use hunting and trapping to control the population. But repeated legal rebuffs and delays have prompted howls of protest from people in the Western Great Lakes, where the predators have killed livestock, pets and hunting dogs and diminished the sense of security. Wildlife and animal-rights groups have long defended the wolves, saying the fears are overblown. The wolves cause relatively little livestock damage and restore the natural balance in the environment, they say. A year ago, wolves were removed from the endangered list in Idaho and Montana, and both states have since held legal wolf hunts. This spring, Minnesota and Wisconsin petitioned the Fish and Wildlife Service to expedite delisting efforts there. Federal officials are preparing a new effort to delist wolves in the Western Great Lakes but are completing scientific research to bolster their case first. "We're tired of losing," said Laura Ragan, a wolf biologist with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. The wolves' supporters have successfully opposed the moves in the Midwest and have sued to reverse the delistings. Wolves occupy just 5% of their range in the lower 48 states before the U.S. was settled, said Wayne Pacelle, president of the Humane Society of the U.S. "The only reason these hunters are clamoring to trap and hunt wolves is for the thrill of getting a trophy," he said. People in Harrison, a green swath of hills, farms, woods and lakes ringed with summer cabins 200 miles north of Madison, tend to disagree. "We hate them," said John Bailey, chairman of the town of 850 and owner of Bailey's Town and Country bar. He said wolves have reduced the deer population, a major source of income from visiting hunters. In addition to Mr. Schoone's cattle losses, Mr. Bailey said another farmer recently lost two pregnant cows and a dog to wolves. He said he had heard stories of people being stalked. "I'm really concerned about it, especially small children," he said. Wolves are shy and generally avoid humans, but they can lose their fear of humans as they come into more frequent contact with them, leading to increased chances for conflicts, experts say. "Whenever somebody has had a negative encounter, they are likely to remain negative toward wolves for a long time," said Adrian P. Wydeven, a wolf specialist with the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources. Laurie Groskopf is one. The 58-year-old part-time wildlife technician for the state lost a Walker hound named Morgan during the training season for bear hunting last summer. Morgan was tracking a bear when she was attacked by wolves that killed and ate most of the dog in a few minutes, said Mike Hagen, 66, who lives with Ms. Groskopf. Ms. Groskopf has won the support of the governing boards of six counties for a resolution calling on the state to cut Wisconsin's wolf population to 350 from 700. Mr. Wydeven said a scientific board recently recommended maintaining the wolf population at 375 to 625. Ms. Groskopf and Mr. Hagen live mostly on meat they hunt and fruit and vegetables they grow. They make their own wine in a large vat in their kitchen and store potatoes by burying them in the yard. The couple now has to drive more than an hour from home to find places where wolves haven't caused problems yet to hunt for raccoons, coyotes, bobcats and bear. Mr. Hagen also has family land where he hunts for deer, but wolves have greatly reduced the deer stock there, he said. The wolves' arrival has "changed our whole life," Ms. Groskopf said after offering a visitor a taste of wine and bear stew. "It's a thrill to see them," she added, "but they need to live in a place where they can be at peace and people can, too."  Credit: By Joe Barrett

Title: U.S. News: Administration Moves to Restore Wildlife Rules
Text: The Biden administration is moving to restore protections for endangered animals and plants that were loosened under former President Donald Trump, a move that had triggered lawsuits from environmental groups. In an announcement on Friday, U.S. Fish and Wildlife officials said they plan to strengthen rules that protect threatened species, including the restoration of an earlier process for designating critical habitat. The new rules are expected to take several months to draft and implement. Fish and Wildlife Service Principal Deputy Director Martha Williams said her office is working with industry groups to "not only protect and recover America's imperiled wildlife but to ensure cornerstone laws like the Endangered Species Act are helping us meet 21st century challenges." Michael Mittelholzer of the National Association of Home Builders criticized the proposed changes, saying that the Trump administration had made common-sense improvements. "Returning to an inefficient ESA permitting process will not only raise the cost of housing, but will also delay countless other infrastructure projects that require either a federal permit or use federal funds," he said. Environmental groups applauded the announcement. "We are currently in the midst of an unprecedented global extinction crisis, and endangered species have no time to waste," said environmental group Earthjustice, which filed one of several lawsuits that challenged the Trump administration's action. Under the Trump administration, wildlife regulators in 2019 weakened protections under the 1973 Endangered Species Act, which extends protections to more than 1,600 plants and animals. The new rules called for regulators to consider economic impacts when making decisions, cut protections for threatened species and changed the critical-habitat designation process. The Trump administration's action came after complaints from developers and other business interests that said portions of the law had become too onerous. Trade groups representing a broad portion of the U.S. business community -- including power-plant owners, manufacturers, developers and pipeline companies -- had pushed for an overhaul. Environmental and animal protection groups, including the Sierra Club and Natural Resources Defense Council, sued over the changes, saying that they violated Congress's intent, and that regulators who implemented the new rules didn't follow the proper procedures. President Biden has ordered a broad review of Trump-era regulations. Justice Department lawyers cited that directive when they asked a judge to pause the lawsuit earlier this year. Credit: By Katy Stech Ferek and Timothy Puko

Title: Environment (A Special Report) --- A Path to Simpler Permits: A pipeline company and the feds may be on the way to creating a revolutionary new environmental agreement
Text: Over the past three years, a pipeline company and the federal government have been hammering out one of the most ambitious environmental agreements in U.S. history. What's it all about? A permit to overhaul a natural-gas pipeline network that stretches for 15,500 miles -- and crosses paths with 43 vulnerable species of flora and fauna along the way. Usually, with big projects like this, developers must get a separate permit every time their plan impinges on an endangered species or environmentally sensitive piece of land. And every time the project crosses state lines, the developer must deal with yet another set of agencies. To streamline things, NiSource Inc., the owner of the pipeline, struck a deal with the federal Fish and Wildlife Service. The company would develop a single environmental plan, describing how it would protect the environment on the entire network. And the wildlife service would take charge of the permitting process, coordinating with all the agencies involved and bringing in consultants to help develop the plan, known as a Habitat Conservation Plan. The scope of the deal is unprecedented. Never before has an environmental agreement crossed so many jurisdictions or addressed such a diverse set of ecological problems in one fell swoop. If it survives a public review in the coming months, it will shave years off the regular permitting process. Even more important, it could provide a much-needed template for other large-scale environmental agreements in the days to come. The U.S. is about to launch the biggest building boom in decades to overhaul the nation's aging infrastructure, but there's no road map for speeding massive projects through the environmental-permitting process. Why? The Endangered Species Act passed in 1973, long after the 1950s infrastructure boom, so "all our [environmental] laws and regulations and public processes been designed around site-specific features," says Lawrence Selzer, president and chief executive of the Conservation Fund, a nonprofit land-conservation group that helped develop NiSource's plan. "We haven't invested in [large infrastructure projects] over the last 30 years, so we have no extant models." The business community is waiting to see whether the cost and time savings materialize. Already, builders of railroad track and electric lines such as CSX Corp. and NextEra Energy Inc. have approached the Conservation Fund to say they're eagerly awaiting the outcome. But the plan also faces objections from environmentalists, who say it's skewed toward the company's convenience and not the protection of plants and animals. If the Fish and Wildlife Service thinks the complaints are valid, it could ask NiSource for an alternative arrangement, which could take years to develop. NiSource came up with the idea for the plan in 2005. The company estimated it was filing about 90 permits a year on rare and endangered species with various state and federal wildlife agencies as part of its maintenance, repair, rerouting and replacement activities. NiSource wanted to simplify that -- and address its pipeline's environmental impact all in one go. So it approached the government with a proposal that covered a mile-wide corridor along the entire length of the pipeline, which runs through Louisiana wetlands where endangered manatee and turtles swim, skirts rivers in Tennessee inhabited by rare fish, and passes through woods in Virginia where bald eagles nest. To be sure, some large-scale environmental plans had been attempted before, says Peter Alagona, an environmental historian at the University of California, Santa Barbara. For instance, one plan approved in 2000 covered how developers would accommodate more than 200 species in Clark County, the vast swath of Southeastern Nevada whose seat is Las Vegas. But, says Mr. Selzer of the Conservation Fund, no other plan had addressed a "linear" space crossing so many state lines. The Fish and Wildlife Service formally agreed to review NiSource's proposal in 2007. The agency saw an "opportunity to develop innovative approaches to achieve regulatory compliance obligations for NiSource's natural gas pipeline activities, while accomplishing broader conservation and recovery goals of the Endangered Species Act," writes agency spokeswoman Georgia Parham in an email. NiSource and the wildlife service turned to outside consultants to help draft important chunks of the plan. At the same time, the federal agency maintained regular contact with its own regional offices and state agencies, and encouraged states to work with the Conservation Fund to come up with criteria for what land should be set aside to be protected under the plan. As for what the effort entails, NiSource says it doesn't wish to speak about the plan before it's published in the federal register this fall. But the Conservation Fund says the plan involves taking a much broader view of environmental issues than usual. Instead of trying to count every single endangered specimen, the states and the Conservation Fund will focus on how to protect important parts of the ecosystem along the pipeline route. The idea: If NiSource protects those important areas, the effects will flow down to all the species along the way. For instance, the pipeline passes near many of the trees under whose bark the Indiana bat roosts in summer. A traditional species-by-species plan might try to save every tree where bats nest. The NiSource approach concentrates on the areas of the woods that are most suited to the bat and also preserves corridors of land around these "hubs" to facilitate feeding and migration for bats and other species, says Ole Amundsen, a strategic conservation program manager at the Conservation Fund. (If it's not possible to have the pipeline and an endangered species live side by side, NiSource will find suitable land to start a new colony.) If the plan gets approved, NiSource would get 50 years' regulatory clearance for all activities on its existing pipeline that may affect federally listed species. But the plan is expected to take heat when the details become public. Environmentalists acknowledge that filing for approval species by species has its shortcomings. Nevertheless, they fear that site-specific issues may be glossed over in NiSource's pursuit of such a wide-ranging and expedited permit. Patrick Rakes, a founder of Conservation Fisheries in Knoxville, Tenn., says the pipeline passes dangerously close to a threatened population of spotfin chub fish near Grinders Creek in Lewis County, Tenn. This "genetically unique population" is one of only four remaining and lives in less than eight miles of the Buffalo River around Grinders Creek, Mr. Rakes says. "It is a population so small that it really cannot support any 'incidental take,' " Mr. Rakes wrote in an email, using the regulatory term for killing endangered animals. Mr. Selzer of the Conservation Fund says Mr. Rakes has opened an important debate. "We need to have enough public and scientific involvement to make sure we make the right decisions," Mr. Selzer says. Yet, he adds, "as much as the purist in me says we can't have any harm to any of these species, we simply cannot continue with our current infrastructure." --- Mr. Curran is a writer in Denton, Texas. He can be reached at reports@wsj.com. Credit: By Rob Curran

Title: Environment: Salmon advocates win first big case against the government
Text: Score one for the salmon.    Judge Malcolm F. Marsh ruled in federal court in Boise, Idaho, that the National Marine Fisheries Service, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and other government agencies responsible for running the vast network of dams and reservoirs on the Snake and Columbia rivers, which traverse four states in the Northwest, broke the law. The agencies pushed through a dam-operating plan that they knew would kill millions of salmon, whose populations are collapsing throughout the Pacific Northwest, he said.    The ruling is the first big courtroom victory for environmentalists in the battle over salmon, which is fast becoming the nation's most high-stakes and contentious conservation fight. A similar ruling favoring the spotted owl began a long-running battle that ended in severe restrictions on logging in federal forests. The stakes in the salmon dispute may be even larger, because it affects the dam system, a pillar of the region's economy.    The dams produce cheap power and irrigation water, but they mince salmon by the millions and are regarded as the main culprit in the fish's dizzying decline. Environmentalists have called for changes in dam operations, such as cutting back on power production during spawning season, but industry and power interests have always fiercely and successfully resisted.    The Boise case focused on salmon in a segment of the Snake River in Idaho, but will reverberate throughout the Northwest. In the ruling, Judge Marsh said that the fisheries service had acted "arbitrarily and capriciously" by finding that the dam-operating plan posed "no jeopardy" to Snake River salmon -- a key ruling by the agency that allowed the dams in the Snake and Columbia to operate much as they always had. That ruling also prevents certain requirements of the Endangered Species Act from kicking in. The agency signed off on the plan and the "no jeopardy" finding despite the objections of its own scientists, who had concluded that the plan would indeed imperil already weak salmon runs.    The judge also criticized the agencies for ignoring some of the very alternatives favored by environmentalists, such as increasing river flows to help young salmon make it to the sea. He said the process by which the federal agencies decided how they'll run the river systems is "seriously, significantly flawed because it is too heavily geared towards a status quo . . . when the situation literally cries out for a major overhaul."    Judge Marsh ordered the agencies to come up with a new plan within 60 days that doesn't jeopardize Snake River salmon.    The fisheries service declined to comment and the other agencies involved couldn't be reached to comment. But salmon advocates hailed it as a turning point in the salmon fight. "It recognizes the flaws in the federal government's attempts to continue business as usual while the salmon continue to decline toward extinction," said Idaho Gov. Cecil D. Andrus, who has been among the leaders of the pro-salmon forces. The case here was brought originally by Idaho at Mr. Andrus's insistence.    Mr. Andrus and others see Judge Marsh's decision as similar to the early spotted owl cases, in which federal judges in Washington and Oregon ruled that the government's timber-management practices were illegal. Environmentalists ultimately used those rulings to win major changes in federal timber policies, and salmon advocates hope for a similar outcome. "Now we have some legal ammunition that we've lacked in the past," said Lorraine Bodi, co-director of American Rivers' Seattle office.    By any measure, the salmon could use the help. Salmon runs in the Pacific Northwest have plunged from 16 million a few decades ago to about two million now, and this spring's counts of returning spawners have been the worst ever. The west's salmon-fishing industry, once a multibillion-dollar business, has been badly damaged -- although U.S. consumers still have plenty of salmon at cheap prices largely because of imports from salmon farms in Norway, Chile and elsewhere.    (See related letter: "Letters to the Editor: Bumper Crops of Wild Salmon" -- WSJ April 26, 1994)    940330-0108    YY94 MM04  Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: After Maxxam Spurns Headwaters Deal, Government Agencies Prepare for Battle
Text: Where the carrot didn't work, government agencies appear poised to use the stick to make financier Charles Hurwitz spare California's ancient Headwaters Forest from extensive logging. On Friday, Mr. Hurwitz's Maxxam Inc., which owns the preserve of redwoods on the Northern California coast, spurned as uneconomical a deal for him to turn over the 3,500-acre forest and some adjoining timberlands in exchange for about $400 million. Officials of Maxxam's Pacific Lumber Co., which oversees the logging, complained that the government attached last-minute restrictions. When asked whether the company now planned to commence logging of the Headwaters area, John Campbell, Pacific Lumber's president and chief executive officer, said, "We will be looking at all our options." However, new Democratic Gov. Gray Davis signals a greater willingness to take on Mr. Hurwitz than his predecessor, Republican Pete Wilson. Moments after Maxxam's rejection, Gov. Davis ordered a doubling of state forestry inspection and enforcement operations in Humboldt County, where the Headwaters is located. Critics of former Gov. Wilson contend he did little to stem an escalation in logging by Pacific Lumber after Mr. Hurwitz bought the Scotia, Calif., company for about $900 million in junk bonds. The company's timber-cutting permit was suspended by the state last fall after one of its contractors felled trees in an unauthorized area, but has been reinstated. Mr. Hurwitz is also bound to face renewed scrutiny from the Clinton administration regarding compliance with the Endangered Species Act, as the Headwaters is home to spotted owls and coho salmon. Pacific Lumber in early 1996 had filed suit against the government over restrictions aimed at protecting those endangered creatures. Under the Headwaters deal, Pacific Lumber would have agreed to drop the suit, which seeks compensation for a "taking" of its land. Pacific Lumber is expected to reopen the suit this week. Government officials had hoped to avert a legal showdown with Mr. Hurwitz by crafting a plan in late 1996 to take control of about 10,000 acres of ancient timberlands, including Headwaters. In return, the government would pay about $350 million in cash and a comparable amount of newer timber acreage valued at about $50 million. Another landowner was to get about $80 million under the deal, which called for payouts of $250 million by the federal government and $230 million by the state of California. Environmentalists asserted that Mr. Hurwitz was being rewarded for what they term his plundering of the forests. Mr. Hurwitz's executives deny that charge. Environmentalists were concerned with terms of a 50-year agreement governing how Pacific Lumber could log on its remaining 211,000 acres in California. "There are various loopholes in the plan that could allow protections to be weakened in coming years," said Kevin Bundy, outreach coordinator for the Environmental Protection Information Center group in Garberville, Calif. But Pacific Lumber viewed the plan as overly restrictive, especially after the government attached the two new conditions. One designated 60,000 acres as a "no harvest" zone pending lengthy watershed assessments. The other restricted logging on 22,000 acres around streams that only fill when it rains. The company said those restrictions would reduce its annual timber cut to 137 million board feet, or 35% below the level officials say they need to remain viable. Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: House refuses to exempt Maxxam unit from order to protect bird's habitat
Text: WASHINGTON -- The House, in a blow to advocates of private-property rights, refused to exempt a California timber company from a federal order to protect the forest habitat of a threatened bird on the West Coast.    Proponents had sought to build on the margins won last year when the House adopted an antiregulatory "property rights" bill in the first months of the new Republican Congress. But the 257-164 vote last night was a reversal of that outcome, reflecting today's changed politics and an increased concern with the propriety of special-interest waivers.    Eighty-one Republicans joined all but 19 Democrats in opposing the exemption that would have benefited Pacific Lumber Co., a unit of Maxxam Inc. Nine smaller property owners would also have been covered by the same language, but the bitter debate was dominated by the controversy surrounding Houston-based Maxxam and its takeover of Pacific Lumber in the mid-80s.    "Let's put an end to the takings" of private property, said Rep. Frank Riggs (R., Calif.), a Pacific ally. But California Democrats angrily denounced Maxxam as a "corporate raider" and said the exemption would "befoul the aisles of this Congress."    The environmental order in question was issued in May and covers millions of acres of largely public lands that are judged critical habitat for the marbled murrelet in the Pacific Northwest. The exemption would have left in place protections for the most sensitive Pacific Lumber lands, the Headwaters Forest. But the company estimates that 32,686 acres of redwood and fir would have been covered by the waiver.    The defeat for Western conservatives came as Speaker Newt Gingrich conceded this week that the GOP doesn't have enough votes to rewrite the Endangered Species Act as it wishes to bolster private property rights. After the "revolutionary" rhetoric last year, the leadership itself is busily repackaging the party under the label: "common sense" Republicans.    The same theme echoed in yesterday's debate on a $12.1 billion natural-resources bill funding major portions of both the Energy and Interior department budgets for the new fiscal year beginning Oct. 1.    House Science Committee Chairman Bob Walker (R., Pa.), a member of the leadership and close ally of Speaker Gingrich, sought to shift $138 million out of fossil-energy research and into national park and Indian education and housing programs. Oil and coal interests, long aligned with the House Appropriations Committee leadership, turned back the drive on a 224-196 vote. But the relatively narrow margin testified to the election-year pressure on lawmakers, hungry for funds to boost popular programs at home.    Meanwhile, in related action:    -- The Senate leadership said it hoped to reach a procedural agreement clearing the way for action early next month on a House-passed bill raising the federal minimum wage by 90 cents an hour. Democrats expressed frustration at the continued delays, but Sen. Trent Lott (R., Miss.), the new majority leader, said, "We are being extra careful because we want to develop a relationship based on trust and respect."    -- The House Appropriations Committee approved a $36.9 billion transportation bill that provides a 6% increase in funding for air-traffic control operations in the new fiscal year beginning Oct. 1. The increase would help pay for 250 additional air-traffic controllers and 373 new staff in aviation safety inspection and oversight, according to Rep. Frank Wolf (R., Va.), chairman of the transportation subcommittee. And $2.4 million is provided for a commission to review aviation safety problems in the aftermath of the recent ValuJet crash in Florida.  Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: U.S. News: Battle Over Drought Remedy --- As California's Fields Grow More Parched, Washington Offers Dueling Solutions
Text: California's drought is becoming a hot issue on Capitol Hill, where bills from Senate Democrats and House Republicans offer rival solutions on how to best aid water-starved farmers. The Golden State has suffered through a three-year drought that is forcing farmers to leave fallow hundreds of thousands of acres. Other Western states have experienced drought conditions for much of the past decade, prompting water managers to embark on billions of dollars in projects to safeguard and stockpile supplies. Because California boasts a bigger agricultural sector than any other state, the drought could have an outsize economic impact nationally, raising produce prices. A weekend storm dumped rain and snow on Northern California, but officials said that put only a small dent in the drought. A bill introduced Tuesday by Sen. Dianne Feinstein (D., Calif.) would aid farmers and communities in drought-ravaged parts of California and Oregon by providing $300 million for such things as new water projects and by making it easier to buy water from neighboring jurisdictions. The legislation also would abide by federal restrictions that protect endangered smelt and other fish that get caught up in pumps that move water from northern California to the semiarid south -- protections the House bill, introduced last week, would weaken. A state survey late last month found the water content of California's mountain snowpack at just 12% of the average for this time of year, the lowest since record-keeping began in 1960. "With so little water available, we must focus on streamlining federal programs and provide what assistance we can to those farmers and communities being hit the hardest," said Ms. Feinstein, who co-wrote the bill with three other Democrats. Last week, the Republican-led House passed a measure sponsored by California GOP Reps. David Valadao, Kevin McCarthy and Devin Nunes that would temporarily exempt the state and federal water-delivery systems there from adhering to provisions of the Endangered Species Act, among other laws. Similar legislation passed by the Republican-led House has died in the Democratic-controlled Senate in previous years. This time, Mr. Valadao said his measure was urgently needed because of an impending cutoff of state and federal supplies to farmers. On Jan. 31, the California Department of Water Resources took the unprecedented step of announcing the possibility of completely halting distribution of state water supplies this year to 25 million urban customers and nearly a million acres of agricultural land. The weekend rains have helped rebuild California's supplies, but officials said much more precipitation would be needed to prevent a cutoff by May 1. If that happens, farmers and communities could turn to groundwater reserves or get water from neighboring districts. The White House already has threatened to veto the House bill, saying a more balanced approach was needed, but has left the door open to the Senate measure. "We're encouraged by progress in the Senate on efforts to ease the pain caused by the drought," a White House spokesman said. "We look forward to continuing to work with the bill's sponsors and other members of Congress as the process moves forward." President Barack Obama is scheduled to visit Fresno, Calif., on Friday, a stop designed to highlight the drought's impact. Mr. Obama brought up the state's situation at a retreat last week with members of the Senate Democratic caucus, saying it was an issue that needed to be addressed this year, a Senate Democratic aide said. "We all want some improvement to the status quo," said Sarah Woolf, board member of the Westlands Water District in Fresno, an agricultural agency that Tuesday issued a statement supporting the Feinstein bill, along with some farm groups. --- Carol Lee contributed to this article. Credit: By Jim Carlton and Siobhan Hughes

Title: Endangered: Sage Grouse, Prairie Chickens, Ranchers
Text: As a fourth-generation cattle rancher in southeast Oregon's high desert outback, I find myself for the first time agreeing with Nevada Sen. Harry Reid, regarding the "major ramifications" listing the greater sage grouse will have on the economies of the rural West ("Sage Grouse Rebellion," Review & Outlook, March 11). It will put rangeland cattle ranching out of business. Any buckaroo and many scientists can tell you that cattle and sage grouse are compatible.Grouse even follow the cattle around. Why? Cattle dung helps produce bugs, which the grouse eat, and grouse prefer grazed areas. The decline of the sage-grouse population coincides with the government's and environmentalists' push to get cattle off the range and to limit predator control. Peak sage-grouse population occurred with peak cattle grazing. I think the sage grouse's worst enemy is the federal government. Mandated removal of livestock from the range often causes desertification of the land. In other instances, it leads to the increase of nonnative grass species and other weeds, resulting in a buildup of fuels. Add federal government mismanagement of firefighting, and you wind up with disastrous rangeland conflagrations. In 2012, a lightning strike sparked a fire on my property. If we ranchers' advice had been followed, the government could have contained the fire with minimal damage. Instead, the Miller Homestead fire consumed 160,801 acres, killed many of my cattle, threatened the hamlet of Frenchglen and destroyed far more sage-grouse breeding and nesting grounds than ever will be preserved by the government's solution, which in my opinion is more about control than preserving sage grouse. My fellow ranchers and I love the land we work, and we work to preserve a vibrant environment, not only for our cattle but for all of God's creatures. Let us do our job. Gary Miller President Frenchglen Rangeland Fire Protection Association Frenchglen, Ore. --- Considering that 91% of all federal lands lie west of the Colorado/Nebraska line, losing ground to sage grouse under the Endangered Species Act is only part of our problem out here in the West. As you note, the federal government owns on average 47% of each Western state. (That compares to an average of less than 5% federal ownership for our Midwestern and Eastern neighbors. Where's Eric Holder with his disparate-impact team when you need him?) These are lands that we can't tax to support education, transportation and other vital programs. Nor can we responsibly manage these lands -- as we have with private and state lands for generations -- to balance human needs with long-term stewardship and conservation goals. Federal payments in lieu of taxes and shared mineral royalties are meant to offset this lack of access to our resources, but those are becoming endangered as well in the current budget environment and only serve to turn us into welfare states anyway -- all for the pleasure of depriving the nation of our enormous natural resource potential. The disconnect between pie-in-the-sky urban desires and the real needs of the rural production economy have never been greater. If we can't prevent the former from imposing their values on the latter, we won't only imperil a way of life, we will geld the nation's economic engine. Carl Graham Director Sutherland Center for Self-Government in the West Salt Lake City --- You talk in sweeping generalities of the potential impacts of conservation efforts on "farming, ranching, mining, road building, water projects and oil and gas drilling" but fail to mention that prairie chickens have declined by more than 90%, or that sage grouse, which once numbered in the millions, have declined to fewer than 200,000. You also fail to mention the harm to humans caused by rampant fossil-fuel extraction resulting in climate change. It's precisely due to the sort of unbridled habitat destruction that has led to the demise of these birds and brought us to a human-caused extinction crisis. Scientists say we're losing life-sustaining biodiversity at thousands of times historic rates, which will be worsened by greenhouse-gas-induced climate change. With your fear mongering about impending economic catastrophe should the law be followed and these imperiled species be saved for generations to come, your editorial actually offers an extremely strong argument for exactly why we need the tools of the Endangered Species Act to help us balance our economic pursuits with our desire to preserve the health of our planet. Randi Spivak Center for Biological Diversity Washington

Title: Farmers Agree To Talk With Regulators
Text: Washington's agricultural interests have agreed to a series of talks with state and federal agencies that could drastically change farming in the state. The talks, slated to begin in September, will establish new guidelines for farming to ensure the survival of threatened and endangered fish. Participants say part of the negotiations will focus on establishing a set of fish-friendly farm-management practices that would meet Endangered Species Act rules and other environmental laws. Such practices could include establishing buffer zones for salmon habitat. The talks also will focus on forming a comprehensive plan to make irrigation districts more fish friendly. To do that, the participants will brainstorm a host of concepts, such as using fish screens, financing changes and enforcing new irrigation practices. The individual districts will then use those ideas to fashion their own salmon-protection plans. Parties to the talks include, among others, the state departments of agriculture and ecology, the federal National Marine Fisheries Service, the federal Fish and Wildlife Service, and major agricultural interests representing the state's farm bureau, dairy federation and horticultural association. Environmental groups and tribal interests have also been asked to participate. That agricultural interests and government agencies are willing to negotiate is a significant step. In the past few months, relations between farmers and the agencies charged with enforcing environmental laws have grown increasingly acrimonious. Unlike the timber industry, which has been hard hit by the listings of the spotted owl and marbled murrelet as endangered species, agriculture has largely escaped scrutiny of environmental regulators in recent years, according to environmentalists and some government agencies. There are basically no comprehensive rules that regulate farm practices to protect wildlife. Then came the listing earlier this year of the Puget Sound Chinook salmon as threatened -- the first time an Endangered Species Act listing has hit such a large urban area. That galvanized the will of politicians and agencies to enforce the listings. And regulators made it known that they would begin scrutinizing farm practices. This spring, the National Marine Fisheries Service told farmers in the Methow Valley in north-central Washington, that they couldn't use six irrigation ditches running through the Okanogan National Forest until the agency drafts a plan that would tell ditch operators what steps they must take to protect fish. Currently, four of the ditches have been allowed to operate after meeting certain National Marine Fisheries Service requirements. Then, during the most recent Legislative session, Gov. Gary Locke's staff believed it wasn't getting support from agricultural interests for its salmon-protection efforts. So the governor said he would proceed with state salmon planning "whether ag went to the table or not," says Patrick Batts, executive director of Washington State Farm Bureau, an Olympia-based trade association representing more than 6,000 family farms. "A lot of farmers felt the governor had painted a bull's-eye on the chest of farmers." That, in turn, has prompted the farmers, once unwilling participants, to go to the table and be part of the rule-making process. "We're in a situation where we have to do something to be able to keep our members farming," says Mr. Batts. "For the state, this would be setting a precedent of having such a broad spectrum of interests sitting down and talking about long-term conservation strategy," says Curt Smitch, a special adviser to the governor on salmon issues. Farmers and government officials say the agricultural plan could be modeled after a similar one recently adopted by the timber industry. That "Forest and Fish" plan adopted by the Legislature this past session gives the timber industry tax breaks and 50 years of regulatory certainty in exchange for not cutting trees along salmon streams on eight million acres of private forest lands. That plan was the product of two years of negotiations. No one expects the agricultural negotiations to go any faster. The timber industry is relatively concentrated, with forest land owned either by the state and federal governments or a handful of companies. By comparison, 37,000 farms grow more than 100 different crops in Washington. "With timber, it's one commodity harvested every 50 to 100 years," says Jim Jesernig, director of Washington state's Department of Agriculture. "With agriculture, it's 100 commodities harvested three to four times a year. The complexity level is a lot higher." Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: In Utah, a Town Digs Deep To Battle Prairie Dogs --- To Keep Critters Out of Airport, Officials Build Barrier Six Feet Underground
Text: PAROWAN, Utah -- There are about 2,790 humans to defend their turf in this farming town. They are up against a foe with superior numbers: 3,435 Utah prairie dogs, give or take a few pups. And the critters have the law on their side. Prairie dogs -- simply "dogs" among locals -- have invaded yards and lots, pockmarking lawns and gardens all around town.
